The Preface

There is no question at all that is of greater importance to mankind, and none that it more concerns every individual person to have well settled, than this: What are the distinguishing qualifications of those who are in favor with God and entitled to his eternal rewards? Or, which comes to the same thing, What is the nature of true religion? And where do the distinguishing marks of that virtue and holiness that is acceptable in the sight of God lie? But though it is of such importance, and though we have clear and abundant light in the word of God to direct us in this matter, there is no point on which professing Christians differ more from one another. It would be endless to count up the variety of opinions on this point that divide the Christian world. They make plain the truth of our Savior’s words: “Small is the gate and narrow the way that leads to life, and only a few find it.”

The consideration of these things has long led me to give attention to this matter, with the utmost diligence and care and the most exact search and inquiry I am capable of. It is a subject on which my mind has been especially intent ever since I first began the study of divinity. But as to the success of my inquiries, that must be left to the judgment of the reader of the following treatise.

I feel keenly that it is much more difficult to judge impartially of the subject of this discourse in the middle of the dust and smoke of such a state of controversy about things of this nature as this land is now in. As it is more difficult to write impartially, so it is more difficult to read impartially. Many will probably be hurt in their spirits to find so much that belongs to religious affection condemned here. And perhaps indignation and contempt will be stirred up in others by finding so much here justified and approved. And it may be that some will be ready to charge me with being inconsistent with myself, in approving some things so much and condemning others so much. I have found that some have always raised this objection against me, ever since the beginning of our recent controversies about religion. It is a hard thing to be a hearty, zealous friend of what has been good and glorious in the recent extraordinary events, and to rejoice much in it, and at the same time to see the evil and harmful tendency of what has been bad, and earnestly to oppose that. Yet I am humbly, but fully, persuaded that we will never be in the way of truth, nor go on in a way acceptable to God and tending to the advancement of Christ’s kingdom, until we do so. There is indeed something very mysterious in it, that so much good and so much bad should be mixed together in the church of God. In the same way it is a mysterious thing, and one that has puzzled and amazed many a good Christian, that something so divine and precious as the saving grace of God, the new and divine nature, should dwell in the same heart with so much corruption, hypocrisy and iniquity in a particular saint. Yet neither of these is more mysterious than it is real. And neither of them is a new or rare thing. It is nothing new that much false religion should prevail at a time of great reviving of true religion, and that at such a time multitudes of hypocrites should spring up among true saints. It was so in the great reformation and revival of religion in Josiah’s time, as appears from Jeremiah 3:10 and 4:3–4, and also from the great apostasy there was in the land so soon after his reign. It was so in the great outpouring of the Spirit on the Jews in the days of John the Baptist, as appears from the great apostasy of that people so soon after so general an awakening, and from the temporary religious comforts and joys of many: “You+ were willing for a season to rejoice in his light” (John 5:35). It was so in the great stirrings among the multitude caused by the preaching of Jesus Christ: of the many who were then called, few were chosen. Of the multitude who were roused and moved by his preaching, and who at one time or another appeared mightily engaged, full of wonder at Christ and lifted up with joy, only a few were true disciples, who stood the shock of the great trials that came afterward and endured to the end. Many were like the stony ground or the thorny ground, and only a few, by comparison, like the good ground. Of the whole heap that was gathered, a great part was chaff, which the wind afterward drove away, and the heap of wheat that was left was small by comparison. All this appears abundantly from the history of the New Testament. It was so in the great outpouring of the Spirit in the apostles’ days, as appears from Matthew 24:10–13; Gal 3:1 and 4:11, 15; Phil 2:21 and 3:18–19; the two epistles to the Corinthians; and many other parts of the New Testament. And so it was in the great Reformation from popery. It plainly appears that in the visible church of God, in times of great reviving of religion, it has been again and again as it is with fruit trees in the spring. There are a multitude of blossoms, all of which look fair and beautiful, and there is a promising appearance of young fruit. But many of them last only a short time; they soon fall off and never come to maturity.

Not that we are to suppose it will always be so. In this world there will never be entire purity, either in particular saints, as a perfect freedom from mixtures of corruption, or in the church of God, without any mixture of hypocrites with saints, and of counterfeit religion and false appearances of grace with true religion and real holiness. Yet it is evident that a time will come of much greater purity in the church of God than there has been in ages past. This is plain from these texts of Scripture: Isa 52:1; Ezek 44:6, 7, 9; Joel 3:17; Zech 14:21; Ps 69:32, 35, 36; Isa 35:8, 10; Isa 4:3–4; Ezek 20:38; Ps 37:9, 10, 11, 29. And one great reason for it will be that at that time God will give his people much greater light to distinguish between true religion and its counterfeits: “And He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver; He will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver. Then they will present offerings to the Lord in righteousness” (Mal 3:3). With this goes verse 18, which continues the prophecy of the same happy times: “So you+ will again distinguish between the righteous and the wicked, between those who serve God and those who do not.”

It is by the mixture of counterfeit religion with true, not discerned and distinguished, that the devil has had his greatest advantage against the cause and kingdom of Christ all along until now. It is plainly by this means above all that he has prevailed against every revival of religion there has ever been since the first founding of the Christian church. By this he hurt the cause of Christianity in and after the apostolic age much more than by all the persecutions of both Jews and heathens. The apostles in all their epistles show themselves much more concerned about the first mischief than the second. By this Satan prevailed against the Reformation begun by Luther, Zwingli and others, to stop its progress and bring it into disgrace, ten times more than by all the bloody, cruel and previously unheard-of persecutions of the church of Rome. By this above all he has prevailed against the revivals of religion there have been in our nation since the Reformation. By this he prevailed against New England about a hundred years ago, to quench the love and spoil the joy of her espousals. And I think I have had opportunity enough to see plainly that by this the devil has prevailed against the recent great revival of religion in New England, so happy and promising in its beginning. Here, most evidently, has been the main advantage Satan has had against us. By this he has defeated us. It is by this means that the daughter of Zion in this land now lies on the ground in the pitiful condition in which we now see her: her garments torn, her face disfigured, her nakedness exposed, her limbs broken, wallowing in the blood of her own wounds and in no way able to rise. And this has come so quickly after her recent great joys and hopes. “Zion stretches out her hands, but there is no one to comfort her. The Lord has decreed against Jacob that his neighbors become his foes. Jerusalem has become an unclean thing among them” (Lam 1:17). I have seen the devil prevail in the same way against two great revivals of religion in this country. Satan goes on with mankind as he began with them. He prevailed against our first parents, cast them out of paradise, and suddenly brought all their happiness and glory to an end, by appearing to be a friend to their happy paradisal state and pretending to advance it to higher degrees. In the same way, that same cunning serpent who deceived Eve by his craftiness has, by turning us aside from the simplicity that is in Christ, suddenly succeeded in robbing us of the fair prospect we had a little while ago of a kind of paradisal state of the church of God in New England.

After religion has revived in the church of God and enemies appear, the people who are engaged to defend its cause are commonly most exposed where they least feel any danger. While they are wholly intent on the opposition that appears openly before them, to stand against it, and neglect to look carefully all around them, the devil comes up behind them and gives a fatal stab unseen. And he has opportunity to strike a more telling blow and wound the deeper, because he strikes at his leisure and as he pleases, hindered by no guard or resistance.

And so it is likely always to be in the church, whenever religion revives remarkably, until we have learned well to distinguish between true and false religion: between saving affections and experiences, and the many fair shows and glittering appearances by which they are counterfeited. When these are not distinguished, the consequences are often unspeakably dreadful. By this means the devil gratifies himself by bringing it about that multitudes offer to God, as though it were a pleasing and acceptable sacrifice to him, what is in fact above all things abominable to him. By this means he deceives great multitudes about the state of their souls, making them think they are something when they are nothing, and so ruins them eternally. And not only that: he establishes many in a strong confidence of their eminent holiness who are, in God’s sight, some of the vilest of hypocrites. By this means he damps and wounds religion in the hearts of the saints in many ways. He obscures it and deforms it by corrupt mixtures. He causes their religious affections to degenerate woefully, and sometimes, for a considerable time, to be like the manna that bred worms and stank. He dreadfully ensnares and confounds the minds of others of the saints, brings them into great difficulties and temptations, and entangles them in a wilderness from which they can by no means free themselves. By this means Satan mightily encourages the hearts of the open enemies of religion, strengthens their hands, fills them with weapons, and makes their fortresses strong, while at the same time religion and the church of God lie exposed to them like a city without walls. By this means he brings it about that men work wickedness under the notion of doing God service, and so sin without restraint, indeed with eager forwardness and zeal, and with all their might. By this means he brings even the friends of religion, without their perceiving it, to do the work of enemies, destroying religion far more effectually than open enemies can, under the notion of advancing it. By this means the devil scatters the flock of Christ and sets them against one another, and that with great heat of spirit, under the notion of zeal for God. Religion by degrees degenerates into empty wrangling. And during the strife Satan leads both parties far out of the right way, driving each to great extremes, one to the right hand and the other to the left, according as he finds they are most inclined, or most easily moved and swayed, until the right path in the middle is almost wholly neglected. And in the middle of this confusion the devil has great opportunity to advance his own interest and make it strong in countless ways, to get the government of all into his own hands, and to work his own will. And by what they see of the terrible consequences of this counterfeit religion, when it is not distinguished from true religion, God’s people in general have their minds unhinged and unsettled in things of religion. They do not know where to set their foot, or what to think or do. Many are brought to doubt whether there is anything at all in religion, and heresy, unbelief and atheism greatly prevail.

Therefore it greatly concerns us to use our utmost endeavors to discern clearly, and to have it well settled and established, what true religion consists in. Until this is done, we may expect that great revivals of religion will last only a short time. Until this is done, there is little good to be expected from all our heated debates, in conversation and from the press, since we do not know clearly and distinctly what we ought to contend for.

My design in the following treatise is to contribute my mite, and to use my best (however feeble) endeavors to this end. It must be noted that my design here is somewhat different from the design of what I published before. That was to show the distinguishing marks of a work of the Spirit of God, including both his common and his saving operations. But what I aim at now is to show the nature and signs of the gracious operations of God’s Spirit, by which they are to be distinguished from all things whatever, of which the minds of men are the subjects, that are not of a saving nature. If I have succeeded in this aim in any tolerable measure, I hope it will tend to promote the interest of religion. And whether or not I have succeeded in bringing any light to this subject, and however my attempt may be reproached in these faultfinding, censorious times, I hope in the mercy of a gracious and righteous God for the acceptance of the sincerity of my endeavors. I hope also for the fairness and the prayers of the true followers of the meek and charitable Lamb of God.

Part I

The Text and the Doctrine

Part I · The Nature and Importance of the Affections

Concerning the Nature of the Affections, and their Importance in Religion.

1 Pet 1:8

Though you+ have not seen Him, you+ love Him; and though you+ do not see Him now, you+ believe in Him and rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory.

In these words the apostle describes the state of mind of the Christians he was writing to, under the persecutions they were then suffering. These persecutions are what he has in view in the two verses before, when he speaks of the trial of their faith, and of their suffering grief in various trials.

Such trials benefit true religion in three ways. First, by them its truth is shown, and it appears to be indeed true religion. Trials, above all other things, tend to distinguish between true religion and false, and to make the difference between them plainly appear. That is why they are called by the name of trials in the verse just before the text, and in countless other places. They try the faith and religion of those who profess religion, to show what sort it is, as apparent gold is tried in the fire and shown to be true gold or not. And the faith of true Christians, tried in this way and proved to be true, is found to praise, and honor, and glory, as that verse before the text says.

Then, these trials benefit true religion further: they not only show its truth, but they make its genuine beauty and loveliness remarkably appear. True virtue never appears so lovely as when it is most oppressed, and the divine excellence of real Christianity is never displayed to such advantage as when it is under the greatest trials. It is then that true faith appears much more precious than gold, and on this account it is found to praise, and honor, and glory.

And again, another benefit such trials bring to true religion is that they purify it and increase it. They not only show it to be true, but also tend to refine it and free it from the mixtures of what is false, which encumber and hinder it, so that nothing may be left but what is true. They tend to make the loveliness of true religion appear to the best advantage, as was observed before. And not only that: they tend to increase its beauty, by establishing and confirming it, making it more lively and vigorous, and purifying it from the things that obscured its luster and glory. As gold that is tried in the fire is purged of its alloy and all remaining dross, and comes out more solid and beautiful, so true faith, tried as gold is tried in the fire, becomes more precious. And so it too is found to praise, and honor, and glory. The apostle seems to have in view each of these benefits that persecutions bring to true religion, in the verse before the text.

And in the text the apostle observes how true religion worked in the Christians he was writing to, under their persecutions, so that these benefits of persecution appeared in them. That is, he observes what kind of working of true religion it was in them by which their religion, under persecution, was shown to be true religion; by which it eminently appeared in the genuine beauty and loveliness of true religion; and by which it also appeared to be increased and purified, and so was likely to be found to praise, and honor, and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ. And there were two kinds of working, or exercise, of true religion in them under their sufferings that the apostle takes notice of in the text, in which these benefits appeared.

1. Love to Christ: “Though you+ have not seen Him, you+ love Him.” The world was ready to wonder what strange principle it was that moved them to expose themselves to such great sufferings: to forsake the things that were seen, and renounce all that was dear and pleasant, all that was the object of sense. To the men of the world around them they seemed to be out of their minds, and to act as though they hated themselves. There was nothing in their view that could lead them to suffer like this, or support them under such trials and carry them through. But although there was nothing seen that influenced and supported them like this, nothing the world saw, or that the Christians themselves ever saw with their bodily eyes, they had a supernatural principle of love to something unseen. They loved Jesus Christ, for they saw him spiritually, though the world did not see him, and though they themselves had never seen him with bodily eyes.

2. Joy in Christ. Though their outward sufferings were very grievous, their inward spiritual joys were greater than their sufferings. These joys supported them and enabled them to suffer with cheerfulness.

There are two things the apostle takes notice of in the text concerning this joy. 1. The way in which it arises, the way in which Christ, though unseen, is its foundation, namely, by faith, which is the evidence of things not seen: “Though you+ do not see Him now, you+ believe in Him and rejoice.” 2. The nature of this joy: “unspeakable and full of glory.” It is unspeakable in its kind: very different from worldly joys and carnal delights, of a far purer, more sublime and heavenly nature, being something supernatural and truly divine, and so excellent beyond all expression. There were no words to set forth its sublimity and its exquisite sweetness. It was unspeakable also in degree, for it pleased God to give them this holy joy with a liberal hand and in large measure in their state of persecution.

Their joy was full of glory. Although the joy was unspeakable, and no words were sufficient to describe it, something might still be said of it, and no words were more fit to represent its excellence than these: that it was full of glory, or, as the original has it, glorified joy. In rejoicing with this joy their minds were filled, as it were, with a glorious brightness, and their natures were exalted and perfected. It was a most worthy and noble rejoicing, which did not corrupt and debase the mind, as many carnal joys do, but greatly beautified and dignified it. It was a foretaste of the joy of heaven, which raised their minds to a degree of heavenly blessedness. It filled their minds with the light of God’s glory, and made them shine themselves with some of that glory imparted to them.

So the proposition, or doctrine, that I would draw from these words is this:

DOCT. True religion, in great Part, consists in holy affections.

The apostle observes and remarks on the workings and exercises of religion in the Christians he was writing to, in which their religion appeared to be true and of the right kind. This was when it had its greatest trial of what sort it was, being tried by persecution as gold is tried in the fire. It was when their religion not only proved true but was at its purest, cleansed of its dross and of the mixtures of what was not true, and when religion appeared in them most in its genuine excellence and native beauty and was found to praise, and honor, and glory. And we see that he singles out the religious affections of love and joy that were then in exercise in them. These are the exercises of religion he takes notice of, in which their religion appeared in this way, true and pure and in its proper glory.

Here I would:

I. Show what is meant by the affections.

II. Observe some things that make it evident that a great part of true religion lies in the affections.

What the Affections Are

Part I · The Nature and Importance of the Affections

I. It may be asked: What are the affections of the mind?

I answer: the affections are nothing other than the more vigorous and strongly felt exercises of the inclination and will of the soul.

God has given the soul two faculties. One is that by which it is capable of perception and contemplation, or by which it discerns and views and judges things; this is called the understanding. The other faculty is that by which the soul does not merely perceive and view things, but is in some way inclined with respect to the things it views or considers: it is either inclined to them, or disinclined and averse from them. In other words, it is the faculty by which the soul does not look on things as an indifferent, unaffected spectator, but either as liking or disliking them, pleased or displeased, approving or rejecting. This faculty is called by various names. It is sometimes called the inclination. As it has respect to the actions that are determined and governed by it, it is called the will. And the mind, with regard to the exercises of this faculty, is often called the heart.

The exercises of this faculty are of two sorts. There are those by which the soul is carried out toward the things in view, in approving of them, being pleased with them, and inclined to them. And there are those in which the soul opposes the things in view, in disapproving them, being displeased with them, averse from them, and rejecting them.

And as the exercises of the inclination and will of the soul are various in their kinds, so they are much more various in their degrees. There are some exercises of being pleased or displeased, inclined or disinclined, in which the soul is carried only a little beyond a state of perfect indifference. And there are other degrees above this, in which the approval or dislike, the pleasure or aversion, is stronger. In these we may rise higher and higher, until the soul comes to act vigorously and perceptibly, and its actings have such strength that (through the laws of the union the Creator has fixed between soul and body) the motion of the blood and animal spirits begins to be perceptibly altered. From this there often arises some bodily sensation, especially about the heart and vital organs, which are the fountain of the fluids of the body. And from this it comes about that the mind, with regard to the exercises of this faculty, is called the heart, perhaps in all nations and ages. And it is to be noted that it is these more vigorous and strongly felt exercises of this faculty that are called the affections.

The will and the affections of the soul are not two faculties. The affections are not essentially distinct from the will, and they do not differ from the mere actings of the will and inclination of the soul except in the liveliness and the felt strength of their exercise.

It must be confessed that language is somewhat imperfect here, and the meaning of words is to a considerable degree loose and unfixed, not precisely limited by custom, which governs the use of language. In one sense the affection of the soul differs not at all from the will and inclination, and the will is never in any exercise any further than it is affected. It is not moved out of a state of perfect indifference in any other way than by being affected one way or another, and it does nothing beyond that. Yet there are many actings of the will and inclination that are not so commonly called affections. In everything we do voluntarily there is an exercise of the will and inclination; it is our inclination that governs us in our actions. But all the actings of the inclination and will in all the common actions of life are not ordinarily called affections. Yet what are commonly called affections are not essentially different from them, but only in the degree and manner of their exercise. In every act of the will whatever, the soul either likes or dislikes, is either inclined or disinclined to what is in view. These acts are not essentially different from the affections of love and hatred. The liking or inclination of the soul to a thing, if it is in a high degree and is vigorous and lively, is the very same thing as the affection of love. And the disliking and disinclination, if it is in a great degree, is the very same as hatred. In every act of the will for, or toward, something not present, the soul is in some degree inclined to that thing, and that inclination, if it is in a considerable degree, is the very same as the affection of desire. And in every degree of the act of the will in which the soul approves of something present, there is a degree of being pleased, and that pleasure, if it is in a considerable degree, is the very same as the affection of joy or delight. And if the will disapproves of what is present, the soul is in some degree displeased, and if that displeasure is great, it is the very same as the affection of grief or sorrow.

Such seems to be our nature, and such the laws of the union of soul and body, that there is never, in any case whatever, any lively and vigorous exercise of the will or inclination of the soul without some effect on the body, in some change in the motion of its fluids, and especially of the animal spirits. And on the other hand, by the same laws of the union of soul and body, the constitution of the body and the motion of its fluids may promote the exercise of the affections. Yet it is not the body but the mind alone that is the proper seat of the affections. The body of a man is no more capable of being really the subject of love or hatred, joy or sorrow, fear or hope, than the body of a tree is, or than the same body of a man is capable of thinking and understanding. As it is the soul alone that has ideas, so it is the soul alone that is pleased or displeased with its ideas. As it is the soul alone that thinks, so it is the soul alone that loves or hates, rejoices or grieves at what it thinks of. Nor are these motions of the animal spirits and fluids of the body anything that properly belongs to the nature of the affections, though in the present state they always accompany them. They are only effects or accompaniments of the affections, entirely distinct from the affections themselves and in no way essential to them. So a spirit without a body may be as capable of love and hatred, joy or sorrow, hope or fear, or other affections, as one that is united to a body.

The affections and passions are frequently spoken of as the same. And yet, in the more common use of speech, there is in some respect a difference. Affection is a word that in its ordinary meaning seems to be somewhat wider than passion: it is used for all vigorous, lively actings of the will or inclination, but passion for those that are more sudden, whose effects on the animal spirits are more violent, and in which the mind is more overpowered and less in its own command.

As all the exercises of the inclination and will are either in approving and liking, or in disapproving and rejecting, so the affections are of two sorts. There are those by which the soul is carried out to what is in view, cleaving to it or seeking it; and there are those by which it is averse from it and opposes it.

Of the first sort are love, desire, hope, joy, gratitude, delight. Of the second kind are hatred, fear, anger, grief, and the like, which there is no need now to stop and define one by one.

And there are some affections in which the two kinds of actings of the will just mentioned are combined. In the affection of pity, for instance, there is something of the first kind toward the person suffering, and something of the second toward what he suffers. And so in zeal there is high approval of some person or thing, together with vigorous opposition to what is thought to be contrary to it.

True Religion Lies Much in the Affections

Part I · The Nature and Importance of the Affections

There are other mixed affections that might also be mentioned, but I hurry on to the second thing proposed, which was to observe some things that make it evident that true religion, in great part, consists in the affections. And here:

1. What has been said of the nature of the affections makes this evident, and may be enough, without adding anything further, to put this matter beyond doubt. For who will deny that true religion consists, in great measure, in vigorous and lively actings of the inclination and will of the soul, or the fervent exercises of the heart?

The religion God requires, and will accept, does not consist in weak, dull and lifeless would-be wishes, raising us only a little above a state of indifference. God in his word greatly insists that we be in good earnest, fervent in spirit, with our hearts vigorously engaged in religion: “Be fervent in spirit, serving the Lord” (Rom 12:11). “And now, O Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you but to fear the Lord your God by walking in all His ways, to love Him, to serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul?” (Deut 10:12). And Deut 6:4–5: “Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is One. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength.” It is such a fervent, vigorous engagement of the heart in religion that is the fruit of a real circumcision of the heart, or true regeneration, and that has the promises of life: “The Lord your God will circumcise your hearts and the hearts of your descendants, and you will love Him with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live” (Deut 30:6).

If we are not in good earnest in religion, and our wills and inclinations are not strongly exercised, we are nothing. The things of religion are so great that the exercises of our hearts cannot be at all suited to their nature and importance unless they are lively and powerful. In nothing is vigor in the actings of our inclinations so necessary as in religion, and in nothing is lukewarmness so hateful. True religion is always a powerful thing, and its power appears first of all in its inward exercises in the heart, which is its principal and original seat. That is why true religion is called the power of godliness, as distinct from its external appearances, which are the form of it: “having a form of godliness but denying its power” (2 Tim 3:5). The Spirit of God, in those who have sound and solid religion, is a spirit of powerful holy affection. And therefore God is said to have given them the Spirit of power, love, and a sound mind (2 Tim 1:7). And such people, when they receive the Spirit of God in his sanctifying and saving influences, are said to be baptized with the Holy Spirit and with fire. This is because of the power and fervor of the exercises the Spirit of God stirs up in their hearts, so that their hearts, when grace is in exercise, may be said to burn within them, as is said of the disciples (Luke 24:32).

The business of religion is again and again compared to those exercises in which men usually have their hearts and strength greatly exercised and engaged: running, wrestling or straining for a great prize or crown, fighting with strong enemies who seek our lives, and making war like those who take a city or kingdom by force.

And though true grace has various degrees, and there are some who are only babes in Christ, in whom the exercise of the inclination and will toward divine and heavenly things is weak by comparison, yet everyone who has the power of godliness in his heart has his inclinations and heart exercised toward God and divine things with such strength and vigor that these holy exercises prevail in him above all carnal or natural affections, and are effectual to overcome them. For every true disciple of Christ loves him more than father or mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, houses and lands; yes, more than his own life. From this it follows that wherever true religion is, there are vigorous exercises of the inclination and will toward divine objects. But by what was said before, the vigorous, lively and strongly felt exercises of the will are nothing other than the affections of the soul.

2. The author of human nature has not only given affections to men, but has made them very much the spring of men’s actions. The affections not only necessarily belong to human nature, but are a very great part of it. So (since by regeneration persons are renewed in the whole man and sanctified throughout) holy affections not only necessarily belong to true religion, but are a very great part of it. And since true religion is of a practical nature, and God has so made human nature that the affections are very much the spring of men’s actions, this also shows that true religion must consist very much in the affections.

Such is man’s nature that he is very inactive except as he is moved by some affection: love or hatred, desire, hope, fear, or some other. We see that these affections are the springs that set men going in all the affairs of life and engage them in all their pursuits. These are the things that drive men forward and carry them along in all their worldly business. And men are especially stirred up and animated by these in all the affairs in which they are earnestly engaged and which they pursue with vigor. We see the world of mankind to be exceedingly busy and active, and the affections of men are the springs of the motion. Take away all love and hatred, all hope and fear, all anger, zeal and heartfelt desire, and the world would be in great measure motionless and dead. There would be no such thing as activity among mankind, or any earnest pursuit whatever. It is affection that engages the covetous man, and the man who is greedy for worldly gain, in his pursuits. It is by the affections that the ambitious man is driven forward in his pursuit of worldly glory. And it is the affections, too, that move the pleasure-loving man in his pursuit of pleasure and sensual delights. The world goes on from age to age in continual commotion and agitation in the pursuit of these things. But take away all affection, and the spring of all this motion would be gone, and the motion itself would cease. And as in worldly things worldly affections are very much the spring of men’s motion and action, so in religious matters the spring of their actions is very much religious affections. He who has only doctrinal knowledge and theory, without affection, is never engaged in the business of religion.

3. Nothing is more plain in fact than that the things of religion take hold of men’s souls no further than they affect them. There are multitudes who often hear the word of God, and in it hear of things that are infinitely great and important and that concern them most nearly. Yet all that is heard seems to be wholly without effect on them and to make no change in their disposition or behavior. And the reason is that they are not affected by what they hear. There are many who often hear of the glorious perfections of God: his almighty power and boundless wisdom, his infinite majesty, and the holiness of God by which he is of purer eyes than to behold evil and cannot look on iniquity, and the heavens are not pure in his sight. They hear of God’s infinite goodness and mercy, and of the great works of God’s wisdom, power and goodness, in which these perfections are wonderfully displayed. They hear in particular of the unspeakable love of God and Christ, and of the great things Christ has done and suffered. They hear of the great things of another world: of eternal misery in bearing the fierceness and wrath of almighty God, and of endless blessedness and glory in the presence of God and the enjoyment of his dear love. They also hear the absolute commands of God, his gracious counsels and warnings, and the sweet invitations of the gospel. I say, they often hear these things, and yet remain as they were before, with no perceptible change in them, either in heart or in practice, because they are not affected by what they hear. And they always will remain so until they are affected. I am bold to assert that there never was any considerable change worked in the mind or conduct of any person by anything of a religious nature that he ever read, heard or saw, unless his affections were moved. Never was a natural man engaged earnestly to seek his salvation; never were any such brought to cry out for wisdom and lift up their voice for understanding, and to wrestle with God in prayer for mercy; never was one humbled and brought to the foot of God by anything he ever heard or imagined of his own unworthiness and his deserving God’s displeasure; nor was one ever led to flee for refuge to Christ, while his heart remained unaffected. Nor was there ever a saint awakened out of a cold, lifeless frame, or recovered from a declining state in religion and brought back from a sad departure from God, without having his heart affected. In a word, there never was anything considerable brought about in the heart or life of any man living by the things of religion unless his heart was deeply affected by those things.

4. The holy Scriptures everywhere place religion very much in the affections, such as fear, hope, love, hatred, desire, joy, sorrow, gratitude, compassion and zeal.

The Scriptures place much of religion in godly fear. So much so that it is often spoken of as the character of those who are truly religious persons that they tremble at God’s word, that they fear before him, that their flesh trembles for fear of him, that they stand in fear of his judgments, that his majesty terrifies them, and the dread of him falls on them, and the like. And a name commonly given to the saints in Scripture is those who fear God, or those who fear the Lord. And because the fear of God is a great part of true godliness, true godliness in general is very commonly called by the name of the fear of God, as everyone who knows anything of the Bible knows.

So too hope in God and in the promises of his word is often spoken of in Scripture as a very considerable part of true religion. It is mentioned as one of the three great things religion consists of (1 Cor 13:13). Hope in the Lord is also frequently mentioned as the character of the saints: “Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God” (Ps 146:5). “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, whose hope is the Lord” (Jer 17:7). “Be strong and courageous, all you+ who hope in the Lord” (Ps 31:24). And so in many other places. Religious fear and hope are joined together again and again, as together making up the character of the true saints: “Surely the eyes of the Lord are on those who fear Him, on those whose hope is in His loving devotion” (Ps 33:18). “The Lord is pleased with those who fear Him, who hope in His loving devotion” (Ps 147:11). Hope is so great a part of true religion that the apostle says we are “saved by hope” (Rom 8:24). And it is spoken of as the helmet of the Christian soldier: “and the helmet of our hope of salvation” (1 Thess 5:8). It is spoken of as the sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, which keeps it from being cast away by the storms of this evil world: “We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain” (Heb 6:19). It is spoken of as a great fruit and benefit that true saints receive by Christ’s resurrection: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! By His great mercy He has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Pet 1:3).

The Scriptures place religion very much in the affection of love: in love to God and the Lord Jesus Christ, and love to the people of God and to mankind. The texts in which this is plain, in both the Old Testament and the New, are countless. But of this more later.

The contrary affection of hatred too, as it has sin for its object, is spoken of in Scripture as no small part of true religion. It is spoken of as that by which true religion may be known and distinguished: “To fear the Lord is to hate evil” (Prov 8:13). And accordingly the saints are called on to give evidence of their sincerity by this: “Hate evil, O you+ who love the Lord!” (Ps 97:10). And the psalmist often mentions it as an evidence of his sincerity: “I will walk in my house with integrity of heart. I will set no worthless thing before my eyes. I hate the work of those who fall away” (Ps 101:2–3). “I hate every false way” (Ps 119:104). So also verse 128. Again, “Do I not hate those who hate You, O Lord?” (Ps 139:21).

So too holy desire, exercised in longings, hungerings and thirstings after God and holiness, is often mentioned in Scripture as an important part of true religion: “Your name and renown are the desire of our souls” (Isa 26:8). “One thing I have asked of the Lord this is what I desire: to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to gaze on the beauty of the Lord and seek Him in His temple” (Ps 27:4). “As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God. My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?” (Ps 42:1–2). “My soul thirsts for You. My body yearns for You in a dry and weary land without water, to see Your power and Your glory, as I have seen You in the sanctuary” (Ps 63:1–2). “How lovely is Your dwelling place, O Lord of Hosts! My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the Lord my heart and my flesh cry out for the living God” (Ps 84:1–2). “My soul is consumed with longing for Your judgments at all times” (Ps 119:20). So Ps 73:25; 143:6–7; 130:6; Song 3:1–2 and 5:8. Such a holy desire and thirst of soul is mentioned at the beginning of Christ’s Sermon on the Mount as one of the great things that make a man truly blessed, or show him to be so: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled” (Matt 5:6). And this holy thirst is spoken of as a great thing in the condition of sharing in the blessings of eternal life: “To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life” (Rev 21:6).

The Scriptures speak of holy joy as a great part of true religion. So it is represented in the text. And as an important part of religion, it is often urged and pressed with great earnestness: “Delight yourself in the Lord, and He will give you the desires of your heart” (Ps 37:4). “Rejoice in the Lord, you+ righteous ones” (Ps 97:12). So Ps 33:1: “Rejoice in the Lord, O righteous ones.” “Rejoice and be glad” (Matt 5:12). “Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord” (Phil 3:1). And Phil 4:4: “Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice!” “Rejoice at all times” (1 Thess 5:16). “Let Israel rejoice in their Maker; let the children of Zion rejoice in their King” (Ps 149:2). It is mentioned among the principal fruits of the Spirit of grace: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy,” and so on (Gal 5:22). The psalmist mentions his holy joy as an evidence of his sincerity: “I rejoice in the way of Your testimonies as much as in all riches” (Ps 119:14).

Religious sorrow, mourning and brokenness of heart are also frequently spoken of as a great part of true religion. These things are often mentioned as distinguishing qualities of the true saints and a great part of their character: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matt 5:4). “The Lord is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit” (Ps 34:18). “The Lord has anointed Me … to bind up the brokenhearted … to comfort all who mourn” (Isa 61:1–2). This godly sorrow and brokenness of heart is often spoken of not only as a great thing in the distinguishing character of the saints, but as something in them that is especially acceptable and pleasing to God: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” (Ps 51:17). “For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: ‘I dwell in a high and holy place, and with the contrite and humble in spirit, to restore the spirit of the lowly and revive the heart of the contrite’ ” (Isa 57:15). Isa 66:2: “This is the one I will esteem: he who is humble and contrite in spirit.”

Another affection often mentioned as one in whose exercise much of true religion appears is gratitude, especially as it is exercised in thankfulness and praise to God. Since this is spoken of so much in the book of Psalms and other parts of the holy Scriptures, I need not mention particular texts.

Again, the holy Scriptures frequently speak of compassion or mercy as a very great and essential thing in true religion. So much so that good men are named in Scripture from it, and a merciful man and a good man are equivalent terms in Scripture: “The righteous perish, and no one takes it to heart; merciful men are swept away” (Isa 57:1). And the Scripture chooses this quality as the one by which, in a special way, a righteous man is described: “The righteous show mercy and give” (Ps 37:21); and verse 26, “They are ever merciful and quick to lend.” And Prov 14:31: “He who honors Him has mercy on the needy.” And Col 3:12: “As the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves+ with hearts of compassion,” and so on. This is one of the great things by which our Savior describes those who are truly blessed: “Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy” (Matt 5:7). And Christ also speaks of this as one of the weightier matters of the law: “Woe to you+, scribes and Pharisees, you+ hypocrites! You+ pay tithes of mint, dill, and cumin. But you+ have disregarded the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness” (Matt 23:23). To the same purpose is Mic 6:8: “He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the Lord require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” And also Hos 6:6: “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice.” This seems to have been a text our Savior especially delighted in, judging by the way he cited it more than once (Matt 9:13 and 12:7).

Zeal too is spoken of as a very essential part of the religion of true saints. It is spoken of as a great thing Christ had in view in giving himself for our redemption: “He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds” (Titus 2:14). And it is spoken of as the great thing lacking in the lukewarm Laodiceans (Rev 3:15, 16, 19).

I have mentioned only a few texts out of a countless multitude all through the Scripture that place religion very much in the affections. But what has been observed may be enough to show that those who would deny that much of true religion lies in the affections, and maintain the contrary, must throw away what we have always acknowledged as our Bible and get some other rule by which to judge the nature of religion.

5. The Scriptures represent true religion as summed up in love, the chief of the affections and the fountain of all the other affections.

So our blessed Savior represents the matter in answer to the lawyer who asked him which was the great commandment of the law: “Jesus declared, ‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’ This is the first and greatest commandment. And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments” (Matt 22:37–40). These last words mean that these two commandments contain all the duty prescribed and the religion taught in the Law and the Prophets. And the apostle Paul again and again represents the matter in the same way, as in Romans 13:8: “He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.” And verse 10: “Love is the fulfillment of the law.” And Gal 5:14: “The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ ” So likewise in 1 Timothy 1:5: “The goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart,” and so on. So the same apostle speaks of love as the greatest thing in religion, and as its vital part, its essence and soul, without which the greatest knowledge and gifts, the most dazzling profession of faith, and everything else that belongs to religion are vain and worthless. And he represents it as the fountain from which all that is good proceeds, all through 1 Corinthians 13; for what is rendered there charity is αγαπη in the original, which in proper English is love.

Now although it is true that the love spoken of here includes the whole of a sincerely benevolent bent of the soul toward God and man, yet it may be considered that, as is evident from what has been observed already, this bent or inclination of the soul, when it is in strongly felt and vigorous exercise, becomes affection, and is nothing other than affectionate love. And surely it is such vigorous and fervent love that Christ speaks of as the sum of all religion, when he speaks of loving God with all our hearts, with all our souls and with all our minds, and our neighbor as ourselves, as the sum of all that was taught and prescribed in the Law and the Prophets.

Indeed, when this affection of love is spoken of here and in other Scriptures as the sum of all religion, it cannot be supposed that this means the act to the exclusion of the habit, or that the exercise of the understanding is excluded, which is implied in all reasonable affection. But it is no doubt true, and evident from these Scriptures, that the essence of all true religion lies in holy love; and that the whole of religion consists in this divine affection, a habitual disposition to it, the light that is its foundation, and the things that are its fruits.

From this it clearly and certainly appears that a great part of true religion consists in the affections. For love is not only one of the affections, but the first and chief of the affections, and the fountain of all the affections. From love arises hatred of the things that are contrary to what we love, or that oppose and thwart us in the things we delight in. And from the various exercises of love and hatred, according to the circumstances of the objects of these affections, as present or absent, certain or uncertain, probable or improbable, arise all the other affections of desire, hope, fear, joy, grief, gratitude, anger, and so on. From a vigorous, affectionate and fervent love to God other religious affections will necessarily arise. From it will arise an intense hatred and abhorrence of sin, fear of sin and a dread of God’s displeasure; gratitude to God for his goodness; delight and joy in God when God is graciously and perceptibly present, and grief when he is absent; a joyful hope when a future enjoyment of God is expected; and fervent zeal for the glory of God. And in the same way, from a fervent love to men all other virtuous affections toward men will arise.

6. The religion of the most eminent saints we have an account of in the Scripture consisted much in holy affections.

I will take particular notice of three eminent saints who have expressed the frame and feelings of their own hearts, and so described their own religion and the manner of their communion with God, in the writings they have left us, which are a part of the sacred canon.

The first instance I will take notice of is David, that man after God’s own heart, who has given us a lively portrait of his religion in the book of Psalms. The holy songs he has left us there are nothing else but the expressions and breathings of devout and holy affections: a humble and fervent love to God; wonder at his glorious perfections and wonderful works; earnest desires, thirstings and pantings of soul after God; delight and joy in God; a sweet and melting gratitude to God for his great goodness; a holy exultation and triumph of soul in the favor, sufficiency and faithfulness of God; his love to, and delight in, the saints, the excellent of the earth; his great delight in the word and ordinances of God; his grief for his own sins and the sins of others; and his fervent zeal for God and against the enemies of God and his church. And these expressions of holy affection, of which the Psalms of David are everywhere full, are all the more to our present purpose because those Psalms are not only the expressions of the religion of so eminent a saint, whom God speaks of as so agreeable to his mind. They were also written, by the direction of the Holy Spirit, for the use of the church of God in its public worship, not only in that age but in later ages, as fitted to express the religion of all saints in all ages, as well as the religion of the psalmist. And it is further to be observed that David, in the book of Psalms, speaks not as a private person but as the psalmist of Israel, as the subordinate head of the church of God and leader in their worship and praises. In many of the Psalms he speaks in the name of Christ, as representing him in these breathings of holy affection, and in many other Psalms he speaks in the name of the church.

Another instance I will observe is the apostle Paul, who was in many respects the chief of all the ministers of the New Testament. He was above all others a chosen vessel of Christ, to bear his name before the Gentiles. He was made the chief instrument of spreading and establishing the Christian church in the world, and of distinctly revealing the glorious mysteries of the gospel for the instruction of the church in all ages. And, as some have thought not without reason, he was the most eminent servant of Christ who ever lived, received to the highest rewards in the heavenly kingdom of his Master. By what is said of him in the Scripture, he appears to have been a person full of affection. And it is very plain that the religion he expresses in his epistles consisted very much in holy affections. It appears by all he says of himself that in the course of his life he was inflamed, driven and entirely swallowed up by a most ardent love to his glorious Lord, counting all things as loss for the surpassing excellence of the knowledge of him, and counting them as dung so that he might gain him. He represents himself as overpowered by this holy affection, and as it were compelled by it to go forward in his service through all difficulties and sufferings (2 Cor 5:14, 15). And his epistles are full of expressions of an overflowing affection toward the people of Christ. He speaks of his dear love to them (2 Cor 12:19; Phil 4:1; 2 Tim 1:2); of his abundant love (2 Cor 2:4); and of his affectionate and tender love, like that of a nurse toward her children: “But we were gentle among you+, like a nursing mother caring for her children. So, being affectionately desirous of you+, we were delighted to share with you+ not only the gospel of God, but our own lives as well. That is how beloved you+ have become to us” (1 Thess 2:7–8). So too he speaks of the deep affection of his heart (Phil 1:8; Phlm 12 and 20). So he speaks of his earnest care for others (2 Cor 8:16), and of his tender pity or mercy toward them (Phil 2:1), and of his concern for others even to anguish of heart: “For through many tears I wrote you+ out of great distress and anguish of heart, not to grieve you+ but to let you+ know how much I love you+” (2 Cor 2:4). He speaks of the great struggle of his soul for them (Col 2:1). He speaks of deep sorrow and unceasing anguish that he had in his heart from compassion for the Jews (Rom 9:2). He speaks of his mouth being opened and his heart opened wide toward Christians: “We have opened our mouth to you+, Corinthians. Our hearts are open wide” (2 Cor 6:11). He often speaks of his affectionate and longing desires (1 Thess 2:8; Rom 1:11; Phil 1:8 and 4:1; 2 Tim 1:4). The same apostle very often in his epistles expresses the affection of joy (2 Cor 1:12 and 7:7, 9, 16; Phil 1:4 and 2:1, 2 and 3:3; Col 1:24; 1 Thess 3:9). He speaks of his rejoicing greatly (Phil 4:10; Phlm 1, 7); of his being glad and rejoicing (Phil 2:1, 7); and of his rejoicing exceedingly (2 Cor 7:13); and of his being filled with comfort, and exceedingly joyful (2 Cor 7:4). He speaks of himself as always rejoicing (2 Cor 6:10). So he speaks of the triumphs of his soul (2 Cor 2:14), and of his glorying in tribulation (2 Thess 1:4 and Rom 5:3). He also expresses the affection of hope: in Philippians 1:20 he speaks of his earnest expectation and his hope. He likewise expresses an affection of godly jealousy (2 Cor 11:2, 3). And it appears from his whole history after his conversion in the Acts, and also from all his epistles and the accounts he gives of himself there, that the affection of zeal, having for its object the cause of his Master and the interest and prosperity of his church, was mighty in him. It continually inflamed his heart and strongly engaged him in the great and constant labors he went through: instructing, exhorting, warning and rebuking others, in the pains of childbirth for them; contending with the powerful and countless enemies who continually opposed him; wrestling with principalities and powers; not fighting like one who beats the air; running the race set before him; continually pressing forward through every kind of difficulty and suffering, so that others thought him quite out of his mind. And how full he was of affection further appears from his being so full of tears. In 2 Corinthians 2:4 he speaks of his many tears, and so in Acts 20:19; and of the tears he shed night and day without ceasing (verse 31).

Now if anyone can consider these accounts the Scripture gives of this great apostle, and that he gives of himself, and yet not see that his religion consisted much in affection, he must have a strange way of managing his eyes, to shut out the light that shines full in his face.

The other instance I will mention is the apostle John, that beloved disciple, who was the nearest and dearest to his Master of any of the twelve, and was admitted by him to the greatest privileges of any of them. He was not only one of the three who were admitted to be present with him on the mount at his transfiguration and at the raising of Jairus’s daughter, and whom he took with him when he was in his agony; and one of the three whom the apostle Paul speaks of as the three main pillars of the Christian church. He was also favored above all in being allowed to lean on his Master’s breast at his last supper, and in being chosen by Christ as the disciple to whom he would reveal his wonderful dealings with his church to the end of time, as we have an account in the book of Revelation; and to close the canon of the New Testament and of the whole Scripture, being preserved much longer than all the rest of the apostles, to set all things in order in the Christian church after their death.

It is evident from all his writings (as divines generally observe) that he was a person remarkably full of affection. His addresses to those he wrote to are unspeakably tender and moving, breathing nothing but the most fervent love, as though he were made up entirely of sweet and holy affection. The proofs of this cannot be given without loss unless we were to copy out his whole writings.

7. He whom God sent into the world to be the light of the world, the head of the whole church, and the perfect example of true religion and virtue for all to imitate, the Shepherd whom the whole flock should follow wherever he goes, even the Lord Jesus Christ, was a person of a remarkably tender and affectionate heart, and his virtue was expressed very much in the exercise of holy affections. He was the greatest instance of ardor, vigor and strength of love, both to God and man, that there ever was. It was these affections that won the victory in that mighty struggle and conflict of his affections in his agonies, when he prayed more earnestly and offered up loud cries and tears, and wrestled in tears and in blood. Such was the power of the exercises of his holy love that they were stronger than death, and in that great struggle they overcame those strong exercises of the natural affections of fear and grief, when he was deeply troubled and distressed and his soul was consumed with sorrow to the point of death. And he also appeared to be full of affection in the course of his life. We read of his great zeal, fulfilling the words of the sixty-ninth Psalm, “Zeal for Your house will consume Me” (John 2:17). We read of his grief for the sins of men: “He looked around at them with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart” (Mark 3:5). We read of his breaking out in tears and cries at the thought of the sin and misery of ungodly men, and at the sight of the city of Jerusalem, which was full of such inhabitants: “As Jesus approached Jerusalem and saw the city, He wept over it and said, ‘If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes’ ” (Luke 19:41–42). With this compare Luke 13:34: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you+ were unwilling!” We read of Christ’s earnest desire: “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you+ before My suffering” (Luke 22:15). We often read of the affection of pity or compassion in Christ (Matt 15:32 and 20:34; Luke 7:13), and of his being moved with compassion (Matt 9:36 and 14:14; Mark 6:34). And how tender his heart appeared to be when Mary and Martha mourned for their brother and came to him with their complaints and tears! Their tears soon drew tears from his eyes. He was moved by their grief and wept with them, though he knew their sorrow would so soon be turned into joy by their brother’s being raised from the dead (see John 11). And how unspeakably affectionate was the last, dying discourse Jesus had with his eleven disciples the evening before he was crucified! He told them he was going away, and foretold the great difficulties and sufferings they would meet with in the world when he was gone. He comforted and counseled them as his dear little children, and left them his Holy Spirit, and with him his peace, his comfort and his joy, as it were in his last will and testament, in the thirteenth, fourteenth, fifteenth and sixteenth chapters of John. And he concluded the whole with that affectionate prayer of intercession for them and his whole church in chapter 17. Of all the discourses ever written, or spoken by the mouth of any man, this seems to be the most affectionate and the most moving.

8. The religion of heaven consists very much in affection.

There is no doubt true religion in heaven, and true religion in its utmost purity and perfection. But according to the Scripture’s representation of the heavenly state, the religion of heaven consists chiefly in holy and mighty love and joy, and the expression of these in most fervent and exalted praises. So the religion of the saints in heaven consists in the same things as that religion of the saints on earth that is spoken of in our text, namely, love and joy unspeakable and full of glory. Now it would be very foolish to claim that because the saints in heaven are not united to flesh and blood, and have no animal fluids to be moved (through the laws of the union of soul and body) with those great emotions of their souls, their exceeding love and joy are therefore no affections. We are not speaking of the affections of the body, but of the affections of the soul, the chief of which are love and joy. When these are in the soul, whether it is in the body or out of it, the soul is affected and moved. And when they are in the soul with the strength with which they are in the saints in heaven, the soul is mightily affected and moved, or, which is the same thing, has great affections. It is true that we do not know by experience what love and joy are in a soul out of a body, or in a glorified body; that is, we have not had experience of love and joy in a soul in these circumstances. But the saints on earth do know what divine love and joy in the soul are, and they know love and joy of the same kind as the love and joy that are in heaven, in the disembodied souls there. The love and joy of the saints on earth are the beginning and dawning of the light, life and blessedness of heaven, and are like their love and joy there; or rather, they are the same in nature, though not the same as it, or like it, in degree and circumstances. This is evident from many Scriptures, such as Prov 4:18; John 4:14 and 6:40, 47, 50, 51, 54, 58; 1 John 3:15; 1 Cor 13:8, 9, 10, 11, 12. It is unreasonable, therefore, to suppose that the love and joy of the saints in heaven not only differ in degree and circumstances from the holy love and joy of the saints on earth, but are so entirely different in nature that they are no affections. And this merely because they have no blood and animal spirits to be set in motion by them. Yet this motion of the blood and animal spirits is not of the essence of these affections in men on the earth, but their effect, although by their reaction they may make some difference in circumstance to the sensation of the mind. There is a sensation of the mind that loves and rejoices which comes before any effects on the fluids of the body. And so this sensation of the mind does not depend on these motions in the body, and so may be in the soul without the body. And wherever there are the exercises of love and joy, there is that sensation of the mind, whether it is in the body or out of it. And that inward sensation, or kind of spiritual sense or feeling, and motion of the soul, is what is called affection. The soul, when it feels in this way (if I may put it so) and is moved in this way, is said to be affected, and especially when this inward sensation and motion are in a very high degree, as they are in the saints in heaven. If we can learn anything of the state of heaven from the Scripture, the love and joy that the saints have there are exceedingly great and vigorous. They impress the heart with the strongest and liveliest sensation of inexpressible sweetness, mightily moving, animating and engaging them, making them like a flame of fire. And if such love and joy are not affections, then the word affection is of no use in language. Will anyone say that the saints in heaven, beholding the face of their Father and the glory of their Redeemer, and contemplating his wonderful works, and in particular his laying down his life for them, have their hearts not at all moved and affected by all they behold or consider?

So, then, the religion of heaven, consisting chiefly in holy love and joy, consists very much in affection. And therefore, without doubt, true religion consists very much in affection. The way to learn the true nature of anything is to go where that thing is found in its purity and perfection. If we would know the nature of true gold, we must look at it not in the ore but when it is refined. If we would learn what true religion is, we must go where there is true religion, and nothing but true religion, and that in its highest perfection, without any defect or mixture. All who are truly religious are not of this world. They are strangers here and belong to heaven. They are born from above; heaven is their native country, and the nature they receive by this heavenly birth is a heavenly nature. They receive an anointing from above. The principle of true religion that is in them is an imparting of the religion of heaven. Their grace is the dawn of glory, and God fits them for that world by conforming them to it.

9. This appears from the nature and design of the ordinances and duties God has appointed as means and expressions of true religion.

Take the duty of prayer. It is plain that in this duty we are not appointed to declare God’s perfections, his majesty, holiness, goodness and all-sufficiency, and our own lowliness, emptiness, dependence and unworthiness, and our needs and desires, in order to inform God of these things, or to incline his heart and prevail on him to be willing to show us mercy. We are appointed to do it in order to affect our own hearts suitably with the things we express, and so to prepare us to receive the blessings we ask. And such gestures and manner of outward behavior in the worship of God as custom has made signs of humility and reverence can be of no further use than as they have some tendency to affect our own hearts or the hearts of others.

And the duty of singing praises to God seems to be appointed wholly to stir up and express religious affections. No other reason can be given why we should express ourselves to God in verse rather than in prose, and do it with music, except that such is our nature and frame that these things tend to move our affections.

The same thing appears in the nature and design of the sacraments God has appointed. God, considering our frame, has not only appointed that we should be told of the great things of the gospel and of the redemption of Christ, and be instructed in them by his word. He has also appointed that they should be, as it were, set before our eyes in perceptible representations in the sacraments, so as to affect us the more with them.

And impressing divine things on the hearts and affections of men is evidently one great and main end for which God has ordained that his word, delivered in the holy Scriptures, should be opened, applied and pressed home on men in preaching. And therefore it does not answer God’s aim in this institution for men merely to have good commentaries and expositions on the Scripture and other good books of divinity. For although these may tend, as well as preaching, to give men a good doctrinal or theoretical understanding of the things of the word of God, they do not have an equal tendency to impress them on men’s hearts and affections. God has appointed a particular and lively application of his word to men in the preaching of it, as a fit means to affect sinners with the importance of the things of religion, with their own misery and need of a remedy, and with the glory and sufficiency of the remedy provided. It is also a means to stir up the pure minds of the saints and enliven their affections, by often bringing the great things of religion to their remembrance and setting them before them in their proper colors, though they know them and have been fully instructed in them already (2 Pet 1:12, 13). And in particular it is a means to promote in them the two affections spoken of in the text, love and joy. Christ gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers, so that the body of Christ might be built up in love (Eph 4:11, 12, 16). The apostle, in instructing and counseling Timothy about the work of the ministry, tells him that the great end of the word a minister is to preach is love or charity (1 Tim 1:3, 4, 5). And another affection God has appointed preaching as a means to promote in the saints is joy; and therefore ministers are called helpers of their joy (2 Cor 1:24).

10. It is an evidence that true religion, or holiness of heart, lies very much in the affection of the heart, that the Scriptures place the sin of the heart very much in hardness of heart. So the Scriptures do everywhere. It was hardness of heart that stirred up grief and displeasure in Christ toward the Jews: “He looked around at them with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart” (Mark 3:5). It is from having such a heart as this that men store up wrath for themselves: “Because of your hard and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath against yourself for the day of wrath, when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed” (Rom 2:5). The reason given why the house of Israel would not obey God was that they were hard-hearted: “But the house of Israel will be unwilling to listen to you, since they are unwilling to listen to Me. For the whole house of Israel is hard-headed and hard-hearted” (Ezek 3:7). The wickedness of that perverse, rebellious generation in the wilderness is ascribed to the hardness of their hearts: “Today, if you+ hear His voice, do not harden your+ hearts as you+ did at Meribah, in the day at Massah in the wilderness, where your+ fathers tested and tried Me, though they had seen My work. For forty years I was angry with that generation, and I said, ‘They are a people whose hearts go astray,’ ” and so on (Ps 95:7–10). This is spoken of as what kept Zedekiah from turning to the Lord: “Zedekiah stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the Lord, the God of Israel” (2 Chr 36:13). This principle is spoken of as the reason men are without the fear of God and depart from God’s ways: “Why, O Lord, do You make us stray from Your ways and harden our hearts from fearing You?” (Isa 63:17). And men’s rejecting Christ and opposing Christianity is laid to this principle: “But when some of them were hardened and refused to believe and publicly maligned the Way …” (Acts 19:9). God’s leaving men to the power of the sin and corruption of the heart is often expressed as God’s hardening their hearts: “Therefore God has mercy on whom He wants to have mercy, and He hardens whom He wants to harden” (Rom 9:18). “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts” (John 12:40). And the apostle seems to speak of an evil heart that turns away from the living God and a hard heart as the same thing: “Do not harden your+ hearts, as you+ did in the rebellion,” and so on (Heb 3:8). Verses 12–13: “See to it, brothers, that none of you+ has a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God. But exhort one another daily, as long as it is called today, so that none of you+ may be hardened by sin’s deceitfulness.” And that great work of God in conversion, which consists in delivering a person from the power of sin and mortifying corruption, is expressed more than once as God’s taking away the heart of stone and giving a heart of flesh (Ezek 11:19 and 36:26).

Now by a hard heart is plainly meant an unaffected heart, a heart not easily moved with virtuous affections: like a stone, without feeling, dull, unmoved and hard to impress. That is why the hard heart is called a heart of stone, and is set against a heart of flesh, which has feeling and is perceptibly touched and moved. We read in Scripture of a hard heart and a tender heart, and no doubt we are to understand these as contrary to each other. But what is a tender heart but a heart that is easily impressed with what ought to affect it? God commends Josiah because his heart was tender. And it is evident from the things mentioned as expressions and evidences of this tenderness of heart that by his heart being tender is meant that it was easily moved with religious and godly affection: “Because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before the Lord when you heard what I spoke against this place and against its people, that they would become a desolation and a curse, and because you have torn your clothes and wept before Me, I have heard you, declares the Lord” (2 Kgs 22:19). And this is one thing in which it is necessary for us to become like little children in order to enter the kingdom of God: we must have our hearts tender, easily affected and moved in spiritual and divine things, as little children have in other things.

It is very plain in some places, in the texts themselves, that by hardness of heart is meant a heart without affection. So, to show that the ostrich is without natural affection for her young, it is said, “She hardens her heart against her young, as if they were not her own” (Job 39:16). So a person who has an unaffected heart in a time of danger is described as hardening his heart: “Blessed is the man who always fears, but he who hardens his heart falls into trouble” (Prov 28:14).

Now therefore, since it is so plain that by a hard heart in Scripture is meant a heart without godly affections, and since the Scriptures also so frequently place the sin and corruption of the heart in hardness of heart, it is evident that the grace and holiness of the heart, on the contrary, must in great measure consist in its having godly affections and being readily open to such affection. Divines are generally agreed that sin, at its root and foundation, consists in what is negative or privative: it has its root and foundation in a privation, or lack, of holiness. And therefore, without doubt, if sin consists very much in hardness of heart, and so in the lack of godly affections of heart, holiness consists very much in those godly affections.

I am far from supposing that all affections show a tender heart. Hatred, anger, vainglory and other selfish and self-exalting affections may greatly prevail in the hardest heart. Yet it is evident that hardness of heart and tenderness of heart are expressions that relate to the affections of the heart. They denote the heart’s being open to, or shut up against, certain affections, of which I will have occasion to speak more later.

On the whole, I think it clearly and abundantly evident that true religion lies very much in the affections. Not that I think these arguments prove that religion in the hearts of the truly godly is ever in exact proportion to the degree of affection and present emotion of the mind. For no doubt there is much affection in the true saints that is not spiritual. Their religious affections are often mixed; not all is from grace, but much is from nature. And though the affections do not have their seat in the body, yet the constitution of the body may contribute very much to the present emotion of the mind. And the degree of religion is to be judged rather by the fixedness and strength of the habit that is exercised in affection, by which holy affection is habitual, than by the degree of the present exercise. And the strength of that habit is not always in proportion to outward effects and displays, or to inward effects in the hurry and vehemence and sudden changes of the course of the thoughts of the mind.
