Yet it is evident that religion consists so much in affection that without holy affection there is no true religion. No light in the understanding is good that does not produce holy affection in the heart. No habit or principle in the heart is good that has no such exercise. And no outward fruit is good that does not proceed from such exercises.

Having considered in this way the evidence for the proposition laid down, I proceed to some inferences.

Inferences

Part I · The Nature and Importance of the Affections

1. From this we may learn how great the error is of those who are for discarding all religious affections, as having nothing solid or substantial in them.

There seems to be too much of a disposition this way prevailing in this land at this time. Many who in the recent extraordinary season appeared to have great religious affections did not show a right temper of mind, and ran into many errors in the time of their affection and the heat of their zeal. The high affections of many seem to have come to nothing so soon, and some who seemed for a while to be mightily lifted up and swallowed up with joy and zeal seem to have returned like the dog to his vomit. And because of this, religious affections in general have lost their credit with great numbers, as though true religion did not consist in them at all. So easily and naturally do we run from one extreme to another. A little while ago we were in the other extreme. There was a prevailing disposition to look on all high religious affections as eminent exercises of true grace, without much inquiry into the nature and source of those affections and the way in which they arose. If persons only appeared to be very much moved and lifted up, so as to be full of religious talk and to express themselves with great warmth and earnestness, and to be filled, or very full, as the phrases were, it was too much the custom to conclude, without further examination, that such persons were full of the Spirit of God and had eminent experience of his gracious influences. This was the extreme that prevailed three or four years ago. But lately, instead of esteeming and wondering at all religious affections without distinction, it is much more common to reject and discard all without distinction. In this the craftiness of Satan appears. While he saw that affections were much in fashion, knowing that the greater part of the land were not versed in such things, and had not had much experience of great religious affections to enable them to judge well of them and distinguish between true and false, he knew he could best play his game by sowing tares among the wheat and mingling false affections with the works of God’s Spirit. He knew this was a likely way to deceive and eternally ruin many souls, to wound religion greatly in the saints and entangle them in a dreadful wilderness, and in time to bring all religion into disrepute. But now, when the bad consequences of these false affections appear, and it has become very plain that some of those emotions which made a dazzling show, and were greatly admired by many, were in reality nothing, the devil sees that it is in his interest to go to work another way. He sees it is in his interest to do his utmost to spread and establish a persuasion that all affections and felt emotions of the mind in things of religion are not to be regarded at all, but are rather to be avoided and carefully guarded against as things of a harmful tendency. This, he knows, is the way to bring all religion down to a mere lifeless formality, to shut out effectually the power of godliness and everything that is spiritual, and to have all true Christianity turned out of doors. For although true religion must indeed have something else besides affection, yet true religion consists so much in the affections that there can be no true religion without them. He who has no religious affection is in a state of spiritual death, and is wholly without the powerful, life-giving, saving influences of the Spirit of God on his heart. As there is no true religion where there is nothing but affection, so there is no true religion where there is no religious affection. On the one hand, there must be light in the understanding as well as an affected, fervent heart; where there is heat without light, there can be nothing divine or heavenly in that heart. So on the other hand, where there is a kind of light without heat, a head stored with notions and theories, with a cold and unaffected heart, there can be nothing divine in that light; that knowledge is no true spiritual knowledge of divine things. If the great things of religion are rightly understood, they will affect the heart. The reason men are not affected by such infinitely great, important, glorious and wonderful things as they often hear and read of in the word of God is without doubt that they are blind. If they were not, it would be impossible, and utterly inconsistent with human nature, for their hearts to be anything other than strongly impressed and greatly moved by such things.

This way of slighting all religious affections is the way to harden the hearts of men exceedingly, to encourage them in their dullness and insensibility, to keep them in a state of spiritual death as long as they live, and to bring them at last to eternal death. The prejudice against religious affections that prevails in the land at this day evidently has a fearful effect. It hardens the hearts of sinners, damps the graces of many of the saints, deadens the life and power of religion, cuts off the effect of the ordinances, and holds us down in a state of dullness and apathy. And it no doubt causes many persons to offend God greatly by entertaining poor and low thoughts of the extraordinary work he has recently done in this land.

And for persons to despise and cry down all religious affections is the way to shut all religion out of their own hearts and to make thorough work of ruining their souls.

Those who condemn high affections in others are certainly not likely to have high affections themselves. And let it be considered that those who have only a little religious affection certainly have only a little religion. And those who condemn others for their religious affections, and have none themselves, have no religion.

There are false affections, and there are true. A man’s having much affection does not prove that he has any true religion. But if he has no affection, it proves that he has no true religion. The right way is not to reject all affections, nor to approve all, but to distinguish between affections, approving some and rejecting others: separating the wheat from the chaff, the gold from the dross, the precious from the vile.

2. If it is true that true religion lies much in the affections, we may infer from this that such means are to be desired as have much tendency to move the affections. Such books, such a way of preaching the word and administering the ordinances, and such a way of worshiping God in prayer and singing praises, are much to be desired as tend to affect deeply the hearts of those who attend these means.

Such means would formerly have been highly approved and applauded by most of the people of the land, as the most excellent and profitable, and as having the greatest tendency to promote the ends of the means of grace. But the prevailing taste seems lately to have changed strangely. The moving manner of praying and preaching that would formerly have been admired and praised, and for this very reason, that it tended so much to move the affections, now in great multitudes immediately stirs up disgust, and moves no other affections than those of displeasure and contempt.

Perhaps formerly most people (at least of the common people) were in the extreme of looking too much for a heartfelt manner in public worship. But now a very great part of the people seem to have gone far into the contrary extreme. Indeed, there may be such means as have a great tendency to stir up the passions of weak and ignorant persons, and yet have no great tendency to benefit their souls. For though they may tend to stir up affections, they may have little or no tendency to stir up gracious affections, or any affections tending to grace. But without doubt, if the things of religion are treated in the means used according to their nature, and set forth truly, in a way that tends to convey correct perceptions and a right judgment of them, the more they tend to move the affections, the better.

3. If true religion lies much in the affections, we may learn from this what great cause we have to be ashamed and confounded before God that we are not more affected by the great things of religion. It appears from what has been said that this comes from our having so little true religion.

God has given mankind affections for the same purpose for which he has given all the faculties and principles of the human soul, namely, that they might serve man’s chief end and the great business for which God created him, that is, the business of religion. And yet how common it is among mankind that their affections are much more exercised and engaged in other matters than in religion! In things that concern men’s worldly interest, their outward delights, their honor and reputation, and their natural relations, their desires are eager, their appetites vehement, their love warm and affectionate, their zeal ardent. In these things their hearts are tender and feeling, easily moved, deeply impressed, much concerned, very deeply affected and greatly engaged; much cast down with grief at worldly losses, and highly lifted up with joy at worldly success and prosperity. But how unfeeling and unmoved most men are about the great things of another world! How dull their affections are! How heavy and hard their hearts are in these matters! Here their love is cold, their desires feeble, their zeal low and their gratitude small. They can sit and hear of the infinite height and depth and length and breadth of the love of God in Christ Jesus: of his giving his infinitely dear Son to be offered up as a sacrifice for the sins of men; and of the unparalleled love of the innocent, holy and tender Lamb of God, shown in his dying agonies, his bloody sweat, his loud and bitter cries and his bleeding heart, and all this for enemies, to redeem them from deserved, eternal burnings and to bring them to unspeakable and everlasting joy and glory. And yet they can be cold and heavy, unfeeling and indifferent! Where is the proper exercise of our affections, if not here? What requires them more? And what can be a fit occasion for their lively and vigorous exercise, if not such an occasion as this? Can anything be set before us that is greater and more important? Anything more wonderful and astonishing? Or anything that concerns our interest more nearly? Can we suppose that the wise Creator planted such principles as the affections in human nature to be of use to us and to be exercised on certain proper occasions, but to lie still on such an occasion as this? Can any Christian who believes the truth of these things entertain such thoughts?

If we ought ever to exercise our affections at all, and if the Creator has not made human nature unwisely, in making these principles a part of it when they are vain and useless, then they ought to be exercised about the objects that are most worthy of them. But is there anything Christians can find in heaven or earth so worthy to be the object of their wonder and love, their earnest and longing desires, their hope, their rejoicing and their fervent zeal, as the things held out to us in the gospel of Jesus Christ? In the gospel, not only are the things declared that are most worthy to affect us, but they are set forth in the most affecting manner. The glory and beauty of the blessed Jehovah, which is in itself most worthy to be the object of our wonder and love, is set forth there in the most affecting manner that can be conceived, as it appears shining in all its luster in the face of an incarnate, infinitely loving, meek, compassionate, dying Redeemer. All the virtues of the Lamb of God, his humility, patience, meekness, submission, obedience, love and compassion, are set before us in a manner more fitted to move our affections than any that can be imagined. For they all had their greatest trial and their highest exercise, and so their brightest display, when he was in the most affecting circumstances: when he was under his last sufferings, those unutterable and unparalleled sufferings he endured from his tender love and pity to us. There too the hateful nature of our sins is shown in the most affecting manner possible, as we see their dreadful effects in what our Redeemer, who undertook to answer for us, suffered for them. And there we have the most affecting displays of God’s hatred of sin, and his wrath and justice in punishing it. We see his justice in its strictness and inflexibility, and his wrath in its terribleness, in his so dreadfully punishing our sins in one who was infinitely dear to him and loving to us. God has so ordered things in the work of our redemption, and in his glorious dealings revealed to us in the gospel, as though everything were purposely arranged to have the greatest possible tendency to reach our hearts in their most tender part, and to move our affections most deeply and strongly. How great cause, then, we have to be humbled to the dust that we are not more affected!

Part II

Affections Raised Very High

Part II · No Certain Sign I

Showing what are no certain Signs that religious Affections are truly gracious, or that they are not.

If anyone, on reading what has just been said, is ready to acquit himself and say, “I am not one of those who have no religious affections; I am often greatly moved when I consider the great things of religion,” let him not be content with this, that he has religious affections. For, as was observed before, we ought not to reject and condemn all affections, as though true religion did not consist in affection at all. But on the other hand, we ought not to approve of all, as though everyone who was religiously affected had true grace and was in that the subject of the saving influences of the Spirit of God. The right way, therefore, is to distinguish among religious affections, between one sort and another. So let us now try to do this, and to that end I would do two things.

I. I would mention some things which are no signs one way or the other, either that affections are such as true religion consists in, or that they are otherwise, so that we may be guarded against judging affections by false signs.

II. I would observe some things in which those affections that are spiritual and gracious differ from those that are not, and by which they may be distinguished and known.

1. FIRST, I would take notice of some things which are no signs that affections are gracious, or that they are not.

I. It is no sign one way or the other that religious affections are very great, or raised very high.

Some are ready to condemn all high affections. If persons appear to have their religious affections raised to an extraordinary pitch, they are prejudiced against them and decide that they are delusions, without further inquiry. But if it is as has been proved, that true religion lies very much in religious affections, then it follows that if there is a great deal of true religion, there will be great religious affections. If true religion in the hearts of men is raised to a great height, divine and holy affections will be raised to a great height.

Love is an affection. But will any Christian say that men ought not to love God and Jesus Christ in a high degree? And will anyone say that we ought not to have a very great hatred of sin and a very deep sorrow for it? Or that we ought not to exercise a high degree of gratitude to God for the mercies we receive from him, and for the great things he has done for the salvation of fallen men? Or that we should not have very great and strong desires after God and holiness? Is there anyone who will profess that his affections in religion are great enough, and will say, “I have no cause to be humbled that I am no more affected with the things of religion than I am; I have no reason to be ashamed that I have no greater exercises of love to God, and sorrow for sin, and gratitude for the mercies I have received”? Who is there who will go and bless God that he is affected enough with what he has read and heard of the wonderful love of God to worms and rebels in giving his only begotten Son to die for them, and of the dying love of Christ? And who will pray that he may not be affected with them in any higher degree, because high affections are improper and very unlovely in Christians, being fanatical and ruinous to true religion?

Our text plainly speaks of great and high affections when it speaks of rejoicing with joy unspeakable and full of glory. Here the most superlative expressions the language can afford are used. And the Scriptures often require us to exercise very high affections. So in the first and great commandment of the law there is a heaping up of expressions, as though words were lacking to express the degree to which we ought to love God: “Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.” So the saints are called on to exercise high degrees of joy. “Rejoice,” says Christ to his disciples, “and be exceedingly glad” (Matt 5:12). So it is said in Ps 68:3, “Let the righteous be glad; let them rejoice before God; let them rejoice exceedingly.” So in the same book of Psalms the saints are often called on to shout for joy, and in Luke 6:23 to leap for joy. So they are abundantly called on to exercise high degrees of gratitude for mercies: to praise God with all their hearts, with hearts lifted up in the ways of the Lord, and their souls magnifying the Lord, singing his praises, talking of his wondrous works, declaring his deeds, and so on.

And we find the most eminent saints in Scripture often professing high affections. So the psalmist speaks of his love as if it were unspeakable: “Oh, how I love Your law!” (Ps 119:97). So he expresses a great degree of hatred of sin: “Do I not hate those who hate You, O LORD, and detest those who rise against You? I hate them with perfect hatred” (Ps 139:21–22). He also expresses a high degree of sorrow for sin. He speaks of his sins going over his head, as a heavy burden that was too heavy for him, and of his roaring all day long, and his moisture being turned into the drought of summer, and his bones being as it were broken with sorrow. So he often expresses great degrees of spiritual desire, in a multitude of the strongest expressions that can be conceived, such as his longing, his soul thirsting as a dry and weary land where there is no water, his panting, his flesh and heart crying out, his soul breaking with the longing it has, and so on. He expresses the exercise of great and extreme grief for the sins of others: “My eyes shed streams of tears because Your law is not obeyed” (Ps 119:136). And in verse 53: “Horror has taken hold of me because of the wicked who reject Your law.” He expresses high exercises of joy: “O LORD, the king rejoices in Your strength. How greatly he exults in Your salvation!” (Ps 21:1). “When I sing praise to You my lips will shout for joy” (Ps 71:23). “Because Your loving devotion is better than life, my lips will glorify You. So I will bless You as long as I live; in Your name I will lift my hands. My soul is satisfied as with the richest of foods; with joyful lips my mouth will praise You. When I remember You on my bed, I think of You through the watches of the night. For You are my help; I will sing for joy in the shadow of Your wings” (Ps 63:3–7).

The apostle Paul expresses high exercises of affection. So he expresses the exercise of pity and concern for the good of others, even to anguish of heart; a great, fervent and abundant love, and earnest and longing desires, and exceeding joy. He speaks of the exultation and triumphs of his soul, and his earnest expectation and hope, and his abundant tears, and the travail of his soul, in pity, grief, earnest desires, godly jealousy and fervent zeal, in many places that have been cited already, which I therefore need not repeat. John the Baptist expressed great joy (John 3:29). Those blessed women who anointed the body of Jesus are represented as in a very high exercise of religious affection on the occasion of Christ’s resurrection: “So they hurried away from the tomb in fear and great joy” (Matt 28:8).

It is often foretold of the church of God, in her future happy seasons here on earth, that they will rejoice exceedingly: “They will walk, O LORD, in the light of Your presence. They will rejoice in Your name all day long, and in Your righteousness they will exult” (Ps 89:15–16). “Rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion! Shout in triumph, O Daughter of Jerusalem! See, your King comes to you,” and so on (Zech 9:9). The same is represented in countless other places. And because high degrees of joy are the proper and genuine fruits of the gospel of Christ, the angel calls this gospel good news of great joy that will be for all the people.

The saints and angels in heaven, who have religion in its highest perfection, are exceedingly affected with what they see and contemplate of God’s perfections and works. They are all like a pure heavenly flame of fire in their love, and in the greatness and strength of their joy and gratitude. Their praises are represented as the sound of many waters, and as the sound of a great thunder. Now the only reason why their affections are so much higher than the holy affections of saints on earth is that they see the things they are affected by more according to their truth, and have their affections more conformed to the nature of things. And therefore, if religious affections in men here below are of the same nature and kind as theirs, the higher they are, and the nearer they come to theirs in degree, the better. For in that they will be so much the more conformed to truth, as theirs are.

From these things it certainly appears that religious affections being in a very high degree is no evidence that they are not such as have the nature of true religion. Therefore those greatly err who condemn persons as fanatics merely because their affections are very high.

And on the other hand, it is no evidence that religious affections are of a spiritual and gracious nature because they are great. It is very plain from the holy Scripture, our sure and infallible rule for judging things of this nature, that there are religious affections which are very high and yet are not spiritual and saving. The apostle Paul speaks of affections in the Galatians which had been exceedingly elevated, and yet he plainly speaks of them as fearing that they were vain and had come to nothing: “What then has become of your+ blessing? For I can testify that, if it were possible, you+ would have torn out your+ eyes and given them to me” (Gal 4:15). And in the eleventh verse he tells them he was afraid for them, that he had spent his labor on them in vain. So the children of Israel were greatly affected with God’s mercy to them when they had seen how wonderfully he worked for them at the Red Sea, where they sang God’s praise, though they soon forgot his works. So they were greatly affected again at Mount Sinai, when they saw the marvelous manifestations God made of himself there. They seemed mightily engaged in their minds, and with great eagerness they answered, when God proposed his holy covenant to them, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient.” But how soon there was an end to all this mighty eagerness and engagement of affection! How quickly they turned aside after other gods, rejoicing and shouting around their golden calf! So great multitudes who were affected with the miracle of raising Lazarus from the dead were elevated to a high degree and made a mighty stir when Jesus, soon after, entered Jerusalem. They exceedingly magnified Christ, as though the ground were not good enough for the donkey he rode to tread on. So they cut down branches of palm trees and spread them in the way; indeed, they pulled off their garments and spread them in the way. And they cried with loud voices, “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!” so as to make the whole city ring again and put everyone in an uproar. We learn from the evangelist John that the reason the people made this stir was that they were affected with the miracle of raising Lazarus (John 12:18). Here was a vast multitude crying Hosanna on this occasion, so that it gave the Pharisees occasion to say, “Look how the whole world has gone after Him!” (John 12:19). But Christ had at that time only a few true disciples. And how quickly this stir came to an end! All of this kind is quelled and dead when this Jesus stands bound, with a mock robe and a crown of thorns, to be mocked, spat on, scourged, condemned and executed. Indeed, there was a great and loud outcry about him among the multitude then, as well as before, but of a very different kind. It is not then Hosanna, Hosanna, but crucify, crucify.

And it is the united voice of all orthodox divines that there may be religious affections raised to a very high degree, and yet nothing of true religion be there.1

1. Mr. Stoddard observes that common affections are sometimes stronger than saving ones. Guide to Christ. P. 21.

Great Effects on the Body

Part II · No Certain Sign II

II. It is no sign that affections have the nature of true religion, or that they do not, that they have great effects on the body.

All affections whatever have, in some respect or degree, an effect on the body. As was observed before, such is our nature, and such are the laws of the union of soul and body, that the mind can have no lively or vigorous exercise without some effect on the body. So subject is the body to the mind, and so closely do its fluids, especially the animal spirits, follow the motions and exercises of the mind, that there cannot be so much as an intense thought without an effect on them. Indeed, it is questionable whether a soul in the body ever so much as thinks one thought, or has any exercise at all, without some corresponding motion, or change of motion, in some degree, of the fluids in some part of the body. But universal experience shows that the exercise of the affections has, in a special way, a tendency to some perceptible effect on the body. And if it is so, that all affections have some effect on the body, we may well suppose that the greater those affections are, and the more vigorous their exercise (other circumstances being equal), the greater the effect on the body will be. So it is no wonder that very great and strong exercises of the affections should have great effects on the body. And therefore, seeing there are very great affections, both common and spiritual, it is no wonder that great effects on the body should arise from both these kinds of affections. And consequently these effects are no signs that the affections they arise from are of one kind or the other.

Great effects on the body are certainly no sure evidence that affections are spiritual. For we see that such effects often arise from great affections about temporal things, when religion has no part in them at all. And if great affections about worldly things, which are purely natural, may have these effects, I do not know by what rule we should decide that high affections about religious things, which arise in the same way from nature, cannot have the same effect.

Nor, on the other hand, do I know of any rule anyone has to decide that gracious and holy affections, when raised as high as any natural affections, and having equally strong and vigorous exercises, cannot have a great effect on the body. No such rule can be drawn from reason. I know of no reason why being affected with a view of God’s glory should not cause the body to faint, as well as being affected with a view of Solomon’s glory. And no such rule has yet been produced from the Scripture. None has ever been found in all the recent controversies there have been about things of this nature. There is a great power in spiritual affections. We read of the power that works in Christians,2 and of the Spirit of God being in them as the Spirit of power,3 and of the effectual working of his power in them,4 indeed, of the working of God’s mighty power in them.5 But man’s nature is weak. Flesh and blood are represented in Scripture as exceedingly weak, and particularly in their unfitness for great spiritual and heavenly operations and exercises (Matt 26:41; 1 Cor 15:43, 50). The text we are considering speaks of joy unspeakable and full of glory. And who that considers what man’s nature is, and what the nature of the affections is, can reasonably doubt that such unutterable and glorious joys may be too great and mighty for weak dust and ashes, so as to overpower it considerably? It is evident from the Scripture that true divine manifestations, or ideas of God’s glory, when given in a great degree, have a tendency, by affecting the mind, to overpower the body. For the Scripture often teaches us that if these ideas or views were given to the degree in which they are given in heaven, the weak frame of the body could not survive under them, and that no man can see God in that way and live. The knowledge the saints have of God’s beauty and glory in this world, and the holy affections that arise from it, are of the same nature and kind as what the saints experience in heaven, differing only in degree and circumstances. What God gives them here is a foretaste of heavenly happiness and an earnest of their future inheritance. And who will limit God in his giving of this earnest, or say that he may give so much of the inheritance, such a part of the future reward, as an earnest of the whole, and no more? And seeing God has taught us in his word that the whole reward is such that it would at once destroy the body, is it not too bold a thing for us to set bounds to the sovereign God in this way? Is it not too bold to say that in giving the earnest of this reward in this world, he will never give so much of it as to lessen the strength of the body in the least, when God has nowhere limited himself like this?

The psalmist, speaking of vehement religious affections he had, speaks of an effect in his flesh or body besides what was in his soul, expressly distinguishing the one from the other, again and again: “My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD; my heart and my flesh cry out for the living God” (Ps 84:2). Here is a plain distinction between the heart and the flesh, as each being affected. So in Ps 63:1: “My soul thirsts for You. My flesh yearns for You in a dry and weary land without water.” Here also is an evident, intended distinction between the soul and the flesh.

The prophet Habakkuk speaks of his body being overpowered by a sense of the majesty of God: “I heard, and my body trembled; my lips quivered at the sound. Decay entered my bones; I trembled where I stood” (Hab 3:16). So the psalmist speaks expressly of his flesh trembling: “My flesh trembles in awe of You” (Ps 119:120).

That such ideas of God’s glory as are sometimes given in this world have a tendency to overpower the body is evident, because the Scripture tells us that this has at times actually been the effect of the external manifestations God has made of himself to some of the saints. These were made for this very end, namely, to give them an idea of God’s majesty and glory. We have such instances in the prophet Daniel and the apostle John. Daniel, giving an account of an external representation of the glory of Christ, says, “No strength remained in me; my face grew deathly pale, and I was powerless” (Dan 10:8). And the apostle John, giving an account of a similar manifestation made to him, says, “When I saw Him, I fell at His feet like a dead man” (Rev 1:17). It is useless to say here that what these saints saw were only external manifestations or symbols of the glory of Christ. It is true that they were outward representations of Christ’s glory, which they saw with their bodily eyes. Yet the end and use of these external symbols or representations was to give these prophets an idea of the thing represented. And that was the true divine glory and majesty of Christ, which is his spiritual glory. They were used only as signs of this spiritual glory, and this is undoubtedly how the prophets received them, made use of them, and were affected by them. According to the end for which God intended these outward signs, they received by them a great and lively perception of the real glory and majesty of God’s nature, of which they were signs. And so they were greatly affected, their souls swallowed up and their bodies overpowered. And I think those are very bold and daring who will say that God cannot, or will not, give the same clear and affecting ideas and perceptions of the same real glory and majesty of his nature to any of his saints without the intervention of any such external shadows of it.

Before I leave this head, I would further observe that the Scripture plainly often uses bodily effects to express the strength of holy and spiritual affections, such as trembling,6 groaning,7 being sick,8 crying out,9 panting,10 and fainting.11 Now suppose these are only figurative expressions, to represent the degree of affection. Yet I hope all will allow that they are fit and suitable figures to represent the high degree of those spiritual affections which the Spirit of God uses them to represent. And I do not see how they would be, if those spiritual affections, however high their degree, have no tendency to any such things, but if, on the contrary, these things are the proper effects and sad tokens of false affections and of the delusion of the devil. I cannot think God would commonly use things which are very foreign to spiritual affections, and are strong marks of the hand of Satan, and smell strongly of the bottomless pit, as beautiful figures to represent the high degree of holy and heavenly affections.

Fluent Talk of Religion

Part II · No Certain Sign III

III. It is no sign that affections are truly gracious affections, or that they are not, that they cause those who have them to be fluent, fervent and abundant in talking of the things of religion.

There are many persons who, if they see this in others, are greatly prejudiced against them. To them, others being so full of talk is enough ground to condemn them as Pharisees and showy hypocrites. On the other hand, there are many who, if they see this effect in anyone, are very ignorantly and rashly eager to decide at once that they are the true children of God and are under the saving influences of his Spirit, and they speak of it as a great evidence of a new creature. They say, “Such a one’s mouth is opened now. He used to be slow to speak, but now he is full and free. He is free now to open his heart and tell his experiences and declare the praises of God. It comes from him as freely as water from a fountain,” and the like. And they are especially captivated into a confident and undoubting persuasion that such persons have been savingly worked on if they are not only free and abundant in their talk, but very full of feeling and earnest in it.

But this is the fruit of only a little judgment and of a scanty and short experience, as events abundantly show. It is a mistake persons often fall into through trusting their own wisdom and discernment, and making their own notions their rule instead of the holy Scripture. The Scripture is full of rules, both for how we should judge our own state and for how we should be guided in our opinion of others. Yet nowhere do we have any rule by which to judge ourselves or others to be in a good state from any such effect. For this is only the religion of the mouth and the tongue. It is what the Scripture represents by the leaves of a tree, which, though the tree ought not to be without them, are nowhere given as an evidence of the goodness of the tree.

That persons are inclined to talk abundantly of the things of religion may be from a good cause, and it may be from a bad one. It may be because their hearts are very full of holy affections, for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. And it may be because their hearts are very full of religious affection which is not holy, for still out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. It is very much the nature of the affections, of whatever kind they are and whatever objects they are exercised about, if they are strong, to incline persons to speak a great deal of what they are affected with, and not only to speak much, but to speak very earnestly and fervently. And therefore persons talking abundantly and very fervently about the things of religion can be evidence of no more than this, that they are very much affected with the things of religion. But this may be so, as has already been shown, and there may be no grace. Whatever men are greatly affected with, they will be earnestly engaged about while the high affection lasts, and they will be likely to show that earnestness in their talk and behavior. So did the greater part of the Jews in all Judea and Galilee for a while, about John the Baptist’s preaching and baptism, when they were willing for a season to rejoice in his light. A mighty stir was made all over the land, and among all sorts of persons, about this great prophet and his ministry. And in the same way the multitude often showed great earnestness and a mighty engagement of spirit in everything that was external about Christ and his preaching and miracles. They were astonished at his teaching, at once receiving the word with joy; they followed him, sometimes night and day, leaving food, drink and sleep to hear him. Once they followed him into the wilderness, going three days without food, to hear him. At times they praised him to the skies, saying, “Never has anyone spoken like this man!” and they were fervent and earnest in what they said. But what did these things come to in the greater part of them?

A person may be too full of talk about his own experiences, commonly turning to it everywhere and in all company. And when it is so, it is a dark sign rather than a good one. A tree that is too full of leaves seldom bears much fruit. And a cloud, though to all appearance very heavy and full of water, seldom gives much rain to the dry and thirsty earth if it brings too much wind with it. The Holy Spirit is pleased several times to use this very thing to represent a great show of religion with the mouth without fruit in the life to answer it: “Like clouds and wind without rain is the man who boasts of gifts never given” (Prov 25:14). And the apostle Jude, speaking of some in the early church who had crept in unnoticed among the saints and, having a great show of religion, were for a while not suspected, says, “They are clouds without water, carried along by the wind” (Jude 4, 12). And the apostle Peter, speaking of the same people, says, “These men are clouds without water, driven by a storm” (2 Pet 2:17).

False affections, if they are equally strong, are much more eager to declare themselves than true ones. For it is the nature of false religion to seek show and notice, as it was with the Pharisees.12

12. That famous experiential divine Mr. Shepard says, “A Pharisee’s trumpet will be heard to the end of the town, when simplicity walks through the town unseen. That is why a man will at times commend himself in a hidden way (and myself always comes in), and tell you a long story of his conversion; and it is a hundred to one that some lie or other slips out with it. Why, the secret meaning is, Please admire me. That is why they complain of their shortcomings and weaknesses: please think what a broken-hearted Christian I am.” Parab. Of the ten virgins, Part I. Page 179, 180. And holy Mr. Flavel says this: “O reader, if your heart were right with God, and you did not cheat yourself with an empty profession of faith, you would have frequent business with God which you would be unwilling for your dearest friend, or the wife of your bosom, to know about. Non est religio, ubi omnia patent. Religion does not lie open to all, to the eyes of men. Duties that are seen maintain our reputation, but secret duties maintain our life. It was the saying of a heathen about his secret friendship with his friend, What need is there for the world to know about it? You and I are theater enough for each other. There are enclosed pleasures in religion which none but renewed, spiritual souls understand by feeling them.” Flavel’s touch-stone of sincerity, ch. 2. Sect. 2.

Affections Not Made by Ourselves

Part II · No Certain Sign IV

IV. It is no sign that affections are gracious, or that they are otherwise, that persons did not make them themselves, or stir them up by their own contriving and their own strength.

There are many in these days who condemn all affections which are stirred up in a way the persons who have them cannot account for, affections that do not seem to be the fruit of any of their own efforts, or the natural result of the faculties and principles of human nature in such circumstances and under such means, but seem to come from the influence of some outside and supernatural power on their minds. How greatly the doctrine of the inward experience, or felt perception, of the immediate power and working of the Spirit of God has been reproached and ridiculed by many lately! They say the manner of the Spirit of God is to work together with the use of means and with our own efforts in a silent, secret and undiscernible way, so that there is no distinguishing by sense between the influences of the Spirit of God and the natural workings of the faculties of our own minds.

And it is true that for anyone to expect to receive the saving influences of the Spirit of God while he neglects a diligent use of the appointed means of grace is unreasonable presumption. And to expect that the Spirit of God will work savingly on their minds without the Spirit making use of means, as serving toward the effect, is fanatical. It is also undoubtedly true that the Spirit of God is very varied in the manner and circumstances of his working, and that at times he works in a more secret and gradual way, and from smaller beginnings, than at others.

But suppose there is indeed a power, entirely different from and beyond our power, or the power of all means and instruments, and above the power of nature, which is required to produce saving grace in the heart, as the country generally professes. Then it is certainly not unreasonable in any way to suppose that this effect should very often be produced in such a way as to make it very plain, apparent and perceptible that it is so. If grace is indeed owing to the powerful and efficacious working of an outside agent, or a divine efficient cause outside ourselves, why is it unreasonable to suppose that it should seem so to those who experience it? Is it a strange thing that it should seem to be as it is? Grace in the heart is in fact not produced by our strength, nor is it the effect of the natural power of our own faculties or of any means or instruments, but it is properly the workmanship and production of the Spirit of the Almighty. When that is so, is it a strange and unaccountable thing that it should seem so to those who experience it, in agreement with the truth and not directly contrary to the truth? And if persons tell of effects they are conscious of in their own minds which seem to them to come not from the natural power or working of their minds but from the supernatural power of some other agent, should that at once be looked on as a sure evidence that they are under a delusion, because things seem to them to be as they are? For this is the objection that is made. It is looked on as clear evidence that the perceptions and affections many persons have are not really from such a cause, because they seem to them to be from that cause. They declare that what they are conscious of plainly seems to them to be not from themselves but from the mighty power of the Spirit of God. And others condemn them for this, and decide that what they experience is not from the Spirit of God but from themselves, or from the devil. This is how unreasonably multitudes are treated by their neighbors at this day.

The Scripture abundantly teaches that grace in the soul is so much the effect of God’s power that it is fitly compared to those effects which are furthest from being owing to any strength in the one who receives them: such as generation, or being begotten; and resurrection, or being raised from the dead; and creation, or being brought out of nothing into being. It teaches that it is an effect in which the mighty power of God is greatly glorified and the exceeding greatness of his power is shown.13 If it is indeed so, then what account can be given of the Almighty, in so great a work of his power, hiding his power so carefully that those who experience it should be able to discern nothing of it? Or what reason or revelation does anyone have to decide that he does so? If we may judge by the Scripture, this does not agree with God’s manner in his works and dispensations. On the contrary, it is God’s manner, in the great works of power and mercy which he works for his people, to order things so as to make his hand visible, his power conspicuous, and men’s dependence on him most evident. He does it so that no flesh should glory in his presence,14 so that God alone might be exalted,15 so that the excellence of the power might be from God and not from man,16 so that Christ’s power might be shown in our weakness,17 and so that no one might say, “My own hand has saved me.”18 So it was in most of the temporal salvations God worked for Israel of old, which were types of the salvation of God’s people from their spiritual enemies. So it was in the redemption of Israel from their bondage in Egypt. He redeemed them with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, and so that his power might be the more conspicuous, he allowed Israel first to be brought into the most helpless and forlorn circumstances. So it was in the great deliverance by Gideon. God would have his army reduced to a handful, and they with no other weapons than trumpets and torches and clay jars. So it was in the deliverance of Israel from Goliath by a youth with a sling and a stone. So it was in that great work of God, his calling of the Gentiles and converting of the heathen world after Christ’s ascension. This came after the world by its wisdom did not know God, and all the efforts of philosophers to reform the world had proved useless for many ages, and it had become abundantly evident by everything that the world was utterly helpless by anything but the mighty power of God. And so it was in most of the conversions of particular persons of which we have an account in the history of the New Testament. They were not worked on in the silent, secret, gradual and imperceptible way that is now insisted on, but with those plain evidences of a supernatural power, wonderfully and suddenly causing a great change, which in these days are looked on as certain signs of delusion and fanaticism.

The apostle in Ephesians 1:18–19 speaks of God’s enlightening the minds of Christians, and so bringing them to believe in Christ, to this end, that they might know the exceeding greatness of his power toward those who believe. The words are, “The eyes of your+ understanding being enlightened, so that you+ may know the hope of His calling, the riches of His glorious inheritance in the saints, and the surpassing greatness of His power to us who believe. These are in accordance with the working of His mighty strength,” and so on. Now when the apostle speaks of their being the subjects of his power in this way, in their enlightening and effectual calling, to the end that they might know what his mighty power was toward those who believe, he can mean nothing else than that they might know it by experience. But if the saints know this power by experience, then they feel it and discern it and are conscious of it, as something perceptibly distinguishable from the natural workings of their own minds. And this does not agree with the notion of God working so secretly and undiscernibly that it cannot be known that they are under the influence of any outside power at all, except as they may argue it from the assertions of Scripture, which is a different thing from knowing it by experience.

So it is very unreasonable and unscriptural to decide that affections are not from the gracious working of God’s Spirit because they perceptibly do not come from the persons themselves who have them.

On the other hand, it is no evidence that affections are gracious that they are not purposely produced by those who have them, or that they arise in their minds in a way they cannot account for.

There are some who make this an argument in their own favor. When speaking of what they have experienced, they say, “I am sure I did not make it myself. It was the fruit of no contriving or effort of mine. It came when I was thinking nothing of it. If I could have the world for it, I cannot make it again when I please.” And from this they decide that what they have experienced must be from the mighty influence of the Spirit of God and is of a saving nature. But they do so very ignorantly and without grounds. What they have experienced may indeed not be from themselves directly, but may be from the working of an invisible agent, some spirit besides their own. But it does not follow from this that it was from the Spirit of God. There are other spirits besides the Holy Spirit who have influence on the minds of men. We are told not to believe every spirit, but to test the spirits to see whether they are from God. There are many false spirits, exceedingly busy with men, who often disguise themselves as angels of light and, in many wonderful ways, with great subtlety and power, imitate the workings of the Spirit of God. And there are many of Satan’s workings which are very distinguishable from the voluntary exercises of men’s own minds. They are so in the dreadful and horrid suggestions and blasphemous thoughts he thrusts in, with which he pursues many persons, and in the vain and fruitless frights and terrors of which he is the author. And the power of Satan may be as immediate and as evident in false comforts and joys as in terrors and horrid suggestions, and in fact it often is. It is not in men’s power to put themselves into such raptures as the Anabaptists in Germany, and many other raving fanatics like them, have experienced.

And besides, it must be considered that persons may have impressions on their minds which may not be of their own producing, nor from an evil spirit, but from the Spirit of God, and yet not be from any saving influence of the Spirit of God, but only a common one. And those who have such impressions may be among those we read of in Heb 6:4–5, “those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have shared in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the coming age,” and yet may be wholly unacquainted with those better things that accompany salvation spoken of in verse 9.

And where neither a good nor an evil spirit has any immediate hand, persons may have strange notions and imaginations, and strong affections accompanying them, arising in a way they cannot account for, which they do not produce voluntarily. This is especially so with those of a weak and nervous constitution of body, whose brain is weak and easily receives impressions. We see that such persons are liable to such impressions about temporal things, and there is equal reason why they should be about spiritual things. As a person who is asleep has dreams of which he is not the voluntary author, so such persons may in the same way have involuntary impressions when they are awake.

Texts of Scripture Brought to Mind

Part II · No Certain Sign V

V. It is no sign that religious affections are truly holy and spiritual, or that they are not, that they come with texts of Scripture remarkably brought to the mind.

It is no sign that affections are not gracious that they are occasioned by Scriptures coming to mind in this way, provided it is the Scripture itself, or the truth which the Scripture so brought contains and teaches, that is the foundation of the affection, and not merely or mainly the sudden and unusual manner of its coming to the mind.

But on the other hand, neither is it any sign that affections are gracious that they arise on the occasion of Scriptures brought suddenly and wonderfully to the mind, whether those affections are fear or hope, joy or sorrow, or any other. Some seem to look on this as good evidence that their affections are saving, especially if the affections stirred up are hope or joy, or any others that are pleasing and delightful. They will mention it as evidence that all is right that their experience came with the word. They will say, “Such and such sweet promises were brought to my mind. They came suddenly, as if they were spoken to me. I had no hand in bringing such a text to my own mind. I was not thinking of anything leading to it. It came all at once, so that I was surprised. I had not thought of it for a long time before. I did not know at first that it was Scripture. I did not remember ever having read it.” And perhaps they will add, “One Scripture came flowing in after another, and so texts from all over the Bible, the sweetest and most pleasant, and the most fitting and suitable that could be devised. They filled me as full as I could hold. I could only stand and wonder. The tears flowed. I was full of joy and could not doubt any longer.” And so they think they have undoubted evidence that their affections must be from God and of the right kind, and that their state is good, but they have no grounds of any kind for it. Where did they get any such rule, that if any affections or experiences arise with promises and comforting texts of Scripture brought to mind in a way they cannot account for, without their calling them to mind, or if a great number of sweet texts follow one another in a chain, this is certain evidence that their experiences are saving? Where is any such rule to be found in the Bible, the great and only sure guide in things of this nature?

What deceives many of the less understanding and less thoughtful sort of people in this matter seems to be this. The Scripture is the word of God, and has nothing wrong in it, but is pure and perfect, and therefore those experiences which come from the Scripture must be right. But then it should be considered that affections may arise on the occasion of the Scripture and not properly come from the Scripture, as the genuine fruit of the Scripture and by a right use of it, but from an abuse of it. All that can be argued from the purity and perfection of the word of God, with respect to experiences, is this: those experiences which are agreeable to the word of God are right and cannot be otherwise. It does not follow that those affections must be right which arise on the occasion of the word of God coming to the mind.

What evidence is there that the devil cannot bring texts of Scripture to the mind and misapply them to deceive persons? There seems to be nothing in this which exceeds the power of Satan. Bringing sounds or letters to persons’ minds is not a work of such mighty power that we have any reason to suppose nothing short of omnipotence can be enough for it. If Satan has power to bring any words or sounds at all to persons’ minds, he may have power to bring words contained in the Bible. No higher sort of power is required in men to make the sounds that express the words of a text of Scripture than to make the sounds that express the words of an idle story or song. And so the same power in Satan which is enough to renew one of those kinds of sounds in the mind is enough to renew the other. The difference in meaning, which depends wholly on custom, does not alter the case as to the ability to make or revive the sounds or letters. Or will anyone suppose that texts of Scripture are such sacred things that the devil would not dare to abuse them or touch them? In this also they are mistaken. He who was bold enough to lay hold of Christ himself and carry him here and there, into the wilderness, onto a high mountain, and to a pinnacle of the temple, is not afraid to touch the Scripture and abuse it for his own purposes. He showed this at the very time he was so bold with Christ, for he then brought one Scripture and another to deceive and tempt him. And if Satan presumed, and was permitted, to put Christ himself in mind of texts of Scripture to tempt him, what reason do we have to decide that he does not dare, or will not be permitted, to put wicked men in mind of texts of Scripture to tempt and deceive them? And if Satan may abuse one text of Scripture in this way, he may abuse another. Its being a very excellent place of Scripture, a comforting and precious promise, does not alter the case as to his boldness or his ability. And if he can bring one comforting text to the mind, he may bring a thousand. He may choose out such Scriptures as most serve his purpose. And he may heap up promises of Scripture which, according to the perverse application he makes of them, tend wonderfully to remove the rising doubts and to confirm the false joy and confidence of a poor deluded sinner.

We know that the devil’s instruments, corrupt and heretical teachers, can and do distort the Scripture to their own and others’ damnation (2 Pet 3:16). We see they have the free use of Scripture, every part of it. There is no text so precious and sacred that they are not permitted to abuse it to the eternal ruin of multitudes of souls. And there are no weapons they use with which they do more damage. And there is no reason of any kind to decide that the devil is not permitted to use the Scripture in this way, as well as his instruments. For when the latter do it, they do it as his instruments and servants, and by his prompting and influence. And no doubt he does himself what he prompts others to do. The devil’s servants only follow their master and do the same work he does himself.

And as the devil can abuse the Scripture to deceive and destroy men, so may men’s own folly and corruptions as well. The sin that is in men acts like its father. Men’s own hearts are deceitful like the devil and use the same means to deceive.

So it is evident that persons may have high affections of hope and joy arising on the occasion of texts of Scripture, indeed precious promises of Scripture, coming suddenly and remarkably to their minds as though they were spoken to them, indeed a great multitude of such texts following one another in a wonderful way. And yet all this may be no argument that these affections are divine, or that they are anything other than the effects of Satan’s delusions.

And I would further observe that persons may have raised and joyful affections which may come with the word of God, and not only with it but from it, and those affections may not be from Satan, nor properly from the corruptions of their own hearts, but from some influence of the Spirit of God with the word, and yet have nothing of the nature of true and saving religion in them. So the hearers on stony ground had great joy from the word, a joy which is represented as arising from the word as growth from a seed. And their affections had in their appearance a very great and exact resemblance to those represented by the growth on the good ground, the difference not appearing until it was shown by what followed, in a time of trial. And yet there was no saving religion in these affections.19

19. Mr. Stoddard, in his Guide to Christ, speaks of it as a common thing for persons, while in a natural condition and before they have ever truly accepted Christ, to have promises of Scripture come to them with a great deal of refreshing, which they take as tokens of God’s love, and hope that God has accepted them, and so they are confident of their good state. Page 8, 9. Edition of 1735.

An Appearance of Love

Part II · No Certain Sign VI

VI. It is no evidence that religious affections are saving, or that they are otherwise, that there is an appearance of love in them.

There are no professing Christians who claim that this is an argument against the truth and saving nature of religious affections. But on the other hand, there are some who suppose it is good evidence that affections are from the sanctifying and saving influences of the Holy Spirit. Their argument is that Satan cannot love, this affection being directly contrary to the devil, whose very nature is enmity and malice. And it is true that nothing is more excellent, heavenly and divine than a spirit of true Christian love to God and men. It is more excellent than knowledge, or prophecy, or miracles, or speaking in the tongues of men and of angels. It is the chief of the graces of God’s Spirit, and the life, essence and sum of all true religion. It is that by which we are most conformed to heaven, and most contrary to hell and the devil. But even so, it is bad reasoning to argue from this that there are no counterfeits of it. It may be observed that the more excellent anything is, the more counterfeits of it there will be. So there are many more counterfeits of silver and gold than of iron and copper. There are many false diamonds and rubies, but who sets out to counterfeit common stones? The more excellent things are, the more difficult it is to make anything that will be like them in their essential nature and inward power. Yet the more numerous the counterfeits will be, and the more art and subtlety will be exercised and displayed in an exact imitation of the outward appearance. So there is the greatest danger of being cheated in buying the medicines that are most excellent and powerful, though it is most difficult to imitate them with anything of the same value and power, and their counterfeits are good for nothing when we have them. So it is with Christian virtues and graces. The subtlety of Satan and men’s deceitful hearts are usually exercised chiefly in counterfeiting those that are in the highest repute. So there are perhaps no graces that have more counterfeits than love and humility, these being the virtues in which the beauty of a true Christian especially appears.

But as to love, it is plain from the Scripture that persons may have a kind of religious love and yet have no saving grace. Christ speaks of many professing Christians who have such love, whose love will not continue, and so they will fall short of salvation: “Because of the multiplication of wickedness, the love of many will grow cold. But the one who endures to the end will be saved” (Matt 24:12–13). These last words plainly show that those spoken of before, whose love would not endure to the end but would grow cold, would not be saved.

Persons may seem to have love to God and Christ, indeed to have very strong and violent affections of this kind, and yet have no grace. For this was evidently the case with many Jews without grace, such as those who praised Jesus so highly, following him day and night without food, drink or sleep, such as the one who said, “I will follow You wherever You go,” and those who cried, “Hosanna to the Son of David!”20

The apostle seems to suggest that there were many in his day who had a counterfeit love to Christ, in Ephesians 6:24: “Grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity.” The last word in the original means in incorruption. This shows that the apostle had a sense that there were many who had a kind of love to Christ whose love was not pure and spiritual.

So also Christian love to the people of God may be counterfeited. It is evident from the Scripture that there may be strong affections of this kind without saving grace, as there were in the Galatians toward the apostle Paul, when they were ready to tear out their eyes and give them to him. And yet the apostle expresses his fear that their affections had come to nothing, and that he had spent his labor on them in vain (Gal 4:11, 15).

20. In agreement with this Mr. Stoddard observes, in his Guide to Christ, that some sinners have pangs of affection, and give an account that they find a spirit of love to God, and that they aim at the glory of God, having that which closely resembles saving grace, and that sometimes their common affections are stronger than saving ones. And he supposes that at times natural men may have such violent pangs of false affection to God that they may think themselves willing to be damned. Page 21, and 65.

Affections of Many Kinds

Part II · No Certain Sign VII

VII. Persons having religious affections of many kinds, accompanying one another, is not enough to determine whether they have any gracious affections or not.

False religion is usually maimed and misshapen, and does not have the wholeness and symmetry of parts that is to be seen in true religion. Yet there may be a great variety of false affections together which may resemble gracious affections.

It is evident that there are counterfeits of all kinds of gracious affections. There are counterfeits of love to God and love to the brethren, as has just been observed. So there are of godly sorrow for sin, as in Pharaoh, Saul and Ahab, and the children of Israel in the wilderness (Exod 9:27; 1 Sam 24:16–17; 26:21; 1 Kgs 21:27; Num 14:39–40). And there are of the fear of God, as in the Samaritans, who feared the LORD and served their own gods at the same time (2 Kgs 17:32–33), and in those enemies of God we read of in Psalm 66:3, who through the greatness of God’s power submit themselves to him, or, as it is in the Hebrew, lie to him, that is, give him a counterfeit reverence and submission. So there are of a gracious gratitude, as in the children of Israel who sang God’s praise at the Red Sea (Ps 106:12), and in Naaman the Syrian after his miraculous cure of his leprosy (2 Kgs 5:15 and following).

So there are of spiritual joy, as in the hearers on stony ground (Matt 13:20), and particularly in many of John the Baptist’s hearers (John 5:35). So there are of zeal, as in Jehu (2 Kgs 10:16), and in Paul before his conversion (Gal 1:14; Phil 3:6), and in the unbelieving Jews (Acts 22:3; Rom 10:2). So persons without grace may have earnest religious desires, which may be like Balaam’s desires. He expressed them under an extraordinary view he had of the happy state of God’s people, as distinguished from all the rest of the world (Num 23:9–10). They may also have a strong hope of eternal life, as the Pharisees had.

And as men in a state of nature are capable of a likeness of all kinds of religious affections, so nothing prevents their having many of them together. And what appears in fact abundantly proves that it is indeed very often so. It seems commonly to be the case that when false affections are raised high, many false affections accompany each other. The multitude that accompanied Christ into Jerusalem after that great miracle of raising Lazarus seem to have been moved with many religious affections at once, and all in a high degree. They seem to have been filled with wonder. There was a show of a high affection of love, and also of a great degree of reverence, in their laying their garments on the ground for Christ to tread on. There was a show of great gratitude to him for the great and good works he had done, as they praised him with loud voices for his salvation. There was a show of earnest desires for the coming of God’s kingdom, which they supposed Jesus was now about to set up, and they showed great hopes and raised expectations of it, expecting it to appear immediately. So they were filled with joy, by which they were so animated in their acclamations as to make the whole city ring with the noise of them. And they appeared great in their zeal and eagerness to accompany Jesus and help him set up his kingdom without further delay, now at the time of the great feast of the Passover. And it is easy, from nature and the nature of the affections, to account for why one affection, when raised very high, should stir up others, especially if the affection raised high is counterfeit love, as it was in the multitude who cried Hosanna. This will naturally draw many other affections after it. For, as was observed before, love is the chief of the affections, and as it were the fountain of them. Let us suppose a person who has been for some time in great turmoil of soul and terror through fear of hell, his heart weakened with distress and dreadful apprehensions, and on the brink of despair. And suppose he is all at once delivered, by being made to believe firmly, through some delusion of Satan, that God has pardoned him, accepts him as the object of his dear love, and promises him eternal life. Suppose this comes through some vision, or strong idea or imagination suddenly stirred up in him, of a person with a beautiful face, smiling on him, with arms open and with blood dropping down, which the person takes to be Christ, without any other enlightening of the understanding to give a view of the spiritual, divine excellence of Christ and his fullness, and of the way of salvation revealed in the gospel. Or perhaps it comes by some voice or words coming as if they were spoken to him, such as, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven,” or, “Do not be afraid … it is your+ Father’s good pleasure to give you+ the kingdom,” which he takes to be spoken to him immediately by God, though there was no previous acceptance of Christ, or the heart’s embrace of him. I say, if we suppose such a case, what various passions would naturally crowd into such a person’s mind, all at once or one after another? It is easy to account, from mere principles of nature, for such a person’s heart being raised to the skies on such an occasion with transports of joy. It is easy to account for his being filled with fervent affection to that imaginary God or Redeemer who he supposes has rescued him in this way from the jaws of such dreadful destruction, the fears of which so overwhelmed his soul, and has received him with such endearment as a special favorite. It is easy to account for his now being filled with wonder and gratitude, and his mouth being opened and full of talk about what he has experienced; and for his thinking and speaking of hardly anything else for a while, seeming to magnify the God who has done so much for him, calling on others to rejoice with him, appearing with a cheerful face and talking with a loud voice. However full of quarreling against the justice of God he was before his deliverance, it is easy to account for its now being easy for him to submit to God, acknowledge his unworthiness, cry out against himself, appear very humble before God, and lie at his feet as tame as a lamb. And it is easy to account for his now confessing his unworthiness and crying out, “Why me? Why me?” (Like Saul, who, when Samuel told him that God had appointed him to be king, answered, “Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin? So why would you say such a thing to me?” This is much in the language of David, the true saint, in 2 Sam 7:18: “Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?”) Nor is it any wonder that he should now delight to be with those who acknowledge and applaud his happy circumstances, and should love all such as esteem and admire him and what he has experienced. Nor is it any wonder that he should have violent zeal against all such as would make nothing of such things, and be inclined to separate openly, and as it were to proclaim war on all who are not of his party. Nor is it any wonder that he should now glory in his sufferings, and be very ready to condemn and censure all who seem to doubt these things or raise any difficulty about them; and that while the warmth of his affections lasts, he should be mightily eager to take pains and deny himself to promote the interest of the party which he imagines favors such things, and should seem earnestly desirous to increase their number, as the Pharisees traveled over sea and land to make one proselyte21. And so I might go on and mention many other things that will naturally arise in such circumstances. A man must have considered human nature only slightly if he thinks such things as these cannot arise in this way without any supernatural intervention of divine power.

As all Christian affections flow from true divine love, so in the same way other false affections naturally flow from a counterfeit love. In both cases love is the fountain, and the other affections are the streams. The various faculties, principles and affections of human nature are like many channels from one fountain. If there is sweet water in the fountain, sweet water will flow out from it into those various channels. But if the water in the fountain is poisonous, then poisonous streams will also flow out into all those channels. So the channels and streams will be alike, corresponding to one another, but the great difference will lie in the nature of the water. Or man’s nature may be compared to a tree with many branches coming from one root. If the sap in the root is good, good sap will also be distributed throughout the branches, and the fruit that is brought forth will be good and wholesome. But if the sap in the root and trunk is poisonous, so it will be in many branches (as in the other case), and the fruit will be deadly. The tree in both cases may be alike; there may be an exact resemblance in shape. But the difference is found only in eating the fruit. It is often like this, in some measure at least, between saints and hypocrites. There is at times a very great likeness between true and false experiences in their appearance, and in what is expressed and related by those who have them. And the difference between them is much like the difference between the dreams of Pharaoh’s chief cupbearer and baker. They seemed to be much alike, so much so that when Joseph interpreted the chief cupbearer’s dream, that he would be delivered from his imprisonment and restored to the king’s favor and his honorable office in the palace, the chief baker’s hopes and expectations were raised, and he told his dream also. But he was woefully disappointed. And though his dream was so much like the happy and hopeful dream of his companion, yet it was quite contrary in its outcome.

21. Associating with godly men does not prove that a man has grace: Ahithophel was David’s companion. Sorrow for the afflictions of the church, and desires for the conversion of souls, do not prove it. These things may be found in carnal men, and so can be no evidences of grace. Stoddard’s nature of saving conversion, p. 82.

Comforts Following Convictions in a Certain Order

Part II · No Certain Sign VIII

VIII. Nothing can be determined with certainty about the nature of the affections from this, that comforts and joys seem to follow awakenings and convictions of conscience in a certain order.

Many persons seem to be prejudiced against affections and experiences that come in the way many divines have much insisted on: first, such awakenings, fears and fearful apprehensions, followed by such humblings under the law in a sense of total sinfulness and helplessness, and then such and such light and comfort. They look on all such schemes, laying down such methods and steps, as devised by men. And particularly if high affections of joy follow great distress and terror, many make that an argument against those affections. But such prejudices and objections have neither reason nor Scripture behind them. Surely it cannot be unreasonable to suppose that before God delivers persons from a state of sin and of exposure to eternal destruction, he should give them some considerable sense of the evil he delivers them from. He does it so that they may be delivered in a way they feel, and understand their own salvation, and know something of what God does for them. Men who are saved are in two exceedingly different states, first a state of condemnation, and then a state of justification and blessedness. And God, in the work of the salvation of mankind, deals with them in a way suited to their intelligent, rational nature. So it seems reasonable, and agreeable to God’s wisdom, that men who are saved should be in these two states in a way they feel. First, they should feel themselves to be in a state of condemnation, and so in a state of woeful calamity and dreadful misery, and afterwards feel themselves to be in a state of deliverance and happiness. They should first have a sense of their absolute, extreme need, and afterwards of Christ’s sufficiency and God’s mercy through him.

And the Scripture shows abundantly that it is God’s manner of dealing with men to lead them into the wilderness before he speaks tenderly to them. It is his manner to order things so that they will be brought into distress, and made to see their own helplessness and their absolute dependence on his power and grace, before he appears to work any great deliverance for them. It is then that God usually has compassion on his professing people, when their strength is gone and no one remains, and when they are brought to see that their false gods cannot help them, and that the rock in which they trusted is vain (Deut 32:36–37). Before God delivered the children of Israel out of Egypt, they were prepared for it by being made to see that they were in trouble, and to cry out to God because of their hard bondage (Exod 2:23; 5:19). And before God worked that great deliverance for them at the Red Sea, they were brought into great distress. The wilderness had shut them in; they could not turn to the right hand or the left; the Red Sea was before them and the great army of Egypt behind. They were brought to see that they could do nothing to help themselves, and that if God did not help them, they would be swallowed up immediately. And then God appeared and turned their cries into songs. So before they were brought to their rest, and to enjoy the milk and honey of Canaan, God led them through the vast and terrifying wilderness, to humble them and teach them what was in their heart, so that in the end he might do them good (Deut 8:2, 16). The woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years was not delivered until she had first spent all her money on earthly physicians, and no one was able to heal her. So she was left helpless, having no more money to spend. And then she came to the great Physician, without money and without price, and was healed by him (Luke 8:43–44). Before Christ would answer the request of the woman of Canaan, he first seemed to refuse her utterly, and humbled her, and brought her to acknowledge herself worthy to be called a dog. And then he showed her mercy and received her as a dear child (Matt 15:22 and following). The apostle Paul, before a remarkable deliverance, was under a burden far beyond his ability to endure, so that he despaired even of life, and had the sentence of death in himself, so that he would not trust in himself but in God, who raises the dead (2 Cor 1:8–10).
