There was first a great storm, and the boat was covered by the waves and just ready to sink, and the disciples were brought to cry to Jesus, “Lord, save us! We are perishing!” And then the winds and the sea were rebuked, and there was a great calm (Matt 8:24–26). The leper, before he is cleansed, must have his mouth stopped by a covering on his upper lip, and was to acknowledge his great misery and utter uncleanness by tearing his clothes and crying, “Unclean, unclean!” (Lev 13:45). And backsliding Israel, before God heals them, are brought to acknowledge that they have sinned and have not obeyed the voice of the LORD, and to see that they lie down in their shame and their disgrace covers them, and that salvation is hoped for in vain from the hills and from the multitude of mountains, and that God alone can save them (Jer 3:23–25). Joseph, who was sold by his brothers and in that was a type of Christ, brings his brothers into great perplexity and distress. He brings them to reflect on their sin and to say, “We are truly guilty,” and at last to give themselves up entirely into his hands as slaves. And then he reveals himself to them as their brother and their savior.

And if we consider the extraordinary manifestations God made of himself to the saints of old, we will find that he commonly manifested himself first in a way that was terrifying, and then by things that were comforting. So it was with Abraham. First great terror and darkness overwhelmed him, and then God revealed himself to him in sweet promises (Gen 15:12–13). So it was with Moses at Mount Sinai. First God appeared to him in all the terrors of his dreadful majesty, so that Moses said, “I am trembling with fear.” And then he made all his goodness pass before him and proclaimed his name, the LORD God, compassionate and gracious, and so on. So it was with Elijah. First there is a stormy wind, and an earthquake, and a devouring fire, and then a still, small, sweet voice (1 Kgs 19). So it was with Daniel. He first saw Christ’s face like lightning, which terrified him and made him faint away. And then he is strengthened and refreshed with comforting words such as these: “Daniel, you are a man who is highly precious” (Dan 10). So it was with the apostle John (Rev 1). And a likeness can be observed between the dispensations and deliverances God works for his people and the manifestations he makes of himself to them, both ordinary and extraordinary.

But there are many things in Scripture which show more directly that this is God’s ordinary manner in working salvation for the souls of men, and in the manifestations God makes of himself and of his mercy in Christ in the ordinary works of his grace on the hearts of sinners. The servant who owed his prince ten thousand talents is first held to his debt. The king pronounces sentence of condemnation on him and commands that he, his wife and his children be sold, and payment be made. In this way he humbles him and brings him to acknowledge that the whole debt is just, and then he forgives him all of it. The prodigal son spends all he has, and is brought to see himself in extreme circumstances, and to humble himself and confess his unworthiness, before he is relieved and feasted by his father (Luke 15). Old, deep-rooted wounds must be probed to the bottom in order to be healed. And the Scripture compares sin, the wound of the soul, to this, and speaks of healing this wound without probing it in this way as vain and deceitful (Jer 8:11). Christ, in the work of his grace on the hearts of men, is compared to rain on the mown grass, grass that has been cut down with a scythe (Ps 72:6). This represents his refreshing, comforting influences on the wounded spirit. Our first parents, after they had sinned, were first terrified with God’s majesty and justice, and had their sin, with all that made it worse, set before them by their judge, before they were relieved by the promise of the seed of the woman. Christians are spoken of as those who have fled for refuge to lay hold of the hope set before them (Heb 6:18). This picture implies great fear and a sense of danger going before. To the same purpose, Christ is called “a shelter from the wind, a refuge from the storm, like streams of water in a dry land, like the shadow of a great rock in an arid land” (Isa 32, at the beginning). And it seems to be the natural meaning of the word gospel, good news, that it is news of deliverance and salvation after great fear and distress. There is every reason to suppose that God deals with particular believers as he dealt with his church. He first made her hear his voice in the law, with terrible thunders and lightnings, and kept her under that schoolmaster to prepare her for Christ. And then he comforted her with the joyful sound of the gospel from Mount Zion. So likewise John the Baptist came to prepare the way for Christ, and to prepare men’s hearts to receive him. He did it by showing them their sins, and by bringing the self-righteous Jews off from their own righteousness. He told them that they were a brood of vipers, and showed them their danger of the coming wrath, telling them that the axe lies ready at the root of the trees, and so on.

And it is indeed God’s manner, as I think the foregoing considerations show beyond doubt, to give men a considerable sense of the greatness and dreadfulness of their sin and misery, and of their extreme wretchedness because of them, before he gives them the comfort of a deliverance from them. If so, surely it is not unreasonable to suppose that persons, often at least, should have great distress and terrible apprehensions of mind while under these views. This is especially so if we consider what these evils are which they see. They are no other than great and manifold sins against the infinite majesty of the great Jehovah, and the suffering of the fierceness of his wrath to all eternity. And it is still more so when we have many plain instances in Scripture of persons who have actually been brought into extreme distress by such convictions before they received saving consolations. There was the multitude at Jerusalem, who were “cut to the heart and asked Peter and the other apostles, ‘Brothers, what shall we do?’” And there was the apostle Paul, who trembled and was astonished before he was comforted. And there was the jailer: “Calling for lights, the jailer rushed in and fell trembling before Paul and Silas … ‘Sirs, what must I do to be saved?’”

From these things it appears very unreasonable in professing Christians to make this an objection against the truth and spiritual nature of the comforting and joyful affections anyone has, that they follow such fearful apprehensions and distresses as have been mentioned.

And on the other hand, it is no evidence that comforts and joys are right because they come after great terrors and overwhelming fears of hell.22 Some persons seem to lay great weight on this. They regard great terrors as evidence of a great work of the law done on the heart, preparing the way well for solid comfort. They do not consider that terror and conviction of conscience are different things. For though convictions of conscience often cause terror, they do not consist in it, and terrors often arise from other causes. Convictions of conscience through the influences of God’s Spirit consist in conviction of the sinfulness of heart and practice, and of the dreadfulness of sin as committed against a God of terrible majesty, infinite holiness and hatred of sin, and strict justice in punishing it. But there are some persons who have frightening apprehensions of hell, a dreadful pit ready to swallow them up, flames just ready to take hold of them, and devils around them ready to seize them, and who at the same time seem to have very little proper enlightening of conscience, really convicting them of their sinfulness of heart and life. The devil, if permitted, can terrify men as well as the Spirit of God can. It is a work natural to him, and he has many ways of doing it in a manner that tends to no good. He may frighten persons exceedingly by impressing on them many external images and ideas: a frowning face, a drawn sword, black clouds of vengeance, words of a fearful doom pronounced,23 hell gaping, devils coming, and the like. He does it not to convince persons of things that are true and revealed in the word of God, but to lead them to vain and groundless conclusions: that their day is past, that they are reprobate, that God cannot be appeased, that he has resolved to cut them off immediately, and so on.

And the terrors some persons have are very much owing to their particular constitution and temperament. Nothing is plainer than that some persons are of such a temperament and frame that their imaginations are more strongly impressed than others’ with everything they are affected with. And the impression on the imagination acts back on the affection and raises it still higher. And so affection and imagination act on one another in turn, until their affection is raised to a vast height, and the person is swallowed up and loses all possession of himself.24

And some speak of a great sight they have of their wickedness who, when the matter comes to be well examined and thoroughly weighed, are really found to have little or no conviction of conscience. They tell of a dreadfully hard heart, and how their heart lies like a stone, when in truth they have none of those things in their minds or thoughts in which the hardness of men’s hearts really consists. They tell of a dreadful load and cesspool of sin, a heap of black and loathsome filth within them, when, if the matter is carefully inquired into, they have nothing in view in which the corruption of nature truly consists. Nor do they have any thought of any particular thing in which their hearts are sinfully defective, or fall short of what ought to be in them, or any exercises of corruption in them at all. And many also think they have great convictions of their actual sins who truly have none. They tell how their sins are set in order before them; they see them standing around them in a row with a dreadful, frightening appearance. And yet in reality not so much as one of the sins they have been guilty of in the course of their lives comes into view in such a way that they are moved by what makes it so heinous.

And if persons have had great terrors which really have been from the awakening and convicting influences of the Spirit of God, it does not follow from this that their terrors must necessarily end in true comfort. The unmortified corruption of the heart may quench the Spirit of God (after he has been striving) by leading men to presumptuous and self-exalting hopes and joys, as well as in other ways. Not every woman who is really in labor brings forth a real child. It may be a monstrous birth, without anything of the form or properties of human nature belonging to it. Pharaoh’s chief baker, after he had lain in the dungeon with Joseph, had a vision that raised his hopes, and he was lifted up out of the dungeon as well as the chief cupbearer, but it was to be hanged.

But suppose comforts and joys not only come after great terrors and awakenings, but there is an appearance of such preparatory convictions and humblings, brought about very distinctly by such steps and in such a method as has often been observed in true converts. Even this is no certain sign that the light and comforts which follow are true and saving. And this is for the following reasons.

(1.) First, as the devil can counterfeit all the saving workings and graces of the Spirit of God, so he can counterfeit the workings that are preparatory to grace. Satan can counterfeit those effects of God’s Spirit which are special, divine and sanctifying, so that there will be a very great resemblance in everything others can observe. If so, he may much more easily imitate those works of God’s Spirit which are common, which men experience while they are still Satan’s own children. These works are in no way so far above him as the others. There are no works of God so high and divine, so far above the powers of nature and out of the reach of the power of all creatures, as those works of his Spirit by which he forms the creature in his own image and makes it a partaker of the divine nature. But if the devil can be the author of such resemblances of these as have been spoken of, without doubt he may be the author of resemblances of those that are of an infinitely lower kind. And it is abundantly evident in fact that there are false humblings and false submissions as well as false comforts.25 How far Saul was brought, though a very wicked man and of a haughty spirit! He, though a great king, was brought in conviction of his sin as it were to fall down, all in tears, weeping aloud, before David, his own subject (and one he had mortally hated for a long time and openly treated as an enemy), and to condemn himself before him, crying out, “You are more righteous than I, for you have rewarded me with good, though I have rewarded you with evil.” And at another time he said, “I have sinned … I have played the fool and have committed a grave error!” (1 Sam 24:16–17; 26:21). And yet Saul seems then to have had very little of the influences of the Spirit of God, for it was after God’s Spirit had departed from him and given him up, and an evil spirit from the LORD troubled him. And if this proud monarch, in a pang of affection, was brought to humble himself so low before a subject he hated, and to whom he still remained an enemy, there may doubtless be appearances of great conviction and humbling before God in men while they still remain his enemies, and even though they remain so to the end. In men who are terrified through fears of hell there is often a great appearance of their being brought off from their own righteousness, when they are not brought off from it in all ways, though they are in many of the ways that are plainer and more visible. They have only exchanged some ways of trusting in their own righteousness for others that are more secret and subtle. Often a great degree of discouragement about many things they used to depend on is taken for being humbled. And that is called a submission to God which is no absolute submission, but has some secret bargain in it that is hard to detect.

(2.) Secondly, if the workings and effects of the Spirit of God in the convictions and comforts of true converts may be counterfeited, then their order may be imitated. If Satan can imitate the things themselves, he may easily put them one after another in such a certain order. If the devil can make A, B and C, it is as easy for him to put A first, B next and C after, as to arrange them in the opposite order. The nature of divine things is harder for the devil to imitate than their order. He cannot imitate divine workings exactly in their nature, though his counterfeits may be very much like them in outward appearance. But he can imitate their order exactly. When counterfeits are made, no divine power is needed to place one of them first and another last. And therefore no order or method of workings and experiences is any certain sign of their divinity. Only that which Satan cannot do, and which cannot possibly be brought about by any power short of divine, is to be trusted as a certain evidence of grace.

(3.) Thirdly, we have no certain rule to determine how far God’s own Spirit may go in workings and convictions which in themselves are not spiritual and saving, while the person who experiences them is never converted, but falls short of salvation at last. There is no necessary connection in the nature of things between anything a natural man may experience while in a state of nature and the saving grace of God’s Spirit. And if there is no connection in the nature of things, then there can be no known and certain connection at all, except by divine revelation. But there is no revealed certain connection between a state of salvation and anything a natural man can experience before he believes in Christ. God has revealed no certain connection between salvation and any qualifications in men except grace and its fruits. And therefore we do not find any convictions under the law, or comforts following those convictions under the law in any certain method or order, ever once mentioned in the Scripture as certain signs of grace or as things found only in the saints, though we do find gracious workings and effects themselves mentioned in this way thousands of times. This should be enough for Christians who are willing to have the word of God, rather than their own philosophy and experiences and conjectures, as their sufficient and sure guide in things of this nature.

(4.) Fourthly, experience strongly confirms that persons seeming to have convictions and comforts following one another in the method and order often observed in true converts is no certain sign of grace.26 I appeal to all the ministers in this land who have had much occasion to deal with souls in the recent extraordinary season. Have there not been many who do not prove well, who have given a fair account of their experiences and have seemed to be converted according to rule, that is, with convictions and affections following one another distinctly and exactly in the order and method that has ordinarily been insisted on as the order of the workings of the Spirit of God in conversion?

And as seeming to have this distinctness of steps and method is no certain sign that a person is converted, so being without it is no evidence that a person is not converted. It might be demonstrated on Scripture principles that a sinner who is not convicted of his sin and misery, of his own emptiness and helplessness, and of his just desert of eternal condemnation, cannot be brought to receive Christ heartily as his Savior, and that therefore such convictions must be implied in some way in what is worked in his soul. Yet nothing proves it necessary that all the things which are implied or presupposed in an act of faith in Christ must be worked plainly and distinctly in the soul, in so many successive and separate works of the Spirit, each one plain and evident, in all who are truly converted. On the contrary, as Mr. Shepard observes, the change made in a saint at the first work is at times like a confused chaos, so that the saints do not know what to make of it. The manner of the Spirit’s proceeding in those who are born of the Spirit is very often exceedingly mysterious and unsearchable. We hear the sound of it, as it were, and its effect can be discerned, but no man can tell where it came from or where it went. And it is often as difficult to know the way of the Spirit in the new birth as in the first birth: “As you do not know the way of the Spirit, or how the bones are formed in a mother’s womb, so you do not know the work of God, the Maker of all things” (Eccl 11:5). The begetting of a principle of grace in the soul seems in Scripture to be compared to the conceiving of Christ in the womb (Gal 4:19). And therefore the church is called Christ’s mother (Song 3:11), and so is every particular believer (Matt 12:49–50). And the conception of Christ in the womb of the blessed virgin by the power of the Holy Spirit seems to be an intended likeness of the conception of Christ in the soul of a believer by the power of the same Holy Spirit. And we do not know the way of the Spirit, or how the bones grow, either in the womb or in the heart that conceives this holy child. The new creature may use the language of Psalm 139:14–15: “I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Marvelous are Your works, and I know this very well. My frame was not hidden from You when I was made in secret.” Of the generation of Christ, both in his person and in the hearts of his people, it may be said, as in Isaiah 53:8, “Who can declare His generation?” We do not know the works of God, the Maker of all things. “It is the glory of God to conceal a matter” (Prov 25:2), and to have his path as it were in the mighty waters, so that his footprints may not be known, and especially in the works of his Spirit on the hearts of men, which are the highest and chief of his works. And therefore it is said in Isa 40:13, “Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD, or informed Him as His counselor?” It is to be feared that some have gone too far toward directing the Spirit of the LORD, marking out his footsteps for him and limiting him to certain steps and methods. Experience plainly shows that in some of the best of Christians God’s Spirit is unsearchable and untraceable in the method of his workings in their conversion. Nor does the Spirit of God proceed discernibly in the steps of a particular established scheme half as often as is imagined. A scheme of what is necessary, according to a rule already received and established by common opinion, has a vast influence (though to many a very imperceptible one) in forming persons’ notions of the steps and method of their own experiences. I know very well what their way is, for I have had much opportunity to observe it. Very often at first their experiences appear like a confused chaos, as Mr. Shepard puts it. But then the parts of their experience are picked out which look most like the particular steps that are insisted on. These are dwelt on in their thoughts, and these are told of from time to time in the account they give. These parts grow brighter and brighter in their view, and others, being neglected, grow more and more obscure. And what they have experienced is imperceptibly stretched to bring it all into exact conformity with the scheme that is established. And it becomes natural for ministers who have to deal with them and guide them, who insist on distinctness and clearness of method, to do the same. But even so, there has been so much to be seen of the workings of the Spirit of God lately that those who have had much to do with souls, and are not blinded with a sevenfold veil of prejudice, must know this: the Spirit is so exceedingly varied in his manner of working that in many cases it is impossible to trace him or find out his way.

What we have chiefly to do with, in our inquiries into our own state or the directions we give to others, is the nature of the effect God has brought about in the soul. As to the steps the Spirit of God took to bring that effect about, we may leave them to him. We are often expressly told in Scripture to test ourselves by the nature of the fruits of the Spirit, but nowhere by the Spirit’s method of producing them.27 Many greatly err in their notions of a clear work of conversion. They call that a clear work where the successive steps of influence and the method of experience are clear. But in truth the clearest work is not where the order of doing is clearest, but where the spiritual and divine nature of the work done, and the effect produced, is clearest.

22. Mr. Shepard speaks of men being cast down as low as hell by sorrow, and lying under chains, quaking in apprehension of terror to come, and then raised up to heaven in joy, not able to live; and yet not torn away from lust; and such are objects of pity now, and are likely to be the objects of terror at the great day. Parable of the ten virgins, P. 1. P. 125.

23. The way of the Spirit’s working, when he does convict men, is by enlightening natural conscience. The Spirit does not work by giving a testimony, but by assisting natural conscience to do its work. Natural conscience is the instrument in the hand of God to accuse, condemn, terrify, and urge to duty. The Spirit of God leads men to consider their danger and makes them affected with it: “The spirit of a man is the lamp of the LORD, searching out his inmost being” (Prov 20:27). Stoddard’s Guide to Christ, p. 44.

24. The famous Mr. Perkins distinguishes between those sorrows that come through convictions of conscience, and melancholy passions rising only from mere imaginations strongly conceived in the brain, which, he says, usually come on suddenly, like lightning into a house. Vol. 1. Of his works, p. 385.

25. The venerable Stoddard observes, “A man may say that now he can justify God however he deals with him, and not be brought off from his own righteousness. And some men do justify God from a partial conviction of the righteousness of their condemnation. Conscience takes notice of their sinfulness and tells them that they may be righteously damned, as Pharaoh justified God (Exod 9:27). And they give some kind of consent to it, but many times it does not continue. They have only a pang on them, which usually dies away after a little time.” Guide to Christ, p. 71.

26. Mr. Stoddard, who had much experience of things of this nature, observed long ago that converted and unconverted men cannot be distinguished with certainty by the account they give of their experience, the same account of experiences being common to both; and that many persons have given a fair account of a work of conversion, and have behaved well in the eyes of the world for several years, but have not proved well at last. Appeal to the learned, p. 75, and 76.

27. Mr. Shepard, speaking of the soul’s embracing Christ, says, “As a child cannot tell how its soul comes into it, nor perhaps when, but afterwards sees and feels that life, so that he would be as bad as a beast who should deny an immortal soul, so it is here.” Parable of the ten virgins, Part II. P. 171. “If the man does not know the time of his conversion, or first embracing Christ, the minister may not draw any absolute conclusion from that, that he is not godly.” Stoddard’s Guide to Christ, p. 83. “Do not think there is no compunction or sense of sin worked in the soul because you cannot discern and feel it so clearly, nor the time of its working and first beginning. I have known many who have come with their complaints that they were never humbled, they never felt it so; yet there it has been, and many times they have seen it by other spectacles and blessed God for it.” Shepard’s sound believer, p. 38. The recent printing in Boston.

Much Time in Religion

Part II · No Certain Sign IX

IX. It is no certain sign that the religious affections persons have are such as have in them the nature of true religion, or that they do not, that they incline persons to spend much time in religion and to be zealously engaged in the external duties of worship.

Lately this has very unreasonably been looked on as an argument against the religious affections some have had, that they spend so much time in reading, praying, singing, hearing sermons, and the like. It is plain from the Scripture that it is the tendency of true grace to make persons delight very much in such religious exercises. True grace had this effect on Anna the prophetess: “She never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying” (Luke 2:37). And grace had this effect on the early Christians in Jerusalem: “With one accord they continued to meet daily in the temple courts and to break bread from house to house, sharing their meals with gladness and sincerity of heart, praising God” (Acts 2:46–47). Grace made Daniel delight in the duty of prayer and solemnly attend to it three times a day. It did the same for David: “Morning, noon, and night, I will pray” (Ps 55:17). Grace makes the saints delight in singing praises to God: “Sing praises to His name, for it is pleasant” (Ps 135:3). And in Ps 147:1: “Hallelujah! How good it is to sing praises to our God, how pleasant and lovely to praise Him!” It also makes them delight to hear the word of God preached. It makes the gospel a joyful sound to them (Ps 89:15), and makes the feet of those who publish this good news beautiful: “How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news,” and so on! (Isa 52:7). It makes them love God’s public worship: “O LORD, I love the house where You dwell, the place where Your glory resides” (Ps 26:8). And in Ps 27:4: “One thing I have asked of the LORD; this is what I desire: to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze on the beauty of the LORD and seek Him in His temple.” And in Ps 84:1–2 and following: “How lovely is Your dwelling place, O LORD of Hosts! My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD. … Even the sparrow has found a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she places her young near Your altars, O LORD of Hosts, my King and my God. How blessed are those who dwell in Your house! They are ever praising You. Blessed are those … whose hearts are set on pilgrimage. As they pass through the Valley of Baca … they go from strength to strength, until each appears before God in Zion.” And verse 10: “Better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere.”

This is the nature of true grace. But on the other hand, persons being inclined to abound and be zealously engaged in the external exercises of religion, and to spend much time in them, is no sure evidence of grace, because such an inclination is found in many who have no grace. So it was with the Israelites of old, whose services were abominable to God. They kept the New Moons and Sabbaths and convocations, and spread out their hands, and multiplied their prayers (Isa 1:12–15). So it was with the Pharisees. They made long prayers and fasted twice a week. False religion may make persons loud and earnest in prayer: “You+ cannot fast as you+ do today to make your+ voice heard on high” (Isa 58:4). Religion which is not spiritual and saving may make men delight in religious duties and ordinances: “For day after day they seek Me and delight to know My ways, like a nation that does what is right and does not forsake the ordinance of their God. They ask Me for righteous ordinances; they delight in drawing near to God” (Isa 58:2). It may make them delight in hearing the word of God preached, as it was with Ezekiel’s hearers: “They come to you as My people come, and sit before you as My people, and hear your words; but they do not put them into practice. Although they express love with their mouths, their hearts pursue dishonest gain. Indeed, you are to them like a singer of love songs with a beautiful voice, who skillfully plays an instrument. They hear your words but do not put them into practice” (Ezek 33:31–32). So it was with Herod. He listened to John the Baptist gladly (Mark 6:20). So it was with others of John’s hearers: for a season they rejoiced in his light (John 5:35). So the hearers on stony ground heard the word with joy.

Experience shows that persons, from false religion, may be inclined to be exceedingly abundant in the external exercises of religion, indeed to give themselves up to them and devote almost their whole time to them. In former times a sort of people called recluses were very numerous in the Roman church. They forsook the world and utterly abandoned the company of mankind, and shut themselves up close in a narrow cell, with a vow never to stir out of it nor to see the face of any human being again (except that they might be visited in case of sickness), to spend all their days in the exercises of devotion and communion with God. There were also great multitudes in ancient times called hermits and anchorites, who left the world to spend all their days in lonely deserts, to give themselves up to religious contemplation and exercises of devotion. Some sorts of them had no dwellings but the caves and hollows of the mountains, and no food but what the earth produced of itself. I once lived for many months next door to a Jew (the houses joined one to another), and I had much opportunity to observe him daily. He seemed to me the most devout person I ever saw in my life. A great part of his time was spent in acts of devotion at his eastern window, which opened next to mine, and he seemed to be most earnestly engaged, not only in the daytime, but at times whole nights.

Praising God with the Mouth

Part II · No Certain Sign X

X. Nothing can be known with certainty about the nature of religious affections from this, that they strongly incline persons to praise and glorify God with their mouths. This is indeed implied in what has just been observed about abounding and spending much time in the external exercises of religion, and it was also hinted at before. But many seem to look on it as a bright evidence of gracious affection when persons appear greatly inclined to praise and magnify God, to have their mouths full of his praises, and to be calling on others with deep feeling to praise and exalt him. So I thought it deserved a more particular consideration.

No Christian will make it an argument against a person that he seems to have such an inclination. Nor can it reasonably be looked on as evidence for a person, if the things already observed and proved are duly considered: namely, that persons without grace may have high affections toward God and Christ; that their affections, being strong, may fill their mouths and incline them to speak much and very earnestly about the things they are affected with; and that there may be counterfeits of all kinds of gracious affection. But it will appear more evidently and directly that this is no certain sign of grace if we consider the instances of it the Scripture gives us in those who had no grace. We often have an account of this in the multitude that was present when Christ preached and worked miracles: “And immediately the man got up, picked up his mat, and walked out in front of them all. As a result, they were all astounded and glorified God, saying, ‘We have never seen anything like this!’” (Mark 2:12). So also in Matt 9:8 and Luke 5:26. Also Matt 15:31: “The crowd was amazed when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled restored, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel.” So we are told that on the occasion of Christ’s raising the son of the widow of Nain, “A sense of awe swept over all of them, and they glorified God. ‘A great prophet has appeared among us!’ they said. ‘God has visited His people!’” (Luke 7:16). So we read of their glorifying Christ, or speaking exceedingly highly of him: “He taught in their synagogues and was glorified by everyone” (Luke 4:15). And how they praised him with loud voices a little before he was crucified, crying, “Hosanna to the Son of David! … Hosanna in the highest! … Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” And after Christ’s ascension, when the apostles had healed the lame man, we are told that all the people were glorifying God for what had happened (Acts 4:21). When the Gentiles in Antioch of Pisidia heard from Paul and Barnabas that God would reject the Jews and take the Gentiles to be his people in their place, they were affected with this goodness of God to the Gentiles, and glorified the word of the Lord. But not all who did so were true believers, only a certain elect number of them, as is suggested in the account we have of it: “When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and all who were appointed for eternal life believed” (Acts 13:48). So of old the children of Israel sang God’s praise at the Red Sea, but soon forgot his works. And it is foretold of false professing Christians, and real enemies of religion, that they would show an eagerness to glorify God: “You+ who tremble at His word, hear the word of the LORD: ‘Your+ brothers who hate you+ and exclude you+ because of My name have said, “Let the LORD be glorified”’” (Isa 66:5).

It is no certain sign that a person is graciously affected if, in the midst of his hopes and comforts, he is greatly affected with God’s unmerited mercy to him who is so unworthy, and seems greatly to exalt and magnify free grace. Those who still remain with unmortified pride and enmity against God may, when they imagine they have received extraordinary kindness from God, cry out about their unworthiness and magnify God’s undeserved goodness to them. And they may do it from no other conviction of their ill desert, and from no higher principle, than Saul had. While he still remained with unsubdued pride and enmity against David, he was brought, though a king, to acknowledge his unworthiness and cry out, “I have played the fool and have committed a grave error!” And with great affection and wonder he magnified and exalted David’s unmerited and unequaled kindness to him (1 Sam 24:16–19; 26:21). And they may do it from no higher principle than the one from which Nebuchadnezzar was affected with God’s dispensation, which he saw and experienced, and praised, exalted and honored the King of heaven. And both he and Darius, in their high affections, called on all nations to praise God (Dan 3:28–30; 4:1–3, 34–35, 37; 6:25–27).

Confidence in a Good Estate

Part II · No Certain Sign XI

XI. It is no sign that affections are right, or that they are wrong, that they make the persons who have them exceedingly confident that what they experience is divine, and that they are in a good state.

Some argue against persons that they are deluded if they claim to be assured of their good state and to be carried beyond all doubt of the favor of God. They suppose that no such thing as a full and absolute assurance of hope is to be expected in the church of God, except in some very extraordinary circumstances, as in the case of martyrdom. This is contrary to the doctrine of Protestants, which their most celebrated writers have maintained against the Papists, and contrary to the plainest evidence of Scripture. It is plain that it was a common thing for the saints of whom we have a history, or particular account, in Scripture to be assured. God revealed and testified his special favor in the plainest and most certain way to Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Daniel and others. Job often speaks of his sincerity and uprightness with the greatest confidence and assurance imaginable, often calling God to witness to it. And he says plainly, “I know that my Redeemer lives … I will see Him for myself … and not as a stranger” (Job 19:25 and following). David, throughout the book of Psalms, almost everywhere speaks of God as his God without any hesitation and in the most confident way, glorying in him as his portion and heritage, his rock and confidence, his shield, salvation and high tower, and the like. Hezekiah appeals to God as one who knew that he had walked before him faithfully and with wholehearted devotion (2 Kgs 20:3). Jesus Christ, in his dying discourse with his eleven disciples in the fourteenth, fifteenth and sixteenth chapters of John (which was as it were Christ’s last will and testament to his disciples and to his whole church), often declares his special and everlasting love to them in the plainest and most definite terms. He promises them a future share with him in his glory in the most absolute way. And he tells them at the same time that he does so to this end, that their joy might be full: “I have told you+ these things so that My joy may be in you+ and your+ joy may be full” (John 15:11). See also the conclusion of his whole discourse, chapter 16:33: “I have told you+ these things so that in Me you+ may have peace. In the world you+ will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!” Christ was not afraid of speaking too plainly and definitely to them. He did not wish to hold them in the least suspense. And he concluded this last discourse of his with a prayer in their presence, in which he speaks with certainty to his Father of those eleven disciples. He speaks of them as having all savingly known him and believed in him, and received and kept his word. He says that they were not of the world, that for their sakes he sanctified himself, and that his will was that they should be with him in his glory. And he tells his Father that he spoke these things in his prayer to this end, that his joy might be fulfilled in them (verse 13). By these things it is evident that it agrees with Christ’s designs, and with the ordering and arrangement Christ has purposely made of things in his church, that sufficient and abundant provision should be made for his saints to have full assurance of their future glory.

The apostle Paul, throughout all his epistles, speaks in an assured strain, always speaking with certainty of his special relation to Christ, his Lord and Master and Redeemer, and of his share in the future reward and his expectation of it. It would be endless to take notice of all the places that might be listed. I will mention only three or four. Gal 2:20: “Christ lives in me. The life I live in the body, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself up for me.” Phil 1:21: “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” 2 Tim 1:12: “I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day.” 2 Tim 4:7–8: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day.”

And the nature of the covenant of grace, and God’s declared ends in the appointment and arrangement of things in that covenant, plainly show that it is God’s design to make ample provision for the saints to have an assured hope of eternal life while living here on earth. For all things in that covenant are so ordered and arranged that everything might be made sure on God’s part. The covenant is ordered and secured in every part. The promises are most full, very often repeated, and set forth in various ways. There are many witnesses and many seals, and God has confirmed his promises with an oath. And God’s declared design in all this is that the heirs of the promises might have an undoubting hope and full joy in an assurance of their future glory: “So when God wanted to make the unchanging nature of His purpose very clear to the heirs of the promise, He guaranteed it with an oath. Thus by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may have strong consolation” (Heb 6:17–18). But all this would be useless for any such purpose as the saints’ strong consolation and hope of obtaining future glory if, in ordinary cases, they could not come to know their share in those sure promises. For God’s promises and oaths, however sure they are, cannot give strong hope and comfort to any particular person any further than he can know that those promises are made to him. And the provision made in Jesus Christ for believers to be made perfect as regards the conscience, as is indicated in Heb 9:9, is made in vain if assurance of freedom from the guilt of sin cannot be attained.

It further appears that assurance is attainable not only in some very extraordinary cases, because all Christians are told to give all diligence to make their calling and election sure, and are told how they may do it (2 Pet 1:5–8). And not knowing whether Christ is in them or not is spoken of as a thing very unbecoming in Christians, and as a sign of something very blameworthy in them: “Do you+ not know for yourselves+ that Jesus Christ is in you+—unless you+ actually fail the test?” (2 Cor 13:5). And it is implied that it is a sign of very blameworthy negligence in Christians if they practice Christianity in such a way as to remain uncertain of the reward, in 1 Cor 9:26: “Therefore I do not run uncertainly.” And to add no more, it is plain that Christians’ knowing their share in the saving benefits of Christianity is a thing ordinarily attainable, because the apostles tell us by what means Christians (and not only apostles and martyrs) used to know this. 1 Cor 2:12: “We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know what God has freely given us.” And 1 John 2:3: “By this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments.” And verse 5: “By this we know that we are in Him.” Chapter 3:14: “We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love our brothers.” Verse 19: “And by this we will know that we belong to the truth, and will assure our hearts in His presence.” Verse 24: “And by this we know that He remains in us: by the Spirit He has given us.” So also chapter 4:13, and chapter 5:2, and verse 19.

Therefore it must be very unreasonable to decide that persons are hypocrites and their affections wrong because they seem to be free of doubt about their own salvation, and the affections they have seem to banish all fears of hell.

On the other hand, it is no sufficient reason to decide that men are saints and their affections gracious because the affections they have are accompanied by an exceeding confidence that their state is good and their affections divine.28. Nothing can be argued with certainty from their confidence, however great and strong it seems to be. We may see a man who boldly calls God his Father, and commonly speaks in prayer in the boldest, most familiar and possessive language: “My Father, my dear Redeemer, my sweet Savior, my beloved,” and the like. It may be a common thing for him to use the most confident expressions before men about the goodness of his state, such as, “I know for certain that God is my Father. I know as surely as there is a God in heaven that he is my God. I know I will go to heaven as well as if I were there. I know that God is now manifesting himself to my soul and is now smiling on me.” And he may seem to have finished forever with any inquiry or examination into his state, as a thing sufficiently known and beyond doubt, and to despise all who so much as suggest that there is some reason to doubt or fear whether all is right. Such things are no signs at all that it is indeed as he is confident it is.29. Such an overbearing, high-handed and violent sort of confidence as this, seen in many, so eager to declare itself with a most glaring show in the sight of men, does not have the face of a true Christian assurance. It savors more of the spirit of the Pharisees. They never doubted that they were saints, and the most eminent of saints. They were bold to go to God and come up near to him, and lift up their eyes and thank him for the great distinction he had made between them and other men. And when Christ suggested that they were blind and without grace, they despised the suggestion: “Some of the Pharisees who were with Him heard this, and they asked Him, ‘Are we blind too?’” (John 9:40). Suppose that with their confidence they had more of the spirit of the tax collector, who, with a sense of his exceeding unworthiness, stood far off and did not dare even to lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast and cried out against himself as a sinner. Then their confidence would look more like the confidence of one who humbly trusts and hopes in Christ and has no confidence in himself.

If we only consider what the hearts of natural men are, what principles rule them, what blindness and deceit, what self-flattery, self-exaltation and self-confidence reign there, we need not wonder at all that their high opinion of themselves and their confidence in their happy circumstances should be as high and strong as mountains and as violent as a storm. This is so once conscience is blinded and convictions killed with false, high affections, and the principles just mentioned are let loose, fed and prompted by false joys and comforts stirred up by some pleasing imaginations impressed by Satan, disguising himself as an angel of light.

Once a hypocrite is established in a false hope in this way, he does not have the things that often occasion the doubting of true saints to make him call his hope into question. First, he does not have that cautious spirit, that great sense of the vast importance of a sure foundation, and that dread of being deceived. The comforts of true saints increase their awakening and caution, and a lively sense of how great a thing it is to appear before an infinitely holy, just and all-knowing judge. But false comforts put an end to these things and dreadfully stupefy the mind. Secondly, the hypocrite does not have the knowledge of his own blindness and the deceitfulness of his own heart, and the low opinion of his own understanding, that the true saint has. Those who are deluded with false manifestations and affections are always highly conceited of their light and understanding. Thirdly, the devil does not assault the hope of the hypocrite as he does the hope of a true saint. The devil is a great enemy to a true Christian hope, not only because it tends greatly to the comfort of the one who has it, but also because it is a thing of a holy, heavenly nature, greatly tending to promote and cherish grace in the heart, and a great incentive to strictness and diligence in the Christian life. But he is no enemy to the hope of a hypocrite, which above all things establishes his hold on the one who has it. A hypocrite may keep his hope without opposition as long as he lives, the devil never disturbing it or attempting to disturb it. But there is perhaps no true Christian whose hope is not assaulted by him. Satan assaulted Christ himself on this point, whether he was the Son of God or not. And the servant is not above his master, nor the disciple above his Lord. It is enough for the disciple who is most privileged in this world to be like his master. Fourthly, the one who has a false hope does not have the sight of his own corruptions that the saint has. A true Christian has ten times as much to do with his heart and its corruptions as a hypocrite. The sins of his heart and practice appear to him in their blackness. They look dreadful, and it often seems a very mysterious thing that any grace can be consistent with such corruption, or should be in such a heart. But a false hope hides corruption and covers it all over, and the hypocrite looks clean and bright in his own eyes.

There are two sorts of hypocrites. One sort are deceived by their outward morality and external religion; many of these are professed Arminians in the doctrine of justification. The other sort are those who are deceived by false manifestations and elevations. These often cry down works and men’s own righteousness and talk much of free grace, but at the same time they make a righteousness of their manifestations and of their humbling, and exalt themselves to heaven with them. Mr. Shepard, in his exposition of the parable of the ten virgins, distinguishes these two kinds of hypocrites by the names of legal and evangelical hypocrites, and often speaks of the latter as the worst. And it is evident that the latter are commonly by far the most confident in their hope, and the hardest to bring off from it. I have hardly known one instance of such a person in my life who has been undeceived. The chief grounds of the confidence of many of them are the very same kind of impulses and supposed revelations (sometimes with texts of Scripture and sometimes without) that so many have lately had about future events. They call these impulses about their good state the witness of the Spirit, entirely misunderstanding the nature of the witness of the Spirit, as I will show later. With those who have had visions and impulses about other things, these have generally revealed such things as they desire and are fond of. And it is no wonder that persons who pay attention to such things have the same sort of visions or impressions about their own eternal salvation, revealing to them that their sins are forgiven, that their names are written in the book of life, that they are in high favor with God, and so on. This is especially so when they earnestly seek, expect and wait for evidence of their election and salvation in this way, as the surest and most glorious evidence of it. Nor is it any wonder that when they have such a supposed revelation of their good state, it raises in them the highest degree of confidence in it. Abundant experience shows that those who are led away by impulses and imagined revelations are extremely confident. They suppose that the great Jehovah has declared these and those things to them, and since they have his immediate testimony, a strong confidence is the highest virtue. So they are bold to say, “I know this or that … I know for certain … I am as sure of it as that I exist,” and the like, and they despise all argument and inquiry in the case. And above all else, it is easy to account for impressions and impulses about something so pleasing, so suited to their self-love and pride, as their being the dear children of God, distinguished in his favor from most in the world, making them strongly confident. This is especially so when, along with their impulses and revelations, they have high affections, which they take to be the most eminent exercises of grace. I have known of several persons who had a foolish desire for something of a temporal nature, through a violent passion that possessed them. They had been earnestly pursuing the thing they desired, and had met with great difficulty and many discouragements in it. But at last they had an impression or supposed revelation that they would obtain what they sought, and they looked on it as a sure promise from the Most High. This made them most ridiculously confident, against every kind of reason to convince them otherwise, and against all events working against them. And nothing prevents persons who are seeking their salvation from being deceived by similar delusive impressions, and being made confident of that in the same way.

The confidence of many of this sort of hypocrites, whom Mr. Shepard calls evangelical hypocrites, is like the confidence of some madmen who think they are kings: they will maintain it against every kind of reason and evidence. And in one sense it is much more immovable than a truly gracious assurance. A true assurance is upheld only by the soul’s being kept in a holy frame, and grace being maintained in lively exercise. If the actings of grace decline greatly in the Christian, and he falls into a lifeless frame, he loses his assurance. But this kind of confidence of hypocrites will not be shaken by sin. They (some of them at least) will keep up their boldness in their hope in the most corrupt frames and wicked ways, which is a sure evidence of their delusion.30.

And here I cannot help observing that there are certain doctrines often preached to the people which need to be delivered with more caution and explanation than they often are. For as many understand them, they tend greatly to establish this delusion and false confidence of hypocrites. The doctrines I speak of are those of Christians living by faith, not by sight; their giving glory to God by trusting him in the dark; living on Christ, and not on experiences; not making their good frames the foundation of their faith. These are indeed excellent and important doctrines when rightly understood, but corrupt and destructive as many understand them. The Scripture speaks of living or walking by faith and not by sight in no other ways than these, namely: being governed by a regard to eternal things, which are the objects of faith and are not seen, and not by a regard to temporal things, which are seen; believing things revealed which we never saw with bodily eyes; and also living by faith in the promise of future things, without yet seeing or enjoying the things promised, or knowing how they can be fulfilled. This will be easily evident to anyone who looks over the Scriptures that speak of faith in opposition to sight, such as 2 Cor 4:18; 5:7; Heb 11:1, 8, 13, 17, 27, 29; Rom 8:24; John 20:29. But this doctrine, as many understand it, is that Christians ought to believe and trust in Christ firmly without spiritual sight or light, even though they are in a dark, dead frame and for the present have no spiritual experiences or manifestations. And it is truly the duty of those who are in darkness in this way to come out of darkness into light, and believe. But that they should confidently believe and trust while they still remain without spiritual light or sight is a doctrine contrary to Scripture, and absurd. The Scripture knows nothing of any such faith in Christ, of the working of God, that is not founded on a spiritual sight of Christ. The believing in Christ which goes with a title to everlasting life is a seeing of the Son and believing in him (John 6:40). True faith in Christ is never exercised any further than persons behold as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, and have the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 3:18; 4:6). Those into whose minds the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, does not shine, do not believe (2 Cor 4:4). Faith that is without spiritual light is not the faith of the children of the light and of the day, but the presumption of the children of darkness. And therefore to press and urge them to believe without any spiritual light or sight tends greatly to further the delusions of the prince of darkness. Not only can men not exercise faith without some spiritual light, but they can exercise faith only in exact proportion to the spiritual light they have. Men will trust in God no further than they know him. And they cannot be in the exercise of faith in him one bit further than they have a sight of his fullness and faithfulness in exercise. Nor can they have the exercise of trust in God any further than they are in a gracious frame. Those who are in a dead, carnal frame doubtless ought to trust in God, because that would be the same thing as coming out of their bad frame and turning to God. But to exhort men to trust in God confidently, and so to keep up their hope and peace, though they are not in a gracious frame and still remain so, is in effect the same thing as exhorting them to trust in God confidently, but not with a gracious trust. And what is that but wicked presumption? It is just as impossible for men to have a strong or lively trust in God when they have no lively exercises of grace, or felt Christian experiences, as it is for them to be in the lively exercises of grace without the exercises of grace.

It is true that it is the duty of God’s people to trust in him when they are in darkness, and though they remain in darkness, in this sense: they ought to trust in God when the face of his providence is dark and looks as though God had forsaken them and did not hear their prayers; when many clouds gather and many enemies surround them with a fearsome look, threatening to swallow them up; when all the events of providence seem to be against them, and all circumstances seem to make the promises of God difficult to fulfill; and when God must be trusted out of sight, that is, when we cannot see how it is possible for him to fulfill his word, and everything but God’s mere word makes it look unlikely, so that if persons believe, they must hope against hope. In this way the ancient patriarchs, and Job, and the psalmist, and Jeremiah, Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, and the apostle Paul gave glory to God by trusting in God in darkness. And we have many instances of such a glorious, victorious faith in the eleventh chapter of Hebrews. But how different a thing this is from trusting in God without spiritual sight while being at the same time in a dead and carnal frame!

There is also such a thing as spiritual light being let into the soul in one way when it is not in another. And so there is such a thing as the saints trusting in God, and also knowing their good state, when they lack some kinds of experience. For instance, they may have clear views of God’s sufficiency and faithfulness, and so trust in him confidently and know that they are his children, and at the same time not have such clear and sweet ideas of his love as at other times. For it was so with Christ himself in his last suffering. And they may have views of much of God’s sovereignty, holiness and all-sufficiency, enabling them to submit to him quietly and exercise a sweet and most encouraging hope in God’s fullness, when they are not satisfied of their own good state. But how different these things are from trusting in God confidently without spiritual light or experience!

Those who insist in this way on persons living by faith when they have no experience and are in very bad frames are also very absurd in their notions of faith. What they mean by faith is believing that they are in a good state. So they count it a dreadful sin for persons to doubt their state, whatever frames they are in and whatever wicked things they do, because, they say, it is the great and heinous sin of unbelief. And in their view the best man, who puts the most honor on God, is the one who keeps his hope of his good state most confidently and immovably when he has the least light or experience, that is to say, when he is in the worst and most wicked frame and way. For that, if you please, is a sign that he is strong in faith, giving glory to God, and against hope believes in hope. But from what Bible do they learn this notion of faith, that it is a man’s confidently believing that he is in a good state?31 If this is faith, the Pharisees had faith in an eminent degree, and some of them, Christ teaches, committed the unpardonable sin against the Holy Spirit. The Scripture represents faith as that by which men are brought into a good state, and therefore it cannot be the same thing as believing that they are already in a good state. To suppose that faith consists in persons believing that they are in a good state is in effect the same as supposing that faith consists in a person’s believing that he has faith, or believing that he believes.

Indeed, persons’ doubting their good state may in several respects arise from unbelief. It may be from unbelief, or because they have so little faith, that they have so little evidence of their good state. If they had more experience of the actings of faith, and so more experience of the exercise of grace, they would have clearer evidence that their state was good, and so their doubts would be removed. And then their doubting of their state may be from unbelief in this way: there may be many things that are good evidences of a work of grace in them, and yet they doubt very much whether they are really in a state of favor with God, because it is they, people so unworthy, who have done so much to provoke God to anger against them. Their doubts in such a case arise from unbelief, in that they arise from a lack of a sufficient sense of, and reliance on, the infinite riches of God’s grace and the sufficiency of Christ for the chief of sinners. They may also be from unbelief when they doubt their state because of the mystery of God’s dealings with them, when they are not able to reconcile such dispensations with God’s favor to them. Or they may be from unbelief when they doubt whether they have any share in the promises because, from the face of providence, the promises appear so unlikely to be fulfilled, and the difficulties in the way are so many and great. Such doubting arises from a lack of dependence on God’s almighty power and on his knowledge and wisdom, as infinitely above theirs. But even so, in such persons, their unbelief and their doubting of their state are not the same thing, though the one arises from the other.

Persons may be greatly to blame for doubting their state on grounds such as these last mentioned. And they may be to blame that they have no more grace, and no more of its present exercises and experiences to be an evidence to them of the goodness of their state. Men are doubtless to blame for being in a dead, carnal frame. But when they are in such a frame and have no felt experience of the exercises of grace, but on the contrary are very much under the power of their lusts and an unchristian spirit, they are not to blame for doubting their state. In the nature of things, it is as impossible for a holy and Christian hope to be kept alive in its clearness and strength in such circumstances as it is to keep the light in the room when the candle is put out, or to keep the bright sunshine in the air when the sun has gone down. Distant experiences, when darkened by present prevailing lust and corruption, will never keep a gracious confidence and assurance alive. Rather, it sickens and declines under this as surely as a little child under repeated blows on the head with a hammer. Nor is it at all to be lamented that persons doubt their state in such circumstances. On the contrary, it is desirable and in every way best that they should. It agrees with the wise and merciful arrangement of things that God has established that it should be so. For God has so contrived and arranged things in his dispensations toward his own people that when their love declines, and its exercises fail or become weak, fear should arise. For then they need it, to restrain them from sin and to stir them to care for the good of their souls, and so to rouse them to watchfulness and diligence in religion. But God has so ordered it that when love rises and is in vigorous exercise, fear should vanish and be driven away. For then they do not need it, having a higher and more excellent principle in exercise to restrain them from sin and stir them up to their duty. There are no other principles under whose influence human nature lies that will ever make men conscientious but one of these two, fear or love. And therefore, if one of these did not prevail as the other declined, God’s people, when fallen into dead and carnal frames, when love is asleep, would indeed be lamentably exposed. And therefore God has wisely ordained that these two opposite principles of love and fear should rise and fall like the two opposite scales of a balance: when one rises, the other sinks. Light and darkness necessarily and unavoidably follow each other. If light prevails, darkness ceases just so much and no more, and if light declines, darkness prevails just so much. So it is in the heart of a child of God. If divine love declines and falls asleep, and lust prevails, the light and joy of hope go out, and dark fear and doubting arise. And if on the contrary divine love prevails and comes into lively exercise, this brings in the brightness of hope and drives away black lust, and fear with it. Love is the Spirit of adoption, or the childlike principle. If that slumbers, men fall under fear, which is the spirit of bondage, or the slavish principle, and so on the contrary. And if love, or the spirit of adoption, is carried to a great height, it drives away all fear completely and gives full assurance, in agreement with the apostle’s words in 1 John 4:18: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear.” These two opposite principles of lust and holy love bring hope and fear into the hearts of God’s children in proportion as they prevail, that is, when left to their own natural influence, without something coming in from outside or by accident: such as the disease of melancholy, ignorance of doctrine, prejudices of upbringing, wrong instruction, false principles, particular temptations, and so on.

The Spirit of God casts out fear in no other way than by the prevailing of love. Nor does his Spirit ever keep fear out when love is asleep. At such a time all the saint’s self-examinations, and poring over past experience in order to establish his peace and get assurance, are in vain. For it is contrary to the nature of things, as God has arranged them, that he should have assurance at such a time.

Those, therefore, who exhort others to be confident in their hope when in dead frames directly thwart God’s wise and gracious arrangement of things. They do it under the notion of living by faith and not by sight, and trusting God in the dark, and living on Christ, and not on experiences; and they warn them not to doubt their good state, lest they be guilty of the dreadful sin of unbelief. And this has a direct tendency to establish the most presumptuous hypocrites, and to keep them from ever calling their state into question, however much wickedness rages and reigns in their hearts and prevails in their lives, under the notion of honoring God by hoping against hope and trusting in God confidently when things look very dark. And doubtless vast harm has been done in this way.

Persons cannot be said to forsake Christ and live on their experiences of the exercises of grace merely because they take them and use them as evidences of grace. For there are no other evidences they can or ought to take. But persons may be said to live on their experiences when they make a righteousness of them. Instead of keeping their eye on God’s glory and Christ’s excellence, they turn their eyes away from these objects outside them onto themselves, to entertain their minds by viewing their own attainments and high experiences and the great things they have met with. They are bright and beautiful in their own eyes, and rich and grown wealthy in their own estimation, and they think God has as admiring an esteem of them on the same account as they have of themselves. This is living on experiences and not on Christ, and it is more abominable in the sight of God than the gross immoralities of those who make no claims to religion. But this is a far different thing from merely making use of experiences as evidences of a share in a glorious Redeemer.

But to return from this digression, I would mention one thing more under the general head I am on.

28. “O professing Christian, look carefully to your foundation: do not be arrogant, but fear. You have perhaps done and suffered many things in and for religion; you have excellent gifts and sweet comforts, a warm zeal for God, and high confidence of your integrity. All this may be right, for all that I, or perhaps you, know; but even so, it is possible it may be false also. You have at times judged yourselves and pronounced yourselves upright; but remember, your final sentence is not yet pronounced by your judge. And what if God should weigh you again in his more just balance and say, Mene, Tekel: you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient? What a shamed man you will be under such a sentence! Quae splendent in conspectu hominis, sordent in conspectu judicis: things that are highly esteemed among men are an abomination in the sight of God; he does not see as man sees. Your heart may be false, and you not know it; indeed, it may be false, and you strongly confident of its integrity.” Flavel’s touchstone of sincerity, ch. 2. Sect. 5. “Some hypocrites are a great deal more confident than many saints.” Stoddard’s discourse on the way to know sincerity and hypocrisy, p. 128.

29. “Does the work of faith in some believers bear on its top branches the full ripe fruits of a blessed assurance? Look what strong confidence and high-built persuasions of a share in God have at times been found in unsanctified ones! Indeed, this false assurance may be so strong that they dare boldly venture to go to the judgment seat of God and defend it there. Does the Spirit of God fill the heart of the assured believer with joy unspeakable and full of glory, giving them through faith a foretaste of heaven itself in those firstfruits of it? How near to this comes what the apostle supposes may be found in apostates!” Flavel’s husbandry spiritualized, ch. 12.

30. Mr. Shepard speaks of it as a presumptuous peace that is not interrupted and broken by evil works. And he says that the Spirit will sigh, and not sing, in that bosom from which corrupt dispositions and passions break out; and that though men in such frames may seem to maintain the consolation of the Spirit, and not suspect their hypocrisy, under the pretense of trusting the Lord’s mercy, yet they cannot escape the condemnation of the word. Parable of the ten virgins, Part 1. P. 139. Dr. Ames speaks of it as a thing by which the peace of a wicked man may be distinguished from the peace of a godly man, that the peace of a wicked man continues whether he performs the duties of piety and righteousness or not, provided he avoids those crimes that appear horrid to nature itself. Cases of conscience, Lib. III. Chapter 7.

31. “Men do not know that they are godly by believing that they are godly. We know many things by faith: ‘By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command’ (Heb 11:3). Faith is the evidence of things not seen (Heb 11:1). This is how men know the Trinity of persons of the Godhead; that Jesus Christ is the Son of God; that he who believes in him will have eternal life; the resurrection of the dead. And if God should tell a saint that he has grace, he might know it by believing the word of God. But it is not in this way that godly men know that they have grace. It is not revealed in the word, and the Spirit of God does not testify it to particular persons.” Stoddard’s nature of saving conversion, p. 83, 84.

Accounts Pleasing to the Godly

Part II · No Certain Sign XII

XII. Nothing can be concluded with certainty about the nature of the religious affections anyone has from this, that their outward manifestations, and the account persons give of them, are very affecting and pleasing to the truly godly, and such as greatly win their charitable judgment and their hearts.

The true saints do not have such a spirit of discernment that they can determine with certainty who are godly and who are not. For though they know by experience what true religion is in its inward exercises, these are what they can neither feel nor see in the heart of another.32 Nothing in others comes within their view but outward manifestations and appearances. But the Scripture plainly suggests that this way of judging what is in men by outward appearances is uncertain at best and liable to deceive: “The LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Sam 16:7). “He will not judge by what His eyes see, and He will not decide by what His ears hear” (Isa 11:3).33 Those who are quick and absolute in deciding persons’ states, boasting of their extraordinary gift of discerning and distinguishing in these great matters, as though all was open and clear to them, are commonly only poor judges and dangerous counselors in cases of the soul. They betray one of these three things: either that they have had only a little experience, or that they are persons of weak judgment, or that they have a great degree of pride and self-confidence, and so of ignorance of themselves. Wise and experienced men will proceed with great caution in such a matter.

When there are many probable appearances of piety in others, it is the duty of the saints to receive them heartily into their charitable judgment, and to love them and rejoice in them as their brethren in Christ Jesus. But even so, the best of men may be deceived when the appearances seem to them exceedingly fair and bright, even so as to win their charitable judgment entirely and conquer their hearts. It has been a common thing in the church of God for such bright professing Christians, who are received among the saints as eminent saints, to fall away and come to nothing.34. And we need not wonder at this if we consider the things already observed, the things it has been shown may appear in men who are altogether without grace. Nothing prevents all these things from meeting together in men while they are without a spark of grace in their hearts. They may have religious affections of many kinds together. They may have a sort of affection toward God that closely resembles dear love to him, and so a kind of love to the brethren, and great appearances of wonder at God’s perfections and works, and sorrow for sin, and reverence, submission, self-abasement, gratitude, joy, religious longings, and zeal for the interest of religion and the good of souls. And these affections may come after great awakenings and convictions of conscience. There may be great appearances of a work of humbling, and counterfeit love and joy and other affections may seem to follow these, and one another, in just the same order that is commonly observed in the holy affections of true converts. And these religious affections may be carried to a great height. They may cause an abundance of tears, indeed may overcome the bodily nature of those who have them, and may make them full of feeling, fervent and fluent in speaking of the things of God, and incline them to do it abundantly. They may be accompanied by many sweet texts of Scripture and precious promises brought to their minds with great impression. And they may incline them to praise and glorify God with their mouths in a very ardent way, and fervently to call on others to praise him, crying out about their unworthiness and exalting free grace. And moreover they may incline them to abound in the external duties of religion, such as prayer, hearing the word preached, singing, and religious conversation. And these things may be accompanied by a great resemblance of a Christian assurance in its greatest height, when the saints mount up on eagles’ wings above all darkness and doubting. I think it has been made plain that all these things may be there, and yet there may be nothing more than the common influences of the Spirit of God, joined with the delusions of Satan and the wicked and deceitful heart. To this I may add that all these things may be accompanied by a sweet natural temper, a good doctrinal knowledge of religion, a long acquaintance with the saints’ way of talking and of expressing their affections and experiences, a natural ability and skill in suiting their expressions and manner of speaking to the inclinations and notions of the hearers, and an attractive propriety of expression and behavior formed by a good upbringing. How great, therefore, the resemblance may be, in all outward expressions and appearances, between a hypocrite and a true saint! Doubtless it is the glorious prerogative of the all-knowing God, as the great searcher of hearts, to be able to separate well between sheep and goats. And what unseemly self-exaltation and arrogance it is in poor, fallible, dark mortals to claim that they can determine and know who are really sincere and upright before God, and who are not!

Many seem to lay great weight on this, and to suppose it to be what may settle the question of others’ real piety: when they not only tell a plausible story, but in giving an account of their experiences they present things and speak in such a way that the hearers feel their talk. That is to say, their talk seems to harmonize with the hearers’ own experience, and the hearers’ hearts are touched and affected and delighted by what they hear them say, and drawn out by it in dear love to them. But there is not the certainty in such things, or the full dependence to be placed on them, that many imagine. A true saint greatly delights in holiness. It is a most beautiful thing in his eyes, and God’s work in savingly renewing a poor soul that was perishing before, and making it holy and happy, appears to him a most glorious work. No wonder, therefore, that his heart is touched and greatly affected when he hears another give a probable account of this work done in his own heart, and when he sees probable appearances of holiness in him, whether those pleasing appearances have anything real to answer them or not. And if he uses the same words commonly used to express the affections of true saints, and tells of many things following one another in an order that agrees with the method of the experience of the one who hears him, and also speaks freely and boldly and with an air of assurance, no wonder the other thinks his experiences harmonize with his own.
