And if, besides all this, he speaks with much affection in giving his account, and above all, if in speaking he seems to show much affection to the one to whom he speaks, such an affection as the Galatians had to the apostle Paul, these things will naturally have a powerful influence to affect and draw the hearer’s heart, and open wide the doors of his charitable judgment toward him. David speaks as one who had felt Ahithophel’s talk, and had once found a sweet savor and relish in it. And therefore his surprise and disappointment were exceedingly great when he fell; it was almost too much for him: “For it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure. … But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend. We shared sweet fellowship together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God” (Ps 55:12–14).

It is with professing Christians, especially those who become so in a time of the outpouring of the Spirit of God, as it is with the blossoms in the spring.35 There are vast numbers of them on the trees, which all look fair and promising, but even so, very many of them never come to anything. And many of those that in a little while wither up and drop off and rot under the trees look as beautiful and bright as the others for a while. And not only so, but they smell sweet and send out a pleasant fragrance. So we cannot with certainty, by any of our senses, distinguish the blossoms that have in them the secret power which will appear afterwards in the fruit, and the inward solidity and strength which will enable them to bear and cause them to be perfected by the hot summer sun that will dry up the others. It is the mature fruit which comes afterwards, and not the beautiful colors and smell of the blossom, that we must judge by. So new converts (professedly so) may appear fair in their talk about the things of religion, and be very savory, and the saints may think they talk with real feeling. They may relish their talk and imagine they perceive a divine savor in it, and yet all may come to nothing.

It is strange how hard it is to bring men to be content with the rules and directions Christ has given them. They must go by other rules of their own invention, which seem to them wiser and better. I know of no directions or counsels Christ ever gave more plainly than the rules he has given us to guide us in judging others’ sincerity, namely, that we should judge the tree chiefly by its fruit. But even so, this will not do, and other ways are found out which are imagined to be more distinguishing and certain. And woeful have been the harmful consequences of this arrogant setting up of men’s wisdom above the wisdom of Christ. I believe many saints have gone far out of the way of Christ’s word in this respect, and some of them have been chastised with whips and (I had almost said) scorpions to bring them back again. But many things that have appeared lately, and appear now, may convince us that ordinarily those who have gone furthest in this way, who have been most highly conceited of their gift of discerning, and have appeared most eager to decide the state of men’s souls absolutely and hastily, have been hypocrites who have known nothing of true religion.

In the parable of the wheat and tares it is said, “When the wheat sprouted and bore grain, then the tares also appeared” (Matt 13:26). It is as though the tares were not discerned or distinguishable from the wheat until then, as Mr. Flavel observes.36 He mentions it as an observation of Jerome’s that wheat and tares are so much alike, until the blade of the wheat comes to bring forth the ear, that it is next to impossible to distinguish them. And then Mr. Flavel adds, “However difficult it is to discern the difference between wheat and tares, yet doubtless the eye of sense can distinguish them much more easily than the quickest and most piercing eye of man can discern the difference between special and common grace. For all saving graces in the saints have their counterfeits in hypocrites. There are similar works in them which a spiritual and very judicious eye may easily mistake for the saving and genuine effects of a sanctifying Spirit.”

As it is the ear or the fruit which distinguishes the wheat from the tares, so this is the true Shibboleth which he who stands as judge at the fords of the Jordan uses to distinguish those who will pass over Jordan into the true Canaan from those who were to be slain at the fords. For the Hebrew word Shibboleth means an ear of grain. And perhaps the fuller pronunciation of Jephthah’s friends, Shibboleth, may represent a full ear with fruit in it, typifying the fruits of the friends of Christ, the antitype of Jephthah. And the thinner pronunciation of the Ephraimites, his enemies, may represent their empty ears, typifying the show of religion in hypocrites, without substance and fruit. This agrees with the doctrine we are abundantly taught in Scripture, namely, that he who is appointed to judge those who pass through death, whether they have a right to enter the heavenly Canaan or not, or whether they should be slain, will judge every man according to his works.

We seem to be taught the same things by the rules given for the priests’ discerning of leprosy. In many cases it was impossible for the priest to determine whether a man had leprosy or was clean by the closest inspection of the appearances on him, until he had waited to see what the appearances would come to, and had shut up the person who showed himself to him for one seven days after another. And when he judged, he was to decide by the hair which grew out of the spot shown to him, which was as it were the fruit it brought forth.

And here, before I finish what I have to say under this head, I would say something about a strange notion some have lately been led away with, of knowing with certainty the good state others are in, as though it were revealed to them immediately from heaven by their love flowing out to them in an extraordinary way. They argue like this. Their love being very great and deeply felt, it may be known with certainty by those who feel it to be a true Christian love. And if it is a true Christian love, the Spirit of God must be its author. And since the Spirit of God, who knows with certainty whether others are the children of God or not, and is a spirit of truth, is pleased by an uncommon influence on them to cause their love to flow out in an extraordinary way toward such a person as a child of God, this infallible Spirit, who deceives no one, must know that that person is a child of God. But such persons might be convinced that their reasoning is false if they would consider this: is it not their duty, and what God requires of them, to love as the children of God those whom they think are the children of God, and whom they have no reason to think otherwise of from all they can see in them, even though God, who searches the hearts, knows that they are not his children? If it is their duty, then it is good, and the lack of it is sin. And therefore surely the Spirit of God may be its author. The Spirit of God, without being a spirit of falsehood, may in such a case help a person to do his duty and keep him from sin. But then they argue from the uncommon degree and special manner in which their love flows out to the person, which they think the Spirit of God would never cause if he did not know the object to be a child of God. But then I would ask them whether it is not their duty to love to a very great degree all those whom they are bound to think are the children of God from all they can see in them, though God, from other things he sees which are out of their sight, knows that they are not. It is men’s duty to love all whom they are bound, in charitable judgment, to look on as the children of God with a vastly dearer affection than they commonly do. As we ought to love Christ to the utmost capacity of our nature, so it is our duty to love those whom we think are so near and dear to him as his members with an exceedingly dear affection, as Christ has loved us. And therefore it is sin in us not to love them so. We ought to pray to God that by his Spirit he would keep us from sin and enable us to do our duty. And may not his Spirit answer our prayers and enable us to do our duty in a particular instance without lying? If he cannot, then the Spirit of God is bound not to help his people do their duty in some instances, because he cannot do it without being a spirit of falsehood. But surely God is sovereign enough for that: he may enable us to do our duty when he pleases and on whatever occasion he pleases. When persons think others are his children, God may have other ends in causing their exceedingly endeared love to flow out to them besides revealing to them whether their opinion of them is right or not. He may have this merciful end in it, to enable them to do their duty and to keep them from that dreadful, infinite evil, sin. And will they say that God may not show them that mercy in such a case? Suppose I am away from home and hear that in my absence my house has burned down, but my family have all escaped the flames in some extraordinary way, and everything in the circumstances of the story as I hear it makes it appear very credible. In such a case it would be sin in me not to feel a very great degree of gratitude to God, even though the story is in fact not true. And is not God so sovereign that he may, if he pleases, show me that mercy on that occasion, and enable me to do my duty to a much greater degree than I used to, and yet not incur the charge of deceitfulness in confirming a falsehood?

It is exceedingly plain from Romans 14:6 that error or mistake may be the occasion of a gracious exercise, and consequently of a gracious influence of the Spirit of God: “He who eats does so to the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and he who abstains does so to the Lord and gives thanks to God.” The apostle is speaking of those who, through erroneous and needless scruples, avoided eating foods that were ceremonially unclean. By this it is very evident that there may be true exercises of grace, a true regard to the Lord, and particularly a true thankfulness, which may be occasioned both by an erroneous judgment and by an erroneous practice. And consequently an error may be the occasion of those truly holy exercises that are from the infallible Spirit of God. And if so, it is certainly too much for us to determine to how great a degree the Spirit of God may give this holy exercise on such an occasion.

This notion of discerning another’s state with certainty by love flowing out is not only not founded on reason or Scripture, but it is contrary to Scripture. It is against the rules of Scripture, which say not a word of any such way of judging the state of others as this, but direct us to judge chiefly by the fruits that are seen in them. And it is against the doctrines of Scripture, which plainly teach us that the state of others’ souls toward God cannot be known by us, as in Revelation 2:17: “To the one who overcomes, I will give the hidden manna. I will also give him a white stone inscribed with a new name, known only to the one who receives it.” And Rom 2:29: “A man is a Jew because he is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code. Such a man’s praise does not come from men, but from God.” By this last expression, such a man’s praise does not come from men, but from God, the apostle refers to the inability of men to judge whether a man is inwardly a Jew or not (as they could easily see by outward marks whether men were outwardly Jews), and means that it belongs to God alone to give the deciding voice in this matter. This is confirmed by the same apostle’s use of the phrase in 1 Corinthians 4:5: “Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time; wait until the Lord comes. He will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men’s hearts. At that time each will receive his praise from God.” The apostle, in the two verses before, says, “I care very little, however, if I am judged by you+ or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. My conscience is clear, but that does not vindicate me. It is the Lord who judges me.” And again, it is further confirmed because in this second chapter to the Romans the apostle directs his speech especially to those who had a high conceit of their own holiness, made their boast of God, and were confident of their own discernment. They were confident that they knew God’s will and approved the things that were excellent, or tested the things that differ (as it is in the margin) (verse 18), and were convinced that they were guides for the blind, a light for those in darkness, instructors of the foolish, teachers of infants, and so they took it on themselves to judge others; see verse 1 and verses 17–20.

And how arrogant the notion must be of those who imagine they can know others’ godliness with certainty, when that great apostle Peter claims to say no more about Silvanus than that he was a faithful brother, as he supposed (1 Pet 5:12). And yet this Silvanus appears to have been a very eminent minister of Christ, an evangelist, a famous light in God’s church at that time, and an intimate companion of the apostles. See 2 Cor 1:19; 1 Thess 1:1; 2 Thess 1:1.

32. “Men may have the knowledge of their own conversion; the knowledge other men have of it is uncertain, because no man can look into the heart of another and see the workings of grace there.” Stoddard’s Nat of saving Conv. Chapter 15. At the beginning.

33. Mr. Stoddard observes that all visible signs are common to converted and unconverted men, and an account of experiences among the rest. Appeal to the learned, p. 75. “O how hard it is for the eye of man to discern between chaff and wheat! And how many upright hearts are now censured whom God will clear! How many false hearts are now approved whom God will condemn! Men ordinarily have no convincing proofs, but only probable signs, which at most produce only a conjectural knowledge of another’s state. And those who judge absolutely either way may possibly wrong the generation of the upright, or on the other side, acquit and justify the wicked. And truly, considering what has been said, it is no wonder that dangerous mistakes are made so often in this matter.” Flavel’s Husb. Spir. Chapter 12.

34. “Do not be offended if you see great cedars fall, stars fall from heaven, great professing Christians die and decay. Do not think they are all such. Do not think that the elect will fall. Truly, some are such that when they fall, one would think a man truly sanctified might fall away, as the Arminians think. ‘They did not belong to us’ (1 John 2:19). I speak this because the Lord is shaking, and I look for great apostasies; for God is testing all his friends throughout the Christian world. In Germany what profession of faith there was! Who would have thought it? The Lord, who delights to show openly what was hidden in secret, sends a sword, and they fall.” Shepard’s Parab. Part I. P. 118, 119. “The saints may approve you, and God condemn you: ‘You have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead’ (Rev 3:1). Men may say, ‘There is a true Nathanael,’ and God may say, ‘There is a self-deceiving Pharisee.’ Reader, you have heard of Judas and Demas, of Ananias and Sapphira, of Hymenaeus and Philetus, once renowned and famous professing Christians, and you have heard how they turned out at last.” Flavel’s touchstone of sincerity, ch. 2. Sect. 5.

35. A time of the outpouring of the Spirit of God, reviving religion and producing its pleasant appearances in new converts, is compared in Scripture to this very thing, namely, the spring season, when the kindly influences of the heavens cause the blossoms to put forth. Song 2:11, 12.

36. Husbandry spiritualized, ch. 12.

Part III

Concerning the Marks

Part III · Distinguishing Signs

Showing what are distinguishing Signs of truly gracious and holy Affections.

I come now to the second thing proposed concerning the trial of religious affections, namely, to take notice of some things in which affections that are spiritual and gracious differ from those that are not.

But before I go on directly to the distinguishing characteristics, I would first mention some things concerning the marks I will lay down, which I want to be noted.

1. I am far from undertaking to give such signs of gracious affections as will be enough to enable anyone to distinguish with certainty true affection from false in others, or to determine positively which of their neighbors are true professing Christians and which are hypocrites. In doing that, I would be guilty of the very arrogance I have been condemning. It is plain that Christ has given rules to all Christians to enable them to judge of those who profess religion, whom they have to deal with, as far as is necessary for their own safety and to keep them from being led into a snare by false teachers and false pretenders to religion. It is also beyond doubt that the Scriptures abound with rules that may be very useful to ministers in counseling and guiding the souls committed to their care, in things that concern their spiritual and eternal state. Yet it is also evident that it was never God’s design to give us any rules by which we may know with certainty which of our fellow professing Christians are his, and so make a full and clear separation between sheep and goats. On the contrary, it was God’s design to reserve this to himself, as his prerogative. And therefore no distinguishing signs that will enable Christians or ministers to do this are ever to be expected, to the end of the world. For no more is ever to be expected from any signs found in the word of God, or gathered from it, than what Christ designed them for.

2. No signs are to be expected that will be enough to enable those saints who are very low in grace, or who have departed far from God and have fallen into a dead, carnal and unchristian frame, to discern their own good state with certainty. It does not agree with God’s design (as has already been observed) that such people should know their good state. Nor is it desirable that they should; on the contrary, it is best in every way that they should not. And we have reason to bless God that he has made no provision for such people to know with certainty the state they are in, in any other way than by first coming out of the bad frame and way they are in.

Indeed, it is not properly because of any defect in the signs given in the word of God that not every living saint, whether strong or weak, and those in a bad frame as well as others, can know his good state with certainty by them. For the rules in themselves are certain and infallible, and every saint has, or has had, those things in himself that are sure evidences of grace; for every act of grace, even the least, is such an evidence. But it is because of a defect in the one to whom the signs are given. In the saint who is very low in grace, or in a bad frame, there is a twofold defect, which makes it impossible for him to know with certainty that he has true grace by the best signs and rules that can be given him. First, there is a defect in the object, that is, in the quality to be viewed and examined. I do not mean an essential defect, for I am supposing the person to be a real saint, but a defect in degree. Grace, being very small, cannot be clearly and certainly discerned and distinguished. When things are very small, we cannot clearly discern their form or distinguish them from one another, though in themselves their forms may be very different. There is no doubt a great difference between the body of a man and the bodies of other animals at the first conception in the womb. Yet if we were to view the different embryos, we might not be able to discern the difference, because of the imperfect state of the object; but as it comes to greater perfection, the difference becomes very plain. The difference between creatures of very contrary qualities cannot be seen so plainly while they are very young, even after they are actually born, as in their more perfect state. The difference between doves and ravens, or doves and vultures, is not so evident when they first come out of the egg; but as they grow to their full perfection, it becomes exceedingly great and obvious. Another defect attending the grace of those I am speaking of is that it is mingled with so much corruption, which clouds and hides it and makes it impossible for it to be known with certainty. Different things in front of us may have in themselves many marks that thoroughly distinguish them from one another. Yet if we see them only in thick smoke, it may still be impossible to distinguish them. A fixed star is easily distinguished from a comet in a clear sky; but if we view them through a cloud, it may be impossible to see the difference. When true Christians are in a bad frame, guilt lies on the conscience. This brings fear, and so hinders the peace and joy of an assured hope.

(2.) Secondly, in such a case there is a defect in the eye. As the feebleness of grace and the prevalence of corruption obscure the object, so they weaken the sight; they darken the sight with respect to all spiritual objects, of which grace is one. Sin is like some diseases of the eyes that make things appear in colors other than those that properly belong to them. It is like many other diseases that put the mouth out of taste, so that a man cannot distinguish good and wholesome food from bad, but everything tastes bitter. Men in a corrupt and carnal frame have their spiritual senses in a poor condition for judging and distinguishing spiritual things.

For these reasons, no signs that can be given will actually satisfy people in such a case. However good and infallible the signs given may be, and however clearly they are laid down, they will not serve them. It is like giving a man rules for distinguishing visible objects in the dark. The things themselves may be very different, and their difference may be described to him very well and distinctly; yet all of it is insufficient to enable him to distinguish them, because he is in the dark. That is why many people in such a case spend their time in fruitless labor, poring over past experiences and examining themselves by signs they hear laid down from the pulpit or read in books, when there is other work for them to do, which is much more expected of them. While they neglect that work, all their self-examination is likely to be in vain, however much time they spend on it. The accursed thing must be destroyed from their camp, and Achan must be put to death; and until this is done they will be in trouble. It is not God’s design that men should obtain assurance in any other way than by mortifying corruption, increasing in grace, and obtaining the lively exercise of it. And although self-examination is a duty of great use and importance, and by no means to be neglected, it is not the principal means by which the saints get satisfaction about their good state. Assurance is not to be obtained so much by self-examination as by action. The apostle Paul sought assurance chiefly in this way, by forgetting what was behind, and reaching forward to what was ahead, pressing on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus, if by any means he might attain to the resurrection of the dead. And it was chiefly by this means that he obtained assurance: “Therefore I do not run uncertainly” (1 Cor 9:26). He obtained assurance of winning the prize more by running than by considering. The swiftness of his pace did more toward his assurance of victory than the strictness of his examination. To give all diligence to grow in grace, by adding to faith virtue, and so on, is the direction the apostle Peter gives us for making our calling and election sure, and having an entrance richly granted to us into Christ’s everlasting kingdom. He is telling us that without this our eyes will be dim, and we will be like men in the dark who cannot plainly see things past or things to come, either the forgiveness of our past sins or our heavenly inheritance, which is future and far off (2 Pet 1:5–11).37

Therefore, good rules for distinguishing true grace from counterfeit may tend to convict hypocrites and be of great use to the saints in many respects. Among other benefits, they may be very useful to the saints in removing many needless scruples and establishing their hope. Yet I am far from claiming to lay down any rules that will be enough by themselves, without other means, to enable all true saints to see their good state, or from supposing that such rules should be the principal means of their satisfaction.

3. Nor is there much encouragement, from the experience of present or past times, to lay down rules or marks for distinguishing true affections from false in hope of convicting any considerable number of that sort of hypocrites who have been deceived by great false manifestations and affections, and who are once settled in a false confidence and a high opinion of their own supposed great experiences and privileges. Such hypocrites are so conceited of their own wisdom, so blinded and hardened by a very great self-righteousness (though a very subtle and secret one, under the disguise of great humility), and so invincibly fond of their pleasing notion of their own great exaltation, that it usually accomplishes nothing at all to lay before them the most convincing evidences of their hypocrisy. Their state is truly deplorable. Next to those who have committed the unpardonable sin, some of this sort of people seem to be furthest out of reach of the means of conviction and repentance. Yet laying down good rules may be a means of keeping people from becoming such hypocrites, and of convicting many hypocrites of other kinds. And God is able to convict even this kind; his grace is not to be limited, and the means are not to be neglected. Besides, such rules may be of use to the true saints, to detect false affections that they may have mingled with true ones, and may be a means of their religion becoming more pure, like gold tried in the fire.

Having laid these things down first, I now go on directly to take notice of the things in which true religious affections are distinguished from false.

37. The way to know your godliness is to renew the visible exercises of grace.—The more the visible exercises of grace are renewed, the more certain you will be. The more frequently these actings are renewed, the more abiding and confirmed your assurance will be.—The more men’s grace is multiplied, the more their peace is multiplied (2 Pet 1:2): “Grace and peace be multiplied to you+ through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.” Stoddard’s way to know sincerity and hypocrisy, p. 139, and 142.

Spiritual, Supernatural and Divine

Part III · Sign I

1. Affections that are truly spiritual and gracious arise from influences and operations on the heart that are spiritual, supernatural and divine.

I will explain what I mean by these terms, and from that their use for distinguishing affections that are spiritual from those that are not will appear.

We find that true saints, or those who are sanctified by the Spirit of God, are called spiritual persons in the New Testament. And their being spiritual is spoken of as their distinctive character, the thing that distinguishes them from those who are not sanctified. This is evident because those who are spiritual are set in opposition to natural men and carnal men. So the spiritual man and the natural man are set in opposition to each other in 1 Cor 2:14–15: “The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned. The spiritual man judges all things.” The Scripture explains itself to mean by a natural man an ungodly man, one who has no grace. So the apostle Jude, speaking of certain ungodly men who had crept in unnoticed among the saints (verse 4 of his epistle), says in verse 19, “These are sensual, not having the Spirit.” The apostle gives this as the reason they behaved in the wicked way he had described. Here the word translated sensual is ψυχικοὶ in the original, the very same word that is translated natural in those verses of 1 Cor chapter 2. In the same way, as the same discourse continues, two verses further on, spiritual men are set against carnal men, and the connection plainly shows that these mean the same as spiritual men and natural men in the verses before: “Brothers, I could not address you+ as spiritual, but as carnal”; that is, as in great measure unsanctified. That by carnal the apostle means corrupt and unsanctified is abundantly evident from Romans 7:25 and 8:1, 4–9, 12–13; Gal 5:16 to the end; and Col 2:18. Now therefore, if by natural and carnal in these texts he meant unsanctified, then no doubt by spiritual, which is set against them, he means sanctified and gracious.

And as the saints are called spiritual in Scripture, so we also find that certain properties, qualities and principles are given the same epithet. So we read of a spiritual mind (Rom 8:6–7), of spiritual wisdom (Col 1:9), and of spiritual blessings (Eph 1:3).

Now it may be observed that the epithet spiritual, in these and other parallel texts of the New Testament, is not used to signify any relation of persons or things to the spirit or soul of man, as the spiritual part of man in contrast to the body, which is the material part. Qualities are not said to be spiritual because they have their seat in the soul and not in the body. For there are some properties that the Scripture calls carnal or fleshly which have their seat in the soul just as much as the properties that are called spiritual. This is the case with pride and self-righteousness, and with a man’s trusting in his own wisdom, which the apostle calls fleshly (Col 2:18). Nor are things called spiritual because they are occupied with things that are immaterial and not bodily. For the wisdom of the wise men and rulers of this world was occupied with spirits and immaterial beings; yet the apostle speaks of these men as natural men, totally ignorant of the things that are spiritual (1 Cor 2). But it is with relation to the Holy Spirit, or Spirit of God, that persons or things are called spiritual in the New Testament. Spirit, as the word is used to signify the third person of the Trinity, is the noun from which the adjective spiritual is formed in the holy Scriptures. So Christians are called spiritual persons because they are born of the Spirit, and because of the indwelling and holy influences of the Spirit of God in them. And things are called spiritual as they are related to the Spirit of God, as in 1 Cor 2:13–14: “And this is what we speak, not in words taught us by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, expressing spiritual things in spiritual words. The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God.” Here the apostle himself expressly indicates that by spiritual things he means the things that come from the Spirit of God, and things taught by the Spirit. The same is still more abundantly apparent from the whole context. Again, Rom 8:6: “To be carnally minded is death, but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.” In what follows, in the ninth verse, the apostle explains what he means by being carnally and spiritually minded, and shows that by being spiritually minded he means having the indwelling and holy influences of the Spirit of God in the heart: “You+, however, are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if the Spirit of God dwells in you+. And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ.” The same is evident from the whole context. But time would fail me to bring forward all the evidence there is of this in the New Testament.

And it must be observed here that although persons and things are called spiritual with relation to the Spirit of God and his influences, yet not all persons who are subject to any kind of influence of the Spirit of God are ordinarily called spiritual in the New Testament. Those who have only the common influences of God’s Spirit are not called so in the places cited above, but only those who have the special, gracious and saving influences of God’s Spirit. This is evident because it has already been proved that by spiritual men is meant godly men, in contrast to natural, carnal and unsanctified men. And it is very plain that by spiritually minded (Rom 8:6) the apostle means graciously minded. The extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, which natural men might have, are sometimes called spiritual, because they are from the Spirit. Yet natural men, whatever gifts of the Spirit they had, were not called spiritual persons in the usual language of the New Testament. For it was not by having the gifts of the Spirit, but by having the virtues of the Spirit, that men were called spiritual. This is apparent from Galatians 6:1: “Brothers, if someone is caught in a trespass, you+ who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of meekness.” Meekness is one of the virtues the apostle had just spoken of in the verses immediately before, where he shows what the fruit of the Spirit is. In the language of the New Testament, those qualities are said to be spiritual which are truly gracious and holy, and belong to the saints alone.

So when we read of spiritual wisdom and understanding (as in Col 1:9: “asking God to fill you+ with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding”), what is meant is the wisdom that is gracious and comes from the sanctifying influences of the Spirit of God. For no doubt by spiritual wisdom is meant what is opposite to what the Scripture calls natural wisdom, just as the spiritual man is set against the natural man. And therefore spiritual wisdom is no doubt the same as the wisdom from above that the apostle James speaks of in Jas 3:17: “The wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peace-loving, gentle,” and so on. For the apostle sets this against natural wisdom in v. 15: “Such wisdom does not come from above, but is earthly, sensual.” The last word, in the original, is the same word that is translated natural in 1 Corinthians 2:14.

So natural men may be the subjects of many influences of the Spirit of God, as is evident from many Scriptures, such as Num 24:2; 1 Sam 10:10, 11:6 and 16:14; 1 Cor 13:1–3; Heb 6:4–6; and many others. Yet in the sense of Scripture they are not spiritual persons. Nor are any of the effects, common gifts, qualities or affections that come from the influence of the Spirit of God on them called spiritual things. The great difference lies in these two things.

(1.) The Spirit of God is given to the true saints to dwell in them as his own lasting home, and to influence their hearts as a principle of new nature, or as a divine, supernatural spring of life and action. The Scriptures represent the Holy Spirit not only as moving the saints and influencing them from time to time, but as dwelling in them as his temple, his own home, and his everlasting dwelling place (1 Cor 3:16; 2 Cor 6:16; John 14:16–17). And he is represented as being so united there to the faculties of the soul that he becomes there a principle, or spring, of new nature and life.

So the saints are said to live by Christ living in them (Gal 2:20). Christ by his Spirit not only is in them, but lives in them, so that they live by his life. His Spirit is so united to them as a principle of life in them. They do not only drink living water; this living water becomes a well or fount of water in the soul, springing up to spiritual and eternal life (John 4:14), and so becomes a principle of life in them. The evangelist himself explains that this living water means the Spirit of God (John 7:38–39). The light of the sun of righteousness does not only shine on them, but is so imparted to them that they shine too, and become little images of the sun that shines on them. The sap of the true vine is not only conveyed into them as the sap of a tree may be conveyed into a vessel, but is conveyed as sap is from a tree into one of its living branches, where it becomes a principle of life. The Spirit of God being imparted and united to the saints in this way, they are properly named from it and are called spiritual.

On the other hand, though the Spirit of God may influence natural men in many ways, yet because it is not imparted to them in this way, as an indwelling principle, they do not take any name or character from it; for since there is no union, it is not their own. Light may shine on a body that is very dark or black. Though that body is the subject of the light, yet because the light becomes no principle of light in it, so as to make the body shine, that body does not properly take its name from the light, so as to be called a luminous body. In the same way the Spirit of God, acting on the soul only, without imparting itself to be an active principle in it, cannot give it the name spiritual. A body that remains black may be said not to have light, though the light shines on it. So natural men are said not to have the Spirit (Jude 19): “sensual,” or natural (as the word is rendered elsewhere), “not having the Spirit.”

(2.) Another reason why the saints and their virtues are called spiritual (and this is the principal thing) is that the Spirit of God, dwelling as a vital principle in their souls, produces there effects in which he exerts and imparts himself in his own proper nature. Holiness is the nature of the Spirit of God; that is why he is called in Scripture the Holy Spirit. Holiness, which is, as it were, the beauty and sweetness of the divine nature, is as much the proper nature of the Holy Spirit as heat is the nature of fire, or as sweetness was the nature of the holy anointing oil, which was the principal type of the Holy Spirit in the Mosaic dispensation. Indeed, I may rather say that holiness is as much the proper nature of the Holy Spirit as sweetness was the nature of the sweet fragrance of that ointment. The Spirit of God so dwells in the hearts of the saints that there, as a seed or spring of life, he exerts and imparts himself in this sweet and divine nature of his. He makes the soul a partaker of God’s beauty and Christ’s joy, so that the saint truly has fellowship with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ, in having in this way the communion or participation of the Holy Spirit. The grace that is in the hearts of the saints is of the same nature as the divine holiness, as far as it is possible for a holiness that is infinitely less in degree to be. It is like the brightness of a diamond that the sun shines on, which is of the same nature as the brightness of the sun, except that it is as nothing to it in degree. That is why Christ says in John 3:6, “That which is born of the Spirit is spirit”; that is, the grace that is begotten in the hearts of the saints is something of the same nature as that Spirit, and so is properly called a spiritual nature, in the same way as what is born of the flesh is flesh, or what is born of corrupt nature is corrupt nature.

But the Spirit of God never influences the minds of natural men in this way. Though he may influence them in many ways, yet in none of his influences does he ever impart himself to them in his own proper nature. Indeed, he never acts in a way that disagrees with his nature, either on the minds of saints or of sinners. But the Spirit of God may act on men in agreement with his own nature without exerting his proper nature in the acts and exercises of their minds. The Spirit of God may act in such a way that his actions agree with his nature, and yet not impart himself at all in his proper nature in the effect of that action. For instance, the Spirit of God moved on the face of the waters, and there was nothing in that action that disagreed with his nature; yet he did not impart himself at all in that action. There was nothing of the proper nature of the Holy Spirit in that motion of the waters. And so he may act on the minds of men in many ways and not impart himself any more than when he acts on inanimate things.

So it is not only the manner of the relation of the Spirit, who is the one who works, to the subject of his working that is different: the Spirit works in the saints as dwelling in them, as an abiding principle of action, whereas he does not work on sinners in that way. The influence and working itself is also different, and the effect produced is exceedingly different. So not only are the persons called spiritual, as having the Spirit of God dwelling in them; the qualities, affections and experiences that the Spirit produces in them are also spiritual. In this they differ vastly, in their nature and kind, from everything a natural man is or can be the subject of while he remains in a natural state, and also from everything that men or devils can be the authors of. It is a spiritual work in this high sense, and therefore, above all other works, it belongs to the Spirit of God alone. There is no work so high and excellent. For there is no work in which God imparts himself so much, and in which the mere creature has, in so high a sense, a participation of God. So it is expressed in Scripture by the saints being made partakers of the divine nature (2 Pet 1:4); having God dwelling in them, and they in God (1 John 4:12, 15, 16, and ch. 3:24); having Christ in them (John 17:21; Rom 8:10); being the temples of the living God (2 Cor 6:16); living by Christ’s life (Gal 2:20); being made partakers of God’s holiness (Heb 12:10); having Christ’s love dwelling in them (John 17:26); having his joy fulfilled in them (John 17:13); seeing light in God’s light, and being made to drink of the river of God’s delights (Ps 36:8–9); having fellowship with God, or sharing and partaking with him (as the word signifies) (1 John 1:3). This does not mean that the saints are made partakers of the essence of God, and so are godded with God and christed with Christ, according to the abominable and blasphemous language and notions of some heretics. But, to use the Scripture’s phrase, they are made partakers of God’s fullness (Eph 3:17–19; John 1:16), that is, of God’s spiritual beauty and happiness, according to the measure and capacity of a creature; for it is evident that this is what the word fullness signifies in the language of Scripture. Grace in the hearts of the saints, then, is the most glorious work of God, in which he imparts of the goodness of his nature. So it is no doubt his own distinctive work, and in an eminent way above the power of all creatures. And the influences of the Spirit of God in this are peculiar to God in this way, and are those in which God, in so high a manner, imparts himself and makes the creature partaker of the divine nature (the Spirit of God imparting itself in its own proper nature). This is what I mean by influences that are divine, when I say that truly gracious affections arise from influences that are spiritual and divine.

Only the true saints have what is spiritual; others have nothing that is divine, in the sense that has been spoken of. Not only do they lack these impartings of the Spirit of God in so high a degree as the saints have them; they have nothing of that nature or kind. For the apostle James tells us that natural men do not have the Spirit. And Christ teaches the necessity of a new birth, or being born of the Spirit, from this: that he who is born of the flesh has only flesh, and no Spirit (John 3:6). They do not have the Spirit of God dwelling in them in any degree. For the apostle teaches that all who have the Spirit of God dwelling in them belong to Christ (Rom 8:9–11). And having the Spirit of God is spoken of as a certain sign that people will have the eternal inheritance, for it is spoken of as the earnest of it (2 Cor 1:22 and 5:5; Eph 1:14). And having anything of the Spirit is mentioned as a sure sign of being in Christ (1 John 4:13): “By this we know that we dwell in Him, because He has given us of His Spirit.” Ungodly men not only have less of the divine nature than the saints; they are not partakers of it at all, which implies that they have nothing of it. For being a partaker of the divine nature is spoken of as the special privilege of the true saints (2 Pet 1:4). Ungodly men are not partakers of God’s holiness (Heb 12:10). A natural man has no experience of any of the things that are spiritual. The apostle teaches us that he is so far from it that he knows nothing about them. He is a complete stranger to them; talk about such things is all foolishness and nonsense to him; he does not know what it means (1 Cor 2:14): “The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned.” And to the same purpose Christ teaches us that the world is wholly unacquainted with the Spirit of God (John 14:17): “the Spirit of truth. The world cannot receive Him, because it neither sees Him nor knows Him.” And it is further evident that natural men have nothing in them of the same nature as the true grace of the saints, because the apostle teaches us that those of them who go furthest in religion have no charity, or true Christian love (1 Cor chapter 13). So Christ elsewhere rebukes the Pharisees, those high pretenders to religion, because they did not have the love of God in them (John 5:42). So natural men have no communion or fellowship with Christ, no participation with him (as these words signify), for this is spoken of as the special privilege of the saints (1 John 1:3, together with verses 6–7; and 1 Cor 1:8–9). And the Scripture speaks of the actual existence of a gracious principle in the soul, even in its first beginning, as a seed planted there, as inconsistent with a man’s being a sinner (1 John 3:9). And natural men are represented in Scripture as having no spiritual light, no spiritual life, and no spiritual being. That is why conversion is often compared to opening the eyes of the blind, raising the dead, a work of creation (in which creatures are made entirely new), and becoming newborn children.

From these things it is evident that the gracious influences the saints are the subjects of, and the effects of God’s Spirit that they experience, are entirely above nature. They are altogether of a different kind from anything that men find within themselves by nature, or only in the exercise of natural principles. They are things to which no improvement of natural qualities or principles, no advancing or raising of them to higher degrees, and no kind of combining of them, will ever bring men. For they differ from what is natural, and from everything that natural men experience, not only in degree and circumstances, but also in kind, and are of a vastly more excellent nature. And this is what I mean by supernatural, when I say that gracious affections come from influences that are supernatural.

From this it follows that in the gracious exercises and affections produced in the minds of the saints through the saving influences of the Spirit of God, there is a new inward perception or sensation of their minds, entirely different in its nature and kind from anything their minds were ever the subjects of before they were sanctified. For suppose God by his mighty power produces something that is new, not only in degree and circumstances, but in its whole nature, something that could not be produced by any raising, varying or combining of what was there before, or by adding anything of the same kind. If God produces something new in this way in a mind, which is a perceiving, thinking, conscious thing, then no doubt something entirely new is felt, or perceived, or thought. Or, which is the same thing, there is some new sensation or perception of the mind, entirely of a new sort, which could not be produced by any raising, varying or combining of the kind of perceptions or sensations the mind had before. Or there is what some metaphysicians call a new simple idea. If grace is, in the sense described above, an entirely new kind of principle, then its exercises are also an entirely new kind of exercises. And if there are in the soul a new sort of exercises that it is conscious of, which the soul knew nothing of before, and which no improvement, combination or management of what it was conscious or aware of before could produce, nor anything like them, then it follows that the mind has an entirely new kind of perception or sensation. Here there is, as it were, a new spiritual sense that the mind has, or a principle of a new kind of perception or spiritual sensation, which in its whole nature is different from any former kinds of sensation of the mind, as tasting is different from any of the other senses. And in the exercise of this new sense of mind, a true saint perceives something in spiritual and divine things as entirely different from anything natural men perceive in them as the sweet taste of honey is different from the ideas men get of honey by only looking at it and feeling it. So the spiritual perceptions that a sanctified and spiritual person has are different from all that natural men have, not only in the way the ideas or perceptions of the same sense may differ from one another, but rather as the ideas and sensations of different senses differ. That is why the work of the Spirit of God in regeneration is often compared in Scripture to giving a new sense: giving eyes to see and ears to hear, unstopping the ears of the deaf, opening the eyes of those who were born blind, and turning from darkness to light. And because this spiritual sense is immensely the most noble and excellent, and without it all other principles of perception and all our faculties are useless and vain, the giving of this new sense, with its blessed fruits and effects in the soul, is compared to raising the dead and to a new creation.

This new spiritual sense, and the new dispositions that attend it, are not new faculties, but new principles of nature. I use the word principles for want of a word with a more definite meaning. By a principle of nature in this place I mean the foundation laid in nature, either old or new, for any particular manner or kind of exercise of the faculties of the soul; or a natural habit or foundation for action, giving a person ability and disposition to exert the faculties in exercises of a certain kind, so that to exert the faculties in that kind of exercises may be said to be his nature. So this new spiritual sense is not a new faculty of understanding, but a new foundation laid in the nature of the soul for a new kind of exercises of the same faculty of understanding. In the same way, the new holy disposition of heart that attends this new sense is not a new faculty of will, but a foundation laid in the nature of the soul for a new kind of exercises of the same faculty of will.

The Spirit of God, in all his operations on the minds of natural men, only moves, impresses, assists, improves, or in some way acts on natural principles; he gives no new spiritual principle. So when the Spirit of God gives a natural man visions, as he did Balaam, he only impresses a natural principle, namely the sense of sight, directly stirring up ideas of that sense. But he gives no new sense, and there is nothing supernatural, spiritual or divine in it. So too, if the Spirit of God impresses on a man’s imagination, either in a dream or when he is awake, any outward ideas of any of the senses, whether voices or shapes and colors, it is only stirring up ideas of the same kind that he has by natural principles and senses. So too, if God reveals to a natural man some secret fact, for instance something that he will later see or hear, this is not infusing or exercising any new spiritual principle, or giving the ideas of any new spiritual sense. It is only impressing, in an extraordinary way, the ideas that will later be received by sight and hearing. So also in the more ordinary influences of the Spirit of God on the hearts of sinners, he only assists natural principles to do to a greater degree the same work that they do of themselves by nature. So the Spirit of God by his common influences may assist men’s natural ingenuity, as he assisted Bezalel and Oholiab in the skilled works of the tabernacle. So he may assist men’s natural abilities in political affairs, and improve their courage and other natural qualities, as he is said to have put his Spirit on the seventy elders, and on Saul, so as to give him another heart. So God may greatly assist natural men’s reason in their reasoning about worldly things or about the doctrines of religion, and may greatly advance the clearness of their perceptions and notions of the things of religion in many respects, without giving any spiritual sense. So in the awakenings and convictions that natural men may have, God only assists conscience, which is a natural principle, to do to a further degree the work it does naturally. Conscience naturally gives men a grasp of right and wrong, and suggests the connection there is between right and wrong and a retribution. The Spirit of God assists men’s consciences to do this to a greater degree, and helps conscience against the numbing influence of worldly objects and of their lusts. And many other ways might be mentioned in which the Spirit acts on, assists and moves natural principles. But after all, it is no more than nature moved, acted on and improved; there is nothing supernatural and divine here. But the Spirit of God, in his spiritual influences on the hearts of his saints, works by infusing or exercising new, divine and supernatural principles: principles that are truly a new and spiritual nature, and vastly more noble and excellent than anything in natural men.

From what has been said it follows that all spiritual and gracious affections are attended by, and arise from, some perception, idea or sensation of mind that in its whole nature is different, indeed exceedingly different, from anything that is or can be in the mind of a natural man. The natural man discerns nothing of it and has no idea of it at all (as 1 Cor 2:14 says). He can conceive of it no more than a man without the sense of taste can conceive of the sweet taste of honey, or a man without the sense of hearing can conceive of the melody of a tune, or a man born blind can have a notion of the beauty of the rainbow.

But here two things must be observed in order to understand this rightly.

[1.] On the one hand it must be observed that not everything that in any respect belongs to spiritual affections is new and entirely different from what natural men can conceive of and do experience. Some things are common to gracious affections and other affections; many circumstances, accompaniments and effects are common. So a saint’s love to God has a great many things belonging to it that it shares with a man’s natural love for a near relative. Love to God makes a man desire the honor of God and desire to please him; so a natural man’s love for his friend makes him desire his friend’s honor and desire to please him. Love to God causes a man to delight in thoughts of God, to delight in the presence of God, and to desire conformity to God and the enjoyment of God; and so it is with a man’s love for his friend. And many other things might be mentioned that are common to both. Yet the idea the saint has of the loveliness of God, and the sensation and the kind of delight he has in that view, which is, as it were, the marrow and quintessence of his love, is peculiar to him, and entirely different from anything a natural man has or can have any notion of. And even in the things that seem to be common there is something distinctive. Both spiritual love and natural love cause desires for the object loved, but they are not the same sort of desires. There is a sensation of soul in the spiritual desires of one who loves God that is entirely different from all natural desires. Both spiritual love and natural love are attended by delight in the object loved, but the sensations of delight are not the same; they are entirely and exceedingly different. Natural men may have conceptions of many things about spiritual affections. But there is something in them, which is, as it were, their nucleus or kernel, of which natural men have no more conception than one born blind has of colors.

It may be clearly illustrated in this way. Suppose two men: one is born without the sense of taste, and the other has it. The second loves honey and is greatly delighted in it, because he knows its sweet taste; the first loves certain sounds and colors. The love of each has many things belonging to it that are common: it causes both of them to desire and delight in the object loved, causes grief when it is absent, and so on. Yet the idea or sensation that the one who knows the taste of honey has of its excellence and sweetness, which is the foundation of his love, is entirely different from anything the other has or can have. And the delight he has in honey is wholly different from anything the other can conceive of, though they both delight in the objects they love. So too, both these persons may in some respects love the same object. The one may love a delicious kind of fruit, which is beautiful to the eye and delicious to the taste, not only because he has seen its pleasant colors, but because he knows its sweet taste. The other, completely ignorant of this, loves it only for its beautiful colors. There are many things that seem in some respect to be common to both: both love, both desire, and both delight. But the love and desire and delight of the one is altogether different from that of the other. The difference between the love of a natural man and that of a spiritual man is like this, except that it must be observed that in one respect it is vastly greater. That is, the kinds of excellence these different kinds of persons perceive in spiritual objects are in themselves vastly more different than the different kinds of excellence perceived in delicious fruit by a man who tastes and a man who has no taste. And in another respect it may not be so great: the spiritual man may have a spiritual sense or taste to perceive that divine and most distinctive excellence only in small beginnings and in a very imperfect degree.

[2.] On the other hand, it must be observed that a natural man may have religious perceptions and affections that are in many respects very new and surprising to him, things he had not conceived of before; and yet what he experiences may be nothing like the exercises of a principle of new nature, or the sensations of a new spiritual sense. His affections may be very new, by natural principles being moved in an extraordinary way, to a very new degree, with a great many new circumstances, a new cooperation of natural affections, and a new combination of ideas. This may come from some extraordinarily powerful influence of Satan and some great delusion; but there is nothing in it except nature acted on in an extraordinary way. Suppose a poor man who had always lived in a cottage, and had never looked beyond the obscure village where he was born, were taken as a joke to a magnificent city and a prince’s court. Suppose he were dressed there in princely robes and set on the throne, with the royal crown on his head and peers and nobles bowing before him, and were made to believe that he was now a glorious monarch. The ideas he would have and the affections he would experience would in many respects be very new, such as he had never imagined before. But all of it is no more than natural principles raised and stirred in an extraordinary way, and ideas of the sort he has by nature newly heightened, varied and combined. There is nothing here like giving him a new sense.

On the whole, I think it is clearly evident that all truly gracious affections arise from special and distinctive influences of the Spirit, producing in the souls of the saints a felt effect or sensation that is entirely different from anything it is possible for a natural man to experience, different not only in degree and circumstances, but in its whole nature. So a natural man not only cannot experience what is individually the same; he cannot experience anything except what is exceedingly different from it, and immensely below it, in its kind. And it is something that the power of men or devils is not sufficient to produce, nor anything like it, nor anything of the same nature.

I have dwelt at length on this matter because it is of great importance and use for clearly exposing and demonstrating the delusions of Satan in many kinds of false religious affections, by which multitudes are deluded, and probably have been in all ages of the Christian church; and for settling and determining many articles of doctrine concerning the operations of the Spirit of God and the nature of true grace.

Now therefore, to apply these things to the purpose of this discourse.

From this it appears that impressions some have made on their imagination, or the imaginary ideas they have of God, or Christ, or heaven, or anything belonging to religion, have nothing in them that is spiritual or of the nature of true grace. Though such things may attend what is spiritual and be mixed with it, yet in themselves they have nothing spiritual, nor are they any part of gracious experience.

Here, for the sake of the common people, I will explain what is meant by impressions on the imagination and imaginary ideas. The imagination is the power of the mind by which it can have a conception or idea of things of an external or outward nature (that is, of the sort of things that are the objects of the outward senses) when those things are not present and are not perceived by the senses. It is called imagination from the word image, because by it a person can have an image of some external thing in his mind when that thing is not present in reality, nor anything like it. All the kinds of things we perceive by our five external senses, seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and feeling, are external things. When a person has an idea or image of any of these sorts of things in his mind when they are not there, and when he does not really see, hear, smell, taste or feel them, that is to have an imagination of them, and these ideas are imaginary ideas. And when such ideas are strongly impressed on the mind, and their image in the mind is very lively, almost as if one saw them or heard them, and so on, that is called an impression on the imagination. So colors and shapes and the form of a face are outward things, because they are the sort of things that are the objects of the outward sense of sight. And therefore when anyone has in his mind a lively idea of any shape or color or form of a face, that is to have an imagination of those things. So too, if he has an idea of the sort of light or darkness that he perceives by the sense of sight, that is to have an idea of outward light, and so it is an imagination. So too, if he has an idea of any marks made on paper, say letters and words written in a book, that is to have an external and imaginary idea of the kind of things we sometimes perceive with our bodily eyes. And when we have ideas of the kind of things we perceive by any of the other senses, such as sounds or voices or spoken words, this is only to have ideas of outward things, namely of the kind of things perceived by the external sense of hearing, and so that also is imagination. And when these ideas are vividly impressed, almost as if they were really heard with the ears, this is to have an impression on the imagination. And so I might go on and give examples of the ideas of things belonging to the other three senses, smelling, tasting and feeling.

Many who have had such things have very ignorantly supposed them to be of the nature of spiritual manifestations. They have had lively ideas of some external shape and the beautiful form of a face, and this they call spiritually seeing Christ. Some have had ideas of a great outward light impressed on them, and this they call a spiritual manifestation of God’s or Christ’s glory. Some have had ideas of Christ hanging on the cross, with his blood running from his wounds, and this they call a spiritual sight of Christ crucified and of the way of salvation by his blood. Some have seen him with his arms open, ready to embrace them, and this they call a manifestation of the sufficiency of Christ’s grace and love. Some have had lively ideas of heaven, and of Christ on his throne there, and shining ranks of saints and angels, and this they call seeing heaven opened to them. Some have had, from time to time, a lively idea of a person with a beautiful face smiling on them, and this they call a spiritual manifestation of the love of Christ to their souls, and tasting the love of Christ. And they consider it sufficient evidence that these things are spiritual manifestations, and that they see them spiritually, because, they say, they do not see these things with their bodily eyes but in their hearts, for they can see them when their eyes are shut. In the same way, the imaginations of some have been impressed with ideas of the sense of hearing. They have had ideas of words, as if they were spoken to them, sometimes the words of Scripture and sometimes other words. They have had ideas of Christ speaking comforting words to them. These things they have called having the inward call of Christ, hearing the voice of Christ spiritually in their hearts, having the witness of the Spirit, and the inward testimony of the love of Christ, and so on.

The common sort of people, who are less thoughtful and understanding, are the more easily led to think that these things are spiritual things, for this reason: spiritual things are invisible, and not things that can be pointed out with the finger, so we are forced to use figurative expressions in speaking of them, and to borrow names from external and perceptible objects to signify them. So we call a clear perception of spiritual things by the name of light, and having such an apprehension of this or that thing by the name of seeing it. And the conviction of the judgment and the persuasion of the will by the word of Christ in the gospel we signify by spiritually hearing the call of Christ. And the Scripture itself abounds with figurative expressions of this kind. People hear these used often, and have pressed on them the necessity of having their eyes opened, having a manifestation of spiritual things, seeing Christ in his glory, having the inward call, and the like. So they ignorantly look and wait for some such external manifestations and imaginary views as have been spoken of. And when they have them, they are confident that now their eyes are opened, now Christ has revealed himself to them, and they are his children. So they are exceedingly moved and elated by their deliverance and happiness, and many kinds of affections are set in violent motion in them all at once.

But it is exceedingly plain that such ideas have nothing in them that is spiritual and divine, in the sense in which it has been demonstrated that all gracious experiences are spiritual and divine. These external ideas are in no way of such a sort that they are entirely, and in their whole nature, different from everything men have by nature, completely different from and vastly above any sensation a man can possibly have by any natural sense or principle, so that, in order to have any sensations of that sort, a man must be given a new spiritual and divine sense. Far from it: they are ideas of the same sort we have by the external senses, which are among the inferior powers of human nature. They are merely ideas of external objects, or ideas of that nature, of the same outward, sensory kind. They are the same sort of sensations of mind (differing not in degree, but only in circumstances) that we have by the natural principles we share with the beasts, namely the five external senses. It is a low, miserable notion of spiritual sense to suppose that it is only conceiving or imagining the sort of ideas we have by our animal senses, senses that the beasts have in as great perfection as we do. It is, as it were, turning Christ, or the divine nature in the soul, into a mere animal. Nothing is lacking in the soul, as it is by nature, to make it capable of being the subject of all these external ideas without any new principles. A natural man is capable of having an idea, and a lively idea, of shapes and colors and sounds when they are absent, and as capable as a regenerate man is; so there is nothing supernatural in them. And it is known by abundant experience that it is not the advancing or perfecting of human nature that makes people more capable of having such lively and strong imaginary ideas. On the contrary, weakness of body and mind, and diseases of the body, make people far more susceptible to such impressions38.

As to a truly spiritual sensation, not only is the way it comes into the mind extraordinary, but the sensation itself is totally different from anything men have or can have in a state of nature, as has been shown. But as to these external ideas, though the way they come into the mind is sometimes unusual, the ideas in themselves are not the better for that. They are still of no different sort from what men have by their senses; they are of no higher kind, and not a bit better. For instance, the external idea a man has now of Christ hanging on the cross and shedding his blood is no better in itself than the external idea the Jews, his enemies, had, who stood around his cross and saw this with their bodily eyes. The imaginary idea men have now of an external brightness and glory of God is no better than the idea the wicked congregation in the wilderness had of the external glory of the Lord at Mount Sinai, when they saw it with bodily eyes. Nor is it any better than the idea that millions of cursed reprobates will have of the external glory of Christ at the day of judgment, who will see, and have a very lively idea of, an external glory of Christ ten thousand times greater than was ever yet conceived in any man’s imagination39. Indeed, the image of Christ that men conceive in their imaginations is not, in its own nature, of any higher kind than the idea the Papists conceive of Christ from the beautiful and moving images of him they see in their churches (though the way they receive the idea may not be so bad). Nor are the affections men have, if they are built primarily on such imaginations, any better than the affections raised in ignorant people by the sight of those images, which are often very great, especially when these images, through the craft of the priests, are made to move and speak and weep, and the like40. The mere way in which people receive these imaginary ideas does not alter the nature of the ideas themselves that are received. Let them be received in whatever way they may, they are still only external ideas, or ideas of outward appearances, and so they are not spiritual. Indeed, if men should actually receive such external ideas by the immediate power of the Most High God on their minds, they would not be spiritual; they would be no more than a common work of the Spirit of God. This is evident in fact in the case of Balaam. God himself impressed on his mind a clear and lively outward representation or idea of Jesus Christ, as the star rising out of Jacob, when he heard the words of God, and knew the knowledge of the Most High, and saw the vision of the Almighty, falling into a trance (Num 24:16–17). Yet he had no spiritual manifestation of Christ of any kind. That morning star never rose spiritually in his heart, for he was only a natural man.

And as these external ideas have nothing divine or spiritual in their nature, and nothing but what natural men are capable of without any new principles, so there is nothing in their nature that requires, for their production, that distinctive, inimitable and unparalleled exercise of the glorious power of God which, as has been shown, there is in the production of true grace. There appears to be nothing in their nature above the power of the devil. It is certainly not above the power of Satan to suggest thoughts to men, for otherwise he could not tempt them to sin. And if he can suggest any thoughts or ideas at all, no doubt imaginary ones, or ideas of external things, are not above his power41; for the external ideas men have are the lowest sort of ideas. These ideas may be raised merely by impressions made on the body, by moving the animal spirits and impressing the brain. Abundant experience certainly shows that changes in the body will stir up imaginary or external ideas in the mind, as often happens in a high fever, melancholy, and so on. These external ideas are as far below the more intellectual exercises of the soul as the body is a less noble part of man than the soul.

And not only is there nothing in the nature of these external ideas, or imaginations of outward appearances, from which we can infer that they are above the power of the devil; it is also certain that the devil can stir up such ideas, and has often done so. They were external ideas that he stirred up in the dreams and visions of the false prophets of old, who were under the influence of lying spirits, whom we often read of in Scripture, as in Deut 13:1; 1 Kgs 22:22; Isa 28:7; Ezek 13:7; Zech 13:4. And they were external ideas that he often stirred up in the minds of the heathen priests, magicians and sorcerers in their visions and ecstasies. And they were external ideas that he stirred up in the mind of the man Christ Jesus when he showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, when those kingdoms were not really in sight.

And if Satan, or any created being, has power to impress the mind with outward representations, then no particular sort of outward representation can be any evidence of a divine power. Almighty power is no more required to represent the shape of a man to the imagination than the shape of anything else. No higher kind of power is needed to form one bodily shape or color in the brain than another. It takes no more glorious power to represent the form of a man’s body than the form of a chip or a block, even if it is a very beautiful human body, with a sweet smile on its face, or arms open, or blood running from hands, feet and side. The sort of power that can represent black or darkness to the imagination can also represent white and shining brightness. The power and skill that can paint a straw or a stick of wood well and exactly on a piece of paper or canvas will be enough, the same in kind, only perhaps further developed, to paint the body of a man with great beauty and in royal majesty, or a magnificent city paved with gold, full of brightness, and a glorious throne, and so on. So it takes no more than the same sort of power to paint the one of these on the brain as the other. The same sort of power that can put ink on paper can put on gold leaf. So it is evident to a demonstration, if we suppose it is in the devil’s power to make any sort of external representation at all on the imagination (as no doubt it is, and no one who believed there was a devil with any agency among mankind ever questioned it): I say, if this is so, it is demonstrably evident that a created power may extend to all kinds of external appearances and ideas in the mind.

From this it again clearly appears that no such things have anything in them that is spiritual, supernatural and divine, in the sense in which it has been proved that all truly gracious experiences are. And though external ideas, because of man’s make and frame, ordinarily attend spiritual experiences in some degree, yet these ideas are no part of the spiritual experience, any more than the motion of the blood and the beating of the pulse that attend experiences are a part of spiritual experience. And no doubt, through men’s infirmity in the present state, and especially through the weak constitution of some people, gracious affections that are very strong do stir up lively ideas in the imagination. Yet it is also beyond doubt that when people’s affections are founded on imaginations, which is often the case, those affections are merely natural and common, because they are built on a foundation that is not spiritual. And so they are entirely different from gracious affections, which, as has been proved, always arise from operations that are spiritual and divine.

These imaginations often raise men’s carnal affections to an exceedingly great height42. And no wonder, when those who have them are ignorantly but without doubt persuaded that they are divine manifestations, which the great Jehovah makes directly to their souls, giving them in an extraordinary way testimonies of his high and special favor.

Again, from what has been observed and proved about the way in which gracious operations and effects in the heart are spiritual, supernatural and divine, it is evident that the immediate suggesting of words of Scripture to the mind has nothing in it that is spiritual.

I have had occasion to say something about this already, and what has been said may be enough to prove it. But if the reader keeps in mind what has been said about the nature of spiritual influences and effects, it will be still more abundantly evident that this is no spiritual effect. For I suppose there is no person of common understanding who will say or imagine that bringing words to the mind (whatever words they may be) is an effect of a kind that the mind of a natural man, while he remains in a state of nature, cannot possibly be the subject of, or anything like it; or that it requires any new divine sense in the soul; or that bringing sounds or letters to the mind is an effect of so high, holy and excellent a nature that no created power can possibly be its cause.

Suggesting words of Scripture to the mind is only stirring up in the mind ideas of certain sounds or letters, and so it is only one way of stirring up ideas in the imagination; for sounds and letters are external things, the objects of the external senses of sight and hearing. Ideas of certain marks on paper, such as any of the twenty-four letters in whatever order, or any sounds of the voice, are just as much external ideas as ideas of any other shapes or sounds whatever. And therefore, by what has already been said about these external ideas, it is evident that they are nothing spiritual. And if at any time the Spirit of God suggests these letters or sounds to the mind, this is a common influence of that Spirit, and not any special or gracious one. And therefore it follows from what has already been proved that the affections that have this effect for their foundation are not spiritual or gracious affections. But let it be noted what it is I am saying, namely: when this effect, the immediate and extraordinary manner of words of Scripture coming to the mind, is what stirs up the affections, and is properly their foundation, then these affections are not spiritual. It may be that people have gracious affections that go along with Scriptures that come to their minds, and the Spirit of God may make use of those Scriptures to stir them up.
