That is the case when what stirs up their affections is some spiritual sense, taste or relish they have of the divine and excellent things contained in those Scriptures, and not the extraordinary and sudden way the words are brought to their minds. They are moved by the instruction they receive from the words, and by the view of the glorious things of God or Christ, and the things belonging to them, that the words contain and teach. They are not moved because the words came suddenly, as though some person had spoken them to them, and they concluded from this that God was, as it were, speaking to them directly. People are often exceedingly moved on this foundation. The words of some great and high promises of Scripture come suddenly to their minds, and they regard the words as directed by God immediately to them, as though the words came out of the mouth of God at that moment, spoken to them. So they take it as a voice from God, immediately revealing to them their happy situation and promising this or that great thing to them; and this is what moves and elates them. There is no new spiritual understanding of the divine things contained in the Scripture, nor any new spiritual sense of the glorious things taught in that part of the Bible, going before their affection and being its foundation. All the new understanding they have, or think they have, as the foundation of their affection is this: that the words are spoken to them, because they come so suddenly and extraordinarily. And so this affection is built wholly on the sand, because it is built on a conclusion for which they have no foundation. For, as has been shown, the sudden coming of the words to their minds is no evidence that their being brought to their minds in that way was from God. And even if it were true that God brought the words to their minds, and they knew it with certainty, that would not be spiritual knowledge; it may exist without any spiritual sense. Balaam might know that the words God suggested to him were indeed suggested to him by God, and yet have no spiritual knowledge. So the affections that are built on the notion that texts of Scripture are sent immediately from God are built on no spiritual foundation, and are vain and delusive. If people whose affections are raised in this way were asked whether they have any new sense of the excellence of the things contained in those Scriptures, they would probably say yes, without hesitation. But it is true in no other way than this: once they have taken up the notion that the words are spoken directly to them, that makes the words seem sweet to them, and they acknowledge the things these Scriptures say to them to be excellent and wonderful things. For instance, suppose these were the words suddenly brought to their minds: “Do not be afraid, … it is your+ Father’s good pleasure to give you+ the kingdom.” They have confidently taken up the notion that the words were, as it were, spoken directly from heaven to them, as an immediate revelation that God was their Father and had given the kingdom to them. So they are greatly moved by it, and the words seem sweet to them. And oh, they say, what excellent things are contained in those words! But the only reason the promise seems excellent to them is that they think it is made directly to them. All the sense they have of any glory in the words comes only from self-love, and from their own imagined share in them. It is not that they had any view or sense of the holy and glorious nature of the kingdom of heaven, and of the spiritual glory of the God who gives it, and of his excellent grace to sinful men in offering and giving them this kingdom of his own good pleasure, going before their imagined share in these things and their being moved by them, and being the foundation of their affection and of their hope of a share in them. On the contrary, they first imagine they have a share in it, and then are highly moved by that, and then can acknowledge these things to be excellent. So the sudden and extraordinary way the Scriptures come to their minds is plainly the first foundation of the whole. This is clear evidence of the wretched delusion they are under.

The first comfort of many people, and what they call their conversion, comes in this way. After awakening and terrors, some comforting, sweet promise comes suddenly and wonderfully to their minds, and the way it comes makes them conclude that it comes from God to them. And this is the very thing that is the whole foundation of their faith and hope and comfort. From this they take their first encouragement to trust in God and in Christ, because they think that God, by some Scripture brought in this way, has now already revealed to them that he loves them, and has already promised them eternal life. This is very absurd. For everyone with a common knowledge of the principles of religion knows that it is God’s way to reveal his love to men, and their share in the promises, after they have believed, and not before; because they must first believe before they have any share in the promises to be revealed. The Spirit of God is a Spirit of truth, and not of lies. He does not bring Scriptures to men’s minds to reveal to them that they have a share in God’s favor and promises when they have none, because they have not yet believed. Yet this would be the case if God’s bringing texts of Scripture to men’s minds to reveal to them that their sins were forgiven, or that it was God’s pleasure to give them the kingdom, or anything of that kind, went before their first faith and was its foundation. No promise of the covenant of grace belongs to any man until he has first believed in Christ. For it is by faith alone that we come to have a share in Christ and in the promises of the new covenant made in him. And therefore whatever spirit applies the promises of that covenant to a person who has not first believed, as being already his, must be a lying spirit; and the faith that is first built on such an application of promises is built on a lie. It is not God’s way to bring comforting texts of Scripture to give men assurance of his love, and that they will be happy, before they have had a faith of dependence43. And if the Scripture that comes to a person’s mind is not properly a promise so much as an invitation, yet if he makes the sudden or unusual way the invitation came to his mind the ground on which he believes he is invited, it is not true faith, because it is built on what is not the true ground of faith. True faith is built on no uncertain foundation. But a judgment that the words of a particular text were suggested to the mind by the immediate power of God at a certain time, as though they were then spoken and directed by God to him, because the words came in a certain way, is a wholly uncertain and unreliable judgment, as has now been shown. And therefore it is a false and sandy foundation for faith, and accordingly the faith built on it is false. The only certain foundation any person has for believing that he is invited to partake of the blessings of the gospel is that the word of God declares that people qualified as he is are invited, and the God who declares it is true and cannot lie. If a sinner is once convinced of the truthfulness of God, and that the Scriptures are his word, he will need nothing more to convince and satisfy him that he is invited. For the Scriptures are full of invitations to sinners, to the chief of sinners, to come and partake of the benefits of the gospel. He will not need any new speaking of God to him; what God has already spoken will be enough for him.

As the first comfort of many people, and their affections at the time of their supposed conversion, are built on grounds like those just mentioned, so are their joys and hopes and other affections from time to time afterward. They often have particular words of Scripture, sweet declarations and promises, suggested to them, which, because of the way they come, they think are sent immediately from God to them at that time. They regard this as their warrant to take them, and they actually make it the main ground of applying them to themselves, of the comfort they take in them, and of the confidence they receive from them. So they imagine that a kind of conversation is carried on between God and them, and that God from time to time, as it were, speaks to them directly, satisfies their doubts, testifies his love to them, promises them support and supplies and his blessing in this or that case, and reveals to them clearly their share in eternal blessings. And so they are often elated, and have a run of sudden and tumultuous kinds of joy, mingled with a strong confidence and a high opinion of themselves. Yet in fact the main ground of these joys and this confidence is not anything contained in or taught by these Scriptures as they stand in the Bible, but the way they came to them. This is certain evidence of their delusion. There is no particular promise in the word of God that is the saint’s, or is made or spoken to him, in any other way than all the promises of the covenant of grace are his, and are made and spoken to him44. It is true that some of these promises may be more especially suited to his case than others, and God by his Spirit may enable him to understand some better than others, and to have a greater sense of the preciousness and glory and suitableness of the blessings contained in them.

But here some may be ready to say, “What! Is there no such thing as a particular spiritual application of the promises of Scripture by the Spirit of God?” I answer, there is no doubt such a thing as a spiritual and saving application of the invitations and promises of Scripture to the souls of men. But it is also certain that its nature is wholly misunderstood by many people, to the great ensnaring of their own souls, and giving Satan a vast advantage against them, and against the interest of religion and the church of God. The spiritual application of a promise of Scripture does not consist in its being immediately suggested to the thoughts by some outside agent, and borne into the mind with a strong persuasion that it is spoken and directed particularly to them at that time. There is nothing of the evidence of the hand of God in this effect, as events have proved in many notorious instances. It is a poor notion of a spiritual application of Scripture. There is nothing at all in its nature beyond the power of the devil, if he is not restrained by God; for there is nothing in the nature of the effect that is spiritual, implying any vital imparting of God. A truly spiritual application of the word of God is of a vastly higher nature, as far above the devil’s power as it is to apply the word of God to a dead corpse so as to raise it to life, or to a stone so as to turn it into an angel. A spiritual application of the word of God consists in applying it to the heart, in spiritually enlightening, sanctifying influences. A spiritual application of an invitation or offer of the gospel consists in giving the soul a spiritual sense or relish of the holy and divine blessings offered. It gives a sense also of the sweet and wonderful grace of the one who offers them, in making so gracious an offer, and of his holy excellence and faithfulness to fulfill what he offers, and his glorious sufficiency for it. So it leads and draws out the heart to embrace the offer, and in this way gives the man evidence of his title to the thing offered. And in the same way, a spiritual application of the promises of Scripture, for the comfort of the saints, consists in enlightening their minds to see the holy excellence and sweetness of the blessings promised, and also the holy excellence of the one who promises, and his faithfulness and sufficiency. So it draws out their hearts to embrace the one who promises and the thing promised; and by this means it gives the felt actings of grace, enabling them to see their grace, and so their title to the promise. An application that does not consist in this divine sense and enlightening of the mind, but consists only in the words being borne into the thoughts as if they were spoken directly at that moment, and so makes people believe, on no other foundation, that the promise is theirs, is a blind application. It belongs to the spirit of darkness, and not of light.

When people have their affections raised in this way, those affections are really not raised by the word of God; the Scripture is not their foundation. It is not anything contained in the Scriptures that come to their minds that raises their affections. It is in fact that effect, namely the strange way the words were suggested to their minds, and a proposition they take up from it which is not actually contained in that Scripture or in any other: such as that his sins are forgiven him, or that it is the Father’s good pleasure to give him in particular the kingdom, or the like. There are propositions to be found in the Bible declaring that people with such and such qualifications are forgiven and loved by God. But there are no propositions to be found in the Bible declaring that such and such particular persons are forgiven and loved by God, apart from any previous knowledge of any qualifications. And therefore when any person is comforted and moved by any such proposition, it is by another word, a newly coined word, and not by any word of God contained in the Bible.45 And so many people are moved in vain and deluded.

Again, it plainly appears from what has been demonstrated that no revelation of secret facts by immediate suggestion is anything spiritual and divine, in the sense in which gracious effects and operations are.

By secret facts I mean things that have been done, or have come to pass, or will come to pass hereafter, which are secret in the sense that they do not appear to the senses, and are not known by any reasoning or any evidence to reason, nor in any other way, but only by revelation, by the immediate suggestion of the ideas of them to the mind. For instance, suppose it were revealed to me that next year this land would be invaded by a fleet from France, or that such and such persons would then be converted, or that I myself would then be converted. Suppose this were done not by enabling me to reason out these events from anything that now appears in providence, but by immediately suggesting and bearing in on my mind, in an extraordinary way, the perception or ideas of these facts, with a strong suggestion or impression on my mind, which I had no hand in myself, that these things would come to pass. Or suppose it were revealed to me that a battle is being fought today between the armies of such and such powers in Europe; or that such a prince in Europe was converted today, or is now in a converted state, having been converted before; or that one of my neighbors is converted, or that I myself am converted. Suppose I had no other evidence of any of these facts from which to reason them out, but only an immediate, extraordinary suggestion or stirring up of these ideas, and a strong impression of them on my mind. This is a revelation of secret facts by immediate suggestion just as much as if the facts were future. For whether the facts are past, present or future does not alter the case, as long as they are secret and hidden from my senses and reason, not spoken of in Scripture, and not known by me in any other way than by immediate suggestion. If it is revealed to me that such a revolution has come to pass today in the Ottoman empire, it is the very same sort of revelation as if it were revealed to me that such a revolution would come to pass there a year from today. For though one is present and the other future, both are equally hidden from me, except by immediate revelation. When Samuel told Saul that the donkeys he went to look for had been found, and that his father had stopped worrying about the donkeys and was worrying about him, this was by the same kind of revelation as that by which he told Saul that in the plain of Tabor three men going up to God at Bethel would meet him (1 Sam 10:2–3), though one of these things was future and the other was not. So when Elisha told the king of Israel the words that the king of Syria spoke in his bedroom, it was by the same kind of revelation as that by which he foretold many things to come.

It is evident that this revelation of secret facts by immediate suggestion has nothing of the nature of a spiritual and divine operation, in the sense mentioned above. There is nothing at all in the nature of the perceptions or ideas themselves that are stirred up in the mind that is divinely excellent, and so is far above all the ideas of natural men, though the way the ideas are stirred up is extraordinary. In things that are spiritual, as has been shown, not only the way the effect is produced, but the effect produced is divine, and so vastly above anything that can be in an unsanctified mind. Now simply having an idea of facts, setting aside the way those ideas are produced, is nothing beyond what the minds of wicked men are capable of without any goodness in them. And all of them either have, or will have, the knowledge of the truth of the greatest and most important facts that have been, are, or will be.

And as to the extraordinary way of producing the ideas or perception of facts, by immediate suggestion, there is nothing in it but what the minds of natural men, while they are still natural men, are capable of, as is evident in Balaam and others spoken of in the Scripture. And therefore it appears that there is nothing belonging to this immediate suggestion of secret facts that is spiritual, in the sense in which it has been proved that gracious operations are spiritual. If there is nothing in the ideas themselves that is holy and divine, and so nothing but what may be in a mind not sanctified, then God can put them into the mind by immediate power without sanctifying it. There is nothing in the idea of a rainbow itself that is of a holy and divine nature, so nothing prevents an unsanctified mind from receiving that idea. So God, if he pleases and when he pleases, may stir up that idea in an unsanctified mind immediately, and in an extraordinary way. So too, there is nothing in the idea or knowledge that such and such particular persons are forgiven and accepted by God and entitled to heaven but what unsanctified minds may have, and will have, concerning many people at the day of judgment. So God can, if he pleases, suggest this to an unsanctified mind now, and impress it on it, extraordinarily and immediately. No principle is lacking in an unsanctified mind to make it capable of such a suggestion or impression; nor is there anything in such minds to exclude such a suggestion or necessarily to hinder it.

And if these suggestions of secret facts are accompanied by texts of Scripture, immediately and extraordinarily brought to mind, about some other facts that seem similar in some respects, that does not make the operation spiritual and divine in nature. For that suggestion of words of Scripture is no more divine than the suggestion of the facts themselves, as has just been demonstrated. And two effects together, neither of which is spiritual, cannot make up one combined effect that is spiritual.

So it follows, from what has already been shown and often repeated, that affections properly founded on such immediate suggestions, or supposed suggestions, of secret facts are not gracious affections. It is possible that such suggestions may be the occasion, or accidental cause, of gracious affections, for a mistake and a delusion may be that. But such a suggestion is never properly the foundation of gracious affections. For gracious affections, as has been shown, are all the effects of an influence and operation that is spiritual, supernatural and divine. But there are many affections, and high affections, that some people have which have suggestions or revelations of this kind for their very foundation. They regard these as spiritual manifestations, which is a gross delusion; and this delusion is truly the spring from which their affections flow.

Here it may be proper to observe that it is exceedingly evident from what has been said that what many people call the witness of the Spirit that they are the children of God has nothing spiritual and divine in it, and consequently that the affections built on it are vain and delusive. What many call the witness of the Spirit is nothing other than an immediate suggestion and impression of the fact, otherwise secret, that they are converted, or made the children of God, and so that their sins are pardoned and that God has given them a title to heaven. This kind of knowledge, namely, knowing that a certain person is converted, delivered from hell, and entitled to heaven, is not a divine sort of knowledge in itself. This sort of fact does not require any higher or more divine kind of suggestion to impress it on the mind than any other fact that Balaam had impressed on his mind. It requires no higher sort of idea or sensation for a man to have the perception of his own conversion impressed on him than to have the apprehension of his neighbor’s conversion impressed on him in the same way. But God, if he pleased, might impress the knowledge of this fact, that he had forgiven his neighbor’s sins and given him a title to heaven, as well as any other fact, without any imparting of his holiness. The excellence and importance of the fact does not at all prevent a natural man’s mind from being capable of an immediate suggestion and impression of it. Balaam had facts as excellent and important and glorious as this impressed immediately on his mind, without any gracious influence: in particular, the coming of Christ, his setting up his glorious kingdom, and the blessedness of the spiritual Israel in his special favor, and their happiness in living and dying. Indeed, Abimelech, king of the Philistines, had God’s special favor to a particular person, Abraham, revealed to him (Gen 20:6–7). So it seems that God revealed to Laban his special favor to Jacob; see Gen 31:24 and Ps 105:15. And if a truly good man should have an immediate revelation or suggestion from God in the same way concerning God’s favor to his neighbor or to himself, it would be no higher kind of influence. It would be no more than a common sort of influence of God’s Spirit, as the gift of prophecy, and all revelation by immediate suggestion, is; see 1 Cor 13:2. It is true that a natural man cannot possibly have that individual suggestion from the Spirit of God, that he is converted, because it is not true. Yet that does not arise from the nature of the influence, or because the kind of influence that suggests such excellent facts is too high for him to be the subject of it, but purely from the lack of a fact to be revealed. The influence that immediately suggests this fact, when it is true, is of no different kind from the influence that immediately suggests other true facts. And so the kind and nature of the influence is not above what natural men share with good men.

But it is a poor, ignoble notion of the witness of the Spirit of God, given to his dear children, to suppose that there is nothing in the kind and nature of that influence of the Spirit of God in imparting this high and glorious benefit except what is common to natural men, or what men may be capable of while they are all the time altogether unsanctified and children of hell; and that therefore the benefit or gift itself has nothing of the holy nature of the Spirit of God in it, nothing of a vital imparting of that Spirit. This notion greatly debases the high and most exalted kind of influence and operation of the Spirit that there is in the true witness of the Spirit46. What is called the witness of the Spirit in Rom 8 is elsewhere in the New Testament called the seal of the Spirit (2 Cor 1:22; Eph 1:13 and 4:30). This alludes to the seal of princes, attached to the document by which they raised any of their subjects to some high honor and dignity, or special privilege in the kingdom, as a token of their special favor. This is evidence that the influence of the Spirit of the Prince of princes, in sealing his favorites, is far from being of a common kind. There is no effect of God’s Spirit whatever that is more divine in its nature, nothing more holy, more peculiar to God, more inimitable, and more distinguishing of divinity. For nothing is more royal than the royal seal; nothing belonging to a prince is more sacred, or more especially marks what belongs to him. It is the very end and purpose of the seal to be the most distinctive stamp and confirmation of the royal authority, the great mark of distinction by which what comes from the king, or belongs to him, may be known from everything else. And therefore no doubt the seal of the great King of heaven and earth, stamped on the heart, is something high and holy in its own nature, some excellent outflow from the infinite fountain of divine beauty and glory. It is not merely making known a secret fact by revelation or suggestion, which is a sort of influence of the Spirit of God that the children of the devil have often been the subjects of. The seal of the Spirit is a kind of effect of the Spirit of God on the heart that natural men, while they remain natural men, are so far from being capable of receiving that they can have no notion or idea of it at all. This agrees with Revelation 2:17: “To the one who overcomes, I will give the hidden manna. I will also give him a white stone inscribed with a new name, known only to the one who receives it.” There is every reason to suppose that what is spoken of here is the same mark, evidence or blessed token of special favor that is elsewhere called the seal of the Spirit.

What has misled many in their notion of the influence of the Spirit of God we are speaking of is the word witness, its being called the witness of the Spirit. So they have taken it to be, not any effect or work of the Spirit on the heart giving evidence from which men may reason that they are the children of God, but an inward, immediate suggestion, as though God spoke inwardly to the man, testified to him, and told him that he was his child, by a kind of secret voice or impression. They have not observed the way the word witness, or testimony, is often used in the New Testament, where such terms often signify not merely declaring and asserting a thing to be true, but holding out evidence from which a thing may be reasoned out and proved to be true. So in Heb 2:4 God is said to bear witness “through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit.” Now the miracles spoken of here are called God’s witness, not because they are of the nature of assertions, but because they are evidences and proofs. So in Acts 14:3: “So Paul and Barnabas spent considerable time there, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the message of His grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders.” And in John 5:36: “But I have testimony more substantial than that of John. For the works that the Father has given Me to accomplish—the very works I am doing—testify about Me that the Father has sent Me.” Again in ch. 10:25: “The works I do in My Father’s name testify on My behalf.” So the water and the blood are said to bear witness (1 John 5:8), not that they spoke or asserted anything, but they were proofs and evidences. So God’s works of providence, in the rain and fruitful seasons, are spoken of as witnesses of God’s being and goodness; that is, they were evidences of these things. And when the Scripture speaks of the seal of the Spirit, the expression properly denotes, not an immediate voice or suggestion, but some work or effect of the Spirit that is left as a divine mark on the soul, to be an evidence by which God’s children may be known. The seals of princes were the distinguishing marks of princes, and so God’s seal is spoken of as God’s mark, as in Rev 7:3: “Do not harm the land or sea or trees until we have sealed the foreheads of the servants of our God,” together with Ezekiel 9:4: “Put a mark on the foreheads of the men sighing and groaning over all the abominations committed there.” When God sets his seal on a man’s heart by his Spirit, there is some holy stamp, some image impressed and left on the heart by the Spirit, as by the seal on the wax. And this holy stamp, or impressed image, displaying clear evidence to the conscience that the one who bears it is a child of God, is the very thing that is called in Scripture the seal of the Spirit, and the witness, or evidence, of the Spirit. And the image the Spirit stamps on the hearts of God’s children is his own image. That is the evidence by which they are known to be God’s children: that they have the image of their Father stamped on their hearts by the Spirit of adoption. In ancient times seals had two things engraved on them, namely the image and the name of the person whose seal it was. So when Christ says to his bride in Song 8:6, “Set me as a seal over your heart, as a seal upon your arm,” it is as much as to say, “Let my name and image remain impressed there.” The seals of princes used to bear their image, so that whatever they set their seal and royal mark on had their image left on it. It was the custom of princes of old to have their image engraved on their jewels and precious stones; and the image of Augustus engraved on a precious stone was used as the seal of the Roman emperors in the times of Christ and the apostles.47 And the saints are the jewels of Jesus Christ, the great sovereign who possesses the empire of the universe; and these jewels have his image stamped on them by his royal signet, which is the Holy Spirit. And no doubt this is what the Scripture means by the seal of the Spirit, especially when it is stamped in so fair and clear a way as to be plain to the eye of conscience, which is what the Scripture calls our spirit. This is truly an effect that is spiritual, supernatural and divine. In itself it is of a holy nature, being an imparting of the divine nature and beauty. The kind of influence of the Spirit that gives and leaves this stamp on the heart is such that no natural man can be the subject of anything of a like nature. This is the highest sort of witness of the Spirit that the soul can possibly be the subject of. If there were any such thing as a witness of the Spirit by immediate suggestion or revelation, this would be vastly more noble and excellent, as far above it as the heaven is above the earth. This the devil cannot imitate. But as to an inward suggestion of the Spirit of God, by a kind of secret voice speaking and immediately asserting and revealing a fact, he can produce something a thousand times more like that than anything he can produce like the holy and divine effect, or work, of the Spirit of God that has now been spoken of.48

Another thing that fully proves that the seal of the Spirit is no revelation of any fact by immediate suggestion, but is grace itself in the soul, is that in Scripture the seal of the Spirit is called the earnest of the Spirit. It is very plain from 2 Corinthians 1:22 that the seal of the Spirit is the same thing as the earnest of the Spirit: God “placed His seal on us, and put His Spirit in our hearts as an earnest of what is to come.” And from Eph 1:13–14: “In Him, having believed, you+ were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, to the praise of His glory.” Now the earnest is part of the money agreed on, paid in hand as a token of the whole, which is to be paid in due time: a part of the promised inheritance, granted now as a token of full possession of the whole hereafter. But surely the kind of imparting of the Spirit of God that is of the nature of eternal glory is the highest and most excellent kind of imparting. It is something in its own nature spiritual, holy and divine, and far from anything common; and therefore it is high above anything of the nature of inspiration, or revelation of hidden facts by suggestion of the Spirit of God, which many natural men have had. What is the earnest and beginning of glory but grace itself, especially in its more lively and clear exercises? It is not prophecy, nor tongues, nor knowledge, but that more excellent divine thing, charity, the love that never fails, which is a foretaste and beginning of the light, sweetness and blessedness of heaven, that world of love or charity. It is grace that is the seed of glory and the dawning of glory in the heart, and therefore it is grace that is the earnest of the future inheritance. What is the beginning or earnest of eternal life in the soul but spiritual life? And what is that but grace? The inheritance Christ has purchased for the elect is the Spirit of God, not in any extraordinary gifts, but in his vital indwelling in the heart, exerting and imparting himself there in his own proper, holy or divine nature. And this is the sum total of the inheritance Christ purchased for the elect. For things are so ordered in the matter of our redemption that the Father provides the Savior, or purchaser, and the purchase is made from him; the Son is the purchaser and the price; and the Holy Spirit is the great blessing or inheritance purchased, as is indicated in Gal 3:13–14. That is why the Spirit is often spoken of as the sum of the blessings promised in the gospel (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:4 and 2:38–39; Gal 3:14; Eph 1:13). This inheritance was the great legacy that Christ left his disciples and church in his last will and testament (John chapters 14, 15 and 16). This is the sum of the blessings of eternal life that will be given in heaven. (Compare John 7:37–39 and John 4:14 with Rev 21:6 and 22:1, 17.) It is through the vital imparting and indwelling of the Spirit that the saints have all their light, life, holiness, beauty and joy in heaven. And it is through the vital imparting and indwelling of the same Spirit that the saints have all their light, life, holiness, beauty and comfort on earth, only imparted in less measure. And this vital indwelling of the Spirit in the saints, in this less measure and small beginning, is the earnest of the Spirit, the earnest of the future inheritance, and the firstfruits of the Spirit, as the apostle calls it in Rom 8:23. There, by the firstfruits of the Spirit, the apostle no doubt means the same vital, gracious principle he speaks of in all the earlier part of the chapter, which he calls Spirit and sets against flesh, or corruption. Therefore this earnest of the Spirit and firstfruits of the Spirit, which has been shown to be the same as the seal of the Spirit, is the vital, gracious, sanctifying imparting and influence of the Spirit, and not any immediate suggestion or revelation of facts by the Spirit.49

And indeed, when the apostle in Rom 8:16 speaks of the Spirit bearing witness with our spirit that we are the children of God, he explains himself sufficiently, if only his words were attended to. What is expressed here is connected with the two verses before, as following from what the apostle had said there, as every reader may see. The three verses together read like this: “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you+ did not receive a spirit of bondage that returns you+ to fear, but you+ received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’ The Spirit Himself bears witness with our spirit that we are God’s children.” Here what the apostle says, if we take it together, plainly shows that what he has in view, when he speaks of the Spirit giving us witness or evidence that we are God’s children, is his dwelling in us and leading us as a spirit of adoption, or spirit of a child, disposing us to behave toward God as toward a Father. This is the witness or evidence the apostle speaks of, that we are children: that we have the spirit of children, or spirit of adoption. And what is that but the spirit of love? The apostle speaks of two kinds of spirit: the spirit of a slave, or the spirit of bondage, which is fear; and the spirit of a child, or Spirit of adoption, which is love. The apostle says we have not received the spirit of bondage, or of slaves, which is a spirit of fear; but we have received the more noble and generous spirit of children, a spirit of love, which naturally disposes us to go to God as children go to a father, and to behave toward God as children. And this is the evidence or witness the Spirit of God gives us that we are children. This is the plain sense of the apostle. And so no doubt the apostle here is speaking of the very same way of casting out doubting and fear and the spirit of bondage that the apostle John speaks of in 1 John 4:18, namely by the prevailing of love, which is the spirit of a child. The spirit of bondage works by fear; the slave fears the rod. But love cries “Abba! Father!” It disposes us to go to God and behave toward God as children, and it gives us clear evidence of our union with God as his children, and so it casts out fear. So it appears that the witness of the Spirit the apostle speaks of is far from being any whisper, or immediate suggestion or revelation. It is that gracious, holy effect of the Spirit of God in the hearts of the saints, the disposition and character of children, appearing in sweet childlike love to God, which casts out fear, or the spirit of a slave.

And the same thing is evident from the whole context. It is plain that the apostle speaks of the Spirit over and over again as dwelling in the hearts of the saints as a gracious principle, set against the flesh, or corruption. And so he does in the words that immediately introduce the passage we are considering, verse 13: “For if you+ live according to the flesh, you+ will die; but if by the Spirit you+ put to death the deeds of the body, you+ will live.”

Indeed, I have no doubt that the apostle has a more special regard to the spirit of grace, or the spirit of love, or spirit of a child, in its more lively actings. For it is only perfect love, or strong love, that witnesses or gives evidence that we are children in such a way as to cast out fear and deliver us wholly from the spirit of bondage. The strong and lively exercises of a spirit of childlike, evangelical, humble love to God give clear evidence of the soul’s relation to God as his child, and this satisfies the soul very greatly and directly. It is far from true that in this case the soul judges only by an immediate witness, without any sign or evidence; for it judges, and is assured, by the greatest sign and the clearest evidence. Yet in this case the saint has no need of many signs, or of any long reasoning on them. And though his sight of his relative union with God, and of his being in God’s favor, is not without a means, because he sees it by means of his love, yet his sight of the union of his heart to God is immediate. Love, the bond of union, is seen intuitively. The saint sees and feels plainly the union between his soul and God; it is so strong and lively that he cannot doubt it. And from this he is assured that he is a child. How can he doubt whether he stands in a childlike relation to God, when he plainly sees a childlike union between God and his soul, and so boldly, and as it were naturally and necessarily, cries, “Abba! Father!”

And where the apostle says the Spirit bears witness with our spirit, by our spirit here is meant our conscience, which is called the spirit of man in Prov 20:27: “The spirit of a man is the lamp of the Lord, searching out his inmost being.” We read elsewhere of the witness of this spirit of ours, in 2 Cor 1:12: “This is our rejoicing: the testimony of our conscience.” And in 1 John 3:19–21: “And by this we will know that we belong to the truth, and will assure our hearts in His presence. For if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things. Beloved, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God.” When the apostle Paul speaks of the Spirit of God bearing witness with our spirit, he is not to be understood as speaking of two spirits that are two separate, parallel, independent witnesses. Rather, it is by the one that we receive the witness of the other. The Spirit of God gives the evidence, by infusing and pouring out the love of God, the spirit of a child, in the heart; and our spirit, or our conscience, receives this evidence and declares it, for our rejoicing.

Many evils have arisen from the false and delusive notion of the witness of the Spirit, that it is a kind of inward voice, suggestion or declaration from God to a man that he is loved by him, and pardoned, elected, or the like, sometimes with a text of Scripture and sometimes without. And many false and vain (though very high) affections have arisen from it. And it is to be feared that multitudes of souls have been eternally ruined by it. That is why I have dwelt longer on this head.

But I go on now to a second characteristic of gracious affections.

38. Fancies and whims abound most in men of weak reason; children, and those who are cracked in their understanding, have the most of them; strength of reason banishes them, as the sun does mists and vapors. But the more rational any gracious person is, the more he is fixed and settled and satisfied in the grounds of religion: indeed, there is the highest and purest reason in religion; and when this change is worked in men, it is carried on in a rational way, Isa 1:18; John 19:9. Flavel’s preparation for sufferings, ch. 6.

39. If any man should see and behold Christ really, immediately, this is not the saving knowledge of him. I know the saints do know Christ as if immediately present; they are not strangers because of their distance: if others have seen him more immediately, I will not dispute it. But if they have seen the Lord Jesus as immediately as if he were here on earth, yet Capernaum saw him so; indeed, some of them were disciples for a time, and followed him, John 6. And yet the Lord was hidden from their eyes. Indeed, all the world will see him in his glory, which will amaze them; and yet this falls far short of having the saving knowledge of him, which the Lord imparts to the elect. So though you see the Lord so really that you become familiar with him, yet, Luke 13:26, “We ate and drank with you,” and so perish. Shepard’s Par. Of the ten virgins, P. I. P. 197, 198.

40. Satan is transformed into an angel of light: and so we have heard that some have heard voices; some have seen the very blood of Christ dropping on them, and the wounds in his side; some have seen a great light shining in the room; some have been wonderfully moved by their dreams; some in great distress have had an inward witness, “your sins are forgiven”; and from this such liberty and joy that they are ready to leap up and down the room. O adulterous generation! This is natural and usual with men: they would gladly see Jesus, and have him present to give them peace; and that is why Papists have his images.—Woe to those who have no other manifested Christ but such a one. Shepard’s Par. Of the ten virgins, P. I. P. 198.

41. Consider how difficult, indeed impossible, it is to determine that such a voice, vision or revelation is from God, and that Satan cannot imitate or counterfeit it; seeing he has left no certain marks by which we may distinguish one spirit from another. Flavel’s causes and cures of mental errors, cause 14.

42. There is a remarkable passage of Mr. John Smith, in his discourse on the shortness of a Pharisaic righteousness, p. 370, 371, of his select discourses, describing the sort of religion that is built on such a foundation as I am speaking of here. I cannot keep from copying the whole of it. Speaking of a sort of Christians whose life is nothing but a strong energy of fancy, he says: so that their religion may not too grossly show itself to be nothing but a piece of art, there may at times be such extraordinary motions stirred up within them, going before all their own thoughts, that they may seem to be a true operation of the divine life; when yet all this is nothing but the energy of their own self-love, touched with some fleshly perceptions of divine things, and stirred up by them. There are things in our Christian religion which, when a carnal, unhallowed mind takes the chair and gets to expound them, may seem very delicious to the fleshly appetites of men: some doctrines and notions of free grace and justification, the magnificent titles of sons of God and heirs of heaven, ever-flowing streams of joy and pleasure that blessed souls will swim in to all eternity, a glorious paradise in the world to come, always springing up with sweet-scented and fragrant beauties, a new Jerusalem paved with gold and spangled with stars, taking in within its vast circuit such numberless varieties that a busy curiosity may occupy itself with them to all eternity. I do not doubt that at times the most fleshly and earthly men, who in their ambition fly to the pomp of this world, may be so ravished with fancies of such things as these that they may seem to be made partakers of the powers of the world to come. I do not doubt that they might be much exalted by them, as the souls of crazed or deranged people seem to be at times, when their fancies play with those quick and nimble spirits that a diseased state of body and an unnatural heat in their heads produce within them. So these blazing comets may rise up above the moon and climb higher than the sun; yet because they have no solid substance of their own, and are of a base and earthly alloy, they will soon vanish and fall down again, being held up only by an external force. They may seem to themselves to have reached higher than those noble Christians who are gently moved by the natural force of true goodness: they seem to be pleniores Deo [that is, more full of God] than those who are really formed and moved by the divine Spirit, and move on steadily and constantly in the way toward heaven. It is as with the seed that was sown on stony ground, which grew up and lengthened out its blade faster than the seed sown in the good and fruitful soil. And while our souls are in this mortal condition, sunk deeply into the body, the motions of our sense and fancy and passions are many times more vigorous, and make stronger impressions on us, than those of the higher powers of the soul, which are more subtle and further removed from these mixed animal perceptions. In the same way, the devotion that is seated there may seem to have more energy and life in it than the devotion that spreads itself gently, with a more delicate kind of touch, over the understanding, and from there flows mildly through our wills and affections. But however much more boisterous the former may be for a time, the latter is of a more lasting, seed-like and thriving nature. For the former, coming in fact from nothing but a sensory and fleshly perception of God and of true happiness, is only of a fleeting and fading nature; and as the sensory powers and faculties grow more languid, or the sun of divine light shines more brightly on us, these earthly devotions, like our kitchen fires, will lose their heat and fervor. But a true heavenly warmth will never be put out, because it is of an immortal nature; and once it is seated vitally in the souls of men, it will regulate and order all the soul’s motions in a proper way, as the natural heat rooted in the hearts of living creatures has the rule and management of the whole body under it. True religion is no piece of artifice; it is no boiling up of our imaginative powers, nor the glowing heats of passion, though these are too often mistaken for it, when in our trickery in religion we cast a mist before our own eyes. But it is a new nature, forming the souls of men; it is a godlike frame of spirit, showing itself most of all in serene and clear minds, in deep humility, meekness, self-denial, universal love to God and all true goodness, without partiality and without hypocrisy, by which we are taught to know God, and knowing him to love him, and to conform ourselves as far as possible to all the perfection that shines in him.

43. Mr. Stoddard, in his Guide to Christ, p. 8, says that at times men, after they have been in trouble for a while, have some promises come to them with a great deal of refreshment, and they hope God has accepted them; and he says that in this case the minister may tell them that God never gives a faith of assurance before he gives a faith of dependence; for he never manifests his love until men are in a state of favor and reconciliation, which is by faith of dependence. When men have comforting Scriptures come to them, they are apt to take them as tokens of God’s love; but men must be brought into Christ, by accepting the offer of the gospel, before they are fit for such manifestations. God’s method is first to make the soul accept the offers of grace, and then to manifest its good state to it. And p. 76, speaking of those who seem to be brought to lie at God’s feet, and who give an account of their embracing Christ, and say that God has revealed Christ to them and drawn their hearts to him, and that they do accept Christ, he says that in this case it is best to examine whether, by the light that was given him, he saw Christ and salvation offered to him, or whether he saw that God loved him or pardoned him: for the offer of grace and our acceptance go before pardon, and therefore much more before the knowledge of it. Mr. Shepard, in his parable of the ten virgins, Part II p. 15, says that grace and the love of Christ (the fairest colors under the sun) may be pretended; but if you receive, under this appearance, that God witnesses his love first by an absolute promise, take care there; for under this appearance you may just as well bring in immediate revelations, and from there come to forsake the Scriptures. And in Part I, p. 86, he says: Is Christ yours? Yes, I see it. How? By any word or promise? No: this is delusion. And p. 136, speaking of those who have no solid ground of peace, he counts among them those who content themselves with the revelation of the Lord’s love without the sight of any work, or without looking to it. And he says soon after: the testimony of the Spirit does not make a man more a Christian, but only shows it to be so; as it is the nature of a witness, not to make a thing true, but to clear it and show it. And p. 140, speaking of those who say they have the witness of the Spirit, which makes a difference between them and hypocrites, he says: the witness of the Spirit does not make the first difference; for first a man is a believer, and in Christ, and justified, called and sanctified, before the Spirit witnesses it; otherwise the Spirit would witness to an untruth, and lie.

44. Mr. Shepard, in his sound believer, p. 159, of the late printing at Boston, says: embrace in your bosom not only a few promises, but all. And then he asks the question: when may a Christian take a promise as spoken to him without presumption? He answers: the rule is very sweet, but certain; when he takes all the Scripture and embraces it as spoken to him, he may then take any particular promise boldly. My meaning is, when a Christian takes hold of, and wrestles with God for, the fulfillment of all the promises of the New Testament; when he sets all the commands before him as a compass and guide to walk by; when he applies all the threatenings to drive him nearer to Christ, the end of them. This no hypocrite can do; this the saints will do; and by this they may know when the Lord speaks in particular to them.

45. Some Christians have rested in a work without Christ, which is abominable: but after a man is in Christ, not to judge by the work is, first, not to judge from a word. For though there is a word that may give a man a dependence on Christ without feeling any work, indeed when he feels none, as absolute promises; yet there is no word giving assurance except one that is made to some work: “He who believes,” or, “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” and so on; until that work is seen, he has no assurance from that promise. Shepard’s parable of the ten virgins. Part I. P. 86. If God should tell a saint that he has grace, he might know it by believing the word of God: but it is not in this way that godly men know that they have grace; it is not revealed in the word, and the Spirit of God does not testify it to particular persons. Stoddard’s nature of saving conversion, p. 84, 85.

46. The late venerable Stoddard, in his younger years, falling in with the opinion of some others, accepted this notion of the witness of the Spirit by way of immediate suggestion; but in the latter part of his life, when he had weighed things more thoroughly and had more experience, he entirely rejected it, as appears from his treatise of the nature of saving conversion, p. 84: The Spirit of God does not testify to particular persons that they are godly. Some think that the Spirit of God does testify it to some; and they ground it on Rom 8:16: “The Spirit Himself bears witness with our spirit that we are God’s children.” They think the Spirit reveals it by giving an inward testimony to it; and some godly men think they have had experience of it: but they may easily be mistaken; when the Spirit of God eminently stirs up a spirit of faith, and pours out the love of God in the heart, it is easy to mistake it for a testimony. And that is not the meaning of Paul’s words. The Spirit reveals things to us by opening our eyes to see what is revealed in the word; but the Spirit does not reveal new truths, not revealed in the word. The Spirit shows the grace of God in Christ, and by this draws out special actings of faith and love, which are evidential; but it does not work by way of testimony. If God only helps us to receive the revelations in the word, we will have comfort enough without new revelations.

47. See Chambers’s dictionary, under the word times.

48. Mr. Shepard argues abundantly against the notion of men knowing their good state by an immediate witness of the Spirit, without judging by any effect or work of the Spirit produced in the heart as an evidence and proof that people are the children of God. Part I. P. 134: “We know that He has chosen you.” How so? Immediately? Some divines think that the angels do not see it so, and that it is peculiar to God to do so; but mediately: “because our gospel came to you … in power … and with much assurance,” to make you enlarged for God, to make you turn “to God from idols,” and so on. Again on the same page: It is heaven to cleave to him in every command; it is death to depart from any command. “By this we know that we are in Him.” If it were possible to ask the angels how they know they are not devils, they would answer, The Lord’s will is ours. So here: how do you know you do not have the nature of devils, and so are not in the state of devils, bound there until the judgment of the great day? Because God has changed our vile nature, and made our wills like his glorious will. And p. 135: The major is the word, the minor experience, and the conclusion the work of the Lord’s Spirit, awakening your spirits to it. Now, some say, how do you know this? You may be mistaken in this way; for many have been deceived in this way. Grant that; and shall a child not take bread when it is given him, though dogs snatch at it? And p. 137: If you look to a Spirit without a work, while you seek consolation, you cannot avoid the condemnation of the word. You say the Spirit has spoken peace to you; but do you love Christ? I do not look to that, but to the Spirit. Why, the word says, “If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse.” So, is the league between your sins and your souls broken? Answer: I do not look to that. Why, John says, “The one who practices sin is of the devil.” Are you new creatures? I do not look to that. Why, the word says that unless you are born again you cannot enter the kingdom of God. Page 176, 177: A man says, I have Christ, and they do not. I ask, where is the Spirit? You have the deed; where is the seal? You have the testator; where is the executor? The Spirit in you? Yes, I have it; it has witnessed that Christ is mine. Answer: It has witnessed; but what has it worked? Where is the power of his death, killing your lusts? Where is the life of the Spirit of Jesus in you? Where is the oil in your vessel? Truly I look for the bridegroom; but I do not regard that; nor are others to regard it, by way of evidence. Then I say the chief evidence is destroyed in the churches. I have known many who have had assurances, yet I never saw them prove right until it witnessed that this was here. What can be the causes of this, and that men should make an uproar in the churches because of this, as though it were building on works? In different men they are different. 1. A readiness to outrun the truth, and to fall from one extreme to another.—2. The apostasy of eminent professing Christians, who have been deceived in their evidencing in this way.—3. Corrupt experience.—4. A heart that never felt the bitterness and bondage of sin as the greatest evil. Page 215, 216: The peace and joy and assurance of that glory which eye never saw, in the saints, is from the witness of the Spirit of glory; not only because God is their God, but because they are his people. It is, I say, from the witness of God in his word; not from themselves, nor from man only, that they approve me; nor from dreams and diabolical breathings; but from the Spirit of God; he brings news of it; and from such a Spirit (so that you may know it) as not only shows you that God is your God, and so you rejoice because of this (for so it is with many a carnal heart, and he has peace, after being in horror, from this, the Lord loves me); but he makes you rejoice because you are the Lord’s people, because he has changed your heart: now the peace is found, and the joy is right: and here I would test the peace of any man. Part II. P. 168, 169: All the heirs of the promises, as heirs who have legacies left them, go to the will of the deceased Father; and what comforts them, what they hold to, is what is sure: such a one will have it, if his name is there. But if one should say, Such a one has promised me such lands—Is it in his will?—No; but since he died, as I was smoking a pipe, he came to me: oh, do not be deceived! Again, in his sound believer there is a long discourse on sanctification as the chief evidence of justification, from p. 221 for many pages following; I will copy only a very small part of it. Tell me how you will know that you are justified. You will say, by the testimony of the Spirit. And cannot the same Spirit shine on your graces, and witness that you are sanctified as well? 1 John 4:13; 3:24; 1 Cor 2:12. Can the Spirit make the one clear to you and not the other? Oh, beloved, it is a sad thing to hear such questions, and such cold answers too, that sanctification possibly may be an evidence. May be! Is it not certain? Assuredly, to deny it is as bad as to affirm that God’s own promises of favor are not true evidences of it, and consequently that they are lies and untruths. Mr. Flavel also strongly opposes this notion of the witness of the Spirit by immediate revelation. Sacramental meditations, Med. 4. Speaking of the sealing of the Spirit, he says: in sealing the believer, he does not make use of an audible voice, nor the ministry of angels, nor immediate and extraordinary revelations; but he makes use of his own graces, implanted in our hearts, and his own promises, written in the Scripture: and by this method he usually brings the doubting, trembling heart of a believer to rest and comfort. Again, Ibid.: Assurance is produced in our souls by the reflective acts of faith: the Spirit helps us to reflect on what he has done in our hearts before; “By this we know that we know Him” (1 John 2:3). To know that we know is a reflective act. Now it is impossible for there to be a reflective act before there has been a direct act. No man can have the evidence of his faith before the habit is infused and the vital act performed. The subject matter to which the Spirit sets his seal is his own sanctifying operation. Afterward, Ibid., he says: the immediate ways of the Spirit’s sealing have ceased. No man may now expect, by any new revelation or sign from heaven, by any voice or extraordinary inspiration, to have his salvation sealed; but he must expect that mercy in God’s ordinary way and method, searching the Scriptures, examining our own hearts, and waiting on the Lord in prayer. The learned Gerson gives the example of one who had long been on the borders of despair, and at last was sweetly assured and settled: he answered, Non ex nova aliqua revelation; not by any new revelation, but by subjecting my understanding to the written word, and comparing my heart with it. And Mr. Roberts, in his treatise of the covenants, speaks of another who panted so intensely after the sealings and assurance of the love of God to his soul that for a long time he earnestly desired some voice from heaven; and at times, walking in the solitary fields, he earnestly desired some miraculous voice from the trees or stones there. This was denied him; but in time a better thing was given, in a scriptural way. Again, Ibid.: This method of sealing is beyond all other methods in the world. For in miraculous voices and inspirations it is possible that there may subess falsum, that there may be found some cheat or imposture of the devil; but the Spirit’s witness in the heart, agreeing with the revelation in the Scripture, cannot deceive us.

49. After a man is in Christ, not to judge by the work is not to judge by the Spirit. For the apostle makes the earnest of the Spirit to be the seal. Now earnest is part of the money bargained for: the beginning of heaven, of its light and life. He who does not see that the Lord is his by that sees no God as his at all. Oh, therefore, do not look for a Spirit without a word to reveal, nor for a word to reveal without first seeing and feeling some work. I thank the Lord, I only pity those who think otherwise. If you are a sheep of Christ, oh, do not wander. Shepard’s parable, P. I. P. 86.

The Excellent Nature of Divine Things

Part III · Sign II

II. The first objective ground of gracious affections is the transcendently excellent and amiable nature of divine things as they are in themselves, and not any conceived relation they bear to self or self-interest.

I say that the supremely excellent nature of divine things is the first, or primary and original, objective foundation of the spiritual affections of true saints. For I do not suppose that every relation divine things bear to the saints themselves and to their own particular interest is wholly excluded from all influence in their gracious affections. This may have, and indeed does have, a secondary and consequential influence in those affections that are truly holy and spiritual, as I shall show shortly.

It was observed before that the affection of love is, as it were, the fountain of all affection, and in particular that Christian love is the fountain of all gracious affections. Now the divine excellence and glory of God and Jesus Christ, of the word of God, the works of God, the ways of God, and so on, is the primary reason why a true saint loves these things. It is not any supposed share he has in them, or any conceived benefit he has received or will receive from them, or any such imagined relation they bear to his interest, so that self-love could properly be said to be the first foundation of his love to these things.

Some say that all love arises from self-love, and that it is impossible in the nature of things for any man to have any love to God, or to any other being, unless love to himself is the foundation of it. But I humbly suppose that they say so for lack of consideration. They argue that whoever loves God, and so desires his glory or the enjoyment of him, desires these things as his own happiness. The glory of God, and the beholding and enjoying of his perfections, are considered as things agreeable to him, tending to make him happy. He places his happiness in them and desires them as things which, if they were obtained, would be delightful to him, or would fill him with delight and joy, and so make him happy. And so, they say, it is from self-love, or a desire for his own happiness, that he desires God to be glorified and desires to behold and enjoy his glorious perfections. But then they ought to consider a little further and ask how the man came to place his happiness in God’s being glorified, and in contemplating and enjoying God’s perfections. There is no doubt that once God’s glory and the beholding of his perfections have become so agreeable to him that he places his highest happiness in these things, he will desire them as he desires his own happiness. But how did these things come to be so agreeable to him that he counts it his highest happiness to glorify God, and so on? Is not this the fruit of love? A man must first love God, or have his heart united to him, before he will count God’s good his own, and before he will desire the glorifying and enjoying of God as his happiness. It is not strong arguing to say that because, after a man has his heart united to God in love, he desires God’s glory and the enjoyment of him as his own happiness as a fruit of this, therefore a desire for this happiness of his own must be the cause and foundation of his love. It would be just as strong to argue that because a father begot a son, therefore his son certainly begot him. Suppose that after a man loves God, and has his heart so united to him as to look on God as his chief good and on God’s good as his own, it is a consequence and fruit of this that even self-love, or love for his own happiness, causes him to desire the glorifying and enjoying of God. It does not follow from this that this very exercise of self-love went before his love to God, and that his love to God was a consequence and fruit of that. Something else, entirely distinct from self-love, might be the cause of this: namely, a change made in the views of his mind and the relish of his heart, by which he perceives a beauty, glory and supreme good in God’s nature as it is in itself. This may be the thing that first draws his heart to God and causes his heart to be united to him, prior to all considerations of his own interest or happiness, although after this, and as a fruit of this, he necessarily seeks his interest and happiness in God.

There is such a thing as a kind of love or affection that a man may have toward persons or things which does properly arise from self-love. In it a preconceived relation to himself, or some regard already shown to him by another, or some benefit already received or depended on, is truly the first foundation of his love, and what his affection wholly arises from; and this comes before any relish of, or delight in, the nature and qualities inherent in the one beloved, as beautiful and lovable. When the first thing that draws a man’s benevolence to another is the beholding of those qualities and properties in him which appear lovely to him in themselves, and the one who has them worthy of esteem and goodwill on that account, love arises in a very different way than when it first arises from some gift bestowed by another, or depended on from him (as a judge loves and favors a man who has bribed him), or from the relation he supposes another has to him (as a man loves another because he looks on him as his child). When love to another arises in this way, it does truly and properly arise from self-love.

That kind of affection to God or Jesus Christ which properly arises from self-love in this way cannot be a truly gracious and spiritual love, as appears from what has been said already. For self-love is a principle entirely natural, as much in the hearts of devils as of angels; and so surely nothing that is merely the result of it can be supernatural and divine in the way described before50. Christ plainly speaks of this kind of love as nothing beyond the love of wicked men (Luke 6:32): “If you+ love those who love you+, what credit is that to you+? Even sinners love those who love them.” And the devil himself knew that a regard for God so mercenary as to be only for benefits received or depended on (which comes to the same thing) is worthless in the sight of God. Otherwise he would never have used such a slander against Job before God, as in Job 1:9–10: “Does Job fear God for nothing? Have You not placed a hedge on every side around him and his household …?” Nor would God ever have implicitly allowed that the objection would have been a good one if the accusation had been true. Yet he did allow it, by allowing the matter to be tried, and Job to be so dealt with that it might appear in the outcome whether Job’s regard for God was mercenary in this way or not, and by making the proof of the sincerity and goodness of his regard rest on that outcome.

It is unreasonable to think anything other than that the first foundation of a true love to God is that by which he is lovely in himself, or worthy to be loved: the supreme loveliness of his nature. This is certainly what chiefly makes him lovable. What chiefly makes a man, or any creature, lovely is his excellence; and so what chiefly makes God lovely, and must undoubtedly be the chief ground of true love, is his excellence. God’s nature, or the divinity, is infinitely excellent; indeed, it is infinite beauty, brightness and glory itself. But how can that be true love of this excellent and lovely nature which is not built on the foundation of its true loveliness? How can that be true love of beauty and brightness which is not for the sake of beauty and brightness? How can that be a true prizing of what is in itself infinitely worthy and precious which is not for the sake of its worthiness and preciousness? This infinite excellence of the divine nature, as it is in itself, is the true ground of all that is good in God in any respect. But how can a man truly and rightly love God without loving him for that excellence in him which is the foundation of all that is in any way good or desirable in him? Those whose affection to God is founded first on his profitableness to them begin their affection at the wrong end. They regard God only for the furthest reach of the stream of divine good, where it touches them and reaches their interest. They have no regard for that infinite glory of God’s nature which is the original good and the true fountain of all good, the first fountain of all loveliness of every kind, and so the first foundation of all true love.

A natural principle of self-love may be the foundation of great affections toward God and Christ without any sight of the beauty and glory of the divine nature. There is a certain gratitude that is a merely natural thing. Gratitude is one of the natural affections of the soul of man, as anger is; and there is a gratitude that arises from self-love in very much the same way that anger does. Anger in men is an affection stirred up against another, or in opposition to another, for something in him that crosses self-love. Gratitude is an affection one has toward another for loving him or gratifying him, or for something in him that suits self-love. And there may be a kind of gratitude without any true or proper love, just as there may be anger without any proper hatred, as in parents toward their children: they may be angry with them and yet at the same time have a strong habitual love for them. This gratitude is the principle at work in wicked men in what Christ declares about them in the sixth chapter of Luke, where he says that “sinners love those who love them”; and in what he declares even about the tax collectors, who were among the most carnal and profligate sort of men (Matt 5:46). This is the very principle that bribery works on in unjust judges; and it is a principle that even the brute beasts exercise: a dog will love his master who is kind to him. And we see in countless instances that mere nature is enough to stir up gratitude in men, or to affect their hearts with thankfulness to others for kindnesses received, and sometimes toward those against whom they have at the same time a habitual enmity. So Saul was more than once greatly affected, and even melted, with gratitude toward David for sparing his life, and yet he remained his habitual enemy. And as men may be affected in this way toward men from mere nature, so they may be toward God. Nothing prevents the same self-love from working in the same way toward God as toward men. And we have clear instances of it in Scripture: in the children of Israel, who sang God’s praises at the Red Sea but soon forgot his works; and in Naaman the Syrian, who was greatly affected by the miraculous cure of his leprosy, so that his heart was engaged from then on to worship the God who had healed him, and him only, except when it would expose him to ruin in his worldly interest. So too Nebuchadnezzar was greatly affected by God’s goodness to him in restoring him to his reason and his kingdom after he had lived with the beasts.

Since gratitude is a natural principle in this way, it makes ingratitude all the more vile and heinous, because it shows a dreadful prevalence of wickedness when wickedness even overbears and suppresses the better principles of human nature. So it is mentioned as evidence of the high degree of wickedness of many of the heathen that they were “without natural affection” (Rom 1:31). But that the lack of gratitude or natural affection is evidence of a high degree of vice is no argument that all gratitude and natural affection has the nature of virtue or saving grace.

Self-love, through the exercise of a merely natural gratitude, may be the foundation of a sort of love to God in many ways. A kind of love may arise from a false notion of God that men have been brought up in, or have somehow absorbed: as though he were only goodness and mercy, and had no avenging justice; or as though the exercises of his goodness were necessary, and not free and sovereign; or as though his goodness depended on what is in them and were, as it were, constrained by them. On such grounds as these men may love a God of their own forming in their imaginations, when they are far from loving such a God as reigns in heaven.

Again, self-love may be the foundation of an affection in men toward God through a great insensibility of their state with regard to God, and for lack of conviction of conscience to make them feel how dreadfully they have provoked God to anger. They have no sense of the heinousness of sin as against God, nor of the infinite and terrible opposition of God’s holy nature to it. And so, having formed in their minds such a God as suits them, and thinking God to be such a one as themselves, who favors them and agrees with them, they may like him very well and feel a sort of love to him, when they are far from loving the true God. And men’s affections may be much moved toward God from self-love by some remarkable outward benefits received from God, as it was with Naaman, Nebuchadnezzar, and the children of Israel at the Red Sea.

Again, a very high affection toward God may arise in men, and often does, from an opinion of God’s favor and love to them as the first foundation of their love to him. After awakenings and distress through fears of hell, they may suddenly get a notion, through some impression on their imagination, or an immediate suggestion, with or without texts of Scripture, or by some other means, that God loves them, has forgiven their sins and made them his children. This is the first thing that causes their affections to flow toward God and Jesus Christ. And then, after this and on this foundation, many things in God may appear lovely to them, and Christ may seem excellent. If such persons are asked whether God appears lovely and lovable in himself, they would perhaps readily answer yes. Yet in truth, if the matter is strictly examined, this good opinion of God was purchased and paid for before they ever gave it, in the distinguishing and infinite benefits they imagined they had received from God. They allow God to be lovely in himself in no other way than this: that he has forgiven them and accepted them, loves them above most in the world, has pledged to use all his infinite power and wisdom in advancing, dignifying and exalting them, and will do for them just what they would have him do. Once they are firm in this persuasion, it is easy to acknowledge God and Christ to be lovely and glorious, and to wonder at them and extol them. It is easy for them to acknowledge Christ to be a lovely person, the best in the world, when they are first firm in the belief that he, though Lord of the universe, is captivated with love to them, has his heart swallowed up in them, prizes them far above most of their neighbors, loved them from eternity, died for them, and will make them reign with him in eternal glory in heaven. When this is the case with carnal men, their very lusts will make him seem lovely. Pride itself will prejudice them in favor of what they call Christ. Selfish, proud man naturally calls that lovely which greatly contributes to his interest and gratifies his ambition.

And as persons of this sort begin, so they go on. Their affections are raised from time to time, primarily on this foundation of self-love and an imagined notion of God’s love to them. Many have a false notion of communion with God, as though it were carried on by impulses and whispers and outward representations made immediately to their imagination. These things they often have, and they take them to be manifestations of God’s great love to them and evidences of their high exaltation above others of mankind; and so their affections are often set going again.

But the exercises of true and holy love in the saints arise in another way. They do not first see that God loves them and then see that he is lovely. They first see that God is lovely, and that Christ is excellent and glorious, and their hearts are first captivated with this view. The exercises of their love usually begin here from time to time, and arise primarily from these views; and then, as a consequence, they see God’s love and great favor to them51. The saint’s affections begin with God, and self-love has a hand in these affections only consequentially and secondarily. False affections, on the contrary, begin with self, and an acknowledgment of an excellence in God, and being affected by it, is only consequential and dependent. In the love of the true saint God is the lowest foundation: the love of the excellence of his nature is the foundation of all the affections that come afterward, in which self-love has its part as a handmaid. The hypocrite, on the contrary, lays himself at the bottom of all as the first foundation, and lays God on top as the superstructure; and even his acknowledgment of God’s glory itself depends on his regard for his private interest.

Self-love may influence men so that they are affected not only by God’s kindness to them individually, but also by his kindness to them as parts of a community. A natural principle of self-love, without any other principle, may be enough to make a man concerned for the interest of the nation he belongs to.
