For instance, in the present war, self-love may make natural men rejoice at our nation’s successes and be sorry for its setbacks, since they have a stake in it as members of the body. In the same way these natural principles may extend further, even to the world of mankind, and men might be affected by the benefits the inhabitants of the earth have beyond those of the inhabitants of other planets, if we knew that there were such and knew how it was with them. So this principle may cause men to be affected by the benefits mankind has received beyond the fallen angels. And so, from this principle, men may be much affected by the wonderful goodness of God to mankind, by his great goodness in giving his Son to die for fallen man, by the marvelous love of Christ in suffering such great things for us, and by the great glory they hear God has provided in heaven for us. They look on themselves as persons who have a stake and a share in it, being members of this species of creatures so highly favored. The same principle of natural gratitude may influence men here as in the case of personal benefits.

But what I have said by no means implies that all gratitude to God is a merely natural thing, and that there is no such thing as a spiritual gratitude, which is a holy and divine affection. It implies no more than that there is a gratitude which is merely natural, and that when persons have affections toward God only or primarily for benefits received, their affection is only the exercise of a natural gratitude. There is no doubt such a thing as a gracious gratitude, which differs greatly from all the gratitude natural men experience. It differs in the following respects:

(1.) True gratitude or thankfulness to God for his kindness to us arises from a foundation laid before, of love to God for what he is in himself; a natural gratitude has no such prior foundation. The gracious stirrings of grateful affection to God for kindness received always come from a stock of love already in the heart, established in the first place on other grounds, namely God’s own excellence; and so the affections are disposed to flow out on occasions of God’s kindness. The saint has seen the glory of God, and his heart has been overcome by it and captivated into a supreme love to him on that account; by this his heart becomes tender and easily affected by kindnesses received. If a man has no love for another, gratitude may still be moved by some extraordinary kindness, as in Saul toward David. But this is not the same kind of thing as a man’s gratitude to a dear friend whom his heart already held in high esteem and love, so that by this means his heart became tender toward him, more easily affected with gratitude, and affected in another way. Self-love is not excluded from a gracious gratitude: the saints love God for his kindness to them, as in Ps 116:1: “I love the Lord, for He has heard my voice—my appeal for mercy.” But something else is included as well: another love prepares the way and lays the foundation for these grateful affections.

(2.) In a gracious gratitude men are affected by the attribute of God’s goodness and free grace, not only as they are concerned in it, or as it affects their interest, but as a part of the glory and beauty of God’s nature. That wonderful and unparalleled grace of God which is manifested in the work of redemption, and shines out in the face of Jesus Christ, is infinitely glorious in itself, and appears so to the angels. It is a great part of the moral perfection and beauty of God’s nature. It would be glorious whether it were exercised toward us or not; and the saint who exercises a gracious thankfulness for it sees it to be so and delights in it as such. Yet his own stake in it serves all the more to engage his mind and raise his attention and affection. Self-love here assists as a handmaid, serving higher principles: it leads the mind out to view and contemplate it, engages and fixes the attention, and heightens the joy and love. God’s kindness to them is a mirror God sets before them in which to behold the beauty of the attribute of his goodness. By this means the exercises and displays of this attribute are brought near to them and set right before them. So in a holy thankfulness to God, the stake our interest has in God’s goodness is not the first foundation of our being affected by it. That foundation was laid in the heart before, in that stock of love to God for his excellence in himself which makes the heart tender and open to such impressions from his goodness to us. Nor is our own interest, or the benefits we have received, the only or the chief objective ground of the present exercises of the affection. That ground is God’s goodness, as part of the beauty of his nature; although the manifestations of that lovely attribute, set immediately before our eyes in its exercise for us, are the special occasion of the mind’s attention to that beauty at that time, and serve to fix the attention and heighten the affection.

Some may perhaps be ready to object to all that has been said from the text 1 John 4:19, “We love Him because He first loved us,” as though this implied that God’s love to the true saints were the first foundation of their love to him.

In answer to this I would observe that the apostle’s purpose in these words is to magnify the love of God to us on this ground: that he loved us while we had no love for him. Anyone who compares this verse and the two following with verses 9, 10 and 11 will see this. And the apostle proves that God loved us when we had no love for him by this argument: that God’s love to the elect is the ground of their love to him. And it is so in three ways. 1. The saints’ love to God is the fruit of God’s love to them, as it is the gift of that love. God gave them a spirit of love to him because he loved them from eternity. In this respect God’s love to his elect is the first foundation of their love to him, as it is the foundation of their regeneration and of the whole of their redemption. 2. The exercises and displays God has made of his wonderful love to sinful men by Jesus Christ in the work of redemption are one of the chief manifestations God has made of the glory of his moral perfection, to both angels and men; and so this is one main objective ground of the love of both to God, which agrees well with what was said before. 3. God’s love to a particular elect person, shown by his conversion, is a great manifestation to him of God’s moral perfection and glory, and a proper occasion for stirring up the love of holy gratitude, in agreement with what was said before. And that the saints love God in these respects because he first loved them fully answers the purpose of the apostle’s argument in that place. So no good argument can be drawn from this text against a spiritual and gracious love in the saints that arises primarily from the excellence of divine things as they are in themselves, and not from any conceived relation they bear to the saints’ interest.

And as it is with the love of the saints, so it is with their joy and spiritual delight and pleasure. Its first foundation is not any consideration or conception of their share in divine things. It consists primarily in the sweet delight their minds have in viewing or contemplating the divine and holy beauty of these things as they are in themselves. And this is indeed the very main difference between the joy of the hypocrite and the joy of the true saint. The former rejoices in himself; self is the first foundation of his joy. The latter rejoices in God. The hypocrite has his mind pleased and delighted, in the first place, with his own privilege and the happiness he supposes he has attained or will attain. True saints have their minds, in the first place, inexpressibly pleased and delighted with the sweet ideas of the glorious and lovely nature of the things of God. This is the spring of all their delights and the cream of all their pleasures; it is the joy of their joy. This sweet and ravishing delight they have in viewing the beautiful and delightful nature of divine things is the foundation of the joy they have afterward in considering that these things are theirs. But the affections of hypocrites depend on one another in the opposite order. They first rejoice, and are elated, that God makes so much of them; and then, on that ground, he seems in a way lovely to them.

The first foundation of the delight a true saint has in God is God’s own perfection; and the first foundation of the delight he has in Christ is Christ’s own beauty. Christ appears in himself the chief among ten thousand, and altogether lovely. The way of salvation by Christ is a delightful way to him because of the sweet and wonderful manifestations of the divine perfections in it. The holy doctrines of the gospel, by which God is exalted and man abased, holiness honored and promoted, sin greatly disgraced and discouraged, and free and sovereign love manifested, are glorious doctrines in his eyes and sweet to his taste, prior to any conception of his share in these things. Indeed the saints rejoice in their share in God, and that Christ is theirs, and they have great reason to. But this is not the first spring of their joy. They first rejoice in God as glorious and excellent in himself, and then secondarily rejoice that so glorious a God is theirs. They first have their hearts filled with sweetness from the view of Christ’s excellence, and the excellence of his grace, and the beauty of the way of salvation by him; and then they have a secondary joy that so excellent a Savior and such excellent grace are theirs.52 But what is the true saint’s superstructure is the hypocrite’s foundation. When hypocrites hear of the wonderful things of the gospel, of God’s great love in sending his Son, of Christ’s dying love to sinners, and the great things Christ has purchased and promised to the saints, and hear these things set out in a lively and eloquent way, they may hear with a great deal of pleasure and be lifted up by what they hear. But if their joy is examined, it will be found to have no other foundation than this: they look on these things as theirs. All this exalts them. They love to hear of the great love of Christ so vastly distinguishing some from others; for self-love, and even pride itself, makes them crave great distinction from others. No wonder that, in this confident opinion of their own good state, they feel well under such doctrine and are pleased in the highest degree to hear how much God and Christ make of them. So their joy is really a joy in themselves, and not in God.

And because the joy of hypocrites is in themselves, it comes about that in their rejoicings and elations they usually keep their eye on themselves. Having received what they call spiritual manifestations or experiences, their minds are taken up with them, wondering at their own experiences. What they are chiefly taken with and elated by is not the glory of God or the beauty of Christ, but the beauty of their experiences. They keep thinking to themselves, What a good experience this is! What a great manifestation this is! What wonderful things I have met with! And so they put their experiences in the place of Christ and his beauty and fullness. Instead of rejoicing in Christ Jesus, they rejoice in their wonderful experiences. Instead of feeding and feasting their souls on the view of what is outside them, namely the innate, sweet, refreshing loveliness of the things set forth in the gospel, their eyes are off these things, or at least they view them only, as it were, sideways. The object that fixes their contemplation is their experience; and they are feeding their souls, and feasting a selfish principle, on a view of their manifestations. They take more comfort in their manifestations than in Christ manifested. This is the true notion of living on experiences and frames; it is not the using of experiences as the signs on which they rely for evidence of their good state, which some call living on experiences. Yet it is very noticeable that some of those who call it so are the most notorious for living on experiences in the true sense of the term.

The affections of hypocrites very often run this way. They are first much affected by some impression on their imagination, or some impulse, which they take to be an immediate suggestion or testimony from God of his love and their happiness and high privilege in some respect, with or without a text of Scripture. They are mightily taken with this as a great manifestation, and from it high affections arise. And when their affections are raised, they view those high affections and call them great and wonderful experiences; and they have a notion that God is greatly pleased with those affections. This affects them still more, and so they are affected by their affections. And so their affections rise higher and higher, until at times they are completely swallowed up; and self-conceit and a fierce zeal rise along with them. And all is built like a castle in the air, on no other foundation than imagination, self-love and pride.

And as the thoughts of persons of this sort are, so is their talk; for out of the abundance of their heart their mouth speaks. As in their high affections they keep their eye on the beauty of their experiences and the greatness of their attainments, so they are great talkers about themselves. The true saint, when under great spiritual affections, is ready from the fullness of his heart to speak much of God and his glorious perfections and works, of the beauty and loveliness of Christ, and of the glorious things of the gospel. But hypocrites in their high affections talk more of the manifestation than of the thing manifested. They are full of talk about the great things they have met with, the wonderful manifestations they have had, how sure they are of God’s love to them, how safe their condition is, how they know they will go to heaven, and so on.

A true saint, when he enjoys true manifestations of the sweet glory of God and Christ, has his mind too much captivated and engaged by what he views outside himself to stop at that time to view himself and his own attainments. It would be a distraction and a loss he could not bear to take his eye off the ravishing object of his contemplation in order to survey his own experience, and to spend time thinking to himself what a high attainment this is, and what a good story I now have to tell others. Nor does the pleasure and sweetness of his mind at that time arise chiefly from considering the safety of his state, or anything he sees of his own qualities, experiences or circumstances. It arises from the divine and supreme beauty of what is the object of his direct view outside himself, which sweetly delights and strongly holds his mind.

As the love and joy of hypocrites all come from the source of self-love, so do their other affections: their sorrow for sin, their humbling and submission, their religious desires and zeal. Everything is, as it were, paid for beforehand, in God’s highly gratifying their self-love and their lusts by making so much of them and exalting them so highly, as things stand in their imagination. It is easy for nature, corrupt as it is, under the notion of being already some of the highest favorites of heaven, and of having a God who so protects them and favors them in their sins, to love this imaginary God who suits them so well, to extol him, submit to him, and be fierce and zealous for him. The high affections of many are all built on the supposition that they are eminent saints. If the opinion they have of themselves were taken away, if they thought they were among the lower rank of saints (though they still supposed themselves to be real saints), their high affections would fall to the ground. If they only saw a little of the sinfulness and vileness of their own hearts, and their deformity in the midst of their best duties and their best affections, it would knock their affections on the head; because their affections are built on self, self-knowledge would destroy them. But truly gracious affections are built elsewhere. They have their foundation outside self, in God and Jesus Christ. And so a discovery of themselves, of their own deformity and the poverty of their experiences, though it will purify their affections, will not destroy them, but in some respects will sweeten and heighten them.

50. There is a natural love to Christ, as to one who does you good, and for your own ends; and a spiritual love, for himself, by which the Lord alone is exalted. Shepard’s parable of the ten virgins, P. I. P. 25.

51. There is a seeing of Christ after a man believes, which is Christ in his love, and so on. But I speak of that first sight of him that precedes the second act of faith; and it is an intuitive, or real, sight of him as he is in his glory. Shepard’s parable of the ten virgins, Part I. P. 74.

52. Dr. Owen, on the SPIRIT, p. 199, speaking of a common work of the Spirit, says: The effects of this work on the mind, which is the first subject affected by it, do not go so far as to give it delight, pleasure and satisfaction in the lovely spiritual nature and excellences of the things revealed to it. The true nature of saving illumination consists in this: it gives the mind such a direct, intuitive insight into spiritual things, and view of them, that in their own spiritual nature they suit, please and satisfy it; so that it is transformed into them, cast into their mold, and rests in them (Rom 6:17; 12:2; 1 Cor 2:13–14; 2 Cor 3:18; 4:6). The work we have insisted on does not reach this far. For whatever manifestation of spiritual things is made to the mind in it, the mind does not find an immediate, direct, spiritual excellence in them, but only with respect to some benefit or advantage to be gained by means of them. It will not give such a spiritual insight into the mystery of God’s grace by Jesus Christ, called his glory shining in the face of Christ (2 Cor 4:6), that the soul, in its first direct view of it, should wonder at it, delight in it, approve it, and find spiritual solace and refreshment in it for what it is in itself. But it imparts such a light, such a knowledge, that a man may like it well in its effects, as a way of mercy and salvation.

The Loveliness of Moral Excellency

Part III · Sign III

III. Those affections that are truly holy are primarily founded on the loveliness of the moral excellence of divine things. Or, to express it another way, a love to divine things for the beauty and sweetness of their moral excellence is the first beginning and spring of all holy affections.

Here, for the sake of the less educated reader, I will explain what I mean by the moral excellence of divine things.

It may be observed that the word moral is not to be understood here in the common, popular sense of the word, as when men speak of morality and a moral behavior, meaning an outward conformity to the duties of the moral law, and especially the duties of the second table; or meaning, at the most, no more than such seeming virtues as proceed from natural principles, as opposed to those virtues that are more inward, spiritual and divine. In that sense the honesty, justice, generosity, good nature and public spirit of many of the heathen are called moral virtues, as distinct from the holy faith, love, humility and heavenly-mindedness of true Christians. I say the word moral is not to be understood in this way here.

But to understand rightly what is meant, it must be observed that divines commonly make a distinction between moral good and evil and natural good and evil. By moral evil they mean the evil of sin, or the evil that is against duty and contrary to what is right and ought to be. By natural evil they do not mean the evil that is properly opposed to duty, but what is contrary to mere nature, without any regard to a rule of duty. So the evil of suffering is called natural evil: pain and torment, disgrace and the like. These things are contrary to mere nature, contrary to the nature of both bad and good, hateful to wicked men and devils as well as to good men and angels. So too natural defects are called natural evils, as when a child is born deformed, or born without the use of reason. These are natural evils, but they are not moral evils, because they do not properly have the nature of the evil of sin. On the other hand, as by moral evil divines mean the evil of sin, or what is contrary to what is right, so by moral good they mean what is contrary to sin: that good in beings who have will and choice by which, as voluntary agents, they are and act as it befits them to be and to act, or in the way that is most fit and suitable and lovely. By natural good they mean a good that is entirely of a different kind from holiness or virtue, namely what perfects or suits nature, considering nature apart from any holy or unholy qualities, and without any relation to any rule or measure of right and wrong.

So pleasure is a natural good; so is honor; so is strength; so is theoretical knowledge, human learning and worldly prudence. So there is a distinction to be made between the natural good that men possess and their moral good; and also between the natural and moral good of the angels in heaven. The great capacity of their understandings, their great strength, and the honorable position they hold as the great ministers of God’s kingdom (for which they are called thrones, dominions, principalities and powers) are the natural good they possess. But their perfect and glorious holiness and goodness, their pure and flaming love to God, to the saints and to one another, is their moral good. So divines make a distinction between the natural and the moral perfections of God. By the moral perfections of God they mean those attributes which God exercises as a moral agent, or by which the heart and will of God are good, right, and infinitely fitting and lovely: such as his righteousness, truth, faithfulness and goodness; or, in one word, his holiness. By God’s natural attributes or perfections they mean those attributes in which, according to our way of conceiving of God, consists not the holiness or moral goodness of God but his greatness: such as his power, his knowledge by which he knows all things, his being eternal, from everlasting to everlasting, his omnipresence, and his fearful and awesome majesty.

The moral excellence of an intelligent, voluntary being is seated more immediately in the heart or will of moral agents. That intelligent being whose will is truly right and lovely is morally good or excellent.

This moral excellence of an intelligent being, when it is true and real, and not only outward, or merely seeming and counterfeit, is holiness. So holiness includes all the true moral excellence of intelligent beings: there is no other true virtue than real holiness. Holiness includes all the true virtue of a good man. His love to God, his gracious love to men, his justice, his charity and heart of compassion, his gracious meekness and gentleness, and all the other true Christian virtues he has belong to his holiness. So the holiness of God, in the wider sense of the word, the sense in which Scripture commonly (if not always) uses the word of God, is the same as the moral excellence of the divine nature, or his purity and beauty as a moral agent, including all his moral perfections: his righteousness, faithfulness and goodness. As in holy men their charity, Christian kindness and mercy belong to their holiness, so the kindness and mercy of God belong to his holiness. Holiness in man is only the image of God’s holiness. There are no more virtues belonging to the image than are in the original. Derived holiness has no more in it than is in that underived holiness which is its fountain. There is no more than grace for grace, or grace in the image answering to grace in the original.

There are two kinds of attributes in God, according to our way of conceiving of him: his moral attributes, which are summed up in his holiness, and his natural attributes of strength, knowledge and so on, which constitute the greatness of God. So there is a twofold image of God in man. There is his moral or spiritual image, which is his holiness, the image of God’s moral excellence (this image was lost by the fall); and there is God’s natural image, consisting in man’s reason and understanding, his natural ability, and his dominion over the creatures, which is the image of God’s natural attributes.

From what has been said it may easily be understood what I mean when I say that a love to divine things for the beauty of their moral excellence is the beginning and spring of all holy affections. It has already been shown, under the former head, that the first objective ground of all holy affections is the supreme excellence of divine things as they are in themselves, or in their own nature. I now go further and say more particularly that the kind of excellence of the nature of divine things which is the first objective ground of all holy affections is their moral excellence, or their holiness. Holy persons, in the exercise of holy affections, love divine things primarily for their holiness. They love God, in the first place, for the beauty of his holiness or moral perfection, as supremely lovely in itself. Not that the saints, in the exercise of gracious affections, love God only for his holiness. All his attributes are lovely and glorious in their eyes; they delight in every divine perfection; the contemplation of the infinite greatness, power and knowledge, and the terrible majesty, of God is pleasant to them. But their love to God for his holiness is what is most fundamental and essential in their love. It is here that true love to God begins; all other holy love to divine things flows from this. This is the most essential and distinguishing thing that belongs to a holy love to God, with regard to its foundation. A love to God for the beauty of his moral attributes leads to, and necessarily causes, a delight in God for all his attributes. For his moral attributes cannot exist without his natural attributes: infinite holiness supposes infinite wisdom and an infinite capacity and greatness; and all the attributes of God, as it were, imply one another.

The true beauty and loveliness of all intelligent beings consists primarily and most essentially in their moral excellence or holiness. In this consists the loveliness of the angels; without it, with all their natural perfections, their strength and their knowledge, they would have no more loveliness than devils. It is moral excellence alone that is, in itself and on its own account, the excellence of intelligent beings. It is this that gives beauty to their natural perfections and qualities, or rather is the beauty of them. Moral excellence is the excellence of natural excellences. Natural qualities are excellent or otherwise according as they are joined with moral excellence or not. Strength and knowledge do not make any being lovely without holiness, but more hateful; though they make beings more lovely when they are joined with holiness. So the elect angels are the more glorious for their strength and knowledge, because these natural perfections of theirs are sanctified by their moral perfection. But though the devils are very strong and of great natural understanding, they are not the more lovely for it. They are more terrifying indeed, but not the more lovely; on the contrary, they are the more hateful. The holiness of an intelligent creature is the beauty of all his natural perfections. And so it is in God, according to our way of conceiving of the divine being: holiness is in a special way the beauty of the divine nature. That is why we often read of the beauty of holiness (Ps 29:2; 96:9; 110:3). This makes all his other attributes glorious and lovely. It is the glory of God’s wisdom that it is a holy wisdom, and not a wicked subtlety and craftiness. What makes his majesty lovely, and not merely dreadful and horrible, is that it is a holy majesty. It is the glory of God’s unchangeableness that it is a holy unchangeableness, and not an inflexible obstinacy in wickedness.

And so a sight of God’s loveliness must begin here. A true love to God must begin with a delight in his holiness, and not with a delight in any other attribute. For no other attribute is truly lovely without this, nor lovely in any other way than as (according to our way of conceiving of God) it derives its loveliness from this. So it is impossible that other attributes should appear lovely in their true loveliness until this is seen; and it is impossible that any perfection of the divine nature should be loved with true love until this is loved. If the true loveliness of all God’s perfections arises from the loveliness of his holiness, then the true love of all his perfections arises from the love of his holiness. Those who do not see the glory of God’s holiness cannot see anything of the true glory of his mercy and grace. They see nothing of the glory of those attributes as any excellence of God’s nature as it is in itself, though they may be affected by them, and love them, as they concern their interest. For these attributes are no part of the excellence of God’s nature, as that nature is excellent in itself, in any other way than as they are included in his holiness, taken more broadly, or as they are a part of his moral perfection.

As the beauty of the divine nature consists primarily in God’s holiness, so does the beauty of all divine things. In this consists the beauty of the saints: that they are saints, or holy ones. It is the moral image of God in them which is their beauty, and that is their holiness. In this consists the beauty and brightness of the angels of heaven: that they are holy angels, and so not devils (Dan 4:13, 17, 23; Matt 25:31; Mark 8:38; Acts 10:22; Rev 14:10). In this consists the beauty of the Christian religion above all other religions: that it is so holy a religion. In this consists the excellence of the word of God: that it is so holy. Ps 119:140: “Your word is completely pure; therefore Your servant loves it.” Verse 128: “I consider all Your precepts right in all things, and I hate every false way.” Verse 138: “The testimonies You have laid down are righteous and altogether faithful.” And verse 172: “My tongue sings of Your word, for all Your commandments are righteous.” And Ps 19:7–10: “The Law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the Lord is trustworthy, making wise the simple. The precepts of the Lord are right, bringing joy to the heart; the commandment of the Lord is pure, giving light to the eyes. The fear of the Lord is clean, enduring forever; the judgments of the Lord are true, being altogether righteous. They are more to be desired than gold, than much pure gold; they are sweeter than honey, than honey from the comb.” In this primarily consists the loveliness and beauty of the Lord Jesus, by which he is the chief among ten thousand and altogether lovely: in that he is “the Holy One of God” (Acts 3:14), and God’s “holy servant” (Acts 4:27), and “the One who is holy and true” (Rev 3:7). All the spiritual beauty of his human nature, consisting in his meekness, lowliness, patience, heavenliness, love to God, love to men, stooping to the lowly and despised, compassion to the miserable, and so on, is all summed up in his holiness. And the beauty of his divine nature, of which the beauty of his human nature is the image and reflection, also consists primarily in his holiness. In this primarily consists the glory of the gospel: that it is a holy gospel, and so bright an outshining of the holy beauty of God and Jesus Christ. In this consists the spiritual beauty of its doctrines: that they are holy doctrines, or doctrines according to godliness. And in this consists the spiritual beauty of the way of salvation by Jesus Christ: that it is so holy a way. And in this chiefly consists the glory of heaven: that it is the holy city, the holy Jerusalem, the habitation of God’s holiness, and so of his glory (Isa 63:15). All the beauties of the new Jerusalem, as it is described in the last two chapters of Revelation, are only various representations of this: see Rev 21:2, 10, 11, 18, 21, 27; 22:1, 3.

And so it is primarily on account of this kind of excellence that the saints love all these things. So they love the word of God because it is completely pure. It is on this account that they love the saints; and it is chiefly on this account that heaven is lovely to them, and those holy tabernacles of God lovely in their eyes. It is on this account that they love God; and it is primarily on this account that they love Christ, and that their hearts delight in the doctrines of the gospel and sweetly rest in the way of salvation revealed there53.

Under the head of the first distinguishing characteristic of gracious affection, I observed that a new supernatural sense is given to those who are regenerated. It is, as it were, a certain divine, spiritual taste, which is in its whole nature different from any former kinds of sensation of the mind, as tasting is different from any of the other five senses. And I observed that something is perceived by a true saint in spiritual and divine things, in the exercise of this new sense of mind, which is as entirely different from anything natural men perceive in them as the sweet taste of honey is different from the ideas men get of honey by looking at it or touching it. Now what I have been speaking of, namely the beauty of holiness, is that thing in spiritual and divine things which is perceived by this spiritual sense, so different from all that natural men perceive in them. This kind of beauty is the quality that is the immediate object of this spiritual sense; this is the sweetness that is the proper object of this spiritual taste. Scripture often represents the beauty and sweetness of holiness as the grand object of a spiritual taste and a spiritual appetite. This was the sweet food of the holy soul of Jesus Christ (John 4:32, 34): “I have food to eat that you+ know nothing about. … My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.” I know of no part of the holy Scriptures where the nature and evidences of true and sincere godliness are so deliberately, so fully and so extensively set out and described as in Psalm 119. The psalmist declares his purpose in the first verses of the psalm, and he keeps his eye on this purpose all the way through and pursues it to the end. And in this psalm the excellence of holiness is represented as the immediate object of a spiritual taste, relish, appetite and delight. God’s law, that grand expression and outflowing of the holiness of God’s nature, and prescription of holiness to the creature, is represented all through as the food and delight, and as the great object of the love, the appetite, the delight and the rejoicing of the gracious nature. That nature prizes God’s commandments above gold, above pure gold, and to it they are sweeter than honey, than honey from the comb; and that on account of their holiness, as I observed before. The same psalmist declares that this is the sweetness a spiritual taste relishes in God’s law (Ps 19:7–10): “The Law of the Lord is perfect … the commandment of the Lord is pure … The fear of the Lord is clean … the precepts of the Lord are right, bringing joy to the heart … the judgments of the Lord are true, being altogether righteous. They are more to be desired than gold, than much pure gold; they are sweeter than honey, than honey from the comb.”

A holy love has a holy object. The holiness of love consists especially in this: that it is the love of what is holy, as holy, or for its holiness; so that it is the holiness of the object which is the quality on which it fixes and in which it comes to rest. A holy nature must love that in holy things chiefly which is most agreeable to itself. But surely what is agreeable to a holy nature in divine things, above all else, is holiness, because holiness must be agreeable to holiness above all other things. For nothing can be more agreeable to any nature than itself: holy nature must be agreeable to holy nature above all things. And so the holy nature of God and Christ, and the word of God, and other divine things, must be agreeable above all other things to the holy nature that is in the saints.

And again, a holy nature no doubt loves holy things especially on account of that for which sinful nature has enmity against them. But what sinful nature is chiefly at enmity against in holy things is their holiness. It is for this that the carnal mind is enmity against God, and against the law of God and the people of God. Now it is fair arguing from contraries: from contrary causes to contrary effects, from opposite natures to opposite tendencies. We know that holiness is of a nature directly contrary to wickedness. So, as it is the nature of wickedness chiefly to oppose and hate holiness, it must be the nature of holiness chiefly to tend toward holiness and delight in it.

The holy nature in the saints and angels in heaven, where its true tendency appears best, is chiefly engaged by the holiness of divine things. This is the divine beauty that chiefly engages the attention, wonder and praise of the bright and burning seraphim (Isa 6:3): “And they were calling out to one another: ‘Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory.’ ” And Rev 4:8: “Day and night they never stop saying: ‘Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!’ ” So too the glorified saints (Rev 15:4): “Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name? For You alone are holy.”

And the Scriptures represent the saints on earth as adoring God primarily on this account, and as wondering at and extolling all God’s attributes, either as deriving their loveliness from his holiness or as being a part of it. So when they praise God for his power, his holiness is the beauty that engages them (Ps 98:1): “Sing to the Lord a new song, for He has done wonders; His right hand and holy arm have gained Him the victory.” So too when they praise him for his justice and terrible majesty (Ps 99:2–3): “Great is the Lord in Zion; He is exalted above all the peoples. Let them praise Your great and awesome name—He is holy!” Verse 5: “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship at His footstool; He is holy!” Verses 8–9: “You were a forgiving God to them, yet an avenger of their misdeeds. Exalt the Lord our God and worship at His holy mountain, for the Lord our God is holy.” So too when they praise God for his mercy and faithfulness (Ps 97:11–12): “Light shines on the righteous, gladness on the upright in heart. Rejoice in the Lord, you+ righteous ones, and praise His holy name.” 1 Sam 2:2: “There is no one holy like the Lord. Indeed, there is no one besides You! And there is no Rock like our God.”

By this, then, all may test their affections, and particularly their love and joy. Various kinds of creatures show the difference of their natures very much in the different things they relish as their proper good, one delighting in what another abhors. Such a difference there is between true saints and natural men. Natural men have no sense of the goodness and excellence of holy things, at least not for their holiness. They have no taste for that kind of good, and so they may be said not to know that divine good, or not to see it; it is wholly hidden from them. But the saints, by the mighty power of God, have it shown to them. They have been given that supernatural, most noble and divine sense by which they perceive it. And it is this that captivates their hearts and delights them above all things. It is the most lovely and sweet thing to the heart of a true saint that is to be found in heaven or earth: what attracts and engages his soul above all else, what he places his happiness in above all things, and what he counts on for comfort and refreshment to his mind in this world and for full satisfaction and blessedness in the next. By this you may examine your love to God, to Jesus Christ and to the word of God, and your joy in them, and also your love to the people of God and your desires for heaven: whether they come from a supreme delight in this sort of beauty, without being moved primarily by your imagined share in them or your expectations from them. There are many high affections, great seeming love and rapturous joys, which have nothing of this holy relish in them.

In particular, by what has been said you may test your manifestations of the glory of God’s grace and love, and the affections arising from them. The grace of God may appear lovely in two ways: either as bonum utile, a profitable good to me, something that greatly serves my interest and so suits my self-love; or as bonum formosum, a good that is beautiful in itself and part of the moral and spiritual excellence of the divine nature. It is in this latter respect that the true saints have their hearts affected, and their love captivated, by the free grace of God in the first place.

From what has been said it appears that if persons have a great sense of the natural perfections of God, and are greatly affected by them, or have any other sight or sense of God than one that consists in, or implies, a sense of the beauty of his moral perfections, it is no certain sign of grace. In particular, men’s having a great sense of the fearful greatness and terrible majesty of God is no certain sign; for this is only God’s natural perfection, and men may see it and yet be entirely blind to the beauty of his moral perfection, having nothing of that spiritual taste which relishes this divine sweetness.

It has already been shown, in what was said on the first distinguishing mark of gracious affections, that what is spiritual is entirely different in its nature from all that any graceless person can possibly experience while he remains graceless. But it is possible for those who are wholly without grace to have a clear sight, and a very great and affecting sense, of God’s greatness, his mighty power and fearful majesty. For this is what the devils have, though they have lost the spiritual knowledge of God, which consists in a sense of the loveliness of his moral perfections. They are entirely without any sense or relish of that kind of beauty; yet they have a very great knowledge of the natural glory of God (if I may speak so), or his fearful greatness and majesty. This they behold, and are affected by their perception of it, and so they tremble before him. All will behold this glory of God at the day of judgment. God will make all rational beings behold it to a great degree indeed, angels and devils, saints and sinners. He will display his infinite greatness and fearful majesty to everyone in a most open, clear and convincing way, and in a light that no one can resist, when he comes in the glory of his Father, and every eye sees him. When they cry to the mountains to fall on them, to hide them from the face of him who sits on the throne, they are represented as seeing the glory of God’s majesty (Isa 2:10, 19, 21). God will make all his enemies behold this, and live in a most clear and affecting view of it in hell to all eternity. God has often declared his unchangeable purpose to make all his enemies know him in this respect, by so often adding these words to the threats he pronounces against them: “and they will know that I am the Lord.” Indeed, he has sworn that all men will see his glory in this respect (Num 14:21): “As surely as I live, all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the Lord.” And this kind of manifestation of God is very often spoken of in Scripture as made, or to be made, in the sight of God’s enemies in this world (Exod 9:16; 14:18; 15:16; Ps 66:3; 46:10; and countless other places). This was a manifestation God made of himself in the sight of that wicked congregation at Mount Sinai, affecting them deeply with it, so that all the people in the camp trembled. Wicked men and devils will see, and have a great sense of, everything that belongs to the glory of God except the beauty of his moral perfection. They will see his infinite greatness and majesty and his infinite power, and will be fully convinced of his omniscience, his eternity and his unchangeableness. And they will see and know everything that belongs to his moral attributes themselves, except their beauty and loveliness. They will see and know that he is perfectly just and righteous and true; that he is a holy God, of purer eyes than to behold evil, who cannot look on iniquity; and they will see the wonderful displays of his infinite goodness and free grace to the saints. Nothing will be hidden from their eyes except the beauty of these moral attributes, and that beauty of the other attributes which arises from it. And so natural men in this world are capable of having a very affecting sense of everything else that belongs to God, except this alone. Nebuchadnezzar had a great and very affecting sense of the infinite greatness and fearful majesty of God, of his supreme and absolute dominion, his mighty and irresistible power, and his sovereignty, and that he and all the inhabitants of the earth were nothing before him. He also had a great conviction in his conscience of God’s justice, and an affecting sense of his great goodness (Dan 4:1–3, 34, 35, 37). And the sense that Darius had of God’s perfections seems to have been very much like his (Dan 6:25 and following). But the saints and angels behold the glory of God that consists in the beauty of his holiness; and it is this sight alone that will melt and humble the hearts of men, wean them from the world, draw them to God, and effectually change them. A sight of the fearful greatness of God may overpower men’s strength and be more than they can endure. But if the moral beauty of God is hidden, the enmity of the heart will remain in its full strength; no love will be kindled; none of this will be effectual to win the will, but it will remain inflexible. Whereas the first glimpse of the moral and spiritual glory of God shining into the heart produces all these effects, as it were with almighty power, which nothing can withstand.

The sense that natural men may have of the fearful greatness of God may affect them in various ways. It may not only terrify them; it may also elevate them and raise their joy and praise, as their circumstances may be. This will be its natural effect, under the influence of mere principles of nature, when they receive, or suppose they receive, some extraordinary mercy from God. It has already been shown that receiving kindness may, by the influence of natural principles, affect the heart with gratitude and praise to God. But if a person, at the same time that he receives remarkable kindness from God, has a sense of his infinite greatness, and that he himself is nothing in comparison with him, surely this will naturally raise his gratitude and praise all the higher for kindness to one so far beneath him. A sense of God’s greatness had this effect on Nebuchadnezzar when he received that extraordinary favor of his restoration, after he had been driven from men and had lived with the beasts. A sense of God’s exceeding greatness raised his gratitude very high, so that he extolled and magnified God in the loftiest terms and called on all the world to do so with him. And much more, if a natural man, at the same time that he is greatly affected by God’s infinite greatness and majesty, holds a strong notion that this great God has made him his child and special favorite, and has promised him eternal glory in his highest love, this will tend, by the course of nature, to raise his joy and praise to a great height.

So it is beyond doubt that too much weight has lately been laid by many persons on manifestations of God’s greatness, fearful majesty and natural perfection working in this way, without any real view of the holy, lovely majesty of God. And experience abundantly bears witness to what reason and Scripture declare on this matter. For there have been very many persons who seemed to be overpowered by the greatness and fearful majesty of God, and were in consequence elevated in the way just described, who have been very far from showing a Christian spirit and disposition in any sort of proportion, or fruits in practice in any way agreeable to it. Their manifestations have worked in a way contrary to the working of truly spiritual manifestations.

Not that a sense of God’s greatness and natural attributes is not exceedingly useful and necessary. For, as I observed before, this is implied in a manifestation of the beauty of God’s holiness. Though that is something beyond it, it supposes it, as the greater supposes the less. And though natural men may have a sense of the natural perfections of God, yet no doubt this is more frequent and common with the saints than with natural men; and grace tends to enable men to see these things in a better way than natural men do. It enables them to see not only God’s natural attributes, but that beauty of those attributes which (according to our way of conceiving of God) is derived from his holiness.

53. For the right embracing of Christ’s person this also is required: to taste the bitterness of sin as the greatest evil. Otherwise a man will never embrace Christ for his holiness, in him and from him, as the greatest good. For we told you that it is the right embracing of Christ for himself when it is for his holiness. For ask a whorish heart what beauty he sees in the person of Christ: after he has looked over his kingdom, his righteousness and all his works, he will see a beauty in them because they serve his purpose, to comfort him only. Ask a virgin: he will see his happiness in all; but what makes the Lord lovely is his holiness, which is in him to make him holy too. As in marriage, it is the personal beauty that draws the heart. And so I have thought it reasonable that he who loves the brethren for a little grace will love Christ much more. Shepard’s parable, P. I. P. 84.

The Mind Enlightened

Part III · Sign IV

IV. Gracious affections arise from the mind’s being enlightened to understand or apprehend divine things rightly and spiritually.

Holy affections are not heat without light. They always arise from some information of the understanding, some spiritual instruction the mind receives, some light or actual knowledge. The child of God is graciously affected because he sees and understands something more of divine things than he did before: more of God or Christ, and of the glorious things set forth in the gospel. He has some clearer and better view than he had before, when he was not affected. Either he receives some understanding of divine things that is new to him, or his former knowledge is renewed after the view of it had decayed. 1 John 4:7: “Everyone who loves … knows God.” Phil 1:9: “that your+ love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight.” Rom 10:2: “they are zealous for God, but not on the basis of knowledge.” Col 3:10: “the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge.” Ps 43:3–4: “Send out Your light and Your truth; let them lead me. Let them bring me to Your holy mountain.” John 6:45: “It is written in the Prophets: ‘And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard the Father and learned from Him comes to Me.” Knowledge is the key that first opens the hard heart and enlarges the affections, and so opens the way for men into the kingdom of heaven. Luke 11:52: “You+ have taken away the key to knowledge.”

Now there are many affections which do not arise from any light in the understanding. And when this is so, it is a sure evidence that these affections are not spiritual, however high they may be54 . Indeed they have some new perceptions which they did not have before. Such is the nature of man that it is impossible for his mind to be affected except by something he perceives, or that his mind conceives of. But in many persons the perceptions or conceptions they are affected by have nothing of the nature of knowledge or instruction in them. For instance, a person may be affected by a lively idea, suddenly stirred up in his mind, of some shape, or a very beautiful, pleasant face, or some shining light, or some other glorious outward appearance. Here something is perceived or conceived by the mind, but there is nothing of the nature of instruction in it. Persons become none the wiser by such things, nor more knowing about God, or a Mediator between God and man, or the way of salvation by Christ, or anything contained in any of the doctrines of the gospel. By these external ideas persons gain no further acquaintance with God in any of the attributes or perfections of his nature, nor any further understanding of his word, or of any of his ways or works. Truly spiritual and gracious affections are not raised in this way. They arise from the enlightening of the understanding to understand the things that are taught of God and Christ in a new way: the coming to a new understanding of the excellent nature of God and his wonderful perfections, some new view of Christ in his spiritual excellences and fullness, or things belonging to the way of salvation by Christ opened to a person in a new way, so that he now sees how it is, and understands those divine and spiritual doctrines which were once foolishness to him. Such enlightenings of the understanding as these are things entirely different in their nature from strong ideas of shapes and colors, outward brightness and glory, or sounds and voices. So the fact that all gracious affections arise from some instruction or enlightening of the understanding is a further proof that affections arising from such impressions on the imagination are not gracious affections, besides the things observed before which make this evident.

From this it also appears that affections arising from texts of Scripture coming to the mind are vain when the ground of the affection is not any instruction received in the understanding from those texts, or anything taught in them, but the way they came to the mind. When Christ makes the Scripture a means of the heart’s burning with gracious affection, it is by opening the Scriptures to their understandings. Luke 24:32: “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” It also appears that an affection occasioned by the coming of a text of Scripture must be vain when it is founded on something supposed to be taught by the text which is really not contained in it, nor in any other Scripture. For such supposed instruction is not real instruction, but a mistake and misapprehension of the mind. For instance, persons may suppose that they are expressly taught by some Scripture coming to their minds that they in particular are loved by God, or that their sins are forgiven, that God is their Father, and the like. This is a mistake or misapprehension. For the Scripture nowhere reveals expressly which individual persons are loved, but only by consequence, by revealing the qualities of persons who are loved by God. So this matter is not to be learned from Scripture in any other way than by consequence, from these qualities; for things are not to be learned from Scripture in any other way than they are taught in Scripture.

In the instances mentioned, affections really arise from ignorance rather than instruction; and so too in some others that might be mentioned. Some, when they find themselves free of speech in prayer, call it God’s being with them; this affects them more, and so their affections are set going and increased. Yet they do not look into the cause of this freedom of speech, which may arise in many other ways besides God’s spiritual presence. So some are much affected by some apt thoughts about Scripture that come into their minds, and call it the Spirit of God teaching them. So they ascribe many of the workings of their own minds, which they have a high opinion of and are pleased and taken with, to the special, immediate influences of God’s Spirit, and so are mightily affected by their privilege. And there are some instances of persons in whom the first ground of their affection seems clearly to be some bodily sensation. The animal spirits, from some cause (and probably sometimes by the devil), are suddenly and unaccountably put into a very agreeable motion, causing persons to feel pleasant sensations in their bodies. The animal spirits are put into such a motion as is usually connected with the exhilaration of the mind, and the soul, by the laws of the union of soul and body, feels pleasure from it. The motion of the animal spirits does not first arise from any affection or perception of the mind whatever. The very first thing that is felt is an exhilaration of the animal spirits and a pleasant external sensation, perhaps in the breast. Then, through ignorance, the person is taken by surprise and begins to think, Surely this is the Holy Spirit coming into me. And then the mind begins to be affected and raised. First there is great joy, and then many other affections, in a very tumultuous way, throwing all nature, both body and mind, into a mighty commotion. For though, as I observed before, it is the soul alone that is the seat of the affections, this does not prevent bodily sensations from being, in this way, an occasion of affections in the mind.

And even if men’s religious affections do truly arise from some instruction or light in the understanding, the affection is still not gracious unless the light which is its ground is spiritual. Affections may be stirred up by the understanding of things that men obtain merely by human teaching, with the common use and development of the faculties of the mind. Men may be much affected by knowledge of the things of religion that they obtain in this way, as some philosophers have been mightily affected, and almost carried beyond themselves, by the discoveries they have made in mathematics and natural science. So men may be much affected by common illuminations of the Spirit of God, in which God assists men’s faculties to a greater degree of the kind of understanding of religious matters which they have in some degree by the ordinary exercise and development of their own faculties alone. Such illuminations may much affect the mind, as in many we read of in Scripture who were once enlightened; but these affections are not spiritual.

If the Scriptures are of any use to teach us anything, there is such a thing as a spiritual, supernatural understanding of divine things which is peculiar to the saints, and of which those who are not saints have nothing. The apostle certainly speaks of a kind of understanding, apprehending or discerning of divine things which natural men have nothing of, in 1 Cor 2:14: “The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned.” A kind of seeing or discerning of spiritual things peculiar to the saints is certainly spoken of in 1 John 3:6: “No one who continues to sin has seen Him or known Him.” 3 John 11: “The one who does evil has not seen God.” And John 6:40: “It is My Father’s will that everyone who sees the Son and believes in Him shall have eternal life.” John 14:19: “The world will see Me no more, but you+ will see Me.” John 17:3: “Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent.” Matt 11:27: “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.” John 12:45: “Whoever sees Me sees the One who sent Me.” Ps 9:10: “Those who know Your name trust in You.” Phil 3:8: “I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord …” Verse 10: “I want to know Christ …” And there are countless other places all over the Bible which show the same. And that there is such a thing as an understanding of divine things which in its nature and kind is wholly different from all the knowledge natural men have is evident from this: there is an understanding of divine things which Scripture calls spiritual understanding. Col 1:9: “We have not stopped praying for you+ and asking God to fill you+ with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding.” It has already been shown that what is spiritual, in the ordinary use of the word in the New Testament, is entirely different in nature and kind from all that natural men experience or can experience.

From this it may be inferred with certainty what spiritual understanding consists in. For if there is in the saints a kind of apprehension or perception which in its nature is entirely different from all that natural men have, or can possibly have until they have a new nature, it must consist in their having a certain kind of ideas or sensations of mind which are simply different from all that is or can be in the minds of natural men. And that is the same as saying that it consists in the sensations of a new spiritual sense, which the souls of natural men do not have, as is evident from what has been observed again and again before. But I have already shown what that new spiritual sense is which the saints are given in regeneration, and what its object is. I have shown that its immediate object is the supreme beauty and excellence of the nature of divine things as they are in themselves. And this agrees with Scripture. The apostle very plainly teaches that the great thing shown by spiritual light, and understood by spiritual knowledge, is the glory of divine things. 2 Cor 4:3–4: “And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.” Together with verse 6: “For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.” And 2 Cor 3:18, just before: “And we, who with unveiled faces all behold the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.” And it must be so. For, as has been observed before, Scripture often teaches that all true religion consists, in sum, in the love of divine things. So the kind of understanding or knowledge which is the proper foundation of true religion must be the knowledge of the loveliness of divine things. For no doubt the knowledge which is the proper foundation of love is the knowledge of loveliness. What that beauty or loveliness of divine things is which is the proper and immediate object of a spiritual sense of mind was shown under the last head discussed: namely, that it is the beauty of their moral perfection. So it is in the view or sense of this that spiritual understanding most immediately and primarily consists. And indeed it is plain that it can be nothing else. For (as has been shown) natural men and devils can see and know everything belonging to divine things except the beauty of their moral excellence and those properties and qualities of divine things of which this beauty is the foundation; and all the rest they will know fully and clearly to all eternity.

From what has been said, then, we necessarily come to this conclusion about what spiritual understanding consists in: namely, that it consists in a sense of the heart of the supreme beauty and sweetness of the holiness or moral perfection of divine things, together with all the discerning and knowledge of the things of religion that depends on, and flows from, such a sense.

Spiritual understanding consists primarily in a sense of heart of that spiritual beauty. I say, a sense of heart; for it is not merely theory that is involved in this kind of understanding. Nor can a clear distinction be made in this matter between the two faculties of understanding and will, as acting distinctly and separately. When the mind has a sense of the sweet beauty and loveliness of a thing, that implies a sense of sweetness and delight in the presence of the idea of it. And this sense of the loveliness or delightfulness of beauty carries in its very nature the sense of the heart: an effect and impression the soul receives as a substance possessed of taste, inclination and will.

There is a distinction to be made between a merely notional understanding, in which the mind only beholds things in the exercise of a theoretical faculty, and the sense of the heart, in which the mind does not only contemplate and behold, but relishes and feels. The sort of knowledge by which a man has a felt perception of loveliness and loathsomeness, or of sweetness and nauseousness, is not the same sort of knowledge as that by which he knows what a triangle is and what a square is. The one is merely theoretical knowledge; the other is felt knowledge, in which more than the mere intellect is involved. The heart is its proper subject: the soul as a being that not only beholds but has inclination, and is pleased or displeased. And yet there is the nature of instruction in it; as he who has perceived the sweet taste of honey knows much more about it than he who has only looked at it and touched it.

The apostle seems to make a distinction between merely theoretical knowledge of the things of religion and spiritual knowledge, in calling the former “the form of knowledge and truth.” Rom 2:20: “because you have in the law the form of knowledge and truth.” The latter is often represented by relishing, smelling or tasting. 2 Cor 2:14: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us triumphantly as captives in Christ and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of the knowledge of Him.” Matt 16:23: “You do not savor the things of God, but the things of men.” 1 Pet 2:2–3: “Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk, so that by it you+ may grow up in your+ salvation, now that you+ have tasted that the Lord is good.” Song 1:3: “The fragrance of your perfume is pleasing; your name is like perfume poured out. No wonder the maidens adore you”; compared with 1 John 2:20: “You+, however, have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you+ know the truth.”

Spiritual understanding consists primarily in this sense, or taste, of the moral beauty of divine things; so that no knowledge can be called spiritual except so far as it arises from this and has this in it. But secondarily it includes all the discerning and knowledge of the things of religion that depends on, and flows from, such a sense.

When the true beauty and loveliness of the holiness, or true moral good, that is in divine things is shown to the soul, it opens, as it were, a new world to its view. This shows the glory of all the perfections of God, and of everything belonging to the divine being; for, as was observed before, the beauty of all arises from God’s moral perfection. This shows the glory of all God’s works, both of creation and of providence. For it is their special glory that God’s holiness, righteousness, faithfulness and goodness are so displayed in them; and without these moral perfections there would be no glory in the power and skill with which they are done. The glorifying of God’s moral perfections is the special end of all the works of God’s hands. By this sense of the moral beauty of divine things the sufficiency of Christ as a mediator is understood. For it is only by the showing of the beauty of the moral perfection of Christ that the believer is let into the knowledge of the excellence of his person, so as to know anything more of it than the devils do. And it is only by the knowledge of the excellence of Christ’s person that anyone knows his sufficiency as a mediator, for the latter depends on and arises from the former. It is by seeing the excellence of Christ’s person that the saints are brought to a sense of the preciousness of his blood and its sufficiency to atone for sin. For the preciousness of Christ’s blood consists in this: that it is the blood of so excellent and lovely a person. And on this depend the merit of his obedience and the sufficiency and prevailing power of his intercession. By this sight of the moral beauty of divine things the beauty of the way of salvation by Christ is seen. For that consists in the beauty of the moral perfections of God, which shines out wonderfully in every step of this method of salvation, from beginning to end. By this the fitness and suitableness of this way is seen. For this consists wholly in its tendency to deliver us from sin and hell, and to bring us to the happiness which consists in the possession and enjoyment of moral good, in a way that sweetly agrees with God’s moral perfections. And the excellent wisdom of that way consists in its being so designed as to attain these ends. By this the excellence of the word of God is seen. Take away all the moral beauty and sweetness in the word, and the Bible is left wholly a dead letter, a dry, lifeless, tasteless thing. By this the true foundation of our duty is seen: God’s worthiness to be esteemed, honored, loved, submitted to and served as he requires of us, and the loveliness of the duties themselves that are required of us. And by this the true evil of sin is seen; for he who sees the beauty of holiness must necessarily see the hatefulness of sin, its contrary. By this men understand the true glory of heaven, which consists in the beauty and happiness that is in holiness. By this the loveliness and happiness of both saints and angels is seen. He who sees the beauty of holiness, or true moral good, sees the greatest and most important thing in the world, which is the fullness of all things, without which all the world is empty, no better than nothing; indeed, worse than nothing. Unless this is seen, nothing is seen that is worth seeing; for there is no other true excellence or beauty. Unless this is understood, nothing is understood that is worthy of the exercise of the noble faculty of understanding. This is the beauty of the Godhead, and the divinity of divinity (if I may speak so), the good of the infinite fountain of good; without which God himself (if that were possible) would be an infinite evil; without which it would have been better for us never to have existed; and without which it would have been better for there to be no being at all. So the man who does not know this in effect knows nothing. His knowledge is only the shadow of knowledge, or the form of knowledge, as the apostle calls it. Well, then, may Scripture represent those who lack that spiritual sense by which the beauty of holiness is perceived as totally blind, deaf and senseless, indeed dead. And well may regeneration, in which this divine sense is given to the soul by its Creator, be represented as opening blind eyes, raising the dead, and bringing a person into a new world. For if what has been said is considered, it will be clear that when a person is given this sense and knowledge, he will view nothing as he did before. Though before he knew all things according to the flesh, from now on he will know them so no longer; and he is a new creation; the old has passed away; all things have become new; in agreement with 2 Corinthians 5:16–17.

And besides the things already mentioned, all true experiential knowledge of religion arises from this sense of spiritual beauty; and this is in itself, as it were, a new world of knowledge. He who does not see the beauty of holiness does not know what a single one of the graces of God’s Spirit is. He has no idea or conception of any gracious exercises of soul, any holy comforts and delights, or any effects of the saving influences of the Spirit of God on the heart. And so he is ignorant of the greatest works of God, the most important and glorious effects of his power on the creature. He is also wholly ignorant of the saints as saints; he does not know what they are. In effect he is ignorant of the whole spiritual world.

Since things are so, it plainly appears that God’s implanting the spiritual, supernatural sense that has been spoken of makes a great change in a man. Were it not for the very imperfect degree in which this sense is commonly given at first, or the small degree of this glorious light that first dawns on the soul, the change made by this spiritual opening of the eyes in conversion would be much greater, and more remarkable in every way, than if a man born blind, with only the other four senses, should remain so for a long time, and then should suddenly be given the sense of sight in the midst of the clear light of the sun, showing him a world of visible objects. For though sight is more noble than any of the other external senses, this spiritual sense which has been spoken of is infinitely more noble than that, or than any other principle of discerning that a man naturally has; and the object of this sense is infinitely greater and more important.

This sort of understanding or knowledge is the knowledge of divine things from which all truly gracious affections proceed; and so it is by this that all affections are to be tested. Those affections that arise wholly from any other kind of knowledge, or result from any other kind of perceptions of mind, are vain.55

From what has been said we may learn where the most essential difference lies between the light or understanding given by the common influences of the Spirit of God on the hearts of natural men and the saving instruction given to the saints. The latter lies primarily and most essentially in beholding the holy beauty that is in divine things, which is the only true moral good, and to which the soul of fallen man is by nature totally blind. The former consists only in a further understanding, through the assistance of natural principles, of those things which men may know in some measure by the ordinary exercise of their faculties alone. And this knowledge consists only in the knowledge of those things belonging to religion which are natural. So, for instance, in the awakenings and convictions of conscience that natural men are often subject to, the Spirit of God gives no knowledge of the true moral beauty which is in divine things. He only assists the mind to a clearer idea of the guilt of sin, or its relation to a punishment and its connection with the evil of suffering (without any sight of its true moral evil, or its odiousness as sin), and to a clearer idea of the natural perfections of God, in which consists not his holy beauty and glory but his fearful and awesome greatness. It is a clear sight of this that will fully awaken the consciences of wicked men at the day of judgment, without any spiritual light. And it is a lesser degree of the same that awakens the consciences of natural men in this world, without spiritual light. The same manifestations are given in some measure in the conscience of an awakened sinner in this world which will be given more fully in the consciences of sinners at the day of judgment. The same kind of sight or perception of God which, in a lesser degree, makes awakened sinners in this world feel the dreadful guilt of sin against so great and terrible a God, and feel its amazing punishment, and fills them with fearful apprehensions of divine wrath, is what will thoroughly convict all wicked men of the infinitely dreadful nature and guilt of sin, and astonish them with apprehensions of wrath, when Christ comes in the glory of his power and majesty, and every eye sees him, and all the tribes of the earth mourn because of him. And in the common illuminations sometimes given to natural men, stirring up in them some kind of religious desire, love and joy, the mind is only assisted to a clearer perception of the natural good that is in divine things. So at times, under common illuminations, men are elated by the ideas of the natural good that is in heaven: its outward glory, its ease, its honor and advancement, being there the objects of the high favor of God and the great regard of men and angels, and so on. So there are many things set forth in the gospel concerning God and Christ and the way of salvation that have a natural good in them, which suits the natural principle of self-love. So in the great goodness of God to sinners, and the wonderful dying love of Christ, there is a natural good which all men love as they love themselves, as well as a spiritual and holy beauty which is seen only by the regenerate. So there are many things belonging to the word of God’s grace delivered in the gospel which may cause natural men, when they hear it, at once to receive it with joy. All the love natural men have for God and Christ, for Christian virtues and good men, comes not from any sight of the loveliness of the holiness, or true moral excellence, of these things, but only for the sake of the natural good there is in them. All natural men’s hatred of sin comes as much from principles of nature as men’s hatred of a tiger for his ferocity, or their aversion to a snake for its poison and harmfulness. And all their love of Christian virtue comes from no higher principle than their love of a man’s good nature, which appears lovely to natural men; but no otherwise than silver and gold appear lovely in the eyes of a merchant, or the blackness of the soil is beautiful in the eyes of the farmer.

From what has been said of the nature of spiritual understanding, it appears that spiritual understanding does not consist in any new doctrinal knowledge, or in having any new proposition suggested to the mind which was not read or heard of before. For it is plain that this suggesting of new propositions is a thing entirely different from giving the mind a new taste or relish of beauty and sweetness.56 It is also evident that spiritual knowledge does not consist in any new doctrinal explanation of any part of Scripture. For this is still only doctrinal knowledge, or the knowledge of propositions. The doctrinal explaining of any part of Scripture only gives us to understand what propositions are contained or taught in that part of Scripture.

So it appears that the spiritual understanding of Scripture does not consist in opening to the mind the mystical meaning of Scripture in its parables, types and allegories; for this is only a doctrinal explanation of Scripture. He who explains what is meant by the stony ground, and the seed’s springing up suddenly and quickly withering away, only explains what propositions or doctrines are taught in it. So he who explains what is typified by Jacob’s ladder, and the angels of God ascending and descending on it, or what was typified by Joshua’s leading Israel through the Jordan, only shows what propositions are hidden in these passages. And many men can explain these types who have no spiritual knowledge. A man might know how to interpret all the types, parables, riddles and allegories in the Bible and not have one beam of spiritual light in his mind. For he may not have the least degree of that spiritual sense of the holy beauty of divine things which has been spoken of, and may see nothing of this kind of glory in anything contained in any of these mysteries, or in any other part of Scripture.
