It is plain from what the apostle says that a man might understand all such mysteries and have no saving grace. 1 Cor 13:2: “If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge … but have not love, I am nothing.” So those are very foolish who are exalted in an opinion of their own spiritual attainments by notions that come into their minds of the mystical meaning of this or that passage of Scripture, as though this were a spiritual understanding of these passages given them immediately by the Spirit of God, and who have their affections highly raised by it. What has been said shows the vanity of such affections.

From what has been said it is also evident that it is not spiritual knowledge for persons to be informed of their duty by having it immediately suggested to their minds that such and such outward actions or deeds are the will of God. If we suppose that it truly is God’s way to signify his will to his people like this, by immediate inward suggestions, such suggestions have nothing of the nature of spiritual light. Such knowledge would be only one kind of doctrinal knowledge. A proposition concerning the will of God is as properly a doctrine of religion as a proposition concerning the nature of God, or a work of God. And having either of these kinds of propositions, or any other proposition, declared to a man, either by speech or by inward suggestion, differs vastly from having the holy beauty of divine things shown to the soul, in which spiritual knowledge most essentially consists. So there was no spiritual light in Balaam, though he had the will of God immediately suggested to him by the Spirit of God from time to time, concerning the way he should go and what he should do and say.

It is clear, then, that being led and directed in this way is not that holy and spiritual leading of the Spirit of God which is peculiar to the saints, and a distinguishing mark of the sons of God, spoken of in Romans 8:14: “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.” Gal 5:18: “But if you+ are led by the Spirit, you+ are not under the law.”

And suppose persons have the will of God concerning their actions suggested to them by some text of Scripture suddenly and extraordinarily brought to their minds. As the words stood in the Bible before they came to their minds, the text related to the actions and behavior of some other person; but they suppose that, as God sent the words to them, he meant something further by them, and meant some particular action of theirs. I say, if persons should have the will of God suggested to them with texts of Scripture in this way, it does not alter the case. The suggestion’s being accompanied by an apt text of Scripture does not make it of the nature of spiritual instruction. For instance, suppose a person in New England were on some occasion at a loss whether it was his duty to go into some popish or heathen land, where he was likely to be exposed to many difficulties and dangers. He prays to God to show him the way of his duty; and after earnest prayer he has the words God spoke to Jacob in Genesis 46 suddenly and extraordinarily brought to his mind, as if they were spoken to him: “Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt … I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will surely bring you back.” As these words stood in the Bible before they came to his mind, they related only to Jacob and his conduct. Yet he supposes that God has a further meaning in them, as they were brought and applied to him: that they are to be understood in a new sense, that by Egypt is meant this particular country he has in mind, that the action intended is his going there, and that the meaning of the promise is that God will bring him back to New England again. There is nothing of the nature of a spiritual or gracious leading of the Spirit in this, for there is nothing of the nature of spiritual understanding in it. To understand texts of Scripture in this way is not to have a spiritual understanding of them. To understand Scripture spiritually is to understand rightly what is in Scripture, and what was in it before it was understood. It is to understand rightly what was always contained in its meaning, and not to make a new meaning. When the mind is enlightened to understand Scripture spiritually and rightly, it is enabled to see in Scripture what was not seen before because of blindness. But if it was because of blindness, that is evidence that the same meaning was in it before; otherwise it would have been no blindness not to see it. It is no blindness not to see a meaning which is not there. Spiritually enlightening the eyes to understand Scripture is opening the eyes. Ps 119:18: “Open my eyes that I may see wondrous things from Your law.” This shows that the reason the same thing was not seen in Scripture before was that the eyes were shut. That would not be the case if the meaning now understood was not there before, but is now newly added to Scripture by the way the Scripture came to my mind. This making of a new meaning for Scripture is the same thing as making a new Scripture. It is properly adding to the word, which is threatened with so dreadful a curse. To understand Scripture spiritually is to have the eyes of the mind opened to behold the wonderful spiritual excellence of the glorious things contained in its true meaning, which have always been contained in it ever since it was written: to behold the lovely and bright displays of the divine perfections, and of the excellence and sufficiency of Christ, and the excellence and suitableness of the way of salvation by Christ, and the spiritual glory of the precepts and promises of Scripture, and so on. These things are, and always were, in the Bible, and would have been seen before if it had not been for blindness, without any new sense being added by the words’ being sent by God to a particular person and spoken to him anew, with a new meaning.

And as to a gracious leading of the Spirit, it consists in two things: partly in instructing a person in his duty by the Spirit, and partly in powerfully inducing him to comply with that instruction. But so far as the gracious leading of the Spirit lies in instruction, it consists in a person’s being guided by a spiritual and distinguishing taste for what has true moral beauty in it. I have shown that spiritual knowledge consists primarily in a taste or relish of the loveliness and beauty of what is truly good and holy. This holy relish is a thing that discerns and distinguishes between good and evil, between holy and unholy, without going to the trouble of a train of reasoning. He who has a true relish of external beauty knows what is beautiful by looking at it. He has no need of a train of reasoning about the proportion of the features to determine whether what he sees is a beautiful face or not; he needs nothing but a glance of his eye. He who has a well-tuned musical ear knows whether the sound he hears is true harmony; he does not first need to go to the trouble of a mathematician’s reasonings about the proportion of the notes. He who has a sound palate knows what is good food as soon as he tastes it, without a physician’s reasoning about it. There is a holy beauty and sweetness in words and actions, as well as a natural beauty in faces and sounds, and sweetness in food. Job 12:11: “Does not the ear test words as the tongue tastes its food?” When a holy and lovely action is suggested to the thoughts of a holy soul, that soul, if it is in the lively exercise of its spiritual taste, at once sees a beauty in it, and so inclines to it and embraces it. On the contrary, if an unworthy, unholy action is suggested to it, its sanctified eye sees no beauty in it and is not pleased with it; its sanctified taste relishes no sweetness in it, but on the contrary finds it nauseous. Indeed, its holy taste and appetite lead it to think of what is truly lovely, and naturally suggest it, as a healthy taste and appetite naturally suggest the idea of their proper object. So a holy person is led by the Spirit as he is instructed and led by his holy taste and disposition of heart. By this, in the lively exercise of grace, he easily distinguishes good and evil, and knows at once what is suitable and lovely behavior toward God and toward man in this case and that. He judges what is right, as it were, spontaneously and of himself, without a particular deduction by any other arguments than the beauty that is seen and the goodness that is tasted. So Christ blames the Pharisees because they did not, even of themselves, judge what was right, without needing miracles to prove it (Luke 12:57). The apostle seems plainly to have this way of judging of spiritual beauty in view in Romans 12:2: “Be transformed by the renewing of your+ mind. Then you+ will be able to test and approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.”

There is such a thing as a good taste of natural beauty (which learned men often speak of), exercised about temporal things in judging them: about the justness of a speech, the goodness of a style, the beauty of a poem, the gracefulness of bearing, and so on. A late great philosopher of our nation writes this about it57: To have a taste is to give things their real value, to be touched with the good and shocked with the ill; not to be dazzled by false luster, but, in spite of all disguises and everything that might deceive or mislead, to judge soundly. Taste and judgment, then, should be the same thing; and yet it is easy to see a difference. The judgment forms its opinions from reflection. On this occasion reason takes a kind of roundabout way to arrive at its end: it supposes principles, it draws consequences, and it judges, but not without a thorough knowledge of the case; so that after it has pronounced, it is ready to give a reason for its decrees. Good taste observes none of these formalities. Before it has time to consult, it has taken its side. As soon as the object is presented to it, the impression is made and the sentiment formed; ask no more of it. As the ear is wounded by a harsh sound, as the smell is soothed by an agreeable odor, before reason has meddled with those objects to judge them, so the taste opens itself at once and goes before all reflection. Reflections may come afterward to confirm it, and show the secret reasons for its conduct; but it was not in its power to wait for them. Frequently it does not know them at all, and whatever pains it takes, it cannot discover what it was that determined it to think as it did. This conduct is very different from what the judgment observes in its decisions; unless we choose to say that good taste is, as it were, a first motion, or a kind of instinct of right reason, which hurries on with rapidity and leads more surely than all the reasonings she could make. It is a first glance of the eye, which shows us the nature and relations of things in a moment.

Now there is such a taste of the mind as this, which philosophers speak of, by which persons are guided in judging the natural beauty, gracefulness, propriety, nobleness and sublimity of speeches and actions, judging, as it were, by the glance of the eye, or by inward sensation and the first impression of the object. So, likewise, there is such a thing as a divine taste, given and maintained by the Spirit of God in the hearts of the saints, by which they are in the same way led and guided in discerning and distinguishing the true spiritual and holy beauty of actions; and they do so the more easily, readily and accurately as they have more or less of the Spirit of God dwelling in them. And so the sons of God are led by the Spirit of God in their behavior in the world.

A holy disposition and spiritual taste, where grace is strong and lively, will enable a soul to determine what actions are right and fitting for Christians not only more quickly but far more exactly than the greatest abilities without it. This may be illustrated by the way some habits of mind and dispositions of heart, of a nature inferior to true grace, will teach and guide a man in his actions. For instance, if a man is a very good-natured man, his good nature will teach him better how to act benevolently among mankind, and will direct him on every occasion to the speeches and actions which agree with the rules of goodness, than the strongest reason will teach a man of a morose disposition. So if a man’s heart is under the influence of an entire friendship and a most tender affection to another, then though he is a man of only ordinary ability, this habit of his mind will direct him far more readily and exactly to a speech and bearing, or manner of behavior, that will be in all respects sweet and kind and agreeable to a benevolent disposition of heart, than the greatest ability without it. He has, as it were, a spirit within him that guides him. The habit of his mind is accompanied by a taste by which he immediately relishes the air and manner that is benevolent and dislikes the contrary; and it causes him to distinguish between the one and the other in a moment, more precisely than the most accurate reasonings can find out in many hours. So the nature and inward tendency of a stone, or other heavy body, let fall from a height, shows the way to the center of the earth more exactly in an instant than the ablest mathematician without it could determine by his most accurate observations in a whole day. This is how a spiritual disposition and taste teaches and guides a man in his behavior in the world. So an eminently humble or meek or charitable disposition will direct a person of small ability to a behavior that agrees with the Christian rules of humility, meekness and charity far more readily and precisely than the most diligent study and elaborate reasonings of a man of the strongest faculties who does not have a Christian spirit within him. So too a spirit of love to God, of holy fear and reverence toward God, of childlike confidence in God, and a heavenly disposition, will teach and guide a man in his behavior.

It is an exceedingly difficult thing for a wicked man, who has no Christian principles in his heart to guide him, to know how to conduct himself like a Christian, with the life and beauty and heavenly sweetness of a truly holy, humble, Christlike behavior. He does not know how to put on these garments, and they do not fit him. Eccl 10:2–3: “A wise man’s heart inclines to the right, but the heart of a fool to the left. Even as the fool walks along the road, his sense is lacking, and he shows everyone that he is a fool.” With verse 15: “The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city.” Prov 10:32: “The lips of the righteous know what is fitting.” Prov 15:2: “The tongue of the wise uses knowledge rightly, but the mouth of the fool spouts folly.” And Prov 16:23: “The heart of the wise man instructs his mouth and adds persuasiveness to his lips.”

The saints, in judging actions by a spiritual taste in this way, do not have particular recourse to the express rules of God’s word for every word and action before them whose good or evil they judge. Yet their taste itself in general is subject to the rule of God’s word, and must be tested by that, and by right reasoning on it. A man with a sound palate judges particular morsels by his taste; yet his palate itself must be judged, whether it is right or not, by certain rules and reasons. But a spiritual taste of soul mightily helps the soul in its reasonings on the word of God, and in judging the true meaning of its rules. It removes the prejudices of a depraved appetite, naturally leads the thoughts in the right channel, casts a light on the word of God, and causes the true meaning to come to mind most naturally, through the harmony there is between the disposition and relish of a sanctified soul and the true meaning of the rules of God’s word. Indeed, this harmony tends to bring the texts themselves to mind on proper occasions, as the particular state of the stomach and palate tends to bring to mind the particular foods and drinks that agree with that state. So the children of God are led by the Spirit of God in judging actions themselves, and in their meditations on God’s holy word, and their judging and applying of its rules. And so God teaches them his statutes, and makes them understand the way of his precepts, which the psalmist prays for so often.

But this leading of the Spirit is something exceedingly different from what some call by that name. Theirs consists not in teaching them God’s statutes and precepts, which he has already given, but in giving them new precepts by immediate inward speech or suggestion; and it has in it no tasting of the true excellence of things, nor any judging or discerning of the nature of things at all. They do not determine what the will of God is by any taste or relish, or by any kind of judgment of the nature of things, but by an immediate dictate concerning the thing to be done. There is no such thing as any judgment or wisdom in the case. Whereas in the leading of the Spirit which is peculiar to God’s children, that true wisdom and holy discretion so often spoken of in the word of God is imparted. It is as high above the other way as the stars are above a glowworm. It is what Balaam and Saul (who were at times led by the Spirit in that other way) never had, and what no natural man can have without a change of nature.

What has been said of the nature of spiritual understanding, as consisting most essentially in a divine, supernatural sense and relish of the heart, shows not only that there is nothing of it in this falsely supposed leading of the Spirit just spoken of. It also shows the difference between spiritual understanding and all kinds and forms of fanaticism: all imaginary sights of God and Christ and heaven; all supposed witnessing of the Spirit, and testimonies of the love of God by immediate inward suggestion; all impressions of future events, and immediate revelations of any secret facts whatever; all fanatical impressions and applications of words of Scripture, as though they were words now immediately spoken by God to a particular person, in a new meaning, and carrying something more in them than the words contain as they stand in the Bible; and all interpretations of the mystical meaning of Scripture by supposed immediate revelation. None of these things consists in a divine sense and relish of the heart of the holy beauty and excellence of divine things, nor have they anything to do with such a sense. They all consist in impressions in the head. They all belong under the head of impressions on the imagination, and consist in stirring up external ideas in the mind: ideas of outward shapes and colors, or of words spoken or letters written, or ideas of external and perceptible things belonging to actions done, or to events accomplished or to be accomplished. A fanatical supposed manifestation of the love of God is made by stirring up in the imagination an idea of a smiling face, or some other pleasant outward appearance, or the idea of pleasant words spoken or written, or some pleasant bodily sensation. So when persons have an imaginary revelation of some secret fact, it is by stirring up external ideas: either of some words implying a declaration of that fact, or of some visible or perceptible circumstances of such a fact. So the supposed leading of the Spirit to do the will of God in outward behavior comes either by stirring up in their minds the idea of words (which are outward things), whether words of Scripture or other words, which they look on as an immediate command of God; or else by stirring up and strongly impressing the ideas of the outward actions themselves. So when an interpretation of a Scripture type or allegory is strongly suggested immediately, in an extraordinary way, it is by suggesting words, as though someone secretly whispered and told the meaning, or by stirring up other ideas in the imagination.

Such experiences and manifestations as these commonly raise the affections of those who are deluded by them to a great height, and make a mighty uproar in both soul and body. And a very great part of the false religion that has been in the world from one age to another consists in such manifestations as these and in the affections that flow from them. In such things consisted the experiences of the ancient Pythagoreans among the heathen, and of many others among them, who had strange ecstasies and raptures and claimed a divine afflatus [inspiration] and immediate revelations from heaven. In such things as these the experiences of the Essenes, an ancient sect among the Jews at and after the times of the apostles, seem to have consisted. In such things as these consisted the experiences of many of the ancient Gnostics and Montanists, and many other sects of ancient heretics in the early ages of the Christian church. And in such things as these consisted the claimed immediate converse with God and Christ, and with the saints and angels of heaven, of the monks, anchorites and recluses who formerly abounded in the church of Rome. In such things consisted the claimed high experiences and great spirituality of many sects of fanatics that swarmed in the world after the Reformation: such as the Anabaptists, Antinomians and Familists, the followers of N. Stork, th. Muncer, Jo. Becold, Henry Pfeifer, David George, Casper Swenckfield, Henry Nicolas, Johannes Agricola Eislebius; the many wild fanatics that were in England in the days of Oliver Cromwell; and the followers of Mrs. Hutchinson in New England. This appears from the particular and full accounts given of all these sects by that eminently holy man Mr. Samuel Rutherford in his Display of the spiritual Antichrist. And in such things as these consisted the experiences of the late French prophets and their followers. And in these things the religion of the many kinds of fanatics of the present day seems to lie. It is chiefly by this sort of religion that Satan transforms himself into an angel of light; and it is what he has always used most successfully to confound hopeful and happy revivals of religion, from the beginning of the Christian church to this day. When the Spirit of God is poured out to begin a glorious work, the old serpent, as fast as possible and by every means, brings in this bastard religion and mingles it with the true; and this has time after time soon brought everything into confusion. Its pernicious consequences are not easily imagined or conceived of until we see and are amazed by its fearful effects and the dismal desolation it has made. Even if the revival of true religion is very great in its beginning, yet if this bastard comes in, there is danger of its doing as Gideon’s bastard Abimelech did, who did not stop until he had killed all of Gideon’s seventy trueborn sons except one, who was forced to flee. Great and strict, then, should be the watch and guard ministers keep against such things, especially at a time of great awakening. For men, especially the common people, are easily bewitched by such things, since they have such a glaring and glittering show of high religion, and the devil hides his own shape and appears as an angel of light, so that men may not be afraid of him but may adore him.

The imagination seems to be where all those delusions of Satan are formed which carry away those who are under the influence of false religion and counterfeit graces and affections. Here is the devil’s grand lurking-place, the very nest of foul and deluding spirits. It is very much to be doubted whether the devil can come at the soul of man at all to affect it, or to stir up any thought or motion, or produce any effect whatever in it, in any other way than by the imagination, which is that power of the soul by which it receives, and has in it, the images or ideas of outward and perceptible things. As to the laws and means the Creator has established for the dealings and communication of unbodied spirits, we know nothing about them. We do not know by what medium they make their thoughts known to each other, or stir up thoughts in each other. But as to spirits united to bodies, the bodies God has united them to are their medium of communication. They have no other medium of acting on other creatures, or of being acted on by them, than the body. So it is not to be supposed that Satan can stir up any thought or produce any effect in the soul of man in any other way than by some motion of the animal spirits, or by causing some motion or alteration in something that belongs to the body. There is this reason to think that the devil cannot produce thoughts in the soul immediately, or in any other way than through the medium of the body: namely, that he cannot immediately see or know the thoughts of the soul. Scripture abundantly declares that to do that belongs to the omniscient God alone. But it is not likely that the devil can immediately produce an effect which is out of the reach of his immediate view. It seems unreasonable to suppose that his immediate agency should be out of his own sight, or that it should be impossible for him to see what he himself immediately does. Is it not unreasonable to suppose that any spirit or intelligent agent should, by the act of his will, produce effects according to his understanding, or agreeable to his own thoughts, and that immediately, and yet the effects produced should be beyond the reach of his understanding, where he can have no immediate perception or discerning at all? But if it is so that the devil cannot produce thoughts in the soul immediately, or in any other way than by the animal spirits, or by the body, then it follows that he never brings anything about in the soul except by the imagination, or by stirring up external ideas. For we know that alterations in the body immediately stir up no other sort of ideas in the mind than external ideas, or ideas of the outward senses, or ideas of the same outward nature. As to reflection, abstraction, reasoning and so on, and the thoughts and inward motions which are the fruits of these acts of the mind, they are not the direct effects of impressions on the body. So it must be only by the imagination that Satan has access to the soul to tempt and delude it, or to suggest anything to it.58 And this seems to be the reason why persons suffering from the disease of melancholy are commonly so visibly and remarkably subject to the suggestions and temptations of Satan. For that is a disease which especially affects the animal spirits, and is accompanied by weakness of the part of the body which is the fountain of the animal spirits, namely the brain, which is, as it were, the seat of the imagination. It is by impressions made on the brain that any ideas are stirred up in the mind by the motion of the animal spirits, or by any changes made in the body. When the brain is weakened and diseased in this way, it is less under the command of the higher faculties of the soul, yields more easily to impressions from outside, and is overpowered by the disordered motions of the animal spirits; and so the devil has a greater advantage to affect the mind by working on the imagination. And so when Satan casts those horrid suggestions into the minds of many melancholy persons, in which they have no hand themselves, he does it by stirring up imaginary ideas, either of some dreadful words or sentences or of other horrid outward ideas. And when he tempts other persons who are not melancholy, he does it by presenting to the imagination, in a lively and alluring way, the objects of their lusts; or by stirring up ideas of words, and so by them stirring up thoughts; or by promoting an imagination of outward actions, events, circumstances and so on. Countless are the ways in which the mind might be led on to all kinds of evil thoughts by stirring up external ideas in the imagination.

If persons keep no guard at these avenues of Satan, by which he has access to the soul to tempt and delude it, they are likely to have enough of him. And especially so if, instead of guarding against him, they lay themselves open to him, and seek and invite him, because he appears as an angel of light and counterfeits the illuminations and graces of the Spirit of God by inward whispers and immediate suggestions of facts and events, pleasant voices, beautiful images and other impressions on the imagination. There are many who are deluded by such things, are lifted up by them and seek after them, who have a continual course of them and can have them almost whenever they want; and especially when their pride and vainglory most need them, to make a show of them before company. It is with them something as it is with those who practice the art of telling where lost things are to be found by impressions made on their imaginations: since they lay themselves open to the devil, he is always at hand to give them the impression they desire.

Before I finish what I would say on this head of imaginations counterfeiting spiritual light, and the affections arising from them, I would again ask (to prevent any misunderstanding of what has been said) that it be observed that I am far from concluding that no affections are spiritual which are accompanied by imaginary ideas. Such is the nature of man that he can hardly think of anything intensely without some kind of outward ideas. They arise and put themselves in the way unavoidably in the course of a man’s thoughts, though they are often very confused and are not what the mind attends to. When the mind is much engaged and the thoughts intense, the imagination is often stronger and the outward idea more lively, especially in persons of certain bodily constitutions. But there is a great difference between these two things: lively imaginations arising from strong affections, and strong affections arising from lively imaginations. The former may happen, and no doubt often does, in the case of truly gracious affections. The affections do not arise from the imagination, nor depend on it at all; on the contrary, the imagination is only the accidental effect or consequence of the affection, through the weakness of human nature. But when the latter is the case, as it often is, that the affection arises from the imagination and is built on it as its foundation, instead of on a spiritual illumination or manifestation, then the affection, however elevated, is worthless and vain. And this is the purpose of what has now been said about impressions on the imagination. Having observed this, I proceed to another mark of gracious affections.

54. Many who have had very strong affections at first conversion afterward become dry, and wither, waste, pine and die away. And now their hypocrisy is manifest: if not to all the world by open profaneness, yet to the discerning eye of living Christians, by a formal, barren, unsavory, unfruitful heart and course; because they never yet had light enough to convict them.—It is strange to see some people carried along with mighty affection against sin and hell, and after Christ. And what is the hell you fear? A dreadful place. What is Christ? They hardly know as much as the devils do; but that is all. Oh, do not trust them! Many have fallen away, and these will fall away, to some lust, or opinion, or pride, or the world; and the reason is that they never had light enough. John 5:35: John was a burning and shining light, and they rejoiced in him for a season; yet glorious as it was, they did not see Christ by it, especially not with divine light. It is rare to see Christians full of both light and affection. And so consider this. Many a man has been well brought up, and is of a sweet, loving nature, mild and gentle and harmless; he likes and loves the best things; his meaning and mind and heart are good, and he has more in his heart than in show; and so he hopes all will go well with him. I say there may be the greatest hypocrisy under the greatest affections, especially if they lack light. You will be hardened in your hypocrisy by them. I never liked violent affections and pangs, but only such as were dropped in by light; because those come from an external principle and do not last, but these do. Men are not frightened by the light of the sun, though it is clearer than the lightning. Shepard’s parable Part I. P. 146.

55. Take care not to content yourselves with every kind of knowledge. Do not worship every image of your own heads; especially you who fall short of the truth, or of the knowledge of it. For when you have some, there may still be something lacking which would make you sincere. There are many men of great knowledge, able to teach themselves and others too, and yet their hearts are unsound. How does this come about? Is it because they have so much light? No, but because they lack much. And so do not content yourselves with every knowledge. There is some knowledge which men have by the light of nature, from the book of creation (which leaves them without excuse); some by the power of education; some by the light of the law, by which men know their sin and evils; some by the letter of the gospel; and so men may know much and speak well, and so in seeing not see; some by the Spirit, and they may see much, so as to prophesy in Christ’s name, and yet be told to depart (Matt 7). Now there is a light of glory by which the elect see things in another way; how, they cannot tell you. It is the beginning of the light of heaven: the same Spirit that fills Christ filling their minds, so that they know all things by this anointing. If you ever have this, you must become babes and fools in your own eyes. God will never write his law in your minds until all the scribblings of it are blotted out. Count all your knowledge loss for the gaining of this. It is sad to see many a man pleasing himself in his own dreaming delusions; yet the poor creature in seeing does not see. This is God’s heavy curse on men under the greatest means, and it lays all waste and desolate. Shepard’s parable, Part I. P. 147.

56. Calvin, in his Institutes, book I. Chap. Ix. § 1, says that it is not the office of the Spirit who is promised to us to make new revelations, unheard of before, or to coin some new kind of doctrine which tends to draw us away from the received doctrine of the gospel, but to seal and confirm to us that very doctrine which is by the gospel. And in the same place he speaks of some who in those days held the contrary notion, claiming to be immediately led by the Spirit, as persons governed by a most haughty self-conceit, and not so properly to be looked on as only laboring under a mistake as driven by a sort of raving madness.

57. Chambers’s dictionary, under the word taste.

58. The imagination is that room of the soul in which the devil often appears. Indeed (to speak exactly) the devil has no efficient power over the rational part of a man. He cannot change the will; he cannot alter the heart of a man. So the utmost he can do in tempting a man to sin is by persuasion and suggestion only. But then how does the devil do this? By working on the imagination. He observes the disposition and bodily constitution of a man, and accordingly suggests things to his imagination and throws his fiery darts into it, and by these the mind and will come to be worked on. So the devil has no commanding efficacy over your will; yet because he can stir and move your imagination in this way, and you, being naturally without grace, cannot withstand these suggestions, it comes about that any sin in your imagination, though only in the outward works of the soul, quickly lays hold on all. And indeed, it is by this means that those horrible delusions arise which are found in many erroneous ways of religion: it is all because their imaginations are corrupted. Indeed, how often are these devilish delusions of the imagination taken for the gracious operations of God’s Spirit?—It is from this that many have laid claim to direct inspiration;—they leave the Scriptures and attend wholly to what they perceive and feel within them. Burgess on original sin, p. 369. The great Turretine, speaking on the question What is the power of angels, says: As to bodies, there is no doubt that they can do a great deal with all sorts of elementary and sublunary bodies, to move them from place to place and to agitate them in various ways. It is also certain that they can act on the external and internal senses, to stir them up or to bind them. But as to the rational soul itself, they can do nothing immediately on it; for it belongs to God alone, who knows and searches the hearts and has them in his hands, also to bend and move them wherever he wills. But angels can act on the rational soul only mediately, by imaginations. Theolog. Elench. Loc. VII quest. 7.

Conviction of the Reality of Divine Things

Part III · Sign V

V. Truly gracious affections are accompanied by a reasonable and spiritual conviction of the judgment, of the reality and certainty of divine things.

This seems to be implied in the text that was laid as the foundation of this discourse: “Though you+ have not seen Him, you+ love Him; and though you+ do not see Him now, you+ believe in Him and rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory.”

All who are truly gracious persons have a solid, full, thorough and effectual conviction of the truth of the great things of the gospel. I mean that they no longer waver between two opinions. The great doctrines of the gospel are no longer doubtful things to them, or matters of opinion which, though probable, are still open to dispute. With them they are settled and determined points, undoubted and indisputable, so that they are not afraid to venture their all on their truth. Their conviction is an effectual conviction, so that the great, spiritual, mysterious and invisible things of the gospel have the influence of real and certain things on them. They have the weight and power of real things in their hearts, and so they rule in their affections and govern them through the course of their lives. As to Christ’s being the Son of God and Savior of the world, and the great things he has revealed about himself, his Father and another world, they do not merely hold a prevailing opinion that these things are true, and so give their assent, as they do in many other matters of doubtful speculation. They see that it is really so: their eyes are opened, so that they see that Jesus really is the Christ, the Son of the living God. And as to the things Christ has revealed of God’s eternal purposes and designs concerning fallen man, and the glorious and everlasting things prepared for the saints in another world, they see that these things are indeed so. Therefore these things carry great weight with them, and have a mighty power on their hearts and influence over their practice, in some measure answerable to their infinite importance.

That all true Christians have this kind of conviction of the truth of the things of the gospel is abundantly plain from the holy Scriptures. I will mention a few places out of many. Matt 16:15–17: “Who do you+ say I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus replied, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah! … this was … revealed to you … by My Father in heaven.” John 6:68–69: “You have the words of eternal life. We believe and know that You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” John 17:6–8: “I have manifested Your name to those You have given Me out of the world. … Now they know that everything You have given Me comes from You. For I have given them the words You gave Me, and they have received them. They knew with certainty that I came from You, and they believed that You sent Me.” Acts 8:37: “If you believe with all your heart, you may.” 2 Cor 4:11–14: “For we who are alive are always consigned to death for Jesus’ sake … death is at work in us … And in keeping with what is written: ‘I believed, therefore I have spoken,’ we who have the same spirit of faith also believe and therefore speak, knowing that the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and present us with you+ in His presence.” Together with verse 16: “Therefore we do not lose heart.” And verse 18: “We fix our eyes not on what is seen,” and so on. And 5:1: “Now we know that if the earthly tent we live in is dismantled, we have a building from God,” and verses 6–8: “Therefore we are always confident, although we know that while we are at home in the body, we are away from the Lord. For we walk by faith, not by sight. We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.” 2 Tim 1:12: “For this reason, even though I suffer as I do, I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day.” Heb 3:6: “And we are His house, if we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope of which we boast.” Heb 11:1: “Now faith is the substance of what we hope for and the evidence of what we do not see,” together with that whole chapter. 1 John 4:13–16: “By this we know that we remain in Him, and He in us: He has given us of His Spirit. And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent His Son to be the Savior of the world. If anyone confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God. And we have come to know and believe the love that God has for us.” Chapter 5:4–5: “For everyone born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith. Who then overcomes the world? Only he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God.”

Truly gracious affections, therefore, are accompanied by the kind of conviction and persuasion of the truth of the things of the gospel, and sight of their evidence and reality, that these and other Scriptures speak of.

There are many religious affections that are not accompanied by such a conviction of the judgment. Some people have many perceptions and ideas which they call divine manifestations, which are affecting but not convincing. For a little while they may seem more persuaded of the truth of the things of religion than they used to be, and may give a ready assent, like many of Christ’s hearers who believed for a while. Yet they have no thorough and effectual conviction. Nor is there any great and lasting change in them in this respect: that whereas before they did not take the great things of the gospel as real, now these things appear new to them in their reality and certainty, and they see them in quite another light than they used to. There are many persons who have been exceedingly raised with religious affections, and think they have been converted, who do not go about the world any more convinced of the truth of the gospel than they used to be; or at least there is no remarkable change. They are not men who live under the influence and power of a conviction that makes real to them the infinite and eternal things the gospel reveals; if they were, it would be impossible for them to live as they do. Because their affections are not accompanied by a thorough conviction of the mind, they are not at all to be depended on. However great a show and noise they make, it is like the blaze of tow, or the crackling of thorns, or like the forward, flourishing blade on stony ground, which has no root, nor depth of earth to keep it alive.

Some persons, under high affections and a confident persuasion of their good state, have something which they very ignorantly call seeing the truth of the word of God, though it is very far from it. It happens like this. Some text of Scripture comes to their minds in a sudden and extraordinary way, declaring to them immediately (as they suppose) that their sins are forgiven, or that God loves them and will save them. Perhaps a chain of Scriptures comes one after another to the same purpose. And they are convinced that it is truth; that is, they are confident that it is certainly so, that their sins are forgiven and God does love them, and so on. They say they know it is so. And when the words of Scripture are suggested to them in this meaning, and, as they suppose, spoken to them immediately by God, they are ready to cry out, “Truth, truth! It is certainly so! The word of God is true!” And this they call seeing the truth of the word of God. Yet the whole of their faith amounts to no more than a strong confidence of their own good state, and so a confidence that those words are true which they suppose tell them they are in a good state. But in fact (as was shown before) there is no Scripture that declares any person to be in a good state directly, or in any other way than by inference. So this, instead of being a real sight of the word of God, is a sight of nothing but a phantom, and is a delusion through and through. Truly to see the truth of the word of God is to see the truth of the gospel: the glorious doctrine the word of God contains about God and Jesus Christ, and the way of salvation by him, and the world of glory that he has entered into and purchased for all who believe. It is not a revelation that such and such particular persons are true Christians and will go to heaven. Therefore those affections which arise from no other persuasion of the truth of the word of God than this arise from delusion, not true conviction, and so are themselves delusive and vain.

But even if the religious affections persons have do indeed arise from a strong persuasion of the truth of the Christian religion, their affections are no better for it unless their persuasion is a reasonable persuasion or conviction. By a reasonable conviction I mean a conviction founded on real evidence, or on what is a good reason or just ground of conviction. Men may have a strong persuasion that the Christian religion is true when their persuasion is not built on evidence at all, but entirely on upbringing and the opinion of others; just as many Muslims are strongly persuaded of the truth of the Muslim religion because their fathers, their neighbors and their nation believe it. A belief in the truth of the Christian religion that is built on the very same grounds as the Muslims’ belief in the Muslim religion is the same sort of belief. And though the thing believed happens to be better, that does not make the belief itself of a better sort. For though the thing believed happens to be true, the belief of it is not owing to its truth but to upbringing. So as the conviction is no better than the Muslims’ conviction, so the affections that flow from it are no better in themselves than the religious affections of Muslims.

But if the belief in Christian doctrines from which persons’ affections arise is not merely from upbringing, but really from reasons and arguments that are offered, it does not necessarily follow from this that their affections are truly gracious. For that, it is required that the belief from which their affections arise should be not only a reasonable but also a spiritual belief or conviction. I suppose no one will doubt that some natural men give a kind of assent of their judgment to the truth of the Christian religion from the rational proofs or arguments offered to demonstrate it. Judas no doubt thought Jesus to be the Messiah from the things he saw and heard; yet all along he was a devil. So in John 2:23–25 we read of many who believed in Christ’s name when they saw the miracles he did, whom Christ nonetheless knew had nothing within them that could be depended on. So Simon the sorcerer believed when he saw the miracles and signs that were done, yet remained “poisoned by bitterness and captive to iniquity” (Acts 8:13, 23). And if there is such a belief or assent of the judgment in some natural men, no one can doubt that religious affections may arise from that assent or belief; as we read of some who believed for a while, who were greatly affected, and at once received the word with joy.

It is evident that there is such a thing as a spiritual belief or conviction of the truth of the things of the gospel: a belief that is peculiar to those who are spiritual, who are regenerated and have the Spirit of God in his holy influences, dwelling in them as a vital principle. So the conviction they have does not differ from that of natural men only in what goes along with it, in that it is accompanied by good works. The belief itself is different: the assent and conviction of the judgment is of a kind peculiar to those who are spiritual, a kind which natural men are wholly without. This is evident from Scripture, if anything at all is. John 17:8: “They believed that You sent Me.” Titus 1:1: “for the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness.” John 16:27: “For the Father Himself loves you+, because you+ have loved Me and have believed that I came from God.” 1 John 4:15: “If anyone confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.” Chapter 5:1: “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God.” Verse 10: “Whoever believes in the Son of God has this testimony within him.”

What a spiritual conviction of the judgment is, we are naturally led to determine from what has already been said under the former head of a spiritual understanding. The conviction of the judgment arises from the illumination of the understanding: passing a right judgment on things depends on having a right perception or idea of them. And so it follows that a spiritual conviction of the truth of the great things of the gospel is a conviction that arises from having a spiritual view or perception of those things in the mind. This is also evident from Scripture, which often represents a saving belief of the reality and divinity of the things set before us and exhibited in the gospel as coming from the Spirit of God enlightening the mind to have right perceptions of the nature of those things; and so, as it were, unveiling them or revealing them, and enabling the mind to view them and see them as they are. Luke 10:21–22: “I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for this was well-pleasing in Your sight. All things have been entrusted to Me by My Father. No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and no one knows who the Father is except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.” John 6:40: “For it is My Father’s will that everyone who sees the Son and believes in Him shall have eternal life.” Here it is plain that true faith arises from a spiritual sight of Christ. And John 17:6–8: “I have manifested Your name to those You have given Me out of the world. … Now they know that everything You have given Me comes from You. For I have given them the words You gave Me, and they have received them. They knew with certainty that I came from You, and they believed that You sent Me.” Here Christ’s manifesting God’s name to the disciples, or giving them a true perception and view of divine things, was that by which they knew that Christ’s doctrine was of God, and that Christ himself was from him and was sent by him. Matt 16:16–17: Simon Peter said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus replied, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah! For this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven.” 1 John 5:10: “Whoever believes in the Son of God has this testimony within him.” Gal 1:14–16: “… extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers. But when God, who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by His grace, was pleased to reveal His Son in me so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles, I did not rush to consult with flesh and blood.”

If, then, a spiritual conviction of the divinity and reality of the things exhibited in the gospel is one that arises from a spiritual understanding of those things, I have already shown what that is: namely, a sense and taste of the divine, supreme and holy excellence and beauty of those things. So the mind is spiritually convinced of the divinity and truth of the great things of the gospel when that conviction arises, either directly or remotely, from such a sense or view of their divine excellence and glory as is exhibited there. This clearly follows from what has already been said, and on this the Scripture is very plain and explicit. 2 Cor 4:3–6: “And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your+ servants for Jesus’ sake. For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.” Together with the last verse of the chapter before, which introduces this: “And we, who with unveiled faces all behold the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.” Nothing can be more evident than that the apostle here speaks of a saving belief of the gospel as arising from the mind’s being enlightened to behold the divine glory of the things the gospel exhibits.

This view or sense of the divine glory and unparalleled beauty of the things exhibited to us in the gospel tends to convince the mind of their divinity in two ways: directly, and more indirectly and remotely. 1. A view of this divine glory convinces the mind directly of the divinity of these things, since this glory is in itself a direct, clear and all-conquering evidence of it; especially when it is clearly shown, or when this supernatural sense is given in a good degree.

He who has his judgment directly convinced and assured in this way of the divinity of the things of the gospel, by a clear view of their divine glory, has a reasonable conviction. His belief and assurance is entirely agreeable to reason, because the divine glory and beauty of divine things is in itself real evidence of their divinity, and the most direct and strong evidence. He who truly sees the divine, transcendent, supreme glory of those things that are divine does, as it were, know their divinity intuitively. He does not only argue that they are divine; he sees that they are divine. He sees in them that in which divinity chiefly consists. For it is in this glory, so vastly and inexpressibly different from the glory of man-made things and from all other glory, that the true notion of divinity mainly consists. God is God, and distinguished from all other beings and exalted above them, chiefly by his divine beauty, which is infinitely different from all other beauty. Those, therefore, who see the stamp of this glory in divine things see divinity in them; they see God in them, and so see them to be divine, because they see in them that in which the truest idea of divinity consists. In this way a soul may have a kind of intuitive knowledge of the divinity of the things exhibited in the gospel. This is not to say that he judges the doctrines of the gospel to be from God without any argument or deduction at all; but it is without any long chain of arguments. There is only one argument, and the evidence is direct: the mind rises to the truth of the gospel by only one step, and that is its divine glory.

It would be very strange if any professing Christian should deny that it is possible for there to be an excellence in divine things so transcendent, and so exceedingly different from what is in other things, that if it were seen it would clearly distinguish them. We cannot rationally doubt that things which are divine, which belong to the Supreme Being, are vastly different from things that are human; that there is a godlike, high and glorious excellence in them which so distinguishes them from the things of men that the difference is beyond words; and therefore an excellence such that, if it is seen, it will have a most convincing and satisfying influence on anyone that they are what they are, namely, divine. No doubt there is such glory and excellence in the divine Being, by which he is so infinitely distinguished from all other beings, that if it were seen he might be known by it. It would therefore be very unreasonable to deny that it is possible for God to give manifestations of this distinguishing excellence in the things by which he is pleased to make himself known, and that this distinguishing excellence may be clearly seen in them. There are natural excellences that very evidently distinguish their subjects or authors to anyone who beholds them. How different the speech of an intelligent man is from that of a little child! And how greatly the speech of some men of great genius, such as Homer, Cicero, Milton, Locke, Addison and others, is distinguished from that of many other intelligent men! There are no limits to be set to the degrees in which mental excellence may be shown in speech. But the appearances of the natural perfections of God, in the manifestations he makes of himself, may no doubt distinguish him unspeakably more clearly than the appearances of those excellences of worms of the dust by which they differ from one another. One who is well acquainted with mankind and their works may know, by looking at the sun, that it is no human work. And it is reasonable to suppose that when Christ comes at the end of the world in the glory of his Father, it will be with such indescribable appearances of divinity as will leave no doubt in the inhabitants of the world, even the most obstinate unbelievers, that he who appears is a divine person. But above all, the manifestations of the moral and spiritual glory of the divine Being (which is the proper beauty of the divinity) bring their own evidence and tend to assure the heart. So the disciples were assured that Jesus was the Son of God, for they beheld his glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). When Christ appeared to his disciples in the glory of his transfiguration, with that outward glory to their bodily eyes, which was a sweet and wonderful symbol and likeness of his spiritual glory, together with his spiritual glory itself manifested to their minds, the manifestation of glory was such as perfectly, and with good reason, assured them of his divinity. This appears from what one of them, namely the apostle Peter, says about it, 2 Pet 1:16–18: “For we did not follow cleverly devised fables when we made known to you+ the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of His majesty. For He received honor and glory from God the Father when the voice came to Him from the Majestic Glory, saying, ‘This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’ And we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain.” The apostle calls that mountain the holy mountain because the manifestation of Christ made there to their minds, with which their minds were especially impressed and enraptured, was the glory of his holiness, or the beauty of his moral excellence; or, as another of these disciples who saw it expresses it, his glory, as full of grace and truth.

Now this distinguishing glory of the divine Being has its brightest appearance and manifestation in the things set before us and exhibited in the gospel: the doctrines taught there, the word spoken there, and the divine counsels, acts and works revealed there. These things contain the clearest, most wonderful and distinguishing representations and exhibitions of the glory of God’s moral perfections that were ever made to the world. And if there is such a distinguishing, evidential manifestation of divine glory in the gospel, it is reasonable to suppose that there may be such a thing as seeing it. What should keep it from being seen? That some do not see it, though they may be discerning men in temporal matters, is no argument that it cannot be seen. If there are such indescribable, distinguishing, evidential excellences in the gospel, it is reasonable to suppose that they are such as cannot be discerned except by the special influence and enlightening of the Spirit of God. Uncommon strength of mind is needed to discern the distinguishing excellences of the works of authors of great genius: those things in Milton which appear tasteless, and even imperfections, to poor judges are his inimitable excellences in the eyes of those who have greater discernment and better taste. And if there is a book of which God is the author, it is most reasonable to suppose that the distinguishing glories of his word are of such a kind that the sin and corruption of men’s hearts would blind men from discerning the beauties of such a book. For that sin and corruption, above all things, alienates men from the Deity, and makes the heart dull and insensible to any sense or taste of those things in which the moral glory of the divine perfections consists. I say, it is only reasonable to suppose this, and that therefore they will not see those beauties except as God is pleased to enlighten them and restore a holy taste, to discern and relish divine beauties.

This sense of the spiritual excellence and beauty of divine things also tends directly to convince the mind of the truth of the gospel, because very many of the most important things declared in the gospel, which are hidden from the eyes of natural men, have a truth that in effect consists in this excellence, or depends so immediately on it and results from it, that when this excellence is seen, the truth of those things is seen. As soon as the eyes are opened to behold the holy beauty and loveliness that is in divine things, a multitude of the most important doctrines of the gospel that depend on it (all of which seem strange and dark to natural men) are seen at once to be true. For instance, in this way the truth of what the word of God declares about the exceeding evil of sin appears. For the same eye that discerns the transcendent beauty of holiness necessarily sees in it the exceeding odiousness of sin; the same taste that relishes the sweetness of true moral good tastes the bitterness of moral evil. And by this means a man sees his own sinfulness and loathsomeness, for he now has a sense to discern objects of this nature. So he sees the truth of what the word of God declares about the exceeding sinfulness of mankind, which he did not see before. He now sees the dreadful pollution of his heart and the desperate depravity of his nature in a new way, for his soul has now been given a sense to feel the pain of such a disease. And this shows him the truth of what the Scripture reveals about the corruption of man’s nature, his original sin, and the ruined, undone condition man is in, and his need of a Savior, his need of the mighty power of God to renew his heart and change his nature. By seeing the true excellence of holiness, men see the glory of all those things which both reason and Scripture show to be in the divine Being; for it has been shown that their glory depends on this. And in this way they see the truth of all that the Scripture declares about God’s glorious excellence and majesty, his being the fountain of all good, the only happiness of the creature, and so on. And this again shows the mind the truth of what the Scripture teaches about the evil of sin against so glorious a God; and also the truth of what it teaches about sin’s just desert of the dreadful punishment it reveals; and also about the impossibility of our offering any satisfaction or sufficient atonement for what is so infinitely evil and heinous. And this again shows the truth of what the Scripture reveals about the necessity of a Savior, to offer an atonement of infinite value for sin. And this sense of spiritual beauty that has been spoken of enables the soul to see the glory of those things the gospel reveals about the person of Christ. So it enables the soul to see the exceeding beauty and dignity of his person, appearing in what the gospel exhibits of his word, works, acts and life. And this perception of the supreme dignity of his person shows the truth of what the gospel declares about the value of his blood and righteousness; and so the infinite excellence of the offering he has made to God for us; and so its sufficiency to atone for our sins and to commend us to God. In this way the Spirit of God shows the way of salvation by Christ. In this way the soul sees the fitness and suitableness of this way of salvation, the wonderful wisdom of its design, and how perfectly the provision the gospel exhibits (as made for us) answers to our needs. When a sense of true divine beauty is given to the soul, the soul discerns the beauty of every part of the gospel scheme. This also shows the soul the truth of what the word of God declares about man’s chief happiness, as consisting in holy exercises and enjoyments. This shows the truth of what the gospel declares about the unspeakable glory of the heavenly state. And what the prophecies of the Old Testament and the writings of the apostles declare about the glory of the Messiah’s kingdom is now all plain; and also what the Scripture teaches about the reasons and grounds of our duty. The truth of all these things revealed in the Scripture, and many more that might be mentioned, appears to the soul only by the imparting of that spiritual taste of divine beauty which has been spoken of. They were hidden things to the soul before.

And besides all this, the truth of all those things the Scripture says about experiential religion is known in this way, for they are now experienced. And this convinces the soul that one who knew the heart of man better than we know our own hearts, and knew perfectly the nature of virtue and holiness, was the author of the Scriptures. And the opening to view, with such clearness, of such a world of wonderful and glorious truth in the gospel, which was unknown before, being quite beyond the sight of a natural eye but now appearing so clear and bright, has a powerful and invincible influence on the soul to persuade it of the divinity of the gospel.

Unless men may come to a reasonable, solid persuasion and conviction of the truth of the gospel by its internal evidences, in the way that has been spoken of, namely by a sight of its glory, it is impossible that those who are unlearned and unacquainted with history should have any thorough and effectual conviction of it at all. Without this they may see a great deal of probability in it. It may be reasonable for them to give much credit to what learned men and historians tell them; and these may tell them so much that it may look very probable and rational to them that the Christian religion is true, so much that they would be very unreasonable not to hold this opinion. But to have a conviction so clear, evident and assuring as to be enough to move them boldly to sell all, to run confidently and fearlessly the risk of losing all things and of enduring the most excruciating and long-continued torments, and to trample the world underfoot and count all things as rubbish for Christ: for this, the evidence they can have from history cannot be enough. It is impossible that men who do not have something of a general view of the historical world, or the course of history from age to age, should grasp the force of arguments for the truth of Christianity drawn from history to such a degree as effectually to move them to venture their all on it. After all that learned men have said to them, countless doubts will remain in their minds. When pressed by some great trial of their faith, they will be ready to say, “How do I know this, or that? How do I know when these histories were written? Learned men tell me these histories were attested in such and such a way in their own day; but how do I know that there were such attestations then? They tell me there is as much reason to believe these facts as any whatever that are related at such a distance; but how do I know that the other facts related of those ages ever happened?” Those who do not have something of a general view of the course of historical events, and of the state of mankind from age to age, cannot see the clear evidence from history of the truth of facts in distant ages; endless doubts and scruples will remain.

But the gospel was not given only for learned men. At least nineteen in twenty, if not ninety-nine in a hundred, of those for whom the Scriptures were written are not capable of any certain or effectual conviction of the divine authority of the Scriptures by such arguments as learned men use. If men who have been brought up in heathenism must wait for a clear and certain conviction of the truth of Christianity until they have learning and acquaintance with the histories of more cultivated nations, enough to see clearly the force of such arguments, it will make the evidence of the gospel immensely cumbersome to them, and will make the spreading of the gospel among them infinitely difficult. Miserable is the condition of the Houssatunnuck Indians, and others who have lately shown a desire to be instructed in Christianity, if they can come at no evidence of the truth of Christianity sufficient to move them to sell all for Christ in any other way than this.

It is unreasonable to suppose that God has provided his people with no more than probable evidences of the truth of the gospel. With great care he has abundantly provided and given them the most convincing, assuring, satisfying and manifold evidence of his faithfulness in the covenant of grace; and, as David says, he has made a covenant “ordered and secured in every part.” It is therefore rational to suppose that at the same time he would not fail to order the matter so that there would be no lack of evidence just as great and clear that this is his covenant, and that these promises are his promises; or, what is the same thing, that the Christian religion is true and that the gospel is his word. Otherwise the great assurances he has given of his faithfulness in his covenant, by confirming it with his oath and establishing it in so many ways by seals and pledges, are in vain. For the evidence that it is his covenant is, properly, the foundation on which all the force and effect of those other assurances stand. We may therefore suppose and conclude without doubt that God has given some sort of evidence, beyond all mere probability, that this covenant and these promises are his: that there are some grounds of assurance of it held out, of which the unlearned and those unacquainted with history are capable, and which, if we are not blind to them, tend to give a higher persuasion than any arguing from history, human tradition and the like. Indeed, God has given what is good ground for the highest and most perfect assurance that mankind have in any case whatever; agreeable to those high expressions the apostle uses, Heb 10:22: “Let us draw near … in full assurance of faith.” And Col 2:2: “that they may be encouraged in heart, knit together in love, and filled with all the riches of the full assurance of understanding, so that they may know the mystery of God, namely Christ.” It is reasonable to suppose that God would give the greatest evidence of those things which are greatest, and whose truth is of greatest importance to us; things of which we, therefore, if we are wise and act rationally, will have the greatest desire to have full, undoubting and perfect assurance. But it is certain that such an assurance cannot be attained by the greater part of those who live under the gospel by arguments drawn from ancient traditions, histories and monuments.

And if we come to fact and experience, there is not the least reason to suppose that one in a hundred of those who have been sincere Christians, and have had a heart to sell all for Christ, came by their conviction of the truth of the gospel in this way. If we read through the histories of the many thousands who have died as martyrs for Christ since the beginning of the Reformation, and have cheerfully undergone extreme tortures in confidence of the truth of the gospel, and consider their circumstances and advantages, how few of them can we reasonably suppose ever came by their assured persuasion in this way, or indeed could possibly have received so full and strong an assurance reasonably from such arguments! Many of them were weak women and children, and the greater part of them unlearned persons. Many of these had been brought up in popish ignorance and darkness and had only newly come out of it, and they lived and died in times when those arguments for the truth of Christianity from antiquity and history had been handled only very imperfectly. And indeed, it is only very lately that these arguments have been set in a clear and convincing light, even by learned men themselves. And since that has been done, there have never been fewer thorough believers among those who have been brought up in the true religion: unbelief never prevailed so much in any age as in this one, in which these arguments are handled to the greatest advantage.

The true martyrs of Jesus Christ are not those who have only been strong in the opinion that the gospel of Christ is true, but those who have seen the truth of it; as the very name of martyrs, or witnesses (by which they are called in Scripture), implies. Those who only declare that they are very much of the opinion that something is true are very improperly called witnesses of its truth. Only those are proper witnesses who can and do testify that they have seen the truth of the thing they assert. John 3:11: “We speak of what we know, and we testify to what we have seen.” John 1:34: “I have seen and testified that this is the Son of God.” 1 John 4:14: “And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent His Son to be the Savior of the world.” Acts 22:14–15: “The God of our fathers has appointed you to know His will, and to see the Righteous One, and to hear His voice. You will be His witness to everyone of what you have seen and heard.” Now the true martyrs of Jesus Christ are called his witnesses; and all the saints who, by their holy practice under great trials, declare that faith which is “the substance of what we hope for and the evidence of what we do not see” are called witnesses (Heb 11:1 and 12:1). For by their profession and practice they declare their assurance of the truth and divinity of the gospel, having had the eyes of their minds enlightened to see divinity in the gospel, or to behold that unparalleled, indescribably excellent and truly divine glory shining in it, which is altogether distinguishing, evidential and convincing. So they may truly be said to have seen God in it, and to have seen that it is indeed divine; and so they can speak in the manner of witnesses. They do not only say that they think the gospel is divine, but say that it is divine, giving this as their testimony, because they have seen it to be so. No doubt Peter, James and John, after they had seen that excellent glory of Christ on the mountain, would have been ready when they came down to speak in the language of witnesses, and to say positively that Jesus is the Son of God; as Peter says, they were “eyewitnesses” (2 Pet 1:16). And so all nations will be ready to say this positively when they behold his glory at the day of judgment; though what will be seen by all will be only his natural glory, not his moral and spiritual glory, which is much more distinguishing. But it must still be noted that among those who have a spiritual sight of the divine glory of the gospel there is a great variety of degrees of strength of faith, as there is a vast variety in the degrees of clearness of their views of this glory. But there is no true and saving faith, or spiritual conviction of the judgment of the truth of the gospel, that has nothing in it of this manifestation of its internal evidence in some degree. The gospel of the blessed God does not go about begging for its evidence as much as some think; it has its highest and most proper evidence in itself. Great use may be made of external arguments; they are not to be neglected, but highly prized and valued, for they may be of great service to awaken unbelievers and bring them to serious consideration, and to confirm the faith of true saints. Indeed, they may in some respects serve toward the begetting of a saving faith in men. Yet what was said before remains true: there is no spiritual conviction of the judgment except what arises from a perception of the spiritual beauty and glory of divine things. For, as has been observed, this perception or view tends to convince the mind of the truth of the gospel in two ways, either directly or indirectly. Having therefore already observed how it does this directly, I proceed now

(2.) To observe how a view of this divine glory convinces the mind of the truth of Christianity more indirectly.

[1.] First, it does so in that the prejudices of the heart against the truth of divine things are removed by it, so that the mind lies open to the force of the reasons that are offered. The mind of man is naturally full of enmity against the doctrines of the gospel. This works against the arguments that prove their truth, and makes them lose their force on the mind. But when the divine excellence of Christian doctrines is shown to a person, this destroys that enmity, removes the prejudices, sanctifies the reason, and makes it open and free. This makes a vast difference to the force that arguments have to convince the mind. This explains the very different effect Christ’s miracles had in convincing the disciples from what they had in convincing the scribes and Pharisees. It was not that the disciples had a stronger reason, or had their reason more cultivated; but their reason was sanctified, and those blinding prejudices which the scribes and Pharisees were under were removed by the sense they had of the excellence of Christ and his doctrine.

[2.] Secondly, it not only removes the hindrances of reason but positively helps reason. It makes even the speculative notions more lively. It assists and engages the attention of the mind to that kind of object, which gives it a clearer view of them and lets it see their mutual relations more clearly. The ideas themselves, which are otherwise dim and obscure, have a light cast on them by this means and are impressed with greater strength, so that the mind can better judge of them. In the same way, he who looks at the objects on the face of the earth when the light of the sun is cast on them is at a greater advantage to discern them in their true forms and mutual relations, and to see the evidences of divine wisdom and skill in their design, than he who sees them in dim starlight or twilight.

What has been said may serve in some measure to show the nature of a spiritual conviction of the judgment, of the truth and reality of divine things, and so to distinguish truly gracious affections from others; for gracious affections are always accompanied by such a conviction of the judgment.

But before I leave this head, it will be necessary to note the ways in which some are deceived in this matter, and to take notice of several things that are sometimes taken for a spiritual and saving belief of the truth of the things of religion, which are in fact very different from it.

(1.) There is a degree of conviction of the truth of the great things of religion that arises from the common enlightenings of the Spirit of God.
