That livelier and more deeply felt perception of the things of religion, as to what is natural in them, such as natural men have who are under awakenings and common illuminations, will give some degree of conviction of the truth of divine things beyond what they had before they were enlightened in this way. For by it they see the manifestations of the natural perfections of God, such as his greatness, power and fearful majesty, that are in the revelation made in the holy Scriptures and in the things exhibited in that revelation. This tends to convince the mind that this is the word of a great and awesome God. From the signs of God’s greatness and majesty in his word and works, of which they have a great sense through the common influence of the Spirit of God, they may have a much greater conviction that these are indeed the word and works of a very great invisible Being. And the lively perception of the greatness of God which natural men may have tends to give them a sense of the great guilt that sin against such a God brings, and of the dreadfulness of his wrath for sin. And this tends to make them believe more easily and fully the revelation the Scripture makes of another world, and of the extreme misery it threatens to inflict there on sinners. And so, from that sense of the great natural good there is in the things of religion, which is sometimes given in common illuminations, men may be more inclined to believe the truth of religion. Persons may have these things, and yet have no sense of the beauty and loveliness of the moral and holy excellence that is in the things of religion, and therefore no spiritual conviction of their truth. Yet such convictions are sometimes mistaken for saving convictions, and the affections flowing from them for saving affections.

(2.) The extraordinary impressions made on the imaginations of some persons, in the visions and immediate strong impulses and suggestions they have, as though they saw sights and had words spoken to them, may and often do produce a strong persuasion of the truth of invisible things. The general tendency of such things, in their final outcome, is to draw men away from the word of God, to make them reject the gospel, and to establish unbelief and atheism. Yet for the present they may, and often do, produce a confident persuasion of the truth of some things revealed in the Scriptures, though their confidence is founded on delusion and so is worth nothing. For instance, suppose some invisible agent immediately and strongly impresses on a person’s imagination the appearance of a bright light, and the glorious form of a person seated on a throne with great outward majesty and beauty, uttering some remarkable words with great force and energy. The person who is the subject of such an operation may from this be confident that there are invisible agents, spiritual beings, from what he has experienced, knowing that he himself had no hand in this extraordinary effect he has experienced. He may also be confident that this is Christ, whom he saw and heard speaking. And this may make him confident that there is a Christ, and that Christ reigns on a throne in heaven as he saw him; and he may be confident that the words he heard him speak are true, and so on. In the same way the lying miracles of the papists may for the present produce in the minds of the ignorant, deluded people a strong persuasion of the truth of many things declared in the New Testament. So when the images of Christ in popish churches are, on some extraordinary occasions, made by priestcraft to appear to the people as if they wept, shed fresh blood, moved, and uttered such and such words, the people may truly be persuaded that it is a miracle worked by Christ himself. From this they may be confident that there is a Christ, and that what they are told of his death and sufferings, resurrection, ascension and present government of the world is true; for they may look on this miracle as a certain evidence of all these things, and a kind of demonstration of them before their eyes. This may be the influence of these lying wonders for the present, though their general tendency is not to convince people that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, but in the end to promote atheism. Even the dealings that Satan has with witches, and their frequent experience of his immediate power, tend to convince them of the truth of some of the doctrines of religion, in particular the reality of an invisible world, or world of spirits, contrary to the doctrine of the Sadducees. The general tendency of Satan’s influences is delusion; but he may still mix some truth with his lies, so that his lies may not be so easily discovered.

There are multitudes who are deluded with a counterfeit faith from impressions on their imagination, in the way just spoken of. They say they know that there is a God, for they have seen him; they know that Christ is the Son of God, for they have seen him in his glory; they know that Christ died for sinners, for they have seen him hanging on the cross, and his blood running from his wounds; they know there is a heaven and a hell, for they have seen the misery of the damned souls in hell and the glory of saints and angels in heaven (meaning some outward representations strongly impressed on their imagination). They know that the Scriptures are the word of God, and that such and such promises in particular are his word, for they have heard him speak them to them: they came to their minds suddenly and immediately from God, without their having any hand in it.

(3.) Persons may seem to have their belief of the truth of the things of religion greatly increased when its foundation is only a persuasion they have received that they themselves have a share in them. First, by some means or other, they take up a confidence that if there is a Christ and a heaven, they are theirs; and this prejudices them more in favor of the truth of these things. When they hear of the great and glorious things of religion, it is with this notion, that all these things belong to them; and so they easily become confident that they are true. They regard it as greatly to their advantage that they should be true. It is very obvious what a strong influence men’s self-interest and inclinations have on their judgments. While a natural man thinks that, if there is a heaven and a hell, the latter and not the former belongs to him, he will be hard to persuade that there is a heaven or hell. But when he comes to be persuaded that hell belongs only to other people and not to him, then he can easily admit the reality of hell, and cry out against others’ senselessness and folly in neglecting the means of escaping it. And being confident that he is a child of God, and that God has promised heaven to him, he may seem strong in the faith of its reality, and may have a great zeal against the unbelief that denies it.

But I proceed to another distinguishing sign of gracious affections.

Evangelical Humiliation

Part III · Sign VI

VI. Gracious affections are accompanied by evangelical humiliation.

Evangelical humiliation is a sense that a Christian has of his own utter insufficiency, despicableness and odiousness, with a frame of heart corresponding to it.

A distinction must be made between a legal and an evangelical humiliation. Men may be the subjects of the former while they are still in a state of nature and have no gracious affection; the latter is peculiar to true saints. The former is from the common influence of the Spirit of God assisting natural principles, and especially natural conscience; the latter is from the special influences of the Spirit of God implanting and exercising supernatural and divine principles. The former comes from the mind’s being assisted to a greater sense of the things of religion as to their natural properties and qualities, and particularly of the natural perfections of God, such as his greatness, awesome majesty and so on, which were manifested to the congregation of Israel in the giving of the law at Mount Sinai; the latter comes from a sense of the transcendent beauty of divine things in their moral qualities. In the former, a sense of the fearful greatness and natural perfections of God, and of the strictness of his law, convinces men that they are exceedingly sinful and guilty and exposed to the wrath of God, as it will convince wicked men and devils at the day of judgment. But they do not see their own odiousness on account of sin; they do not see the hateful nature of sin. A sense of this is given in evangelical humiliation, by the showing of the beauty of God’s holiness and moral perfection. In a legal humiliation men are made to feel that they are little and nothing before the great and awesome God, and that they are undone and wholly unable to help themselves, as wicked men will be at the day of judgment. But they do not have a frame of heart corresponding to it, consisting in a disposition to abase themselves and exalt God alone. This disposition is given only in evangelical humiliation, by overcoming the heart and changing its inclination through the showing of God’s holy beauty. In a legal humiliation the conscience is convicted, as the consciences of all will be most perfectly convicted at the day of judgment; but because there is no spiritual understanding, the will is not bowed, nor the inclination changed. This is done only in evangelical humiliation. In legal humiliation men are brought to despair of helping themselves; in evangelical humiliation they are brought voluntarily to deny and renounce themselves. In the former they are subdued and forced to the ground; in the latter they are brought sweetly to yield, and freely and with delight to lay themselves down at the feet of God.

Legal humiliation has no spiritual good in it, nothing of the nature of true virtue; whereas evangelical humiliation is that in which the excellent beauty of Christian grace very much consists. Legal humiliation is useful as a means toward evangelical humiliation, as a common knowledge of the things of religion is a means required toward spiritual knowledge. Men may be legally humbled and have no humility. So the wicked at the day of judgment will be thoroughly convinced that they have no righteousness but are altogether sinful, exceedingly guilty and justly exposed to eternal damnation, and will fully feel their own helplessness, without the least mortification of the pride of their hearts. But the essence of evangelical humiliation consists in such humility as befits a creature that is in itself exceedingly sinful, under a dispensation of grace: a low esteem of himself, as in himself nothing, and altogether contemptible and odious, accompanied by a mortification of the disposition to exalt himself, and a free renunciation of his own glory.

This is a great and most essential thing in true religion. The whole frame of the gospel, and everything belonging to the new covenant, and all God’s dealings with fallen man, are designed to bring about this effect in the hearts of men. Those who are without it have no true religion, whatever profession they may make, and however high their religious affections may be. Hab 2:4: “Look at the proud one; his soul is not upright—but the righteous will live by his faith”; that is, he will live by his faith in God’s righteousness and grace, and not by his own goodness and excellence. God has abundantly shown in his word that this is what he has a special regard for in his saints, and that nothing is acceptable to him without it. Ps 34:18: “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit.” Ps 51:17: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.” Ps 138:6: “Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly.” Prov 3:34: “He … gives grace to the humble.” Isa 57:15: “For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: ‘I dwell in a high and holy place, and with the contrite and humble in spirit, to restore the spirit of the lowly and revive the heart of the contrite.’ ” Isa 66:1–2: “This is what the LORD says: ‘Heaven is My throne, and earth is My footstool. … This is the one I will esteem: he who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word.’ ” Mic 6:8: “He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” Matt 5:3: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Matt 18:3–4: “Truly I tell you+, unless you+ change and become like little children, you+ will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.” Mark 10:15: “Truly I tell you+, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.” The centurion of whom we have an account in Luke 7 acknowledged that he was not worthy to have Christ come under his roof, and that he was not worthy to come to him. See the manner in which the woman who was a sinner came to Christ, Luke 7:37 and following: “When a sinful woman from that town learned that Jesus was dining there, she brought an alabaster jar of perfume. As she stood behind Him at His feet weeping, she began to wet His feet with her tears and wipe them with her hair.” She did not think the hair of her head, which is the natural crown and glory of a woman (1 Cor 11:15), too good to wipe the feet of Christ with. Jesus most graciously accepted her, and says to her, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” The woman of Canaan submitted to Christ when he said, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs,” and as it were acknowledged that she deserved to be called a dog; at which Christ says to her, “O woman, your faith is great! Let it be done for you as you desire” (Matt 15:26–27). The prodigal son said, “I will get up and go back to my father and say to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants’ ” (Luke 15:18 and following). See also Luke 18:9 and following: “To some who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt, He also told this parable,” and so on. … “But the tax collector stood at a distance, unwilling even to lift up his eyes to heaven. Instead, he beat his breast and said, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner!’ I tell you+, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” Matt 28:9: “They came to Him, grasped His feet, and worshiped Him.” Col 3:12: “As the elect of God … clothe yourselves+ with … humility.” Ezek 20:41, 43: “When I bring you+ from the peoples … I will accept you+ as a pleasing aroma,” and so on. … “There you+ will remember your+ ways and all the deeds with which you+ have defiled yourselves+, and you+ will loathe yourselves+ for all the evils you+ have done.” Chapter 36:26–27, 31: “I will give you+ a new heart … And I will put My Spirit within you+ and cause you+ to walk in My statutes,” and so on. … “Then you+ will remember your+ evil ways and wicked deeds, and you+ will loathe yourselves+ for your+ iniquities and abominations.” Chapter 16:63: “so that when I am pacified toward you for all you have done, you will remember and be ashamed and never again open your mouth because of your disgrace, declares the Lord GOD.” Job 42:6: “Therefore I abhor myself, and I repent in dust and ashes.”

So if we would make the holy Scriptures our rule in judging the nature of true religion, and in judging our own religious qualifications and state, it greatly concerns us to regard this humiliation as one of the most essential things belonging to true Christianity.59 This is the principal part of the great Christian duty of self-denial. That duty consists in two things, namely: first, in a man’s denying his worldly inclinations, and forsaking and renouncing all worldly objects and enjoyments; and secondly, in denying his natural self-exaltation, renouncing his own dignity and glory, and being emptied of himself, so that he freely and from his very heart, as it were, renounces himself and annihilates himself. This is what the Christian does in evangelical humiliation. And this latter is the greatest and most difficult part of self-denial. Although the two always go together, and the one never truly exists where the other does not, yet natural men can come much nearer to the former than to the latter. Many anchorites and recluses have abandoned the wealth and pleasures and common enjoyments of the world (though without any true mortification) who were far from renouncing their own dignity and righteousness. They never denied themselves for Christ, but only sold one lust to feed another, sold a beastly lust to pamper a devilish one; and so they were never the better, but their latter end was worse than their beginning. They turned out one black devil to let in seven white ones that were worse than the first, though fairer in appearance. It is inexpressible, and almost inconceivable, how strong a self-righteous, self-exalting disposition there naturally is in man, and what he will not do and suffer to feed and gratify it. And what lengths have been gone to in a seeming self-denial in other respects: by Essenes and Pharisees among the Jews; by papists, many sects of heretics, and fanatics among professing Christians; by many Muslims; and by Pythagorean philosophers and others among the heathen! And all to offer sacrifice to this Moloch of spiritual pride or self-righteousness, and so that they may have something in which to exalt themselves before God and above their fellow creatures.

The humiliation that has been spoken of is what all the most glorious hypocrites, who make the most splendid show to the world of mortification and of high religious affection, grossly fail in. If this were not so much insisted on in Scripture as a most essential thing in true grace, one would be tempted to think that many of the heathen philosophers were truly gracious. In them there was so bright an appearance of many virtues, and also great illuminations, and inward fervors and elevations of mind, as though they were truly the subjects of divine inflowings and heavenly gifts.60

It is true that many hypocrites make great pretenses to humility, as to other graces; and very often there is nothing whatever that they make a higher profession of. They try to make a great show of humility in speech and behavior; but they commonly make bungling work of it, though glorious work in their own eyes. They cannot find out what humble speech and behavior is, or how to speak and act so that there may really be a savor of Christian humility in what they say and do. That sweet, humble air and manner is beyond their art, since they are not “led by the Spirit,” nor naturally guided to a behavior befitting holy humility by the vigor of a lowly spirit within them. And so many of them have no other way but to be much in declaring that they are humble, and in telling how they were humbled to the dust at such and such times, and in abounding in very low expressions that they use about themselves, such as, “I am the least of all saints! I am a poor vile creature! I am not worthy of the least mercy, or that God should look on me! Oh, I have a dreadfully wicked heart! My heart is worse than the devil! Oh, this cursed heart of mine!” and so on. Such expressions are very often used, not with a heart that is broken, not with spiritual mourning, not with the tears of her who washed Jesus’ feet with her tears, not as remembering and being ashamed, and never opening their mouths again because of their disgrace, when God is pacified, as the expression is in Ezek 16:63. They are used with a light air, with smiles on the face, or with a pharisaical affectation. And we must believe that they are humble in this way, and see themselves as so vile, on the strength of their own say-so; for nothing of any savor of humility appears in them, in the manner of their conduct and the deeds they do. There are many who are full of expressions of their own vileness who nevertheless expect, as their due, to be looked on by others as eminent and bright saints; and it is dangerous for anyone so much as to hint the contrary, or to treat them in any other way than as if we regarded them as among the chief of Christians. There are many who are much in crying out about their wicked hearts and their great shortcomings and unprofitableness, and who speak as though they looked on themselves as the lowest of the saints. Yet if a minister were seriously to tell them the same things in private, and to indicate that he feared they were very low and weak Christians, and thought they had reason solemnly to consider their great barrenness and unprofitableness, and their falling so far short of many others, it would be more than they could stomach. They would think themselves greatly wronged, and there would be danger of a rooted prejudice in them against such a minister.

There are some who are abundant in talking against legalistic doctrines, legalistic preaching and a legal spirit, who understand very little of the thing they talk against. A legalistic spirit is a more subtle thing than they imagine; it is too subtle for them. It lurks and works and prevails in their hearts, and they are most notoriously guilty of it at the very time when they are denouncing it. So far as a man is not emptied of himself, and of his own righteousness and goodness, in whatever form or shape, so far he is of a legalistic spirit. A spirit of pride in a man’s own righteousness, morality, holiness, affection, experience, faith, humbling, or any goodness whatever, is a legalistic spirit. It was no pride in Adam before the fall to be of a legal spirit, because in his circumstances he might seek acceptance by his own righteousness. But a legalistic spirit in a fallen, sinful creature can be nothing else but spiritual pride; and, conversely, a spiritually proud spirit is a legalistic spirit. There is no man living who is lifted up with a high conceit of his own experiences and manifestations, and on account of them glitters in his own eyes, who does not trust in his experiences and make a righteousness of them. However he may use humble terms, and speak of his experiences as the great things God has done for him, and perhaps call on others to glorify God for them, yet he who is proud of his experiences claims something for himself, as though his experiences were some dignity of his. And if he looks on them as his own dignity, he necessarily thinks that God looks on them so too. For he necessarily thinks his own opinion of them to be true, and so judges that God looks on them as he does; and so he unavoidably imagines that God looks on his experiences as a dignity in him, as he looks on them himself, and that he glitters as much in God’s eyes as he does in his own. And so he trusts in what is inherent in him to make him shine in God’s sight and commend him to God. With this encouragement he goes before God in prayer; this makes him expect much from God; and this makes him think that Christ loves him and is willing to clothe him with his righteousness, because he supposes that Christ is taken with his experiences and graces. And this is a high degree of living on his own righteousness; and such persons are on the highway to hell. Poor deluded wretches, who think they look so glittering in God’s eyes when they are a smoke in his nostrils, and many of them more odious to him than the most impure beast in Sodom who makes no pretense to religion! To do as these do is to live on experiences, according to the true meaning of the phrase; and not to do as those do who only make use of spiritual experiences as evidences of a state of grace, and in that way receive hope and comfort from them.

There is a sort of men who indeed abundantly cry down works and cry up faith in opposition to works, and set themselves up very much as evangelical persons in opposition to those who are of a legalistic spirit, and make a fair show of advancing Christ and the gospel and the way of free grace; and yet they are in fact some of the greatest enemies of the gospel way of free grace, and the most dangerous opposers of pure, humble Christianity.61

There is a pretended great humbling, a being dead to the law and emptied of self, which is one of the biggest and most puffed-up things in the world. There are some who have made a great profession of experiencing a thorough work of the law on their own hearts, and of being brought fully off from works, whose conduct has savored more of a self-righteous spirit than that of anyone I ever had opportunity to observe. And some who think themselves quite emptied of themselves, and are confident that they are abased in the dust, are as full as they can hold of the glory of their own humility, and lifted up to heaven with a high opinion of their abasement. Their humility is a swelling, self-conceited, confident, showy, noisy, assuming humility. It seems to be the nature of spiritual pride to make men conceited and ostentatious about their humility. This appears in that firstborn of pride among the children of men who would be called his holiness, the man of sin himself, who exalts himself above all that is called God or is worshiped. He styles himself servant of servants; and to make a show of humility, he washes the feet of a number of poor men at his inauguration.

For persons to be truly emptied of themselves, poor in spirit and broken in heart, is quite another thing, with other effects, than many imagine. It is astonishing how greatly many are deceived about themselves in this matter, imagining themselves most humble when they are most proud, and when their behavior is really most haughty. The deceitfulness of the heart of man appears in nothing so much as in this matter of spiritual pride and self-righteousness. The subtlety of Satan appears at its height in his management of persons with respect to this sin. And perhaps one reason may be that here he has the most experience: he knows the way it comes in; he is acquainted with its secret springs; it was his own sin. Experience gives a vast advantage in leading souls, whether in good or in evil.

But though spiritual pride is so subtle and secret an iniquity, and commonly appears under a pretext of great humility, there are two things by which it may (perhaps universally and surely) be detected and distinguished.

The first thing is this: he who is under the power of this disease is apt to think highly of his attainments in religion in comparison with others. It is natural for him to fall into the thought that he is an eminent saint, that he stands very high among the saints, and has distinguishingly good and great experiences. That is the secret language of his heart: “God, I thank You that I am not like the other men” (Luke 18:11); and, “I am holier than you!” (Isa 65:5). So such men are apt to put themselves forward among God’s people, and as it were to take a high seat among them, as if there were no doubt that it belonged to them. As it were by nature, they do what Christ condemns in Luke 14:7 and following: they take the place of honor. This they do by being forward to take on themselves the place and business of the chief: to guide, teach, direct and manage. They are confident that they are guides for the blind, a light for those in darkness, instructors of the foolish, teachers of infants (Rom 2:19–20). It is natural for them to take it for granted that it belongs to them to play the part of dictators and masters in matters of religion; and so, without saying so, they aim to be called Rabbi by men, which means Master, as the Pharisees did (Matt 23:6–7 and following). They are apt to expect that others should regard them and defer to them as masters in matters of religion.62

But he whose heart is under the power of Christian humility is of the opposite disposition. If the Scriptures are to be relied on at all, such a man is apt to think his attainments in religion comparatively small, and to esteem himself low among the saints, one of the least of saints. Humility, or true lowliness of mind, disposes persons to think others better than themselves. Phil 2:3: “In humility consider others better than yourselves+.” So they are apt to think the lowest place belongs to them, and their inward disposition naturally leads them to obey that command of our Savior in Luke 14:10. It is not natural to them to take it on themselves to play the part of teachers. On the contrary, they are disposed to think that they are not the persons for it, that others are fitter for it than they; as it was with Moses and Jeremiah (Exod 3:11; Jer 1:6), though they were such eminent saints and men of great knowledge. It is not natural to them to think that it belongs to them to teach, but to be taught. They are much more eager to hear and to receive instruction from others than to dictate to others. Jas 1:19: “Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak.” And when they do speak, it is not natural to them to speak with a bold, masterly air; humility disposes them rather to speak trembling. Hos 13:1: “When Ephraim spoke trembling, he was exalted in Israel. But he incurred guilt through Baal, and he died.” They are not apt to assume authority, and to take it on themselves to be chief managers and masters, but rather to be subject to others. Jas 3:1–2: “Not many of you+ should become teachers.” 1 Pet 5:5: “All of you+, be subject to one another, and clothe yourselves+ with humility.” Eph 5:21: “Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.”

There are some persons whose experiences naturally work in this way, to make them think highly of their experiences; and they often speak of their experiences themselves as very great and extraordinary. They speak freely of the great things they have met with. This may be said and meant in a good sense. In one sense every degree of saving mercy is a great thing: it is indeed a great thing, indeed an infinitely great thing, for God to give the least crumb of the children’s bread to such dogs as we are in ourselves; and the more humble a person is who hopes that God has given such mercy to him, the more apt he will be to call it a great thing that he has met with, in this sense. But if by the great things which they have experienced they mean spiritual experiences that are great by comparison, great compared with other people’s experiences, or beyond what is ordinary, which is evidently often the case, then for a person to say, “I have met with great things,” is the very same as to say, “I am an eminent saint,” and have more grace than ordinary. For to have great experiences, if the experiences are true and worth telling, is the same as to have great grace. There is no true experience but the exercise of grace, and the degree of grace and holiness is exactly according to the degree of true experience. The persons who talk like this about their experiences expect, when they give an account of them, that others should admire them. Indeed, they do not call it boasting to talk in this way about their experiences, nor do they regard it as any sign of pride. For they say they know that it was not they who did it; it was free grace; these are the great things that God has done for them; they would acknowledge the great mercy God has shown them, and not make light of it. But so it was with the Pharisee Christ tells us of in Luke 18. In words he gave God the glory for making him differ from other men: “God, I thank You,” he says, “that I am not like the other men.”63 Their ascribing it in words to the grace of God that they are holier than other saints does not keep their readiness to think so highly of their holiness from being a sure evidence of the pride and vanity of their minds. If they were under the influence of a humble spirit, their attainments in religion would not be so apt to shine in their own eyes, nor would they be so much taken up with admiring their own beauty. The Christians who really are the most eminent saints, and so have the most excellent experiences, are the greatest in the kingdom of heaven, and humble themselves like a little child (Matt 18:4). For they look on themselves as only little children in grace, and on their attainments as only the attainments of babes in Christ; and they are astonished at and ashamed of the low degrees of their love and their thankfulness, and their little knowledge of God. When Moses had been speaking with God on the mountain, and his face shone so bright in the eyes of others as to dazzle their eyes, he “was unaware that his face had become radiant.” There are some persons who are known for professing great things in religion, and some will admit that they do; but eminently humble saints, who will shine brightest in heaven, are not at all apt to make high professions. I do not believe there is an eminent saint in the world who makes a high profession. Such men will be much more likely to profess themselves the least of all saints, and to think that every saint’s attainments and experiences are higher than their own.64

Such is the nature of grace and of true spiritual light that they naturally dispose the saints in the present state to look on their grace and goodness as little, and their deformity as great. And those who have the most grace and spiritual light of anyone in this world have the most of this disposition. This will appear most clear and evident to anyone who soberly and thoroughly weighs the nature and reason of things, and considers the following things.

That grace and holiness is worthy to be called little which is little in comparison with what it ought to be. And so it seems to one who is truly gracious. For such a man has his eye on the rule of his duty: conformity to that rule is what he aims at; it is what his soul struggles and reaches after; and it is by that rule that he estimates and judges what he does and what he has. To a gracious soul, and especially to one eminently gracious, that holiness appears little which is little of what it should be, little of what he sees infinite reason and obligation for. If his holiness appears to him to be at a vast distance from this, it naturally appears despicable in his eyes, and not worth mentioning as any beauty or loveliness in him. For a similar reason a hungry man naturally counts what is set before him as only a little food, a small matter not worth mentioning, if it is nothing in comparison with his appetite. Or again, the child of a great prince, who is jealous for the honor of his father and sees the respect men show him, naturally looks on that honor and respect as very little and not worth regarding if it is nothing in comparison with what the dignity of his father requires.

But the nature of true grace and spiritual light is that it opens to a person’s view the infinite reason there is that he should be holy in a high degree. And the more grace he has, the more this is opened to his view, and the greater sense he has of the infinite excellence and glory of the divine Being, and of the infinite dignity of the person of Christ, and of the boundless length and breadth, and depth and height, of the love of Christ to sinners. And as grace increases, the field opens more and more to a distant view, until the soul is swallowed up with the vastness of the object, and the person is astonished to think how much it befits him to love this God and this glorious Redeemer who has so loved man, and how little he does love. And so the more he apprehends, the more the smallness of his grace and love appears strange and wonderful; and so he is more ready to think that others are beyond him. For, wondering at the littleness of his own grace, he can scarcely believe that so strange a thing happens to other saints. It is amazing to him that one who is really a child of God, and has actually received the saving benefits of that unspeakable love of Christ, should love no more. And he is apt to look on it as a thing peculiar to himself, a strange and exceptional case; for he sees only the outside of other Christians, but he sees his own inside.

Here the reader may possibly object that love to God really increases in proportion as the knowledge of God increases; so how should an increase of knowledge in a saint make his love appear less in comparison with what is known? To this I answer that although grace and the love of God in the saints correspond to the degree of knowledge or sight of God, yet they are not in proportion to the object seen and known. The soul of a saint, by having something of God opened to its sight, is convinced of much more than is seen. Something is seen that is wonderful, and that sight brings with it a strong conviction of something vastly beyond it that is not immediately seen. So the soul at the same time is astonished at its ignorance, that it knows so little, as well as that it loves so little. And as the soul in a spiritual view is convinced of infinitely more in the object, still beyond its sight, so it is convinced of the soul’s capacity for knowing vastly more, if only the clouds and darkness were removed. This makes the soul, in the enjoyment of a spiritual view, complain greatly of spiritual ignorance and lack of love, and long and reach after more knowledge and more love.

Grace and the love of God in the most eminent saints in this world are truly very little in comparison with what they ought to be. For the highest love that anyone ever attains in this life is poor, cold, exceedingly low, and not worth naming in comparison with what our obligations appear to be from considering these two things together, namely: 1. The reason God has given us to love him, in the manifestations he has made of his infinite glory in his word and in his works, and particularly in the gospel of his Son and what he has done for sinful man by him. And 2. The capacity there is in the soul of man, by the intellectual faculties God has given it, for seeing and understanding these reasons God has given us to love him. How small indeed is the love of the most eminent saint on earth in comparison with what these things, considered together, require! And grace tends to convince men of this, especially eminent grace; for grace is of the nature of light, and brings truth to view. And so he who has much grace apprehends, much more than others, that great height to which his love ought to rise; and he sees better than others how little a way he has risen toward that height. And so, estimating his love by the whole height of his duty, it appears astonishingly little and low in his eyes.

And the eminent saint, having such a conviction of the high degree in which he ought to love God, is shown by it not only the littleness of his grace but the greatness of his remaining corruption. To judge how much corruption or sin we have remaining in us, we must take our measure from the height to which the rule of our duty extends. The whole of the distance we are from that height is sin; for failing in duty is sin, or else our duty is not our duty; and the further we fall short of our duty, the more sin we have. Sin is nothing other than a disagreement, in a moral agent, with the law or rule of his duty. And so the degree of sin is to be judged by the rule: so much disagreement with the rule, so much sin, whether it is in defect or excess. Therefore, if men in their love to God do not come up halfway to the height that duty requires, then they have more corruption in their hearts than grace, because more goodness is lacking than is there; and all that is lacking is sin. It is an abominable defect, and it appears so to the saints, especially to those who are eminent. It appears exceedingly abominable to them that Christ should be loved so little, and thanked so little for his dying love; in their eyes it is hateful ingratitude.

And then the increase of grace tends in another way to make the saints think their deformity vastly greater than their goodness. It not only tends to convince them that their corruption is much greater than their goodness, which is indeed the case; it also tends to make the deformity in the least sin, or the least degree of corruption, appear so great as vastly to outweigh all the beauty in their greatest holiness; for this also is indeed the case. For the least sin against an infinite God has an infinite hatefulness or deformity in it; but the highest degree of holiness in a creature does not have an infinite loveliness in it. And so its loveliness is as nothing in comparison with the deformity of the least sin. That every sin has infinite deformity and hatefulness in it is most demonstrably evident. For the evil, or iniquity, or hatefulness of sin consists in the violating of an obligation, or in being or doing contrary to what we should be or do, or are obliged to. And so the greater the obligation that is violated, the greater the iniquity and hatefulness of the violation. But certainly our obligation to love and honor any being is in some proportion to his loveliness and honorableness, or to his worthiness to be loved and honored by us, which is the same thing. We are surely under greater obligation to love a more lovely being than a less lovely one; and if a being is infinitely lovely, or worthy to be loved by us, then our obligations to love him are infinitely great. And so whatever is contrary to this love has infinite iniquity, deformity and unworthiness in it. But on the other hand, with respect to our holiness or love to God, there is not an infinite worthiness in that. The sin of the creature against God is ill-deserving and hateful in proportion to the distance there is between God and the creature: the greatness of the object, and the lowness and inferiority of the subject, aggravate it. But it is the reverse with regard to the worthiness of the creature’s respect to God: it is worthless, and not worthy, in proportion to the lowness of the subject. The greater the distance between God and the creature, the less the creature’s respect is worthy of God’s notice or regard. The great degree of superiority increases the obligation on the inferior to regard the superior, and so makes the lack of regard more hateful. But the great degree of inferiority diminishes the worth of the inferior’s regard; because the more inferior he is, the less he is worthy of notice; the less he is, the less what he can offer is worth. For he can offer no more than himself in offering his best respect; and so, as he is little and of little worth, so his respect is of little worth. And the more a person has of true grace and spiritual light, the more it will appear like this to him: the more he will appear to himself infinitely deformed by reason of sin, and the less the goodness in his grace or good experience will appear in proportion to it. For indeed it is nothing compared with it: it is less than a drop to the ocean; for the finite bears no proportion at all to the infinite. But the more a person has of spiritual light, the more things appear to him, in this respect, as they really are. From this it most demonstrably appears that true grace is of such a nature that the more a person has of it, with remaining corruption, the less his goodness and holiness appear in proportion to his deformity; and not only to his past deformity, but to his present deformity, in the sin that now appears in his heart, and in the abominable defects of his highest and best affections and brightest experiences.

The nature of many high religious affections and great manifestations (as they are called) in many persons I have been acquainted with is to hide and cover over the corruption of their hearts, and to make it seem to them as if all their sin were gone, and to leave them without complaints of any hateful evil left in them (though perhaps they cry out much about their past unworthiness). This is a sure and certain evidence that their manifestations (as they call them) are darkness and not light. It is darkness that hides men’s pollution and deformity; but light let into the heart reveals it, searches it out in its secret corners, and makes it plainly appear; especially that penetrating, all-searching light of God’s holiness and glory. It is true that saving manifestations may for the present hide corruption in one sense: they restrain its positive exercises, such as malice, envy, covetousness, lewdness, grumbling and so on. But they bring corruption to light in what is lacking: that there is not more love, not more humility, not more thankfulness. These defects appear most hateful in the eyes of those who have the most eminent exercises of grace; they are very burdensome, and make the saints cry out about their leanness and their odious pride and ingratitude. And whatever positive exercises of corruption arise at any time and mingle themselves with eminent actings of grace, grace will greatly magnify the view of them, and make them appear far more heinous and horrible.

The more eminent the saints are, and the more they have of the light of heaven in their souls, the more they appear to themselves as the most eminent saints in this world appear to the saints and angels in heaven. How can we rationally suppose the most eminent saints on earth appear to them, if they are seen in any other way than covered over with the righteousness of Christ, and their deformities swallowed up and hidden in the brilliance of the beams of his abundant glory and love? How can we suppose our most ardent love and praises appear to those who behold the beauty and glory of God without a veil? How does our highest thankfulness for the dying love of Christ appear to those who see Christ as he is, who know as they are known, and see the glory of the person of him who died, and the wonders of his dying love, without any cloud or darkness? And how do they look on the deepest reverence and humility with which worms of the dust on earth approach that infinite majesty which they behold? Do these appear great to them, or even worthy of the name of reverence and humility, in those whom they see to be at such an infinite distance from that great and holy God in whose glorious presence they are? The reason why the highest attainments of the saints on earth appear so low to them is that they dwell in the light of God’s glory and see God as he is. And in this respect it is with the saints on earth as it is with the saints in heaven, in proportion as they are more eminent in grace.

I would not be understood to mean that the saints on earth have in every respect the worst opinion of themselves when they have the most exercise of grace. In many respects it is otherwise. With respect to the positive exercises of corruption, they may appear to themselves freest and best when grace is most in exercise, and worst when the actings of grace are lowest. And when they compare themselves with themselves at different times, they may know, when grace is in lively exercise, that it is better with them than it was before (though before, at the time, they did not see as much badness as they see now). And when afterward they sink again in the frame of their minds, they may know that they sink, and have a new proof of their great remaining corruption, and a rational conviction of a greater vileness than they saw before; and they may have far more of a sense of guilt, and a kind of legal sense of their sinfulness, than when grace is in lively exercise. But still it is true, and demonstrable from the considerations already mentioned, that the children of God never have so much of a felt and spiritual conviction of their deformity, and so great, keen and abasing a sense of their present vileness and odiousness, as when they are highest in the exercise of true and pure grace; and they are never so much disposed to set themselves low among Christians as then. And so he who is greatest in the kingdom, or most eminent in the church of Christ, is the same one who humbles himself like the least infant among them; agreeable to that great saying of Christ, Matt 18:4.

A true saint may know that he has some true grace; and the more grace there is, the more easily it is known, as was observed and proved before. But it does not follow that an eminent saint readily has a sense that he is an eminent saint when compared with others. I will not deny that it is possible for one who has much grace and is an eminent saint to know it. But he will not be apt to know it; it will not be obvious to him. That he is better than others, and has higher experiences and attainments, is not a foremost thought with him, nor is it something that readily presents itself from time to time. It is not in his way, but lies far out of sight. He must take pains to convince himself of it; there will be need of a great command of reason, and a high degree of strictness and care in arguing, to convince himself. And if he is rationally convinced, by a very strict consideration of his own experiences compared with the great appearances of low degrees of grace in some other saints, it will hardly seem real to him that he has more grace than they; and he will be apt to lose the conviction he has obtained with such pains. Nor will it seem at all natural to him to act on that supposition. And this may be laid down as an infallible thing: the person who is apt to think that he, compared with others, is a very eminent saint, much distinguished in Christian experience, in whom this is a first thought that rises of itself and naturally presents itself, is certainly mistaken. He is no eminent saint, but is under the great prevailing of a proud and self-righteous spirit. And if this is habitual with the man, and is steadily the prevailing disposition of his mind, he is no saint at all; he does not have the least degree of any true Christian experience, as surely as the word of God is true.

And the sort of experiences that appears to have this tendency, and is found from time to time to have this effect, of lifting up the person who has them with a great conceit of those experiences, is certainly vain and delusive. Those supposed manifestations that naturally swell a person with admiration of the eminence of his manifestations, and fill him with the notion that now he has seen and knows more than most other Christians, have nothing of the nature of true spiritual light in them. All true spiritual knowledge is of such a nature that the more a person has of it, the more he feels his own ignorance; as is evident from 1 Corinthians 8:2: “The one who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought to know.” When Agur had a great manifestation of God, and a sense of the wonderful height of his glory and of his marvelous works, and cries out about his greatness and incomprehensibility, he had at the same time the deepest sense of his brutish ignorance, and looked on himself as the most ignorant of all the saints. Prov 30:2–4: “Surely I am more brutish than any man, and I lack the understanding of a man. I have not learned wisdom, and I have no knowledge of the Holy One. Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in His hands? Who has bound up the waters in His cloak? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is His name, and what is the name of His Son? Tell me, if you know!”

For a man to be highly conceited of his spiritual and divine knowledge is for him to be wise in his own eyes, if anything is. And so it comes under those prohibitions, Prov 3:7: “Be not wise in your own eyes”; Rom 12:16: “Do not be wise in your own sight.” And it brings men under that woe, Isa 5:21: “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight.” Those who are wise in their own eyes in this way are among the least likely of anyone in the world to receive good. Experience shows the truth of Prov 26:12: “Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.”

To this some may object that the psalmist, at a time when we must suppose he was in a holy frame, speaks of his knowledge as eminently great, far greater than that of other saints, Ps 119:99–100: “I have more insight than all my teachers, for Your testimonies are my meditation. I discern more than the elders, for I obey Your precepts.”

To this I answer two things:

[1.] First, no restraint is to be laid on the Spirit of God as to what he may reveal, for the benefit of his church, to a prophet who is speaking or writing under immediate inspiration. The Spirit of God may reveal to such a man, and dictate to him to declare to others, secret things that would otherwise be hard, indeed impossible, for him to find out. He may reveal to him mysteries that would otherwise be beyond the reach of his reason, or things in a distant place that he cannot see, or future events that it would be impossible for him to know and declare if they were not extraordinarily revealed to him. So the Spirit of God might reveal to David this distinguishing benefit he had received by being much occupied with God’s testimonies, and use him as his instrument to record it for the benefit of others, to stir them up to the same duty and to use the same means to gain knowledge. Nothing can be gathered about the natural tendency of the ordinary gracious influences of the Spirit of God from what David declares of his distinguishing knowledge under the extraordinary influences of God’s Spirit, immediately dictating the divine mind to him by inspiration, and using David as his instrument to write what he pleased for the benefit of his church. We can no more argue so than we can reasonably argue that it is the natural tendency of grace to incline men to curse others, and to wish on them the most dreadful misery that can be thought of, because David under inspiration often curses others and prays that such misery may come on them.

[2.] Secondly, it is not certain that the knowledge David speaks of here is spiritual knowledge, in which holiness fundamentally consists. It may be that greater revelation which God made to him of the Messiah and the things of his future kingdom, and the far clearer and more extensive knowledge he had of the mysteries and doctrines of the gospel than others had, as a reward for his keeping God’s testimonies. In this it is apparent from the book of Psalms that David far exceeded all who had gone before him.

(2.) Secondly, another infallible sign of spiritual pride is persons’ being apt to think highly of their humility. False experiences are commonly accompanied by a counterfeit humility, and it is the very nature of a counterfeit humility to be highly conceited of itself. False religious affections generally tend, especially when raised to a great height, to make persons think that their humility is great, and so to take much notice of their great attainments in this respect and admire them. But eminently gracious affections (I do not hesitate to say it) always tend the opposite way, and have universally the opposite effect in those who have them. They do indeed make them deeply feel how much reason there is that they should be deeply humbled, and make them earnestly thirst and long for it; but they make their present humility, what they have already attained, appear small, and their remaining pride great and exceedingly abominable.

Why a proud person should be apt to think his humility great, and a very humble person think his humility small, may easily be seen if it is considered that it is natural for persons, in judging the degree of their own humbling, to take their measure from what they esteem their proper height, or the dignity in which they properly stand. What may be a great humbling in one is no humbling at all in another, because the degree of honor or importance in which each properly stands is very different. For some great man to stoop to untie the shoes of another great man, his equal, or to wash his feet, would be noticed as an act of abasement in him; and he, having a sense of his own dignity, would look on it so himself. But if a poor slave is seen stooping to untie the shoes of a great prince, nobody will take any notice of this as an act of humbling himself, or a sign of any great degree of humility. Nor would the slave himself, unless he were horribly proud and ridiculously conceited of himself. And if, after he had done it, he should show in his talk and behavior that he thought his abasement in it great, and had his mind much on it as evidence that he was very humble, would not everybody cry out at him, “Who do you think you are, that you should think what you have done such a deep humbling?” This would make it plain beyond question that this slave was swollen with a high degree of pride and vanity of mind, as much as if he declared in plain terms, “I think myself to be some great one.” And the matter is no less plain and certain when worthless, vile and loathsome worms of the dust are apt to put such a construction on their acts of abasement before God, and to think it a sign of great humility in them that, under their affections, they find themselves so willing to acknowledge themselves to be so low and unworthy, and to behave themselves as those who are so inferior. The very reason why such outward acts and such inward exercises look like great abasement in such a man is that he has a high conceit of himself. If he thought of himself more justly, these things would appear as nothing to him, and his humility in them worthy of no regard; he would rather be astonished at his pride, that one so infinitely despicable and vile is brought no lower before God. When he says in his heart, “This is a great act of humbling myself; it is certainly a sign of great humility in me that I should feel this way and act so,” his meaning is, “This is great humility for me, for such a one as I am, who am so important and worthy.” He considers how low he is now brought, and compares this with the height of dignity on which he thinks in his heart he properly stands; and the distance appears very great, and he calls it all pure humility, and admires it as such. But in him who is truly humble, and really sees his own vileness and loathsomeness before God, the distance appears the other way. When he is brought lowest of all, it does not appear to him that he is brought below his proper station, but that he has not yet come down to it; he appears to himself still vastly above it. He longs to get lower so that he may come to it, but he appears to be at a great distance from it; and this distance he calls pride. And so his pride appears great to him, and not his humility. For although he is brought much lower than he used to be, yet it does not appear to him worthy of the name of humbling for one so infinitely low and detestable as he is to come down to a place which, though lower than what he used to assume, is still vastly higher than what is proper for him. Just so, men would hardly count it worthy of the name of humility in a contemptible slave who formerly pretended to be a prince, to have his spirit brought down so far as to take the place of a nobleman, when this is still so far above his proper station.

All men in the world, in judging the degree of their own and others’ humility as it appears in any act of theirs, consider two things, namely: the real degree of dignity in which they stand, and the degree of abasement and the relation it bears to that real dignity. So submitting to the same low place, or low act, may be evidence of great humility in one, while it shows little or no humility in another. But truly humble Christians have so low an opinion of their own real dignity that all their self-abasement, when considered in relation to that and compared with it, appears very small to them. It does not seem to them to be any great humility, or any abasement worth making much of, for such poor, vile, abject creatures as they are to lie at the feet of God.

The degree of humility is to be judged by the degree of abasement and the degree of the cause for abasement. But he who is truly and eminently humble never thinks his humility great, considering the cause. The cause why he should be abased appears so great, and the abasement of the frame of his heart falls so far short of it, that he takes much more notice of his pride than of his humility.

Everyone who has been familiar with souls under convictions of sin knows that those who are greatly convicted of sin are not apt to think themselves greatly convicted. And the reason is this: men judge the degree of their own convictions of sin by two things considered together, namely, the degree of sense they have of guilt and pollution, and the degree of cause they have for such a sense in the degree of their real sinfulness. It is really no evidence of any great conviction of sin for some men to think themselves very sinful, beyond most others in the world, because they really are so, very plainly and notoriously. And so a far smaller conviction of sin may incline such a man to think so than another; he must be very blind indeed not to have a sense of it. But he who is truly under great convictions of sin naturally thinks this to be his case. It appears to him that the cause he has to feel guilt and pollution is greater than others have; and so he ascribes his sense of this to the greatness of his sin, and not to the greatness of his sensibility. It is natural for one under great convictions to think himself one of the greatest of sinners in reality, and also that it is so very plainly and evidently; for the greater his convictions are, the plainer and more evident it seems to him. And so it necessarily seems to him so plain, and so easy to see, that it may be seen without much conviction. That man is under great convictions whose conviction is great in proportion to his sin. But no man who is truly under great convictions thinks his conviction great in proportion to his sin. For if he does, it is a certain sign that he inwardly thinks his sins small; and if that is the case, that is a certain evidence that his conviction is small. And this, by the way, is the main reason why persons under a work of humbling have no sense of it at the time.

And as it is with conviction of sin, so by the same reasoning it is with persons’ conviction or sense of their own lowness and vileness, their own blindness, their own impotence, and all that low sense a Christian has of himself in the exercise of evangelical humiliation. So in a high degree of this, the saints are never disposed to think their sense of their own lowness, filthiness, impotence and so on to be great, because it never appears great to them, considering the cause.

An eminent saint is not apt to think himself eminent in anything. All his graces and experiences are ready to appear to him comparatively small, but especially his humility. There is nothing belonging to Christian experience and true piety that is so much out of his sight as his humility. He is a thousand times quicker to discern his pride than his humility: that he easily discerns and is apt to take much notice of, but he hardly discerns his humility. By contrast, the deluded hypocrite who is under the power of spiritual pride is blind to nothing so much as to his pride, and quick-sighted to nothing so much as to the shows of humility in him.

The humble Christian is more apt to find fault with his own pride than with other men’s. He is apt to put the best construction on others’ words and behavior, and to think that none are so proud as himself. But the proud hypocrite is quick to see the speck in his brother’s eye in this respect, while he sees nothing of the beam in his own. He is very often much in crying out about others’ pride, finding fault with others’ clothing and way of living; and he is affected ten times as much by his neighbor’s ring or ribbon as by all the filthiness of his own heart.

From the disposition there is in hypocrites to think highly of their humility, it comes about that counterfeit humility is forward to put itself on view. Those who have it are apt to be much in speaking of their humblings, and to set them out in high terms, and to make a great outward show of humility in affected looks, gestures or manner of speech, or in shabbiness of clothing, or some affected singularity. So it was of old with the false prophets (Zech 13:4); so it was with the hypocritical Jews (Isa 58:5); and so Christ tells us it was with the Pharisees (Matt 6:16). But it is the opposite with true humility. Those who have it are not apt to display their eloquence in setting it out, or to speak of the degree of their abasement in strong terms.65 True humility does not affect to show itself in any singular outward shabbiness of clothing or way of living; agreeable to what is implied in Matthew 6:17: “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face.” Col 2:23: “Such restrictions indeed have an appearance of wisdom, with their self-prescribed worship, their false humility, and their harsh treatment of the body.” Nor is true humility a noisy thing; it is not loud and boisterous. The Scripture represents it as of the opposite nature. Ahab, when he had a visible humility, a resemblance of true humility, “walked around softly” (1 Kgs 21:27). A penitent in the exercise of true humbling is represented as still and silent, Lam 3:28: “Let him sit alone in silence, for God has disciplined him.” And silence is mentioned as what accompanies humility, Prov 30:32: “If you have foolishly exalted yourself or if you have plotted evil, put your hand over your mouth.”

So I have shown particularly and at length the nature of the true humility that accompanies holy affections, as it appears in its tendency to make persons think little of their attainments in religion compared with the attainments of others, and particularly of their attainments in humility; and I have shown the opposite tendency of spiritual pride, to dispose persons to think their attainments in these respects great. I have dwelt longer on this matter because I regard it as a matter of great importance: it affords a certain distinction between true and counterfeit humility; and this disposition of hypocrites to look on themselves as better than others is what God has declared to be very hateful to him, a smoke in his nostrils, and a fire that burns all day long (Isa 65:5). It is mentioned as an instance of the pride of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, that holy city (as it was called), that they esteemed themselves far better than the people of Sodom, and so looked on them as worthy to be overlooked and disregarded by them. Ezek 16:56: “Your sister Sodom was not even mentioned by your mouth in the day of your pride.”

Let not the reader pass over these things lightly in applying them to himself. If you have once taken in that it is a bad sign for a person to be apt to think himself a better saint than others, a blinding prejudice will arise in your own favor; and there will probably be need of great strictness of self-examination to determine whether it is so with you. If, when the question is put, you answer, “No, it seems to me that none are so bad as I,” do not let the matter pass off like that. Examine again whether you do not think yourself better than others on this very account, because you imagine you think so lowly of yourself. Do you not have a high opinion of this humility? And if you answer again, “No, I do not have a high opinion of my humility; it seems to me I am as proud as the devil,” still examine again whether self-conceit does not rise up under this cover; whether on this very account, that you think yourself as proud as the devil, you do not think yourself to be very humble.

From this opposition between the nature of a true and of a counterfeit humility, as to the esteem their possessors have of themselves, arises a manifold contrariety of disposition and behavior.

A truly humble person, having such a low opinion of his righteousness and holiness, is poor in spirit. For a person to be poor in spirit is to be poor, in his own sense and understanding, as to what is in him, and to be of a disposition corresponding to it. And so a truly humble person, especially one eminently humble, naturally behaves himself in many respects as a poor man does. “The poor man pleads for mercy, but the rich man answers harshly.” A poor man is not disposed to quick and high resentment when he is among the rich. He is apt to yield to others, for he knows others are above him. He is not stiff and self-willed; he is patient with hard fare; he expects nothing other than to be despised, and takes it patiently. He does not take it badly that he is overlooked and little regarded; he is prepared to be in a low place; he readily honors his superiors; he takes rebukes quietly; he readily honors others as above him; he easily lets himself be taught, and does not claim much for his own understanding and judgment. He is not overly particular or moody, and has his spirit subdued to hard things. He is not presumptuous, nor apt to take much on himself, but it is natural for him to be subject to others. So it is with the humble Christian. Humility is (as the great Mastricht expresses it) a kind of holy pusillanimity.

A man who is very poor is a beggar; so is he who is poor in spirit. This is a great difference between affections that are gracious and those that are false. Under the former the person still remains a poor beggar at God’s gates, exceedingly empty and needy; but the latter make men appear to themselves rich, grown wealthy, and not in great need. In their own imagination they have a great stock to live on.66

A poor man is modest in his speech and behavior; so, and much more, and more certainly and universally, is one who is poor in spirit: he is humble and modest in his behavior among men. It is in vain for anyone to claim that they are humble, and as little children before God, when they are haughty, presumptuous and impudent in their behavior among men. The apostle tells us that the design of the gospel is to cut off all glorying, not only before God but also before men (Rom 4:1–2). Some who claim great humbling are very haughty, brazen and presumptuous in their outward appearance and behavior; but they ought to consider these Scriptures. Ps 131:1: “My heart is not proud, O LORD, my eyes are not haughty. I do not aspire to great things or matters too lofty for me.” Prov 6:16–17: “There are six things that the LORD hates, seven that are detestable to Him: haughty eyes,” and so on. Chapter 21:4: “Haughty eyes and a proud heart … are sin.” Ps 18:27: “You humble those with haughty eyes.” And Ps 101:5: “The one with haughty eyes and a proud heart, I will not endure.” 1 Cor 13:4–5: “Love … does not boast … It is not rude.” There is a certain lovely modesty and fear, arising from humility, that belongs to Christian behavior among men, which the Scripture often speaks of. 1 Pet 3:15: “Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you+ … with gentleness and fear.” Rom 13:7: “fear to whom fear is due.” 2 Cor 7:15: “when he remembers that you+ were all obedient as you+ welcomed him with fear and trembling.” Eph 6:5: “Slaves, obey your+ earthly masters with respect and fear.” 1 Pet 2:18: “Servants, submit yourselves+ to your+ masters with all fear.” 1 Pet 3:2: “when they see your+ pure conduct, coupled with fear.” 1 Tim 2:9: “I want the women to adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty, and with self-control.” In this respect a Christian is like a little child: a little child is modest before men, and his heart is apt to be filled with fear and awe among them.

The same spirit will dispose a Christian to honor all men. 1 Pet 2:17: “Honor all men.” A humble Christian is disposed to honor not only the saints in his behavior, but others also, in all those ways that do not imply a visible approval of their sins. So Abraham, the great pattern of believers, honored the children of Heth. Gen 23:11–12: Abraham rose and “bowed down before the people of the land.” This was a remarkable instance of humble behavior toward those who were outside of Christ, and whom Abraham knew to be accursed, so that he would by no means allow his servant to take a wife for his son from among them; and Esau’s wives, being of these children of Heth, were a grief of mind to Isaac and Rebekah. So Paul honored Festus, Acts 26:25: “I am not insane, most excellent Festus.” Christian humility will dispose persons to honor not only wicked men who are outside the visible church, but also false brethren and persecutors. So Jacob, when he was in an excellent frame, having just wrestled all night with God and received the blessing, honored Esau, his false and persecuting brother. Gen 33:14–15: Jacob “bowed to the ground seven times as he approached his brother” Esau. So he called him lord, and commanded all his family to honor him in the same way.

So I have tried to describe the heart and behavior of one who is governed by a truly gracious humility, as exactly in agreement with the Scriptures as I am able.

Now it is out of such a heart as this that all truly holy affections flow. Christian affections are like Mary’s precious ointment, which she poured on Christ’s head, and which filled the whole house with a sweet fragrance. That was poured out of an alabaster jar; so gracious affections flow out to Christ out of a pure heart. That was poured out of a broken jar: until the jar was broken the ointment could not flow, nor spread its fragrance; so gracious affections flow out of a broken heart. Gracious affections are also like those of Mary Magdalene (Luke 7, at the end), who also pours precious ointment on Christ out of a broken alabaster jar, anointing the feet of Jesus with it, after she had washed them with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head. All gracious affections that are a sweet fragrance to Christ, and that fill the soul of a Christian with a heavenly sweetness and fragrance, are broken-hearted affections. A truly Christian love, whether to God or to men, is a humble, broken-hearted love. The desires of the saints, however earnest, are humble desires; their hope is a humble hope; and their joy, even when it is “unspeakable and full of glory,” is a humble, broken-hearted joy, and leaves the Christian poorer in spirit, more like a little child, and more disposed to a universal lowliness of behavior.

59. Calvin, in his Institutes, book II, chapter 2, § 11, says: I was always exceedingly pleased with that saying of Chrysostom, “The foundation of our philosophy is humility”; and yet more pleased with that of Augustine: “As the rhetorician, when asked what was the first thing in the rules of eloquence, answered, Delivery; what was the second, Delivery; what was the third, still he answered, Delivery; so if you should ask me about the precepts of the Christian religion, I would answer, first, second, third and forever, humility.”

60. Although the Pythagoreans were so famous for Judaic mysterious wisdom, and for many moral as well as natural accomplishments, yet they were not free from boasting and pride. This was indeed a vice most widespread, and as it were inborn, among all the philosophers, but in a more particular way among the Pythagoreans. So Hernius, Hist. Philosoph. L. 3, chapter 11: “The manners of the Pythagoreans were not free from boasting. They were all ΠΕΡΙΑΥΤΟΛΟΓΟΙ, such as abounded in the sense and praise of their own excellences, and in boasting almost to the point of immodesty and impudence, as the great Heinsius ad Horat. has rightly observed.” Thus indeed proud nature delights to walk in the sparks of its own fire. And although many of these old philosophers could, by the strength of their own lights and heats, together with some common elevations and raisings of spirit (perhaps from a more than ordinary, though not special and saving, assistance of the Spirit), abandon many grosser vices, yet they were all deeply sunk in that miserable, cursed abyss of spiritual pride. So all their natural, moral and philosophic attainments fed, nourished and strengthened this hell-bred plague of their hearts, and made it most deeply rooted. Indeed, even those of them who seemed most modest, such as the Academics, who professed that they knew nothing, and the Cynics, who greatly decried the pride of others both in their words and in their dress, abounded in the most notorious and visible pride. So natural, and so morally essential to corrupt nature, is this venomous root, fountain and plague of spiritual pride, especially where there is any natural, moral or philosophic excellence to feed it. That is why Augustine rightly judged all these philosophic virtues to be nothing but splendid sins. Gale, court of the Gentiles, Part II, B. II, chapter 10, § 17.

61. Do not take every opinion and doctrine from men or angels that bears a fair show of advancing Christ; for they may be only the fruits of evangelical hypocrisy and deceit, which, being received themselves, may deceive others too. Matt 7:15: “Beware of” those who “come to you+ in sheep’s clothing,” in the innocence, purity and meekness of Christ and his people, “but inwardly they are ravenous wolves”: proud, cruel, censorious, who “slander what they do not understand. By their fruit you+ will recognize them.” Do not think, beloved, that Satan will not seek to send delusions among us. And do you+ think these delusions will come out of the popish pack, whose inventions smell above ground here? No, he must come, and will come, with more evangelical, finely spun devices. It is a rule observed among the Jesuits at this day, if they would conquer religion by subtlety, never to oppose religion with a contrary religion, but to set it against itself: so to oppose the gospel by the gospel. And look: as churches pleading for works had newly invented works, so when faith is preached men will have their new inventions of faith. I do not speak this against the doctrine of faith, where it is preached; I am glad of it. Nor do I say it because I would have men content themselves with every form of faith, for I believe that most men’s faith needs confirming or trying. But I speak to prevent danger on that side. Shepard’s parable, Part I, p. 122.

62. There are two things in which it appears that a man has only common gifts, and no inward principle. 1. These gifts always puff up, and make a man something in his own eyes, as the Corinthian knowledge did; and many a layman thinks himself fit to be a minister. Shepard’s parable, Part I, p. 181, 182.

63. Calvin, in his Institutes, B. 3, chapter 12, § 7, speaking of this Pharisee, observes that in his outward confession he acknowledges that the righteousness he has is the gift of God; but (he says) because he trusts that he is righteous, he goes away out of the presence of God unaccepted and odious.

64. Luther, as his words are cited by Rutherford in his Display of the spiritual Antichrist, p. 143, 144, says this: Such is the life of a Christian that he who has begun seems to himself to have nothing, but strives and presses forward so that he may take hold. That is why Paul says, “I do not consider myself yet to have taken hold of it.” For indeed nothing is more harmful to a believer than the presumption that he has already taken hold and has no further need of seeking. That is also why many fall back and pine away in spiritual complacency and slothfulness.
