So Bernard says, “To stand still in God’s way is to go back.” Therefore this remains for him who has begun to be a Christian: to think that he is not yet a Christian, but to seek to be a Christian, so that he may glory with Paul, “I am not, but I desire to be”: a Christian not yet finished, but only in his beginnings. Therefore he is not a Christian who is a Christian, that is, he who thinks himself a finished Christian and has no sense of how he falls short. We reach after heaven, but are not in heaven. Woe to him who is wholly renewed, that is, who thinks himself to be so. That man without doubt has never so much as begun to be renewed, nor did he ever taste what it is to be a Christian.

65. It is an observation of Mr. Jones, in his excellent treatise of the canon of the new Testament, that when the evangelist Mark, who was the companion of St. Peter and is supposed to have written his gospel under the direction of that apostle, mentions Peter’s repentance after denying his Master, he does not use such strong terms to set it out as the other evangelists. He only uses these words: “When he thought about it, he wept” (Mark 14:72); whereas the other evangelists say: “He went outside and wept bitterly” (Matt 26:75; Luke 22:62).

66. This Spirit always keeps a man poor and vile in his own eyes, and empty. … When a man has gained some knowledge and can talk about it fairly well, and has some tastes of the heavenly gift, some sweet inflowings of grace, his conscience is fairly well quieted. And if he has had some answer to his prayers, and has sweet affections, he grows full; and having ease of conscience, he casts off his sense of sin and his daily groaning under it. And so the spirit of prayer dies: he loses his esteem for God’s ordinances, does not feel such need of them, or gets no good, feels no life or power by them. … This is the woeful condition of some, and yet they do not know it. But now he who is filled with the Spirit, the Lord empties; and the more so the longer he lives. So though others think he does not need much grace, he counts himself the poorest. Shepard’s parable of ten virgins, Part II, p. 132. After all fillings, be always empty, hungry, feeling need, and praying for more. Ibid. p. 151. Truly, brethren, when I see the curse of God on many Christians who have now grown full of their talents, gifts, peace, comforts, abilities and duties, I stand adoring the riches of the Lord’s mercy to a little handful of poor believers, not only in making them empty, but in keeping them so all their days. Shepard’s sound believer, the late edition in Boston, p. 158, 159.

A Change of Nature

Part III · Sign VII

VII. Another thing in which gracious affections are distinguished from others is that they are attended with a change of nature.

All gracious affections arise from a spiritual understanding, in which the excellence and glory of divine things are shown to the soul, as was shown before. But all spiritual manifestations are transforming. They do not only alter the present exercise, sensation and frame of the soul; they have such power and efficacy that they alter the very nature of the soul. 2 Cor 3:18: “And we all, with unveiled faces, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.” Power like this is properly divine power, and belongs to the Spirit of the Lord alone. Other power may make a great alteration in men’s present frames and feelings, but only the power of a Creator can change the nature, or give a new nature. And no manifestations or illuminations will have this supernatural effect except those that are divine and supernatural. But all manifestations that are truly divine do have this effect. The soul is deeply affected by these manifestations, and so affected as to be transformed.

So it is with the affections the soul has in its conversion. The ways Scripture represents conversion strongly imply and signify a change of nature: being born again; becoming new creatures; rising from the dead; being renewed in the spirit of the mind; dying to sin, and living to righteousness; putting off the old man, and putting on the new man; being grafted into a new stock; having a divine seed implanted in the heart; being made partakers of the divine nature, and so on.

Therefore, if there is no great, remarkable and abiding change in persons who think they have experienced a work of conversion, all their imaginations and claims are vain, however they have been affected.67 Conversion (if we may give any credit to the Scripture) is a great and universal change of the man, turning him from sin to God. A man may be restrained from sin before he is converted. But when he is converted, he is not only restrained from sin; his very heart and nature are turned from it to holiness, so that from then on he becomes a holy person and an enemy to sin. Suppose, then, that after a person’s high affections at his supposed first conversion, it comes in a little while to this: there is no very perceptible or remarkable alteration in him as to the bad qualities and evil habits that were visible in him before. He is ordinarily under the sway of the same kind of dispositions he used to have, and the same things seem to belong to his character. He appears as selfish, as carnal, as dull and perverse, as unchristian and unsavory as ever. Then this is greater evidence against him than the brightest story of experiences that was ever told is for him. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, neither high profession nor low profession, neither a fair story nor a broken one, counts for anything, but a new creature.

If a very great alteration is visible in a person for a while, but it does not last, and afterward he returns, in a settled way, to be much as he used to be, it appears to be no change of nature. For nature is an abiding thing. A pig, which is of a filthy nature, may be washed, but its swinish nature remains. And a dove, which is of a clean nature, may be soiled, but its clean nature remains.68

Allowances must indeed be made for the natural temperament. Conversion does not entirely root out the natural temperament. The sins a man was most inclined to by his natural constitution before his conversion, he may still be most apt to fall into. But conversion will still make a great alteration even with respect to these sins. Though grace, while it is imperfect, does not root out an evil natural temperament, it has great power and efficacy to correct it. The change worked in conversion is a universal change. Grace changes a man with respect to whatever is sinful in him. The old man is put off and the new man put on. They are sanctified throughout, and the man becomes a new creature: old things have passed away, and all things have become new. All sin is mortified, sins of constitution as well as others. Suppose that before his conversion a man was especially inclined by his natural constitution to lewdness, or drunkenness, or malice. Converting grace will make a great alteration in him with respect to these evil dispositions. However much he may still be most in danger of these sins, they will no longer have dominion over him, nor will they properly be his character any more. Indeed, true repentance in some respects turns a man especially against his own iniquity: that in which he has been most guilty and has chiefly dishonored God. The man who forsakes other sins but spares his leading sin, the iniquity he is chiefly inclined to, is like Saul when he was sent against God’s enemies the Amalekites. He had a strict charge to spare none of them alive but to destroy them utterly, small and great. He utterly destroyed the common people, but spared the king, the chief of them all, alive.

Some foolishly make it an argument in favor of their manifestations and affections that, when these are gone, they are left wholly without any life or sense, or anything beyond what they had before. They think it shows that what they experienced was wholly of God and not of themselves, because (they say) when God has departed, all is gone; they can see and feel nothing, and are no better than they used to be.

It is very true that all grace and goodness in the hearts of the saints is entirely from God, and they depend on him for it universally and immediately. But these persons are still mistaken about the way in which God imparts himself and his Holy Spirit when he imparts saving grace to the soul. He gives his Spirit to be united to the faculties of the soul, and to dwell there in the manner of a principle of nature. So the soul, in being endowed with grace, is endowed with a new nature; and nature is an abiding thing. All the exercises of grace are entirely from Christ. But those exercises are not from Christ in the way that something alive moves and stirs something that is without life, which still remains without life. They are from him as having life imparted to the soul, so that through Christ’s power it has a vital nature inherent in itself. In the soul where Christ savingly is, there he lives. He does not only live outside it, so as to move it by force; he lives in it, so that it too is alive. Grace in the soul is as much from Christ as the light in a glass held out in the sunbeams is from the sun. But this pictures the way grace is imparted to the soul only in part. For the glass remains as it was; its nature is not changed at all, and it is as much without any light in its own nature as ever. But the soul of a saint receives light from the Sun of righteousness in such a way that its nature is changed, and it properly becomes a luminous thing. Not only does the sun shine in the saints; they also become little suns, partaking of the nature of the fountain of their light. In this respect the way they receive their light is like that of the lamps in the tabernacle rather than that of a reflecting glass. Though those lamps were lit by fire from heaven, they thereby became burning, shining things themselves. The saints do not only drink of the water of life that flows from the original fountain; this water becomes a fountain of water in them, springing up there and flowing out of them (John 4:14; and 7:38, 39). Grace is compared to a seed implanted, which is not only in the ground but has hold of it, has root there and grows there, and is an abiding principle of life and nature there.

As it is with the spiritual manifestations and affections given at first conversion, so it is with all illuminations and affections of that kind that persons have afterward: they are all transforming. There is a divine power and energy in them like that in the first manifestations. They still reach the bottom of the heart, and affect and alter the very nature of the soul, in proportion to the degree in which they are given. And by them a transformation of nature is continued and carried on to the end of life, until it is brought to perfection in glory. That is why Scripture represents the progress of the work of grace in the hearts of the saints as a continued conversion and renewal of nature. So the apostle exhorts those at Rome, loved by God and called to be saints, who had received God’s redeeming mercies, to be transformed by the renewing of their mind. Rom 12:1, 2: “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices … Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” Compare chapter 1:7. So too the apostle writes to the saints and faithful in Christ Jesus who were at Ephesus (Eph 1:1). These were people who were once dead in trespasses and sins, but had now been made alive, raised up, and seated together in the heavenly realms in Christ, created in Christ Jesus for good works. They were once far away but had now been brought near by the blood of Christ. They were no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built together into a dwelling place for God through the Spirit. Writing to these people, I say, the apostle tells them that he did not stop praying for them, that God would give them a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Christ, the eyes of their understanding being enlightened, so that they might know, or experience, the surpassing greatness of God’s power toward those who believe, in accordance with the working of his mighty power, which he exerted in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his own right hand in the heavenly realms (Eph 1:16 to the end). In this the apostle has in view the glorious power and work of God in converting and renewing the soul, as is very plain from what follows. So the apostle exhorts the same persons to put off the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts, and to be renewed in the spirit of their minds, and to put on the new man, which is created after God in righteousness and true holiness (Eph 4:22, 23, 24).

There is a sort of high affections that some have from time to time which leave them without any appearance at all of an abiding effect. They go off suddenly, so that from the very height of their emotion and seeming rapture they pass at once to being quite dead, empty of all sense and activity. Surely it is not usually so with high gracious affections.69 They leave a sweet savor and relish of divine things on the heart, and a stronger bent of soul toward God and holiness. So Moses’s face not only shone while he was on the mountain, conversing with God in an extraordinary way; it went on shining after he came down from the mountain. When men have been conversing with Christ in an extraordinary way, a perceptible effect of it remains on them. There is something remarkable in their disposition and frame; and if we take note of it and trace it to its cause, we will find it is because they have been with Jesus (Acts 4:13).

67. I would not judge of the whole soul’s coming to Christ so much by sudden pangs as by an inward bent. For the whole soul may be carried to Christ in affectionate expressions and actions; but without this bent, and change of affections, it is unsound. Shepard’s parable, Part I. P. 203.

68. It is with the soul as with water: all the cold may be gone, but the native principle of cold remains still. You may remove the burning of lusts, but not the blackness of nature. Where the power of sin lies, there may be a change of conscience from complacency to terror, a change of life from profaneness to outward respectability and the fashions of the world, to escape its pollutions, a change of lusts, indeed a quenching of them for a time; but the nature is never changed, in the best hypocrite that ever was. Shepard’s parable, Part I. P. 194.

69. Do you think the Holy Spirit comes on a man, as on Balaam, by an immediate acting, and then leaves him, and then he has nothing? Shepard’s Par. Part I. P. 126.

The Spirit of Jesus Christ

Part III · Sign VIII

VIII. Truly gracious affections differ from those that are false and delusive in that they tend to, and are attended with, the lamb-like, dove-like Spirit and disposition of Jesus Christ. In other words, they naturally beget and promote such a spirit of love, meekness, quietness, forgiveness and mercy as appeared in Christ.

The evidence for this in the Scripture is very abundant. If we judge the nature of Christianity and the proper spirit of the gospel by the word of God, this spirit is what may, above all others, be called the Christian spirit. It may be regarded as the true and distinguishing disposition of the hearts of Christians as Christians. When some of Christ’s disciples, through thoughtlessness and weakness, said something that did not agree with such a spirit, Christ told them that they did not know what kind of spirit they were of (Luke 9:55). This implies that the spirit I am speaking of is the proper spirit of his religion and kingdom. All who are truly godly and real disciples of Christ have this spirit in them. And not only that: they are of this spirit. It is the spirit by which they are so possessed and governed that it is their true and proper character. This is evident from what the wise man says in Prov 17:27 (plainly having in view such a spirit as this): “A man of understanding is of a calm spirit.” It is evident too from the particular description Christ gives in Matt 5 of the qualities and disposition of those who are truly blessed, who will obtain mercy, and who are God’s children and heirs: “Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth. … Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy. … Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God.” And that this spirit is the special character of the elect of God is clear from Colossians 3:12, 13: “Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves+ with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience. Bear with one another and forgive” one another. The apostle also speaks of that spirit and disposition which he presents as the most excellent and essential thing in Christianity, that without which none are true Christians, and without which the most glorious profession and gifts are nothing. He calls this spirit love, and he describes it like this (1 Cor 13:4, 5): “Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs.” And in Gal 5, where the same apostle sets out on purpose the distinguishing marks and fruits of true Christian grace, he dwells chiefly on the things that belong to such a disposition and spirit as I am speaking of, verses 22, 23: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, meekness, and self-control.” So does the apostle James in describing true grace, or “the wisdom from above.” He does it with the declared aim that others who are of a contrary spirit may not deceive themselves and lie against the truth by professing to be Christians when they are not, Jas 3:14–17: “But if you+ harbor bitter jealousy and strife in your+ hearts, do not boast in it or lie against the truth. Such wisdom does not come from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where jealousy and strife exist, there will be disorder and every evil practice. But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit.”

Everything that belongs to holiness of heart does indeed belong to the nature of true Christianity and the character of Christians. But a spirit of holiness, as it appears in some particular graces, may more especially be called the Christian spirit or disposition. There are some lovely qualities and virtues that agree more especially with the nature of the gospel order and the Christian profession. One reason is that there is a special agreement between them and those divine attributes which God has more remarkably shown and glorified in the work of redemption by Jesus Christ, the grand subject of the Christian revelation. There is also a special agreement between them and the virtues Jesus Christ so wonderfully exercised toward us in that work, and the blessed example he has set us in it. Another reason is that they agree especially with the particular drift and design of the work of redemption, and with the benefits we receive by it, and the relation it brings us into, to God and to one another. These virtues are such as humility, meekness, love, forgiveness and mercy. These things, therefore, belong especially to the character of Christians as such.

These things are spoken of as being especially the character of Jesus Christ himself, the great head of the Christian church. They are spoken of so in the prophecies of the Old Testament, as in the one cited in Matt 21:5: “Say to the Daughter of Zion, ‘See, your King comes to you, meek and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’ ” Christ himself speaks of them so in Matt 11:29: “Learn from Me; for I am meek and humble in heart.” The same appears from the name by which Christ is so often called in Scripture, namely THE LAMB. And as these things are especially the character of Christ, so they are also especially the character of Christians. Christians are Christlike. None deserve the name of Christians who are not so in their prevailing character. “The new man … is being renewed … in the image of its Creator” (Col 3:10). All true Christians, “beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image,” by his Spirit (2 Cor 3:18). The elect are all predestined “to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom 8:29). “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly man, so also must we bear the image of the heavenly man. … As was the earthly man, so also are those who are of the earth; and as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are of heaven” (1 Cor 15:47, 48, 49). Christ is full of grace, and Christians all “received of his fullness, and grace for grace.” That is, there is grace in Christians answering to grace in Christ, a correspondence like that between the wax and the seal: there is character for character. Such kinds of graces, such a spirit and disposition, the same things that belong to Christ’s character, belong to theirs. His image consists especially in that disposition in which Christ’s character especially consists. Christians who shine by reflecting the light of the Sun of righteousness shine with the same sort of brightness, the same mild, sweet and pleasant beams. These lamps of the spiritual temple, which are kindled by fire from heaven, burn with the same sort of flame. The branch is of the same nature as the stock and root, has the same sap, and bears the same sort of fruit. The members have the same kind of life as the head. It would be strange if Christians were not of the same disposition and spirit that Christ is of, when they are his flesh and his bone, indeed are “one with Him in spirit” (1 Cor 6:17), and live in such a way that it is not they who live, but Christ who lives in them. A Christian spirit is Christ’s mark, which he sets on the souls of his people: his seal in their foreheads, bearing his image and inscription. Christians are the followers of Christ, and they are so as they obey that call of Christ in Matt 11:28, 29: “Come to Me … learn from Me; for I am meek and humble in heart.” They follow him as the Lamb, Rev 14:4: “They follow the Lamb wherever He goes.” True Christians are, as it were, clothed with the meek, quiet and loving disposition of Christ; for all who are in Christ have put on Christ. And in this respect the church is clothed with the sun, not only by being clothed with his imputed righteousness, but also by being adorned with his graces (Rom 13:14). Christ the great Shepherd is himself a Lamb, and believers are also lambs; the whole flock are lambs. John 21:15: “Feed My lambs.” Luke 10:3: “I am sending you+ out like lambs among wolves.” The redemption of the church by Christ from the power of the devil was typified long ago by David’s delivering the lamb out of the mouth of the lion and the bear.

That such virtue as has been spoken of is the very nature of the Christian spirit, the spirit that works in Christ and in his members, and its distinguishing nature, is evident from this: the dove is the very symbol or emblem God chose to represent it. Those things are the fittest emblems of other things which best represent that which is most distinguishing in their nature. The Spirit that descended on Christ when he was anointed by the Father descended on him like a dove. The dove is a well-known emblem of meekness, harmlessness, peace and love. But the same Spirit that descended on the head of the church descends to the members. “God sent the Spirit of His Son into” their “hearts” (Gal 4:6). “And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ” (Rom 8:9). There is only one Spirit for the whole mystical body, head and members (1 Cor 6:17; Eph 4:4). Christ breathes his own Spirit on his disciples (John 20:22). As Christ was anointed with the Holy Spirit descending on him like a dove, so Christians also “have an anointing from the Holy One” (1 John 2:20, 27). And they are anointed with the same oil. It is the same “fine oil on the head” that runs down “to the skirts of his robes,” and on both it is a spirit of peace and love. Ps 133:1, 2: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony! It is like fine oil on the head, running down on the beard, running down Aaron’s beard to the skirts of his robes.” The oil on Aaron’s garments had the same sweet and inimitable fragrance as that on his head, the smell of the same sweet spices. Christian affections and Christian behavior are only the flowing out of the fragrance of Christ’s sweet ointments. Because the church has a dove-like temper and disposition, it is said of her that she has doves’ eyes. Song 1:15: “How beautiful you are, my darling! Oh, how very beautiful! Your eyes are like doves.” And 4:1: “How beautiful you are, my darling—how very beautiful! Your eyes are like doves behind your veil.” The same is said of Christ in 5:12: “His eyes are like doves.” And the church is often compared to a dove in Scripture. Song 2:14: “O my dove in the clefts of the rock …” 5:2: “Open to me, … my darling, my dove.” And 6:9: “My dove, my perfect one, is unique.” Ps 68:13: “You+ shall be like the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with shimmering gold.” And 74:19: “Do not deliver the soul of Your dove to beasts.” The dove that Noah sent out of the ark, which could find no rest for the sole of her foot until she returned, was a type of a true saint.

Meekness is so much the character of the saints that the meek and the godly are used as synonymous terms in Scripture. So in Ps 37:10, 11 the wicked and the meek are set in opposition to one another, as the wicked and the godly: “Yet a little while, and the wicked will be no more … But the meek will inherit the land.” So too Ps 147:6: “The Lord sustains the meek, but casts the wicked to the ground.”

It is doubtless very much on this account that Christ represents all his disciples, all the heirs of heaven, as little children. Matt 19:14: “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.” Matt 10:42: “And if anyone gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones because he is My disciple, truly I tell you+, he will never lose his reward.” Matt 18:6: “But if anyone causes one of these little ones … to stumble,” and so on. Verse 10: “See that you+ do not look down on any of these little ones.” Verse 14: “Your+ Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish.” John 13:33: “Little children, I am with you+ only a little while longer.” Little children are innocent and harmless. They do not do a great deal of mischief in the world; men need not be afraid of them; they are not a dangerous sort of persons. Their anger does not last long. They do not store up injuries in deep resentment, harboring deep and rooted malice. So Christians are children in malice (1 Cor 14:20). Little children are not cunning and deceitful, but plain and simple. They are not skilled in the arts of pretense and deceit, and are strangers to crafty disguises. They are yielding and pliable, not willful and obstinate. They do not trust their own understanding, but rely on the instructions of their parents and others of greater understanding. Here, then, is a fit and lively emblem of the followers of the Lamb. Being like little children in this way is not only highly commendable, something Christians approve of and aim at, and which some of extraordinary progress attain. It is their universal character, and absolutely necessary for entering the kingdom of heaven, unless Christ was mistaken. Matt 18:3: “Truly I tell you+, unless you+ are converted and become like little children, you+ will never enter the kingdom of heaven.” Mark 10:15: “Truly I tell you+, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.”

But here some may be ready to say: Is there no such thing as Christian fortitude and boldness for Christ, being good soldiers in the Christian warfare, and coming out boldly against the enemies of Christ and his people?

To this I answer that there doubtless is such a thing. The whole Christian life is compared to a warfare, and fitly so. And the most eminent Christians are the best soldiers, endowed with the greatest degrees of Christian fortitude. It is the duty of God’s people to be steadfast and vigorous in their opposition to the designs and ways of those who are trying to overthrow the kingdom of Christ and the cause of religion. But many persons seem to be quite mistaken about the nature of Christian fortitude. It is an exceedingly different thing from a brutal fierceness, or the boldness of beasts of prey. True Christian fortitude consists in strength of mind, through grace, exerted in two things. The first is ruling and suppressing the evil and unruly passions and affections of the mind. The second is steadfastly and freely exerting and following good affections and dispositions, without being hindered by sinful fear or the opposition of enemies. But the passions that are restrained and kept under in the exercise of this Christian strength and fortitude are the very passions that are vigorously and violently exerted in a false boldness for Christ. And the affections that are vigorously exerted in true fortitude are those Christian, holy affections that are directly contrary to them. Though Christian fortitude appears in withstanding and counteracting the enemies outside us, it appears much more in resisting and suppressing the enemies within us; for they are our worst and strongest enemies, and have the greatest advantage against us. The strength of the good soldier of Jesus Christ appears in nothing more than in steadfastly keeping the holy calm, meekness, sweetness and benevolence of his mind amid all the storms, injuries, strange behavior, and surprising acts and events of this evil and unreasonable world. The Scripture seems to suggest that true fortitude consists chiefly in this. Prov 16:32: “He who is slow to anger is better than a warrior, and he who controls his temper is greater than one who captures a city.”

The most direct and surest way in the world to judge rightly what a holy fortitude is, in fighting with God’s enemies, is to look to the captain of all God’s hosts, our great leader and example. We should see in what his fortitude and valor appeared in his chief conflict. That was the time of the greatest battle that ever was or ever will be fought with these enemies, when he fought with them all alone, and of the people there was no one with him. Then he exercised his fortitude in the highest degree he ever did, and won that glorious victory which will be celebrated in the praises and triumphs of all the hosts of heaven throughout all eternity. We should look, that is, to Jesus Christ at the time of his last sufferings, when his enemies on earth and in hell made their most violent attack on him, surrounding him on every side like tearing and roaring lions. Here, surely, we will see the fortitude of a holy warrior and champion in the cause of God in its highest perfection and greatest luster, an example fit for the soldiers who fight under this captain to follow. But how did he show his holy boldness and valor at that time? Not in the exercise of any fiery passions. Not in fierce and violent speeches, vehemently denouncing and crying out against the intolerable wickedness of his opponents, giving them what they deserved in plain terms. He showed it in not opening his mouth when he was afflicted and oppressed, in going like a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before its shearers is silent, not opening his mouth. He showed it in praying that the Father would forgive his cruel enemies, because they did not know what they were doing; in shedding not the blood of others, but his own, with all-conquering patience and love. Indeed, one of his disciples, who made an eager show of boldness for Christ and confidently declared that he would sooner die with Christ than deny him, began to lay about him with a sword. But Christ meekly rebukes him, and heals the wound he gives. And never were the patience, meekness, love and forgiveness of Christ so gloriously displayed as at that time. Never did he appear so much a Lamb, and never did he show so much of the dove-like Spirit, as at that time. If, then, we see any of Christ’s followers, in the midst of the most violent, unreasonable and wicked opposition from God’s enemies and his own, keeping under all this temptation the humility, quietness and gentleness of a lamb, and the harmlessness, love and sweetness of a dove, we may well judge that here is a good soldier of Jesus Christ.

When persons are fierce and violent, and exert their sharp and bitter passions, it shows weakness instead of strength and fortitude. 1 Cor 3, at the beginning: “Brothers, I could not address you+ as spiritual, but as carnal—as infants in Christ. … For you+ are still carnal. For since there is jealousy and dissension among you+, are you+ not carnal? Are you+ not walking in the way of man?”

There is a pretended boldness for Christ that arises from no better principle than pride. A man may be eager to expose himself to the dislike of the world, and even to provoke their displeasure, out of pride. For it is the nature of spiritual pride to make men seek distinction and singularity, and so often to set themselves at war with those they call carnal, so that they may be more highly exalted among their own party. True boldness for Christ is universal: it overcomes all, and carries men above the displeasure of friends and foes alike, so that they will forsake all rather than Christ, and will rather offend all parties and be thought little of by all than offend Christ. And the duty that tests whether a man is willing to be despised by those of his own party, and thought the least worthy of their regard, is a much more proper test of his boldness for Christ than his being eager to expose himself to the reproach of opponents. The apostle did not seek glory from heathens and Jews only, nor from Christians either, as he declares in 1 Thess 2:6.70 He is bold for Christ who has Christian fortitude enough to confess his fault openly, when he has committed one that requires it, and as it were to come down on his knees before his opponents. Things like these are far greater evidence of holy boldness than resolutely and fiercely confronting opponents.

As some are much mistaken about the nature of true boldness for Christ, so they are about Christian zeal. It is indeed a flame, but a sweet one; or rather, it is the heat and fervor of a sweet flame. For the flame of which it is the heat is no other than that of divine love, or Christian love, the sweetest and most benevolent thing that is or can be in the heart of man or angel. Zeal is the fervor of this flame as it goes out ardently and vigorously toward the good that is its object, in desiring it and pursuing it; and so, as a consequence, in opposing the evil that is contrary to it and hinders it. There is indeed opposition, and vigorous opposition, that is a part of it, or rather goes along with it. But it is against things, not persons. Bitterness against the persons of men is no part of it, but is very contrary to it. So much is this so that the warmer true zeal is, and the higher it is raised, the further persons are from such bitterness, and the fuller of love, both to the evil and to the good. This appears from what has just been observed: in its very nature and essence it is nothing other than the fervor of a spirit of Christian love. And as for the opposition to things that there is in it, it is first and chiefly against the evil things in the person himself who has this zeal, against the enemies of God and holiness that are in his own heart (since these are most in his view, and what he has most to do with), and only secondarily against the sins of others. Therefore there is nothing in a true Christian zeal that is contrary to that spirit of meekness, gentleness and love, the spirit of a little child, a lamb and a dove, that has been spoken of. It entirely agrees with it, and tends to promote it.

But to say something in particular about this Christian spirit I have been speaking of, as it is exercised in these three things, forgiveness, love and mercy, I would observe that the Scripture is very clear and explicit about the absolute necessity of each of these, as belonging to the temper and character of every Christian.

It is so with a forgiving spirit, a disposition to overlook and forgive injuries. Christ gives it to us as both a negative and a positive evidence. He teaches us explicitly that if we are of such a spirit, it is a sign that we ourselves are in a state of forgiveness and favor; and that if we are not of such a spirit, we are not forgiven by God. And he seems to take special care that we should take good notice of it and always keep it in mind. Matt 6:12, 14, 15: “And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. … For if you+ forgive men their trespasses, your+ heavenly Father will also forgive you+. But if you+ do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your+ Father forgive yours+.” Christ says the same again at another time (Mark 11:25, 26). And again in Matthew 18:22 to the end, in the parable of the servant who owed his lord ten thousand talents, who would not forgive his fellow servant a hundred denarii, and was therefore handed over to the torturers. In the application of the parable Christ says in verse 35: “That is how My heavenly Father will treat each of you+ unless you+ forgive your+ brother from your+ heart.”

And the Scripture is very plain and abundant that all true saints are of a loving, benevolent and beneficent disposition. The apostle tells us that without it, though we “speak in the tongues of men and of angels,” we are “only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal”; and though we “have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge,” yet without this spirit we are “nothing.” And there is no other virtue or disposition of the mind that is so often and so explicitly insisted on in the marks laid down in the New Testament for knowing true Christians. It is often given as a sign that is especially distinguishing, by which all may know Christ’s disciples, and by which they may know themselves; and it is often laid down as both a negative and a positive evidence. Christ calls the law of love, above all others, his commandment. John 13:34: “A new commandment I give you+: Love one another. As I have loved you+, so you+ also must love one another.” And 15:12: “This is My commandment, that you+ love one another as I have loved you+.” And verse 17: “This is My command to you+: Love one another.” And he says in 13:35: “By this everyone will know that you+ are My disciples, if you+ love one another.” And in 14:21 (still with special reference to this which he calls his commandment): “Whoever has My commandments and keeps them is the one who loves Me.” The beloved disciple, who had so much of this sweet temper himself, dwells on it at length in his epistles. None of the apostles does so much as he does in laying down explicit signs of grace by which those who profess religion may test themselves. And in his signs he insists on scarcely anything else but a spirit of Christian love and a practice that agrees with it. 1 John 2:9, 10: “If anyone claims to be in the light but hates his brother, he is still in the darkness. Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no cause of stumbling in him.” 3:14: “We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love our brothers. The one who does not love remains in death.” Verses 18, 19: “Little children, let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth. And by this we will know that we belong to the truth, and will assure our hearts in His presence.” Verses 23, 24: “This is His commandment: … that we should love one another. … Whoever keeps His commandments remains in God, and God in him. And by this we know that He remains in us: by the Spirit He has given us.” 4:7, 8: “Beloved, let us love one another, because love comes from God. Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.” Verses 12, 13: “No one has ever seen God; but if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us. By this we know that we remain in Him, and He in us: He has given us of His Spirit.” Verse 16: “God is love; whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him.” Verse 20: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ but hates his brother, he is a liar. For anyone who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen.”

And the Scripture is as plain as it is possible for it to be that none are true saints but those whose true character it is to be of a disposition to pity and relieve their fellow creatures who are poor, needy and afflicted. Ps 37:21: “The righteous are gracious and giving.” Verse 26: “They are ever generous and quick to lend.” Ps 112:5: “It is well with the man who is generous and lends freely.” Verse 9: “He has scattered abroad his gifts to the poor.” Prov 14:31: “Whoever honors Him is kind to the needy.” Prov 21:26: “The righteous give without restraint.” Jer 22:16: “He took up the cause of the poor and needy, and so it went well with him. Is this not what it means to know Me?” declares the Lord. Jas 1:27: “Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress,” and so on. Hos 6:6: “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.” Matt 5:7: “Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy.” 2 Cor 8:8: “I am not making a demand, but I am testing the sincerity of your+ love in comparison to the earnestness of others.” Jas 2:13, 14, 15, 16: “For judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. … What good is it, my brothers, if someone claims to have faith, but has no deeds? Can such faith save him? Suppose a brother or sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you+ tells him, ‘Go in peace; stay warm and well fed,’ but does not provide for his physical needs, what good is that?” 1 John 3:17: “If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him?” In the description he gives us of the day of judgment in Matt 25 (the most detailed we have in the whole Bible), Christ represents that judgment will be passed on that day according to whether men have been found to be of a merciful spirit and practice or not. Christ’s design in giving such a description of the proceedings of that day is plainly to impress on all his followers the conviction that unless this was their spirit and practice, there was no hope of their being accepted and acknowledged by him on that day. This, therefore, is a conviction we ought to be possessed with. We find in Scripture that a righteous man and a merciful man are synonymous expressions. Isa 57:1: “The righteous perish, and no one takes it to heart; merciful men are swept away, while no one considers that the righteous are taken away from the presence of evil.”

So we see how full, clear and abundant the evidence from Scripture is that those who are truly gracious are under the government of that lamb-like, dove-like Spirit of Jesus Christ, and that this is essentially and eminently the nature of the saving grace of the gospel, and the proper spirit of true Christianity. We may therefore determine without doubt that all truly Christian affections are attended with such a spirit, and that this is the natural tendency of the fear and hope, the sorrow and joy, the confidence and zeal of true Christians.

Let no one take me to mean that true Christians have no remains of a contrary spirit, and can never in any instance be guilty of behavior that does not agree with such a spirit. But this I affirm, and will affirm until I deny the Bible to be worth anything: that everything in Christians that belongs to true Christianity has this tendency and works this way. And there is no true Christian on earth who is not so under the prevailing power of such a spirit that he is properly named from it, and it is truly and justly his character. Therefore ministers and others have no warrant from Christ to encourage persons whose character and behavior are contrary to it to think they are converted because they tell a fair story of illuminations and manifestations. In doing so they would set up their own wisdom against Christ’s, and judge without, and against, the rule by which Christ has declared that all men should know his disciples. Some persons place religion so much in certain passing illuminations and impressions (especially if they come in a particular method and order), and so little in the spirit and temper persons are of, that they greatly deform religion, and form notions of Christianity quite different from what it is as portrayed in the Scriptures. The Scripture knows of no true Christians who are of a sordid, selfish, cross and contentious spirit. Nothing more absurd can be invented than a morose, hard, close-fisted, haughty, spiteful true Christian. We must learn the way of bringing men to rules, and not of bringing rules to men and so straining and stretching the rules of God’s word to take in ourselves and some of our neighbors, until we make them of no effect at all.

It is true that allowances must be made for men’s natural temperament with regard to these things, as with others. But not such allowances as to allow that men who were once wolves and serpents are now converted, without any remarkable change in the spirit of their mind. The change made by true conversion is usually most remarkable and perceptible with respect to the wickedness the person was most notoriously guilty of before. Grace has as great a tendency to restrain and mortify the sins that are contrary to the spirit that has been spoken of as it has to mortify drunkenness or lewdness. Indeed, the Scripture represents the change worked by gospel grace as appearing especially in an alteration of the first sort. Isa 11:6–9: “The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the goat; the calf and young lion and fatling will be together, and a little child will lead them. The cow will graze with the bear, their young will lie down together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox. The infant will play by the cobra’s den, and the toddler will reach into the viper’s nest. They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the Lord as the sea is full of water.” And Isa 65:25 is to the same purpose. Accordingly we find that in the early times of the Christian church converts were remarkably changed in this respect. Titus 3:3 and following: “For at one time we too were foolish, disobedient, misled, and enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures—living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another. But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared, He saved us … through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.” And Col 3:7, 8: “When you+ lived among them, you+ also used to walk in these ways. But now you+ also put aside all such things as these: anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language from your+ lips.”

70. Mr. Shepard, speaking of hypocrites who seek applause, says: “This is why men forsake their friends, and trample underfoot the scorn of the world: they have credit elsewhere. To keep their place in the love of godly men, they will suffer much.” Parable of the ten virgins, Part I. P. 180.

Tenderness of Spirit

Part III · Sign IX

IX. Gracious affections soften the heart, and are attended and followed with a Christian tenderness of spirit.

False affections, however much persons may seem to be melted by them while they are new, still tend in the end to harden the heart. A disposition to some kinds of passions may be established, such as those that imply self-seeking, self-exaltation and opposition to others. But false affections, with the delusion that attends them, finally tend to dull the mind and shut it against those affections in which tenderness of heart consists. And their effect at last is this: in the settled frame of their minds, persons become less affected by their present and past sins and less conscientious about future sins. They are less moved by the warnings and cautions of God’s word, or by God’s chastisements in his providence. They are more careless of the frame of their hearts, and of the manner and tendency of their behavior. They are less quick-sighted to discern what is sinful, and less afraid of the appearance of evil, than they were while they were under awakenings by the law and fears of hell. Now that they have had such and such impressions and affections, they have a high opinion of themselves and regard their state as safe. So they can be much more at ease than before in living in the neglect of duties that are troublesome and inconvenient. They are much slower and more partial in obeying difficult commands. They are nowhere near so alarmed at the sight of their own defects and transgressions. They are emboldened to indulge themselves more with respect to the labor, the painstaking care and the exactness of their walk. They yield more easily to temptations and to the urgings of their lusts. And they take far less care of their behavior when they come into the holy presence of God, in the time of public or private worship. Formerly, perhaps, under the convictions of the law, they took great pains in religion and denied themselves in many things. But now that they think themselves out of danger of hell, they largely put off the burden of the cross, spare themselves the trouble of difficult duties, and allow themselves more of the comfort of enjoying their ease and their lusts.

Persons like these, instead of embracing Christ as their Savior from sin, trust in him as the Savior of their sins. Instead of fleeing to him as their refuge from their spiritual enemies, they make use of him as the defense of their spiritual enemies from God, and to strengthen them against him. They make Christ the minister of sin, the great officer and deputy of the devil, to strengthen his cause and make him, above all things in the world, strong against JEHOVAH. So they may sin against him with good courage and without any fear, being effectually secured against the restraints of his most solemn warnings and most fearful threatenings. They trust in Christ to preserve to them the quiet enjoyment of their sins, and to be their shield to defend them from God’s displeasure. Meanwhile they come close to him, even to his bosom, the place of his children, to fight against him with their deadly weapons hidden under their robes.71 Yet some of these, at the same time, make a great profession of love to God and assurance of his favor, and of great joy in tasting the sweetness of his love.

It was in this way that those trusted in Christ whom the apostle Jude speaks of, who crept in among the saints unnoticed, but were really ungodly men, turning the grace of God into a license for immorality (Jude 4). These are the ones who trust in their being righteous, and because God has promised that the righteous will surely live, that is, will certainly be saved, they are emboldened to commit iniquity. God threatens them in Ezekiel 33:13: “If I tell the righteous man that he will surely live, but he then trusts in his righteousness and commits iniquity, then none of his righteous works will be remembered; he will die because of the iniquity he has committed.”

Gracious affections have a quite contrary tendency: they turn a heart of stone more and more into a heart of flesh. A holy love and hope are principles far more efficacious on the heart than a slavish fear of hell, to make it tender, to fill it with a dread of sin, or of whatever might displease and offend God, and to engage it to watchfulness, care and strictness. Gracious affections, as was observed before, flow out of a contrite heart, or (as the word means) a bruised heart, bruised and broken with godly sorrow. This makes the heart tender, as bruised flesh is tender and easily hurt. Godly sorrow has much greater influence to make the heart tender than mere sorrow under the law from selfish principles.

The tenderness of the heart of a true Christian is beautifully pictured by our Savior when he compares such a person to a little child. The flesh of a little child is very tender, and so is the heart of one who is newborn. This is represented in what we are told of Naaman’s cure from his leprosy by washing in the Jordan at the prophet’s direction, which was undoubtedly a type of the renewing of the soul by the washing of regeneration. We are told in 2 Kgs 5:14 that he “went down and dipped himself in the Jordan seven times, according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored and became like that of a little child.” Not only is the flesh of a little child tender, but his mind is tender. A little child’s heart is easily moved, worked on and bowed; so is a Christian’s in spiritual things. A little child is quick to be moved by sympathy, to weep with those who weep, and can hardly bear to see others in distress; so it is with a Christian (John 11:35; Rom 12:15; 1 Cor 12:26). A little child is easily won by kindness; so is a Christian. A little child is easily moved to grief by earthly evils; his heart melts and he begins to weep. So tender is the heart of a Christian with regard to the evil of sin. A little child is easily frightened at the appearance of outward evils, or of anything that threatens to hurt it; so a Christian is quick to be alarmed at the appearance of moral evil, and of anything that threatens to hurt the soul. A little child, when it meets enemies or fierce beasts, is not inclined to trust its own strength, but flees to its parents for refuge; so a saint is not self-confident in engaging spiritual enemies, but flees to Christ. A little child is apt to suspect evil in places of danger: afraid in the dark, afraid when left alone or far from home. So a saint is apt to feel his spiritual dangers deeply, to be wary of himself, full of fear when he cannot see his way plain before him, afraid to be left alone and to be at a distance from God. Prov 28:14: “Blessed is the man who always fears, but he who hardens his heart falls into trouble.” A little child is apt to be afraid of those over him, to dread their anger, and to tremble at their frowns and threats; so is a true saint with respect to God. Ps 119:120: “My flesh trembles in awe of You; I stand in fear of Your judgments.” Isa 66:2: “This is the one I will esteem: he who is humble … who trembles at My word.” Verse 5: “You+ who tremble at His word, hear the word of the Lord.” Ezra 9:4: “Then everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel gathered around me.” 10:3: “According to the counsel of my lord and of those who tremble at the command of our God.” A little child approaches those over him with awe; so the saints approach God with holy awe and reverence. Job 13:11: “Would His majesty not terrify you+? Would the dread of Him not fall upon you+?” Holy fear is so much the nature of true godliness that Scripture calls it by no name more often than the fear of God.

So gracious affections do not tend to make men bold, forward, noisy and boisterous, but rather to make them speak with trembling (Hos 13:1: “When Ephraim spoke with trembling, he was exalted in Israel. But he incurred guilt through Baal, and he died”), and to clothe them with a kind of holy fear in all their behavior toward God and man, in keeping with Psalm 2:11; 1 Pet 3:15; 2 Cor 7:15; Eph 6:5; 1 Pet 3:2; Rom 11:20.

But here some may object and say: Is there no such thing as a holy boldness in prayer and the duties of divine worship? I answer that there is doubtless such a thing, and it is chiefly to be found in eminent saints, persons of great degrees of faith and love. But this holy boldness is not in the least opposed to reverence, though it is opposed to disunion and servility. It abolishes or lessens the disposition that arises from moral distance or alienation, and also from distance of relation, such as that of a slave. But it does not at all lessen the disposition that befits our natural distance, by which we are infinitely inferior. No boldness in poor sinful worms of the dust who have a right view of God and of themselves will prompt them to approach God with less fear and reverence than the spotless and glorious angels in heaven, who cover their faces before his throne (Isa 6, at the beginning). Rebekah (who in her marriage with Isaac was, in almost all its circumstances, plainly a great type of the church, the bride of Christ), when she meets Isaac, gets down from her camel, takes a veil and covers herself. And this though she was brought to him as his bride, to be with him in the nearest relation and most intimate union in which human beings are ever united to one another.72 Elijah, that great prophet who had so much holy familiarity with God, at a time of special nearness to God, even when he conversed with him on the mountain, wrapped his face in his cloak. This was not because he was terrified with any slavish fear by the terrible wind and earthquake and fire. It was after these were all over, and God spoke to him as a friend in a still, small voice. 1 Kgs 19:12, 13: “And after the fire came a still, small voice. When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak.” And Moses, with whom God spoke face to face as a man speaks with his friend, and who was distinguished from all the prophets by the familiarity with God he was admitted to, did the same. At the time when he was brought nearest of all, when God showed him his glory on that same mountain where he afterward spoke to Elijah, Moses hurried to bow his head toward the earth, and worshiped (Exod 34:8). In some persons there is a most unfitting and intolerable boldness in their addresses to the great JEHOVAH, a show of holy boldness and a display of eminent nearness and familiarity. The very thought of it would make them shrink into nothing with horror and shame if they saw the distance there is between God and them. They are like the Pharisee, who boldly came up near, confident of his own eminence in holiness. If they saw their vileness, they would instead be more like the tax collector, who stood at a distance, and did not dare even to lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, God, have mercy on me, a sinner. It befits sinful creatures such as we are to approach a holy God (with faith, indeed, and without terror, yet) with contrition, and penitent shame and confusion of face. It is foretold that this would be the disposition of the church in the time of her highest privileges on earth, in her latter day of glory, when God would remarkably comfort her by revealing his covenant mercy to her. Ezek 16:60 to the end: “I will establish an everlasting covenant with you. Then you will remember your ways and be ashamed. … So I will establish My covenant with you, and you will know that I am the Lord, so that when I am pacified toward you for all you have done, you will remember and be ashamed and never again open your mouth because of your disgrace, declares the Lord God.” The woman we read of in the seventh chapter of Luke was an eminent saint, and by Christ’s own testimony (verse 47) she had much of that true love which casts out fear. She approached Christ in a lovely and acceptable way when she came with that humble modesty, reverence and shame, when she stood at his feet weeping behind him, as one not fit to appear before his face, and washed his feet with her tears.

One reason why gracious affections are attended with this tenderness of spirit that has been spoken of is that true grace tends to promote convictions of conscience. Persons usually have convictions of conscience before they have any grace. And if afterward they are truly converted, and have true repentance, and joy and peace in believing, this tends to put an end to terrors, but has no tendency to put an end to convictions of sin; rather it tends to increase them. It does not dull a man’s conscience; it makes it more sensitive. It makes it discern more easily and thoroughly the sinfulness of what is sinful, receive a greater conviction of the heinous and dreadful nature of sin, and be capable of a quicker and deeper sense of it. It makes him more convicted of his own sinfulness and the wickedness of his heart, and so it tends to make him more wary of his heart. Grace tends to give the soul a further and better conviction of the same things about sin that it was convicted of under a work of the law by the Spirit of God: namely, its great contrariety to the will, the law and the honor of God, the greatness of God’s hatred of it and displeasure against it, and the dreadful punishment it exposes to and deserves. And not only that: it convicts the soul of something further about sin that it saw nothing of while it was only under the law’s convictions, and that is the infinitely hateful nature of sin, and its dreadfulness on that account. And this makes the heart tender with respect to sin, like David’s heart, which struck him when he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe. The heart of a true penitent is like a burnt child that dreads the fire. On the contrary, the one who has had a counterfeit repentance and false comforts and joys is like iron that has been suddenly heated and quenched: it becomes much harder than before. A false conversion puts an end to convictions of conscience, and so either takes away or greatly diminishes the conscientiousness that was shown under a work of the law.

All gracious affections tend to promote this Christian tenderness of heart that has been spoken of: not only a godly sorrow, but also a gracious joy. Ps 2:11: “Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling.” So also does a gracious hope. Ps 33:18: “Surely the eyes of the Lord are on those who fear Him, on those whose hope is in His loving devotion.” And Ps 147:11: “The Lord is pleased with those who fear Him, who hope in His loving devotion.” Indeed, the most confident and assured hope that is truly gracious has this tendency. The higher a holy hope is raised, the more there is of this Christian tenderness. The banishing of a slavish fear by a holy assurance is attended with a proportionate increase of a reverential fear. The lessening of the fear of the fruits of God’s displeasure in future punishment is attended with a proportionate increase of the fear of his displeasure itself; the lessening of the fear of hell, with an increase of the fear of sin. The vanishing of doubts about the person’s state is attended with a proportionate increase of wariness of his heart, a distrust of its strength, wisdom, stability, faithfulness and so on. The less apt he is to be afraid of natural evil, having “his heart … steadfast, trusting in the Lord,” and so not fearing “bad news,” the more apt he is to be alarmed at the appearance of moral evil, the evil of sin. As he has more holy boldness, so he has less self-confidence and less of a forward, presuming boldness, and more modesty. As he is surer than others of deliverance from hell, so he has more of a sense that he deserves it. He is less apt than others to be shaken in faith, but more apt than others to be moved by solemn warnings, by God’s frowns, and by the calamities of others. He has the firmest comfort, but the softest heart; he is richer than others, but poorest of all in spirit; the tallest and strongest saint, but the least and tenderest child among them.

71. These are hypocrites who believe, but fail in regard to the use of the gospel and of the Lord Jesus. And we read of these in Jude 3, namely, of some men who turned grace into licentiousness. For in this the exceeding evil of a man’s heart appears: that not only the law, but also the glorious gospel of the Lord Jesus, works in him all kinds of unrighteousness. And it is all too common for men at the first work of conversion to cry, oh, for grace and Christ, and afterward to grow licentious, to live and lie in the breaking of the law, and to take their warrant for their course from the gospel. Shepard’s parable Part. I. P. 126. Again, p. 232, Mr. Shepard speaks of such hypocrites as those who are like strange eggs put into the same nest where honest men have lived, and so have been hatched there. While they are young they keep to their nest, and live by crying and opening their mouths wide after the Lord and the food of his word. But when their wings are grown, and they have gained some affections, some knowledge, some hope of mercy, they are hardened by these to fly from God. And he adds: Can that man be good whom God’s grace makes worse? Again, Part II. P. 167: When men flee to Christ in times of peace so that they may keep their sins with greater peace of conscience, so that sin makes them flee to Christ as well as misery, not that they may destroy and abolish sin, but that they may be kept in their sins with peace, then men may be said to lay hold of Christ only by a seeming faith.—Many a heart secretly says this: If I can have my sin, and peace, and a quiet conscience for the present, and God merciful to pardon it afterward. That is why he relies (as he says) only on the mercy of God in Christ. And now this hardens and blinds him, and makes him complacent, and his faith is sermon-proof: nothing stirs him.—And if it were not for their faith they would despair, but this keeps them up. And now they think that if they have any trouble of mind, it is the devil troubling them. And so they make Christ and faith protectors of sin, not purifiers from sin, which is most dreadful: turning grace into licentiousness, as they did with sacrifice. So these would sin under the shadow of Christ, because the shadow is good and sweet, Mich. 3. 11. They had subtle, sly ends in good duties, for a man’s sin may lie there; “yet they lean upon the Lord.”—When the money changers came into the temple: you are making it a den of robbers. Robbers, when they are hunted, flee to their den or cave, and there they are safe against all searchers and hue and cry. So it is here. But Christ whipped them out. So when men are pursued with the cries and fears of conscience, away to Christ they go, as to their den: not as saints, to pray and mourn out the life of their sin there, but to preserve their sin. This is vile. Will the Lord receive such?

72. Dr. Ames, in his cases of conscience, book III. Chap. Iv., speaks of a holy modesty in the worship of God as one sign of true humility.

Symmetry and Proportion

Part III · Sign X

X. Another thing in which truly gracious and holy affections differ from false ones is beautiful symmetry and proportion.

Not that the symmetry of the virtues and gracious affections of the saints is perfect in this life. It is often defective in many things: through the imperfection of grace, for lack of proper instruction, through errors in judgment, or some particular defect of natural temperament, or defects in upbringing, and many other disadvantages that might be mentioned. But there is in no way that monstrous disproportion in the gracious affections and the various parts of true religion in the saints which is very commonly to be seen in the false religion and counterfeit graces of hypocrites.

In the truly holy affections of the saints is found that proportion which is the natural consequence of the universality of their sanctification. They have the whole image of Christ on them. They have “taken off the old man” and “have put on the new man,” entire in all his parts and members. “God was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Him”: there is every grace in him. He is “full of grace and truth,” and those who are Christ’s “received of his fullness, and grace for grace” (John 1:14, 16). That is, every grace that is in Christ is in them: “grace for grace,” that is, grace answering to grace. There is no grace in Christ without its image in believers to answer it. The image is a true image, and there is something of the same beautiful proportion in the image as in the original: there is feature for feature and member for member. There is symmetry and beauty in God’s workmanship. The natural body that God has made consists of many members, and all are in beautiful proportion. So it is in the new man, which consists of various graces and affections. The body of one who was born a perfect child may fall short of exact proportion through illness, and through the weakness and wounds of some of its members. Yet the disproportion is in no way like that of those who are born deformed.

It is with hypocrites as it was with Ephraim long ago, at a time when God greatly complains of their hypocrisy: “Ephraim is an unturned cake” (Hos 7), half baked and half raw. There is commonly no uniformity at all in their affections.

In many of them there is a great partiality with regard to the various kinds of religious affections: great affections in some things, and no proportion at all in others. A holy hope and a holy fear go together in the saints, as has been observed from Ps 33:18 and 147:11. But in some of these persons there is the most confident hope, while they are empty of reverence, self-suspicion and caution, and have to a great degree cast off fear. In the saints, joy and holy fear go together, however great the joy may be, as it was with the disciples on that joyful morning of Christ’s resurrection. Matt 28:8: “So they hurried away from the tomb in fear and great joy.”73 But many of these rejoice without trembling: their joy is of a sort that is truly opposed to godly fear.

But in particular, one great difference between saints and hypocrites is this: the joy and comfort of the former is attended with godly sorrow and mourning for sin. They have sorrow not only to prepare them for their first comfort, but also after they are comforted and their joy is established. So it is foretold of the church of God that they would mourn and loathe themselves for their sins after they had returned from the captivity and were settled in the land of Canaan, the land of rest, the land that flows with milk and honey. Ezek 20:42, 43: “Then you+ will know that I am the Lord, when I bring you+ into the land of Israel, the land that I swore to give your+ fathers. There you+ will remember your+ ways and all the deeds with which you+ have defiled yourselves+, and you+ will loathe yourselves+ for all the evils you+ have done.” So also in Ezekiel 16:61, 62, 63. A true saint is like a little child in this respect. He never had any godly sorrow before he was born again, but since then he often has it in exercise. So a little child, before it is born, while it remains in darkness, never cries; but as soon as it sees the light it begins to cry, and from then on it is often crying. Christ has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows, so that we are freed from the sorrow of punishment, and may now sweetly feed on the comforts Christ has purchased for us. Yet that does not prevent our feeding on these comforts from being attended with the sorrow of repentance. So in the past the children of Israel were commanded always to eat the Passover lamb with bitter herbs.74 True saints are spoken of in Scripture not only as those who have mourned for sin, but as those who do mourn, whose way it still is to mourn. Matt 5:4: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.”

In hypocrites there is often not only an essential deficiency in the various kinds of religious affections, but also a strange partiality and disproportion in the same affections with regard to different objects.

So, as to the affection of love, some make high claims and a great show of love to God and Christ, and perhaps have been greatly affected by what they have heard or thought about them. But they do not have a spirit of love and benevolence toward men. They are inclined to contention, envy, revenge and evil-speaking. Perhaps they will let an old grudge against a neighbor rest in their hearts for seven years on end, if not twice seven years, living in real ill will and bitterness of spirit toward him. And perhaps in their dealings with their neighbors they are not very strict and conscientious in keeping the rule of doing to others as they would have others do to them. 1 John 4:20: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ but hates his brother, he is a liar. For anyone who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen.” And on the other hand, there are others who appear to have a great deal of benevolence toward men, and are very good-natured and generous in their way, but have no love to God.

And as to love to men, some have overflowing affections toward some people, but their love is far from being of so extensive and universal a nature as a truly Christian love is. They are full of tender affection toward some, and full of bitterness toward others. They are bound to their own party, to those who approve of them, love them and admire them, but are fierce against those who oppose and dislike them. Matt 5:45, 46: “that you+ may be sons of your+ Father in heaven. He causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good. … If you+ love those who love you+, what reward will you+ get? Do not even tax collectors do the same?” Some show great affection to their neighbors, and claim to be delighted beyond words with the company of the children of God away from home, and at the same time are disagreeable and churlish toward their wives and other close relatives at home, and very negligent of the duties of those relations. And then there is the great love to sinners and opposers of religion, and the great concern for their souls, that appears in some, even to extreme distress and agony. It singles out one particular person from among a multitude as its object, while there is at the same time no general compassion for sinners who are in equally miserable circumstances, or none but what is monstrously out of proportion. This seems not to be of the nature of a gracious affection. Not that I suppose it at all strange that pity for the perishing souls of sinners should rise to a degree of agony, if other things answer to it; or that a truly gracious compassion for souls should be exercised much more toward some persons than toward others who are equally miserable, especially on some particular occasions. Many things may happen at such a time to fix the mind and affect the heart with respect to a particular person. And no doubt some saints have been in great distress for the souls of particular persons, so as to be, as it were, in labor for them. But suppose persons appear at particular times in racking agonies for the soul of some single person, far beyond what has usually been heard or read of in eminent saints, and yet appear to have a spirit of meek and fervent love, charity and compassion toward mankind in general in a far less degree than those saints had. Such agonies, I say, are greatly to be suspected, for reasons already given: namely, that the Spirit of God usually gives graces and gracious affections in a beautiful symmetry and proportion.

And as there is a monstrous disproportion in the love of some in its exercises toward different persons, so there is in their seeming exercises of love toward the same persons. Some men show a love to others as to their outward man: they are generous with their worldly goods and often give to the poor, but have no love for or concern for the souls of men. Others claim a great love for men’s souls, but are not compassionate and charitable toward their bodies. Making a great show of love, pity and distress for souls costs them nothing; but to show mercy to men’s bodies they must part with money out of their pockets. But a true Christian love to our brothers extends to both their souls and their bodies. In this it is like the love and compassion of Jesus Christ. He showed mercy to men’s souls by laboring for them in preaching the gospel to them, and showed mercy to their bodies by going about doing good, healing every kind of sickness and disease among the people. We have a remarkable instance in Mark 6:34 and following of Christ having compassion on both men’s souls and their bodies at once, and showing compassion by feeding both: “When Jesus stepped ashore and saw a large crowd, He had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And He began to teach them many things.” Here was his compassion for their souls. And in what follows we have an account of his compassion for their bodies, because they had been a long while with nothing to eat: he fed five thousand of them with five loaves and two fish. And if the compassion of professing Christians toward others does not work in the same ways, it is a sign that it is no true Christian compassion.

Furthermore, it is a sign that affections are not of the right sort if persons seem to be much affected by the bad qualities of their fellow Christians, such as the coldness and lifelessness of other saints, but are not affected in any proportion by their own defects and corruptions. A true Christian may be affected by the coldness and lack of savor in other saints, and may mourn much over it. But at the same time he is not so apt to be affected by the badness of anybody’s heart as by that of his own. This is most in his view; this he is quickest to discern; this he sees most of the weight of, and is most ready to cry out against. And it takes a lesser degree of virtue to bring a man to pity himself and be concerned at his own calamities than to be rightly affected by the calamities of others. And if men have not attained the lesser, we may determine that they never attained the greater.

And here, by the way, I would observe that it may be laid down as a general rule that if persons claim to have come to high attainments in religion but have never yet reached the lesser attainments, it is a sign of a vain claim. For example, persons may claim that they have got beyond mere morality to live a spiritual and divine life, but really have not come so far as to be moral persons. Or they may claim to be greatly affected by the wickedness of their hearts, and yet not be affected by the plain violations of God’s commands in their practice, which is a lesser attainment. Or they may claim to have been brought even to be willing to be damned for the glory of God, and yet have no readiness to suffer a little in their property, their reputation and their worldly convenience for the sake of their duty. Or they may claim that they are not afraid to venture their souls on Christ and commit their all to God, trusting his bare word and the faithfulness of his promises for their eternal welfare, and yet at the same time not have enough confidence in God to dare to trust him with a little of their property given to godly and charitable uses.
