When it is so with persons, I say, their claims are plainly vain. A man on a journey who imagines he has got far beyond a certain place on his road, and never yet came to it, must be mistaken. And the man who never yet got halfway up the hill has not yet reached the top. But this is by the way.

What has been observed of the affection of love is also to be observed of other religious affections. Those that are true extend in some proportion to the various things that are their due and proper objects; but when they are false, they are commonly strangely out of proportion. So it is with religious desires and longings. In the saints these go out to things that are spiritual and excellent in general, and in some proportion to their excellence, importance or necessity, or to the saints’ own close concern in them. But in false longings it is often far otherwise. They will strangely run with impatient vehemence after something of less importance, while other things of greater importance are neglected. For instance, some persons are from time to time seized with a vehement inclination, and an unaccountably violent pressure, to tell others what they experience and to exhort others. Yet at the same time there is no inclination in any measure equal to it toward other things that true Christianity tends to as much as, indeed more than, that: such as pouring out the soul before God in secret, earnest prayer and praise to him, and more conformity to him, and living more to his glory, and so on. We read in Scripture of groans too deep for words, and of the soul consumed with longing, and of longings, thirstings and pantings, much more often for these latter things than for the former.

So too with hatred and zeal. When these come from right principles, they are against sin in general, in some proportion to the degree of its sinfulness. Ps 119:104: “I hate every false way.” So verse 128. But a false hatred and zeal against sin is against some particular sin only. So some seem to be very zealous against profaneness and pride in clothing, who themselves are notorious for covetousness and stinginess, and perhaps for backbiting, envy toward those above them, a turbulent spirit toward rulers, and rooted ill will toward those who have injured them. False zeal is against the sins of others, while men have no zeal against their own sins. But he who has true zeal exercises it chiefly against his own sins, though he also shows a proper zeal against prevailing and dangerous iniquity in others. And some claim to have a great abhorrence of their own sins of heart, and cry out much about their inward corruption; and yet they make light of sins in practice, and seem to commit them without much restraint or remorse, though these involve sin in both heart and life.

As there is a much greater disproportion in the exercises of false affections than in those of true ones with regard to different objects, so there is also with regard to different times. True Christians are not always the same. Indeed, there is a very great difference at different times, and the best have reason to be greatly ashamed of their unsteadiness. Yet there is in no way, in the hearts of those who are true virgins, who follow the Lamb wherever He goes, the instability and inconstancy there is in false-hearted professing Christians. The righteous man is truly said to be one whose heart is steadfast, trusting in God (Ps 112:7), to have his heart established by grace (Heb 13:9), and to hold to his way. Job 17:9: “Yet a righteous one holds to his way, and the one with clean hands grows stronger.” It is spoken of as a mark of the hypocrisy of the Jewish church that they were like a swift young camel, running here and there in her ways.

If, then, persons are religious only by fits and starts, it is a sign that their affections are unsound. Suppose they now and then seem to be raised up to the clouds in their affections, and then suddenly fall down again, lose everything, and become quite careless and carnal, and this is their way of carrying on religion. Suppose they appear greatly moved and mightily engaged in religion only in extraordinary seasons: in the time of a remarkable outpouring of the Spirit, or some other uncommon dispensation of providence, or on the real or supposed receipt of some great mercy, when they have received some extraordinary earthly mercy, or suppose that they are newly converted, or have lately had what they call a great manifestation. But they quickly return to such a frame that their hearts are chiefly on other things, and the prevailing bent of their hearts and the stream of their affections is ordinarily toward the things of this world. They are like the children of Israel in the wilderness. Their affections were highly raised by what God had done for them at the Red Sea, and they sang his praise, and soon began craving the meat pots of Egypt. But then again, when they came to Mount Sinai and saw the great displays God made of himself there, they seemed to be greatly engaged again, and very eager to enter into covenant with God, saying, “All that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient”; but then they quickly made themselves a golden calf. When it is so with persons, I say, it is a sign of the unsoundness of their affections.75 They are like the waters during a shower of rain, which during the shower and a little after run like a brook and flow abundantly, but are soon quite dry; and when another shower comes, they will flow again. But a true saint is like a stream from a living spring, which, though it may be greatly increased by a shower of rain and diminished in time of drought, still runs constantly (John 4:14: “the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up,” and so on). Or he is like a tree planted by such a stream, which has a constant supply at the root and is always green, even in time of the greatest drought. Jer 17:7, 8: “But blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, whose confidence is in Him. He is like a tree planted by the waters that sends out its roots toward the stream. It does not fear when the heat comes, and its leaves are always green. It does not worry in a year of drought, nor does it cease to produce fruit.” Many hypocrites are like comets, which appear for a while with a mighty blaze, but are very unsteady and irregular in their motion (and are therefore called wandering stars, Jude 13); their blaze soon disappears, and they appear only once in a great while. But the true saints are like the fixed stars, which, though they rise and set and are often clouded, are steadfast in their orbit, and may truly be said to shine with a constant light. Hypocritical affections are like a forced motion, like that of the air when it is moved by winds (Jude 12). But gracious affections are more a natural motion, like the stream of a river, which has many turns this way and that, and may meet with obstacles, and run more freely and swiftly in some places than in others, yet in general tends the same way with a steady and constant course until it reaches the ocean.

And as there is a strange unevenness and disproportion in false affections at different times, so there often is in different places. Some are greatly affected from time to time when they are in company, but have nothing that bears any proportion to it in secret: in private meditation, secret prayer, and conversing with God when they are alone and separated from all the world.76 A true Christian doubtless delights in religious fellowship and Christian conversation, and finds much in it to affect his heart. But he also delights at times to withdraw from all mankind, to converse with God in solitary places. And this too has its own advantages for fixing his heart and engaging its affections. True religion disposes persons to be much alone in solitary places for holy meditation and prayer. So it worked in Isaac (Gen 24:63). And, which is much more, so it worked in Jesus Christ. How often do we read of his withdrawing into mountains and solitary places for holy communion with his Father? It is difficult to conceal great affections, but gracious affections are of a much more silent and secret nature than counterfeit ones. So it is with the gracious sorrow of the saints. So it is with their sorrow for their own sins.77 So the future gracious mourning of true penitents, at the beginning of the glory of the latter days, is represented as being so secret as to be hidden from the companions of their bosom. Zech 12:12, 13, 14: “The land will mourn, each clan on its own: the clan of the house of David on its own, and their wives on their own; the clan of the house of Nathan on its own, and their wives on their own; the clan of the house of Levi on its own, and their wives on their own; the clan of Shimei on its own, and their wives on their own; and all the remaining clans, each clan on its own, and their wives on their own.” So it is with their sorrow for the sins of others. The saints’ pains and labor for the souls of sinners are chiefly in secret places. Jer 13:17: “But if you+ do not listen, I will weep in secret because of your+ pride. My eyes will overflow with tears, because the Lord’s flock has been taken captive.” So it is with gracious joys: in this respect, as in others, they are hidden manna (Rev 2:17). The psalmist seems to speak of his sweetest comforts as those that were to be had in secret. Ps 63:5: “My soul is satisfied as with the richest of foods; with joyful lips my mouth will praise You. When I remember You on my bed, I think of You through the watches of the night.” Christ calls his bride away from the world into secluded places, so that he may give her his sweetest love. Song 7:11, 12: “Come, my beloved, let us go to the countryside; let us spend the night among the wildflowers. … There I will give you my love.” The most eminent divine favors the saints received that we read of in Scripture came in their times alone. The chief manifestations God made of himself and his covenant mercy to Abraham were when he was alone, apart from his large household, as anyone who reads his history carefully will judge. Isaac received that special gift of God to him, Rebekah, who was so great a comfort to him, and by whom he obtained the promised seed, while he was walking alone, meditating in the field. Jacob had withdrawn for secret prayer when Christ came to him, and he wrestled with him and obtained the blessing. God revealed himself to Moses in the bush when he was in a solitary place in the desert, at Mount Horeb (Exod 3, at the beginning). And afterward, when God showed him his glory, and he was admitted to the highest degree of communion with God he ever enjoyed, he was alone on the same mountain, and stayed there forty days and forty nights, and then came down with his face shining. God came to those great prophets Elijah and Elisha, and conversed freely with them, chiefly when they were alone. Elijah conversed alone with God at Mount Sinai, as Moses did. And when Jesus Christ had his greatest foretaste of his future glory, when he was transfigured, it was not when he was with the multitude, or with the twelve disciples. He had withdrawn into a solitary place on a mountain with only three chosen disciples, and he charged them to tell no one until he had risen from the dead. When the angel Gabriel came to the blessed virgin, and when the Holy Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, she seems to have been alone, and to have been hidden from the world in this matter. Her nearest and dearest earthly friend, Joseph, who was engaged to her (though he was a just man), knew nothing of it. And she who first shared in the joy of Christ’s resurrection was alone with Christ at the tomb (John 20). And when the beloved disciple was favored with those wonderful visions of Christ, and of his future dealings with the church and the world, he was alone on the island of Patmos. Not that we do not also have instances of great privileges the saints have received when they were with others, or that there is not much in Christian conversation, and in social and public worship, that tends greatly to refresh and gladden the hearts of the saints. But all I aim at in what has been said is to show that it is the nature of true grace that, however much it loves Christian company in its place, it delights in a special way in being alone and in secret communion with God. So if persons appear greatly engaged in social religion but little in the religion of the private room, and are often highly affected when they are with others but little moved when they have none but God and Christ to converse with, it looks very dark for their religion.

73. Renewed care and diligence follow the sealings of the Spirit. Now the soul is at the feet of Christ, as Mary was at the tomb, with fear and great joy. He who travels the road with a rich treasure about him is afraid of a thief in every bush. Flavel’s sacramental meditations, Medi. 4.

74. If repentance accompanies faith, it is no presumption to believe. Many know their sin, and so they believe in Christ and trust in Christ, and there is an end of their faith. But what confession and sorrow for sin, what more love to Christ follows this faith? Truly none. Indeed, their faith is the reason they have none. For they think: If I trust in Christ to forgive me, he will do it, and there is an end of the matter. Truly this hedge-faith, this bramble-faith, which catches hold of Christ and pricks and scratches Christ by more impenitence and more contempt of him, is mere presumption, which will one day be burned up and destroyed by the fire of God’s jealousy. Shame on that faith which serves only to keep a man from being tormented before his time! Your+ sins would be your+ sorrows, if your+ faith did not quiet you+. But suppose faith is accompanied with repentance, mourning for sin, and a higher esteem of God’s grace in Christ, so that nothing breaks your heart more than the thought of Christ’s unchangeable love to one so vile; and this love makes you love much, and love him the more; and as your sin increases, so you desire your love to increase; and now the stream of your thoughts runs on how you may live to him who died for you. This was Mary’s faith, who sat at Christ’s feet weeping, washing them with her tears, and loving much, because much was forgiven. Shepard’s sound believer. P. 128, 129. You+ will know godly sorrow (says Dr. Preston, in his discourse on Paul’s conversion) by its continuance. It is constant; but worldly sorrow is only a passion of the mind: it changes, it does not last. Though for the present it may be violent and strong and work much outwardly, it comes only in fits and does not continue, like a flash flood, which violently overflows the banks for the present, but will go away again; it is not always so. But godly sorrow is like a spring, which keeps running constantly, winter and summer, wet and dry, in heat and cold, early and late. So this godly sorrow is always the same in a regenerate man: take him when you will, he is still sorrowing for sin. This godly sorrow stands like the center of the earth, which does not move, but still remains. I am persuaded that many a man’s heart is kept from breaking and mourning because of this. He says (perhaps) that he is a vile sinner, “but I trust in Christ,” and so on. If they do go to Christ to destroy their sin, this makes them more complacent in their sin. For (they say) “I cannot help it, and Christ must do all.” Whereas faith makes the soul mourn after the Lord all the more. Shep. Parable of the ten virgins, Part II. P. 168.

75. Dr. Owen (on the Spirit, book III. Chap. Ii. § 18.), speaking of a common work of the Spirit, says: This work operates greatly on the affections. We have given instances in fear, sorrow, joy and delight about spiritual things, which are stirred up and set to work by it. But it still falls short of a thorough work on the affections themselves in two things. For 1st, it does not fix them. And 2nd, it does not fill them. 1. It is required that our affections be fixed on heavenly and spiritual things, and true grace will bring it about. Col 3:1, 2: “Therefore, since you+ have been raised with Christ, strive for the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your+ affections on things above.” The joys, the fears, the hopes, the sorrows concerning spiritual and eternal things which the work mentioned before produces are fleeting, uncertain and unstable, not only as to their degrees but as to their very being. Sometimes they are like a river ready to overflow its banks: men cannot help pouring them out on every occasion. And sometimes they are like waters that fail: not a drop comes from them. Sometimes they are hot and sometimes cold, sometimes up and sometimes down, sometimes all heaven and sometimes all world, without evenness, without stability. But true grace fixes the affections on spiritual things. As to the degrees of their exercise, there may be, and there is, a great variety in them, according as they are stirred up, aided and assisted by grace and its means, or obstructed and hindered by temptations and distractions coming between. But the constant bent and inclination of renewed affections is toward spiritual things, as the Scripture everywhere testifies, and as experience confirms. There is (says Dr. Preston) a certain love by fits which God does not accept: when men come and offer God great promises, like the waves of the sea, as big as mountains. Oh, they think they will do much for God! But their minds change, and they become like those high waves which at last fall level with the other waters. If a man should offer you great kindnesses, and you should afterward come to him to make use of him, and he should look at you strangely, as if he had never been acquainted with you, how would you value such love? If we are now on, now off, in our love, God will not value such love. Discourse on the divine love of Christ. Mr. Flavel, speaking of these changeable professing Christians, says: Such professing Christians have more of the moon than of the sun: little light, less heat, and many changes. They deceive many, indeed they deceive themselves, but they cannot deceive God. They lack the ballast and settledness in themselves that would have kept them tight and steady. Touchstone of sincerity, ch. 2. § 2.

76. The Lord is neglected in secret, yet honored openly; because there is no wind in their rooms to blow their sails, and so there they stand still. That is why many men keep their profession when they lose their affection. By the one they have a name to live (and that is enough), though their hearts are dead. And that is why, as long as you love and commend them, they love you; but if not, they will forsake you. They were warm only by another’s fire, and so, having no principle of life within, they soon grow dead. This is the water that turns a Pharisee’s mill. Shepard’s Par. Part I. P. 180. The hypocrite (says Mr. Flavel) is not for the private room, but the synagogue (Matt 6:5, 6). It is not his food and drink to withdraw from the noise of the world to enjoy God in secret. Touchstone of sincerity, ch. 7. § 2. Dr. Ames, in his cases of conscience, Lib. III. Chapter 5., speaks of it as a thing by which sincerity may be known, that persons are obedient in the absence as well as in the presence of onlookers, in secret as much as, indeed more than, in public, citing Phil 2:12 and Matt 6:6.

77. Mr. Flavel, in listing the things in which the sorrow of saints over their sins is distinguished from the sorrow of hypocrites, says: Their troubles for sin are more private and silent troubles than others’ are; their sore runs in the night. Touchstone of sincerity, ch. 6. § v.

Longing After Spiritual Attainments

Part III · Sign XI

XI. Another great and very distinguishing difference between gracious affections and others is that the higher gracious affections are raised, the more a spiritual appetite and longing of soul after spiritual attainments is increased. False affections, on the contrary, rest satisfied in themselves.78

The more a true saint loves God with a gracious love, the more he desires to love him, and the more uneasy he is at his lack of love to him. The more he hates sin, the more he desires to hate it, and laments that he has so much love for it remaining. The more he mourns for sin, the more he longs to mourn for sin. The more his heart is broken, the more he desires it to be broken. The more he thirsts and longs after God and holiness, the more he longs to long, and to breathe out his very soul in longings after God. The kindling and raising of gracious affections is like kindling a flame: the higher it is raised, the more ardent it is, and the more it burns, the more vehemently it tends and seeks to burn. So the spiritual appetite after holiness and after an increase of holy affections is much more lively and keen in those who are eminent in holiness than in others; and more when grace and holy affections are in their liveliest exercise than at other times. It is as much the nature of one who is spiritually newborn to thirst after growth in holiness as it is the nature of a newborn baby to thirst after its mother’s breast; and the baby has the sharpest appetite when it is in the best health. 1 Pet 2:2, 3: “Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk, so that by it you+ may grow up in your+ salvation, now that you+ have tasted that the Lord is good.” The most the saints have in this world is only a taste, a foretaste of that future glory which is their proper fullness. It is only an earnest of their future inheritance in their hearts (2 Cor 1:22; and 5:5; and Eph 1:14). The most eminent saints in this state are only children compared with their future state, which is their proper state of maturity and perfection, as the apostle observes in 1 Cor 13:10, 11. The greatest eminence and perfection the saints reach in this world has no tendency to make them sated or to lessen their desires for more. On the contrary, it makes them more eager to press forward, as is evident from the apostle’s words in Phil 3:13, 14, 15: “Forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead, I press on toward the goal. … All of us who are PERFECT should embrace this point of view.”

The reasons for it are these. The more holy affections persons have, the more they have of that spiritual taste I have spoken of elsewhere, by which they perceive the excellence and relish the divine sweetness of holiness. And the more grace they have while in this state of imperfection, the more they see their imperfection and emptiness, and their distance from what ought to be; and so the more they see their need of grace, as I showed at length before when speaking of the nature of evangelical humiliation. Besides, grace, as long as it is imperfect, is of a growing nature and in a growing state. And we see that it is so with all living things: while they are in a state of imperfection and in their growing state, their nature seeks growth, and all the more as they are healthier and more thriving. Therefore the cry of every true grace is like that cry of true faith in Mark 9:24: “I do believe; help my unbelief!” And the greater the spiritual manifestations and affections the true Christian has, the more earnest a beggar he becomes for grace and spiritual food, so that he may grow; and the more earnestly he pursues it in the use of proper means and efforts. For true and gracious longings after holiness are no idle, ineffectual desires.

But here some may object and say: How is this consistent with what everyone grants, that spiritual enjoyments are of a soul-satisfying nature?

I answer that it will appear not at all inconsistent with what has been said, if we consider in what way spiritual enjoyments are said to be of a soul-satisfying nature. Certainly they are not so in the sense of being so cloying that the man who has anything of them, though only in a very imperfect degree, desires no more. But spiritual enjoyments are of a soul-satisfying nature in the following respects. 1. In their kind and nature they are fully suited to the nature, capacity and need of the soul of man. So those who find them desire no other kind of enjoyment. They sit down fully content with the kind of happiness they have, desiring no change, and no longer inclined to wander about, saying, “Who can show us the good?” The soul is never cloyed, never weary, but perpetually gives itself up, with all its powers, to this happiness. But this does not mean that those who have something of this happiness desire no more of the same. 2. They are satisfying also in this respect, that they answer the expectation of the appetite. When the appetite for anything is strong, the expectation is strong as a result. Appetite for a particular object implies expectation in its very nature. This expectation is not satisfied by worldly enjoyments: the man expected to gain a great increase of happiness, but he is disappointed. But it is not so with spiritual enjoyments; they fully answer and satisfy the expectation. 3. The gratification and pleasure of spiritual enjoyments is lasting. It is not so with worldly enjoyments. In a sense they satisfy particular appetites. But in being satisfied the appetite is glutted, and then the pleasure is over; and as soon as that is over, the general appetite of human nature for happiness returns, but empty, with nothing to satisfy it. So the glutting of a particular appetite only takes away from the general thirst of nature and leaves it empty. 4. Spiritual good is satisfying in that there is enough in it to satisfy the soul in degree, if only the obstacles were removed and the enjoying faculty duly applied. There is room enough here for the soul to stretch itself out; here is an infinite ocean of it. If men are not satisfied here in degree of happiness, the cause lies with themselves: it is because they do not open their mouths wide enough.

But these things do not show that a soul that has tasted a little has no appetite stirred up for more of the same, or that his appetite will not increase the more he tastes, until he comes to the fullness of enjoyment. So bodies that are drawn toward the globe of the earth tend toward it more strongly the nearer they come to the attracting body, and are not at rest outside its center. Spiritual good is of a satisfying nature; and for that very reason the soul that tastes it and knows its nature will thirst after it, and after a fullness of it, so that it may be satisfied. And the more he experiences and the more he knows this excellent, unparalleled, exquisite and satisfying sweetness, the more earnestly will he hunger and thirst for more, until he comes to perfection. And therefore it is the nature of spiritual affections that the greater they are, the greater the appetite and longing after grace and holiness.

But it is otherwise with joys and other religious affections that are false and counterfeit. If before there was a great desire of some sort after grace, then as these affections rise, that desire ceases or is lessened. Perhaps before, while the man was under the convictions of the law and very afraid of hell, he earnestly longed to obtain spiritual light in his understanding, and faith in Christ, and love to God. But now that these false affections have risen, which deceive him and make him confident that he is converted and his state is good, there are no more earnest longings after light and grace. For his end has been met: he is confident that his sins are forgiven and that he will go to heaven, and so he is satisfied. And especially when false affections are raised very high, they put an end to longings after grace and holiness. The man is now far from seeing himself as a poor, empty creature. On the contrary, he is rich and has grown wealthy, and can hardly conceive of anything more excellent than what he has already attained.

That is why many persons’ earnestness in seeking comes to an end once they have obtained what they call their conversion, or at least once they have had those high affections that make them fully confident of it. Before, while they regarded themselves as in a state of nature, they were engaged in seeking after God and Christ, cried earnestly for grace, and strove in the use of means. But now they act as though they thought their work was done. They live on their first work, or on some high experiences that are past, and there is an end to their crying and striving after God and grace.79 But the holy principles that move a true saint have a far more powerful influence than slavish fear to stir him up to earnestness in seeking God and holiness. That is why seeking God is spoken of as one of the distinguishing marks of the saints, and those who seek God is one of the names by which the godly are called in Scripture. Ps 24:6: “Such is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face, O God of Jacob.” Ps 69:6: “May those who seek You not be dishonored through me.” Verse 32: “The humble will see and rejoice. You+ who seek God, let your+ hearts be revived!” And 70:4: “May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You; may those who love Your salvation always say, ‘Let God be magnified!’ ” And the Scriptures everywhere represent the seeking, striving and labor of a Christian as coming chiefly after his conversion, and his conversion as only the beginning of his work. Almost everything said in the New Testament about men’s watching, paying earnest heed to themselves, running the race set before them, striving and agonizing, wrestling not against flesh and blood but against rulers and powers, fighting, putting on the whole armor of God and standing, having done everything, to stand, pressing forward, straining toward what is ahead, persisting in prayer, crying to God day and night: almost everything said in the New Testament about these things, I say, is spoken of the saints and directed to them. Where these things are applied once to sinners seeking conversion, they are spoken ten times of the saints carrying on the great business of their high calling. But many in these days have fallen into a strange way, contrary to Scripture, of having all their striving and wrestling over before they are converted, and so having an easy time of it afterward, sitting down to enjoy their sloth and idleness, as those whose wants are now supplied, and who have become rich and full. But when the Lord fills the hungry with good things, these rich are likely to be sent away empty (Luke 1:53).

But doubtless there are some hypocrites who have only false affections and who will think they can stand this test. They will readily say that they do not want to rest satisfied with past attainments, but to keep pressing forward: they do desire more, they long after God and Christ, and desire more holiness, and do seek it. But the truth is that their desires are not properly the desires of an appetite for holiness for its own sake, or for the moral excellence and holy sweetness that is in it, but only for ulterior ends. They long for clearer manifestations so that they may be better satisfied about the state of their souls. Or, because self is gratified in great manifestations, in being made so much of by God and so exalted above others, they long to taste the love of God (as they call it) more than to have more love to God. Or perhaps they have a kind of forced, imagined or manufactured longing, because they think they must long for more grace, or else it will be a dark sign against them. But things like these are far different from the natural, and as it were necessary, appetite and thirst of the new man after God and holiness. There is an inward burning desire after holiness in a saint, as natural to the new creature as vital heat is to the body. There is a holy breathing and panting after the Spirit of God to increase holiness, as natural to a holy nature as breathing is to a living body. And holiness or sanctification is more directly its object than any manifestation of God’s love and favor. This is the food and drink that is the object of the spiritual appetite. John 4:34: “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.” Where we read in Scripture of the desires, longings and thirstings of the saints, righteousness and God’s laws are much more often mentioned as their object than anything else. The saints crave pure spiritual milk, not so much to testify God’s love to them as so that by it they may grow up in holiness. I have shown before that holiness is the good which is the immediate object of a spiritual taste. But undoubtedly the same sweetness that is the chief object of a spiritual taste is also the chief object of a spiritual appetite. Grace is the godly man’s treasure. Isa 33:6: “The fear of the Lord is his treasure.” Godliness is the gain he is covetous and greedy for (1 Tim 6:6). Hypocrites long for manifestations more for the present comfort of the manifestation, and the high manifestation of God’s love in it, than for any sanctifying influence it has. But neither a longing after great manifestations or great tastes of the love of God, nor a longing to be in heaven, nor a longing to die, is in any measure so distinguishing a mark of true saints as longing after a more holy heart, and living a more holy life.

But I have now come to the last distinguishing mark of holy affections that I will mention.

78. Truly there is no work of Christ that is right (says Mr. Shepard) but it carries the soul to long for more of it. Par. Of the ten virgins, Part I. P. 136. And again: There is in true grace an infinite circle: a man receives by thirsting, and by receiving thirsts for more. But this is why the Spirit is not poured out abundantly on churches: because men shut it out by shutting themselves in and contenting themselves with their common graces and gifts (Matt 7:29). Examine whether it is not so. Ibid, p. 182. And on p. 210 he says: This I say: true grace, as it comforts, so it never fills, but puts an edge on the appetite: more of that grace, Lord! So Paul, Phil 3:13, 14. So David: out of my poverty I have given, and so on (1 Chr 29:3, 17, 18). It is a sure way never to be deceived in lighter strokes of the Spirit, to be thankful for any of it, but to be content with no measure of it. And this cuts the thread of difference between a superficial, lighter stroke of the Spirit and one that is sound.

79. It is common to see a false heart most diligent in seeking the Lord when he has been at his worst, and most careless when he is at his best. That is why many at their first conversion sought the Lord earnestly, but afterward their affections and efforts die, so that now they think they are as good as the word can make them.—A hypocrite’s last end is to satisfy himself, so he has enough. A saint’s is to satisfy Christ, so he never has enough. Shepard’s parable Part I. P. 157. Many a man, perhaps, may say: I have nothing in myself, and all is in Christ; and comfort himself there, and so fall asleep. Hands off! Do not touch this ark, or the Lord will strike you dead. A Christ made of rags would serve your turn as well. Ibid p. 71. A hypocrite’s light goes out, and does not grow. That is why many who have stood a long time take all their comfort from their first work, and droop in old age. Ibid p. 77. And on p. 93, 94, Mr. Shepard, describing those who have a dead hope, says: Those who content themselves with any measure of holiness and grace do not look for Christ’s coming and company. For saints who do look for him, though they do not have the holiness and grace they would like, still do not rest satisfied with any measure. 1 John 3:3: “Everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as Christ is pure.”—The saints are not content with any adornment until they are made glorious, and so fit for fellowship with that bridegroom.—When a man does not stop until he gets a certain measure of faith and grace, and now that he has got it, contents himself with it as a good sign that he will be saved, he is not looking for Christ. Or when men are heavily laden with sin, then embrace Christ, and then are comforted, sealed, and have joy that fills them; and now the work is done.—And when men will not content themselves with any measure, but wish they had more, if only grace would grow while they count the hours and sit idle; and so God must do it all, but they do not purge themselves and make a work of it. Again, p. 109: There is not a hypocrite living who does not come to Christ for his own ends, for he cannot work beyond his principle. Now when men have served their own turn out of another man, away they go, and keep what they have. A hypocrite comes to Christ as a man comes to a rich shop: he will not go to the cost of buying the whole shop, but only as much as serves his turn. Commonly men in horror seek as much of Christ as will ease them, and so they profess; and so they seek as much of Christ as will give them credit; and so their desires after Christ are soon satisfied. Appetitus Finis est infinitus. [The desire for the end is infinite.] Woe to you who can paint such a Christ in your head, and receive such a Christ into your heart, as must be a pander to your sloth. The Lord will avenge this wrong done to his glory with greater sorrows than any ever felt: to make Christ not only food and drink to feed you, but clothes to cover your sloth.—Why, what can we do? What can we do?—Why, as the first Adam passes on not only guilt but power, so the second passes on both righteousness and strength. Ibid p. 158. When the Lord has given some light and affection, and some comfort, and some reformation, now a man grows full here. Saints do things for God, and carnal hearts do something too; but a little fills them, and quiets them, and so damns them. That is why men are very diligent in the use of means at the first work on them; but after that they come to neglect prayer, sleep through sermons, and become careless, sapless and lifeless.— Ibid p. 210. It is evidence of a lack of grace when a man says to himself, as the glutton said to his soul, “You have plenty of good things laid up for many years. Take your rest.” So you have repentance, and grace, and peace enough for many years; and so the soul takes its rest, and grows sluggish and negligent. Oh, if you die in this condition, this night your soul will be taken away to hell. Ibid. P. 227.

Christian Practice

Part III · Sign XII

XII. Gracious and holy affections have their exercise and fruit in Christian practice.——I mean that they have such influence and power over the one who has them that they make a practice universally conformed to Christian rules, and directed by them, the practice and business of his life.

This implies three things. 1. That his behavior or practice in the world is universally conformed to Christian rules and directed by them. 2. That he makes a business of such a holy practice above all things: that it is a business he is chiefly engaged in and devoted to, and pursues with the highest earnestness and diligence, so that he may be said to make this practice of religion, in a special way, his work and business. And 3. That he persists in it to the end of his life. So it may be said to be not only his business at certain seasons (the business of Sabbath days, or of certain extraordinary times, or the business of a month, or a year, or seven years, or his business under certain circumstances), but the business of his life: the business he perseveres in through all changes and under all trials, as long as he lives.

The necessity of each of these in all true Christians is most clearly and fully taught in the word of God.

(1.) It is necessary that men be universally obedient:80 1 John 3:3, etc.: “Everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as Christ is pure.—But you+ know that Christ appeared to take away sins, and in Him there is no sin. No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning. No one who continues to sin has seen Him or known Him.—The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Christ is righteous. The one who practices sin is of the devil.” Chapter 5:18: “We know that anyone born of God does not keep on sinning; the one who was born of God keeps himself, and the evil one cannot touch him.” John 15:14: “You+ are My friends if you+ do what I command you+.” Jas 2:10: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it.” 1 Cor 6:9: “Do you+ not know that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters,” etc., “will inherit the kingdom of God.” Gal 5:19, 20: “The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity, and debauchery; idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions, and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like. I warn you+, as I did before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.” That is as much as to say, those who practice any sort of wickedness. Job 31:3, 4, 5, 6, 7: “Does not disaster come to the unjust and calamity to the workers of iniquity? Does He not see my ways and count my every step? … Let God weigh me with honest scales, that He may know my integrity. If my steps have turned from the path, if my heart has followed my eyes, or if impurity has stuck to my hands,” etc. Ezek 33:15: “If he … walks in the statutes of life without practicing iniquity, then he will surely live.” If only one member is corrupt and we do not cut it off, it will carry the whole body to hell (Matt 5:29, 30). Saul was commanded to kill all God’s enemies, the Amalekites; and he killed all but Agag, and sparing his life proved to be his ruin. Caleb and Joshua entered into God’s promised rest because they wholly followed the Lord (Num 14:24; and 32:11, 12; Deut 1:36; Josh 14:6, 8, 9, 14). Naaman’s hypocrisy appeared in this: however greatly he seemed to be moved with gratitude to God for healing his leprosy, and though he pledged himself to serve him, yet in one thing he wanted to be excused. And Herod, though he feared John and kept him safe, and heard him gladly, and did many things, was yet condemned, because in one thing he would not listen to him: in parting with his beloved Herodias. So it is necessary that men part with their dearest iniquities, which are like their right hand and right eye: the sins that most easily beset them, and that they are most exposed to by their natural inclinations, evil customs or particular circumstances, as well as with others. Joseph would not make himself known to his brothers, who had sold him, until Benjamin, the beloved child of the family, the one hardest to part with, was given up. In the same way Christ will not reveal his love to us until we part with our dearest lusts, and until we are brought to comply with the most difficult duties, and those we have the greatest aversion to.

And it is important to observe that, for a man to be truly said to be universally obedient, his obedience must not consist only in negatives, or in universally avoiding wicked practices, sins of commission. He must also be universal in the positives of religion. Sins of omission are as much breaches of God’s commands as sins of commission. In Matthew 25, Christ represents those on the left hand as condemned and cursed to everlasting fire for sins of omission: “I was hungry and you+ gave Me nothing to eat,” etc. So a man cannot be said to be universally obedient, and of a Christian conduct, merely because he is no thief, no oppressor, no cheat, no drunkard, no tavern-haunter, no whoremonger, no carouser, no night-walker, not unclean, not profane in his language, no slanderer, no liar, not furious, not malicious, no reviler. He who goes this far and no farther is falsely said to be of a conduct that becomes the gospel. For this it is also necessary that he be of a serious, religious, devout, humble, meek, forgiving, peaceful, respectful, gracious to those beneath him, benevolent, merciful, charitable and beneficent walk and conduct. Without such things as these he does not obey the laws of Christ, laws that he and his apostles abundantly insisted on as of the greatest importance and necessity.

(2.) For men to be true Christians, it is necessary that they pursue the business of religion and the service of God with great earnestness and diligence, as the work they devote themselves to and make the main business of their lives. All Christ’s own people not only do good works but are zealous for good works (Titus 2:14). No man can do the service of two masters at once. Those who are God’s true servants give themselves up to his service and make it, as it were, their whole work, employing their whole hearts and the chief of their strength in it. Phil 3:13: “One thing I do.” Christians in their effectual calling are not called to idleness, but to labor in God’s vineyard, and to spend their day doing a great and laborious service. All true Christians comply with this call (as is implied in its being an effectual call) and do the work of Christians. Everywhere in the New Testament this work is compared to those exercises in which men usually exert their strength with the greatest earnestness, such as running, wrestling and fighting. All true Christians are good and faithful soldiers of Jesus Christ, and fight the good fight of faith, for none but those who do so ever take hold of eternal life. Those who fight like men beating the air never win the crown of victory. Those who run in a race all run, but only one wins the prize; and those who are slack and negligent in their course do not run in such a way as to win it. The kingdom of heaven is not to be taken except by violence. Without earnestness there is no getting along in that narrow way that leads to life, and so no arriving at the state of glorious life and happiness it leads to. Without earnest labor there is no climbing the steep and high hill of Zion, and so no arriving at the heavenly city on its top. Without constant labor there is no stemming the swift stream we swim in, so as ever to come to the fountain of the water of life at its head. We need to watch and pray always, in order to escape those dreadful things that are coming on the ungodly, and to be counted worthy to stand before the Son of Man. We need to put on the whole armor of God, and to do everything to stand, in order to avoid a total overthrow and being utterly destroyed by the flaming arrows of the devil. We need to forget what is behind, and to be straining toward what is ahead, and pressing on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, in order to obtain that prize. Slothfulness in the service of God, in his professed servants, is as damning as open rebellion. For the slothful servant is a wicked servant, and will be thrown into the outer darkness among God’s open enemies (Matt 25:26, 28). Those who are slothful are not followers of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises. Heb 6:11, 12: “We want each of you+ to show this same diligence to the full assurance of hope to the very end. Then you+ will not be slothful, but followers of those who through faith and patience inherit what has been promised.” And all who follow that cloud of witnesses who have gone before to heaven throw off every weight and the sin that so easily besets them, and run with endurance the race set before them (Heb 12:1). The true faith by which persons rely on the righteousness of Christ and the work he has done for them, and truly feed and live on him, is always accompanied by such a spirit of earnestness in the Christian work and course. This was typified of old by the way the children of Israel fed on the Passover lamb. They were told to eat it like people in haste, with their loins girded, their shoes on their feet and their staff in their hand. Exod 12:11: “This is how you+ are to eat it: You+ must be fully dressed for travel, with your+ sandals on your+ feet and your+ staff in your+ hand. You+ are to eat in haste; it is the Lord’s Passover.”

(3.) Every true Christian perseveres in this way of universal obedience, and of diligent and earnest service of God, through all the various kinds of trials he meets with, to the end of his life. That all true saints, all who obtain eternal life, persevere in this way in the practice of religion and the service of God is a doctrine so abundantly taught in Scripture that to list all the texts that imply it one by one would be endless. I will content myself with referring to some in the margin.81

But that part of perseverance in obedience which Scripture chiefly insists on as a special mark of the truth of grace is that professing Christians continue in the practice of their duty, and stay steadfast in a holy walk, through the various trials they meet with.

By trials I mean here the things that occur, and that a professing Christian meets with in his course, which especially make his continuing in his duty and faithfulness to God hard for nature. Again and again Scripture calls these things trials or temptations (words that mean the same thing). They are of various kinds. Many things make it hard for persons to continue in the way of their duty because they tend to cherish and feed, or to stir up and provoke, their lusts and corruptions. Many things make it hard to continue in the way of duty because they are alluring and tend to entice persons to sin, or because they tend to remove restraints and make them bold in iniquity. Other things try the soundness and steadfastness of professing Christians because they tend to make their duty look terrible to them, and so to frighten and drive them away from it: such as the sufferings their duty will expose them to, pain, ill will, contempt and reproach, or the loss of outward possessions and comforts. If persons, after they have made a profession of religion, live any considerable time in this world, so full of changes and so full of evil, they cannot help meeting with many trials of their sincerity and steadfastness. Besides, it is God’s way in his providence to bring trials on his professing friends and servants on purpose, so that he may make them manifest, and may set before their own consciences, and often before the world, sufficient matter to show convincingly the state they are in. This appears from innumerable Scriptures; some are referred to in the margin.82

True saints may be guilty of some kinds and degrees of backsliding. They may be overcome by particular temptations, and may fall into sin, indeed into great sins. But they can never fall away so far as to grow weary of religion and the service of God, and habitually to dislike it and neglect it, whether for its own sake or because of the difficulties that come with it. This is evident from Galatians 6:9; Rom 2:7; Heb 10:36; Isa 43:22; Mal 1:13. They can never backslide so far as to continue no longer in a way of universal obedience, or so that it ceases to be their manner to observe all the rules of Christianity and do all the duties required, even the most difficult, and in the most difficult circumstances.83 This is abundantly clear from the things already observed. Nor can they ever fall away so far as to be habitually more engaged in other things than in the business of religion, or so that it becomes their way and manner to serve something else more than God, or so as to cease, as a settled thing, to serve God with such earnestness and diligence that they are still habitually devoted and given up to the business of religion. This cannot be, unless those words of Christ can fall to the ground, “No one can serve two masters,” and those of the apostle, “Whoever chooses to be a friend of the world renders himself an enemy of God”; and unless a saint can change his God and still be a true saint. Nor can a true saint ever fall away so far that it comes to this: that ordinarily there is no remarkable difference between his walk and behavior since his conversion and what it was before. Those who are truly converted are new men, new creatures: new not only within but without. They are sanctified throughout, in spirit, soul and body. Old things have passed away; all things have become new. They have new hearts, and new eyes, new ears, new tongues, new hands, new feet, that is, a new conduct and practice. They walk in newness of life, and continue to do so to the end of life. And as for those who fall away and visibly cease to do so, it is a sign they never were risen with Christ.84 And especially when men’s opinion that they are converted, and so in a safe state, is the very cause of their coming to this, it is a most evident sign of their hypocrisy.85 And this holds whether their falling away is into their former sins or into some new kind of wickedness, the corruption of nature only turned into a new channel instead of being mortified. So it is when persons who think themselves converted, though they do not return to their former profaneness and lewdness, yet, from the high opinion they have of their experiences, graces and privileges, gradually settle more and more into a self-righteous and spiritually proud temper of mind, and into the kind of behavior and conduct that naturally arises from it. When it is like this with men, however far they may seem to be from their former evil practices, this alone is enough to condemn them, and may make their last state far worse than the first. For this seems to be the very case of the Jews of that generation whom Christ speaks of in Matt 12:43, 44, 45. They had been awakened by John the Baptist’s preaching and brought to a reformation of their former licentious ways, by which the unclean spirit was, as it were, turned out, and the house swept and put in order. Yet, being empty of God and of grace, they became full of themselves. They were lifted up in an exceedingly high opinion of their own righteousness and eminent holiness, and grew used to a self-exalting behavior to match. So they exchanged the sins of tax collectors and prostitutes for those of the Pharisees, and in the end had seven devils worse than the first.

So I have explained what exercise and fruit I mean when I say that gracious affections have their exercise and fruit in Christian practice.

The reason gracious affections have such a tendency and effect appears from many things already observed in the earlier parts of this discourse.

The reason for it appears from this: that gracious affections arise from operations and influences that are spiritual, and that the inward principle they flow from is something divine: an imparting of God, a participation of the divine nature, Christ living in the heart, the Holy Spirit dwelling there in union with the faculties of the soul, as an inward vital principle, exerting his own proper nature in the exercise of those faculties. This is enough to show us why true grace should have such activity, power and efficacy. No wonder that what is divine is powerful and effectual, for it has omnipotence on its side. If God dwells in the heart and is vitally united to it, he will show that he is God by the efficacy of his working. Christ is not in the heart of a saint as in a tomb, or as a dead Savior who does nothing, but as in his temple, and as one who is alive from the dead. For in the heart where Christ savingly is, there he lives, and exerts himself according to the power of that endless life he received at his resurrection. So every saint who has the benefit of Christ’s sufferings is made to know and experience the power of his resurrection. The Spirit of Christ, who is the immediate spring of grace in the heart, is all life, all power, all act. 1 Cor 2:4: “with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power.” 1 Thess 1:5: “Our gospel came to you+ not only in word, but also in power, in the Holy Spirit.” 1 Cor 4:20: “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power.” That is why saving affections, though often they do not make as great a noise and show as others, yet have in them a hidden solidity, life and strength. By it they take hold of the heart and carry it away, leading it into a kind of captivity (2 Cor 10:5), and gain a full and steadfast determination of the will for God and holiness. Ps 110:3: “Your people shall be willing in the day of Your power.” And this is how holy affections have a governing power in the course of a man’s life. A statue may look very much like a real man, and a handsome man. Indeed, to the eye it may resemble a very lively, strong and active man. But it lacks an inward principle of life and strength, and so it does nothing, it brings nothing about; there is no action or working to match the show. False manifestations and affections do not go deep enough to reach and govern the spring of men’s actions and practice. The seed on stony ground had no depth of soil, and the root did not go deep enough to bring forth fruit. But gracious affections go to the very bottom of the heart and take hold of the very innermost springs of life and activity. It is chiefly in this that the power of true godliness appears: in its being effectual in practice. And the efficacy of godliness in this respect is what the apostle has in view when he speaks of the power of godliness (2 Tim 3:5). This is very plain, for he is declaring there in particular how some professing Christians would notoriously fail in the practice of religion; and then in the 5th verse he observes that in being of such an unholy practice they deny the power of godliness, though they have the form of it. It is true that the power of godliness is exerted first of all within the soul, in the felt, lively exercise of gracious affections there. Yet the chief evidence of this power of godliness is in those exercises of holy affections that are practical, and in their being practical: in conquering the will, and conquering the lusts and corruptions of men, and carrying men on in the way of holiness through all temptation, difficulty and opposition.

Again, the reason gracious affections have their exercise and effect in Christian practice appears from this (which has also been observed before): that the first objective ground of gracious affections is the transcendently excellent and lovely nature of divine things as they are in themselves, and not any supposed relation they bear to self or self-interest. This shows why holy affections will make men holy in their practice universally. What makes men partial in religion is that they seek themselves, and not God, in their religion, and take up religion not for its own excellent nature, but only to serve a purpose. He who takes up religion only to serve a purpose will take up no more of it than he imagines serves that purpose. But he who takes up religion for its own excellent and lovely nature takes up all that has that nature. He who embraces religion for its own sake embraces the whole of religion. This also shows why gracious affections will make men practice religion perseveringly and at all times. In the course of time religion may change greatly, in many respects, in how well it agrees with men’s private interest. So he who complies with it only from selfish views is liable to forsake it when times change. But the excellent nature of religion, as it is in itself, does not vary. It is always the same, at all times and through all changes; it never alters in any respect.

The reason gracious affections issue in holy practice appears further from the kind of excellence of divine things that, as has been observed, is the foundation of all holy affection, namely, their moral excellence, or the beauty of their holiness. No wonder that a love to holiness for holiness’ sake inclines persons to practice holiness, and to practice everything that is holy. Since holiness is the main thing that stirs, draws and governs all gracious affections, no wonder that all such affections tend to holiness. What men love, they desire to have, to be united to and to possess. The beauty men delight in, they desire to be adorned with. The acts men delight in, they are necessarily inclined to do.

And what has been observed of that divine teaching and leading of the Spirit of God which there is in gracious affections shows the reason for this tendency of such affections to a universally holy practice. For, as has been observed, the Spirit of God in this divine teaching and leading of his gives the soul a natural relish of the sweetness of what is holy, and of everything that is holy, so far as it comes into view, and stirs up a distaste and disgust for everything that is unholy.

The same also appears from what has been observed of the nature of the spiritual knowledge that is the foundation of all holy affection: that it consists in a sense and view of that excellence in divine things which is supreme and transcendent. For by this, these things appear worthy above all others to be chosen and held to. By the sight of the transcendent glory of Christ, true Christians see him to be worthy to be followed, and so are powerfully drawn after him. They see him to be worthy that they should forsake all for him. By the sight of that surpassing loveliness they are thoroughly disposed to be subject to him, and committed to labor with earnestness and activity in his service, and made willing to go through all difficulties for his sake. And it is the manifestation of this divine excellence of Christ that makes them constant to him. For it makes so deep an impression on their minds that they cannot forget him. They will follow him wherever he goes, and it is useless for anyone to try to draw them away from him.

The reason for this practical tendency and issue of gracious affections appears further from what has been observed of such affections being accompanied by a thorough conviction of the judgment of the reality and certainty of divine things. No wonder that those who were never thoroughly convinced that there is any reality in the things of religion will never go to the labor and trouble of such an earnest, universal and persevering practice of religion, through all difficulties, self-denials and sufferings, depending on something they are not convinced of. But on the other hand, those who are thoroughly convinced of the certain truth of those things must be governed by them in their practice. For the things revealed in the word of God are so great, and so infinitely more important than all other things, that it is inconsistent with human nature for a man fully to believe their truth and not be influenced by them above all things in his practice.

Again, the reason for this expression and effect of holy affections in practice appears from what has been observed of a change of nature that accompanies such affections. Without a change of nature, men’s practice will not be thoroughly changed. Until the tree is made good, the fruit will not be good. Men do not gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles. The pig may be washed, and look clean for a little while, but without a change of nature it will still wallow in the mire. Nature is a more powerful principle of action than anything that opposes it. Though it may be forcibly restrained for a while, it will in the end overcome what restrains it. It is like the stream of a river: it may be stopped for a while with a dam, but if nothing is done to dry up the spring, it will not be stopped forever; it will find a course, either in its old channel or a new one. Nature is something more constant and lasting than any of the things on which carnal men’s reformation and righteousness are founded. When a natural man denies his lust, and lives a strict, religious life, and seems humble, painstaking and earnest in religion, it is not natural; it is all a force against nature, as when a stone is thrown violently upward. That force will gradually be spent, but nature will remain in its full strength, and so it prevails again, and the stone comes back down. As long as corrupt nature is not mortified, but the principle is left whole in a man, it is useless to expect that it will not govern. But if the old nature is truly mortified, and a new and heavenly nature infused, then it may well be expected that men will walk in newness of life, and continue to do so to the end of their days.

The reason for this practical exercise and effect of holy affections may also be partly seen from what has been said of the spirit of humility that accompanies them. A spirit of obedience consists very much in humility. A proud spirit is a rebellious spirit, but a humble spirit is a yielding, submissive, obedient spirit. We see among men that a servant who is of a haughty spirit is not inclined to be submissive and obedient to his master’s will in everything; but it is otherwise with a servant who is of a lowly spirit.

And the lamblike, dovelike spirit that has been spoken of, which accompanies all gracious affections, fulfills (as the apostle observes, Rom 13:8, 9, 10, and Gal 5:14) all the duties of the second table of the law. Christian practice consists very much in these duties, and the outward practice of Christianity chiefly consists in them.

And the reason gracious affections are accompanied by the strict, universal and constant obedience that has been spoken of appears further from what has been observed of the tenderness of spirit that accompanies the affections of true saints. It gives them so quick and lively a sense of pain at the presence of moral evil, and such a dread of the appearance of evil.

And one great reason the Christian practice that flows from gracious affections is universal, constant and persevering appears from what has been observed of those affections themselves, from which this practice flows: that they are universal and constant, in all kinds of holy exercises, toward all objects, in all circumstances and at all seasons, in a beautiful symmetry and proportion.

And much of the reason holy affections are expressed and shown in such earnestness, activity, commitment and perseverance in holy practice as has been spoken of appears from what has been observed of the spiritual appetite and longing for further attainments in religion, which always accompanies true affection, and does not decay but increases as those affections increase.

So we see how the tendency of holy affections to such a Christian practice as has been explained appears from each of the characteristics of holy affection spoken of before.

And this point may be further illustrated and confirmed if we consider where the holy Scriptures abundantly place sincerity and soundness in religion. They place it in making a full choice of God as our only Lord and portion, forsaking all for him; in a full determination of the will for God and Christ, after counting the cost; in our hearts taking up and complying with the religion of Jesus Christ, with all that belongs to it, embracing it with all its difficulties, as it were hating our dearest earthly enjoyments, and even our own lives, for Christ; in giving up ourselves, with all that we have, wholly and forever, to Christ, without keeping anything back or making any reserve; or, in one word, in the great duty of self-denial for Christ, that is, in denying, as it were disowning and renouncing, ourselves for him, making ourselves nothing so that he may be all. See the texts to this effect referred to in the margin.86 Now surely, having a heart to forsake all for Christ tends to actually forsaking all for him, so far as there is occasion and we are put to the trial. And having a heart to deny ourselves for Christ tends to denying ourselves in deed when Christ and self-interest stand in competition. Giving up ourselves, with all that we have, in our hearts, without making any reserve there, tends to our behaving universally as his, as subject to his will and devoted to his ends. Our hearts entirely taking up the religion of Jesus, with all that belongs to it and with all the difficulties that come with it, after deliberately counting the cost, tends to a universal taking up of the same in act and deed: to actually going through all the difficulties we meet with in the way of religion, and so holding out with patience and perseverance.

The tendency of grace in the heart to holy practice is very direct, and the connection most natural, close and necessary. True grace is not an inactive thing. There is nothing in heaven or earth of a more active nature, for it is life itself, and the most active kind of life, spiritual and divine life. It is no barren thing. There is nothing in the universe that by its nature has a greater tendency to fruit. Godliness in the heart has as direct a relation to practice as a fountain has to a stream, or as the luminous nature of the sun has to the beams it sends out, or as life has to breathing, or the beating of the pulse, or any other vital act; or as a habit or principle of action has to action. For it is the very nature and idea of grace that it is a principle of holy action or practice. Regeneration, the work of God in which grace is infused, has a direct relation to practice. For practice is the very end of it, the end in view of which the whole work is done. In this mighty and manifold change worked in the soul, everything is designed and framed so as to tend directly to this end. Eph 2:10: “For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works.” Indeed, it is the very end of the redemption of Christ. Titus 2:14: “He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds.” 2 Cor 5:15: “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them and was raised again.” Heb 9:14: “How much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God!” Col 1:21, 22: “Once you+ were alienated from God and were hostile in your+ minds, engaging in evil deeds. But now He has reconciled you+ by Christ’s physical body through death to present you+ holy, unblemished, and blameless in His presence.” 1 Pet 1:18: “For you+ know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you+ were redeemed from the empty way of life”—. Luke 1:74, 75: “deliverance from hostile hands, that we may serve Him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before Him all the days of our lives.” God often speaks of holy practice as the end of that great redemption that was a type, the redemption from Egyptian bondage, as in Exod 4:23: “Let My son go so that he may serve Me.” So also ch. 4:23, and 7:16, and 8:1, 20, and 9:1, 13, and 10:3. And this is also declared to be the end of election. John 15:16: “You+ did not choose Me, but I chose you+. And I appointed you+ to go and bear fruit—fruit that will remain.” Eph 1:4: “For He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in His presence. In love …” Chapter 2:10: “created … to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life.” Holy practice is as much the end of all God does with his saints as fruit is the end of all the farmer does for the growth of his field or vineyard, as Scripture often represents the matter: Matt 3:10; chapter 13:8, 23, 24–30, 38; chapter 21:19, 33, 34; Luke 13:6; John 15:1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8; 1 Cor 3:9; Heb 6:7, 8; Isa 5:1–8; Song 8:11, 12; Isa 27:2, 3.87 And so everything in a true Christian is designed to reach this end. This fruit of holy practice is what every grace, and every manifestation, and every single thing that belongs to Christian experience, has a direct tendency to.88

The constant and unbreakable connection between a Christian principle and profession in the true saints and the fruit of holy practice in their lives was typified of old in the make of the golden lampstand in the temple. It is beyond doubt that the golden lampstand, with its seven branches and seven lamps, was a type of the church of Christ. The Holy Spirit himself has been pleased to put the matter beyond doubt by representing his church by such a golden lampstand with seven lamps in the fourth chapter of Zechariah, and by representing the seven churches of Asia by seven golden lampstands in the first chapter of Revelation. That golden lampstand in the temple was made everywhere, throughout its whole frame, with knops and flowers (Exod 25:31 to the end, and ch. 37:17–24). The word translated knop means in the original an apple or pomegranate. There was a knop and a flower, a knop and a flower: wherever there was a flower, there was an apple or pomegranate with it. The flower and the fruit were constantly joined, without fail. The flower contained the principles of the fruit, and a beautiful, promising appearance of it; and it never was a deceptive appearance. The principle or show of fruit always had real fruit accompanying it or following it. So it is in the church of Christ. There is the principle of fruit in grace in the heart. There is a lovely profession, signified by the open flowers of the lampstand. And there is fruit to match, in holy practice, constantly accompanying this principle and profession. Every branch of the golden lampstand, made up in this way of golden apples and flowers, was crowned on its top with a burning, shining lamp. For it is by this means that the saints shine as lights in the world: by making a fair and good profession of religion, and having their profession always joined with fruit to match it in practice. This agrees with our Savior’s words in Matt 5:15, 16: “Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a basket. Instead, they set it on a stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house. In the same way, let your+ light shine before men, that they may see your+ good works and glorify your+ Father in heaven.” A fair and beautiful profession and golden fruits accompanying one another are the lovely ornaments of the true church of Christ. That is why we find that apples and flowers were the ornaments not only of the lampstand in the temple, but of the temple itself, which is a type of the church, which the apostle tells us is the temple of the living God. See 1 Kgs 6:18: “The cedar paneling inside the temple was carved with knops and open flowers.” The ornaments and crown of the pillars at the entrance of the temple were of the same sort: they were lilies and pomegranates, that is, flowers and fruits mixed together (1 Kgs 7:18, 19). So it is with all those who are as pillars in the temple of God, who will never again go out, or never be thrown out as intruders, as it is with all true saints. Rev 3:12: “The one who overcomes I will make a pillar in the temple of My God, and he will never again leave it.”

Much the same thing seems to be signified by the ornaments on the skirt of the ephod, the garment of Aaron the high priest, which were golden bells and pomegranates. That these skirts of Aaron’s garment represent the church, or the saints (who are, as it were, the garment of Christ), is plain, for they are evidently spoken of in this way in Ps 133:1, 2: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony! It is like fine oil on the head, running down on the beard, running down Aaron’s beard to the skirts of his robes.” That ephod of Aaron signified the same thing as the seamless coat of Christ, our great high priest. As Christ’s coat had no seam but was woven in one piece from the top, so it was with the ephod (Exod 39:22). As God took care in his providence that Christ’s coat should not be torn, so God took special care that the ephod should not be torn (Exod 28:32, and ch. 39:23). The golden bells on this ephod, by their precious material and pleasant sound, well represent the good profession the saints make, and the pomegranates the fruit they bring forth. And in the hem of the ephod bells and pomegranates were constantly joined, as is observed again and again: there was a golden bell and a pomegranate, a golden bell and a pomegranate (Exod 28:34, and ch. 39:26). So it is in the true saints: their good profession and their good fruit constantly accompany one another. The fruit they bring forth in their lives always answers to the pleasant sound of their profession.

Again, the very same thing is represented by Christ in his description of his bride, Song 7:2: “Your waist is a mound of wheat encircled by the lilies.” Here again are beautiful flowers and good fruit accompanying one another. The lilies were fair and beautiful flowers, and the wheat was good fruit.

As this fruit of Christian practice is always found in true saints, as they have opportunity and trial, so it is found in them only. None but true Christians live such an obedient life, so universally devoted to their duty and given up to the business of a Christian, as has been explained. All unsanctified men are workers of iniquity. They are of their father the devil, and the lusts of their father they will do. There is no hypocrite who will go through with the business of religion, and both begin and finish the tower. They will not endure the trials God usually brings on those who profess religion, but will turn aside to their crooked ways. They will not be thoroughly faithful to Christ in their practice and follow him wherever he goes. Whatever lengths they may go in religion in some instances, and though they may appear exceedingly strict and mightily engaged in the service of God for a season, yet they are servants of sin. The chains of their old taskmasters are not broken; their lusts still have a reigning power in their hearts; and so to these masters they will bow down again.89 Dan 12:10: “Many will be purified, made spotless, and refined, but the wicked will continue to act wickedly. None of the wicked will understand.” Isa 26: “Though grace is shown to the wicked man, he does not learn righteousness. In the land of righteousness he acts unjustly.” Isa 35:8: “And there will be a highway called the Way of Holiness. The unclean will not travel it.” Hos 14:9: “The ways of the Lord are right, and the righteous walk in them but the rebellious stumble in them.” Job 27:8, 9, 10: “What is the hope of the hypocrite …? Will he delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?” An unsanctified man may hide his sin, and may in many things and for a season refrain from sin. But he will not be brought finally to renounce his sin and give it a bill of divorce. Sin is too dear to him for him to be willing to do that. “Evil is sweet in his mouth,” and so “he conceals it under his tongue”; “he cannot bear to let it go and keeps it in his mouth” (Job 20:12, 13). It is chiefly in this that the narrowness of the gate and of the way that leads to life consists, on account of which carnal men will not go in by it: namely, that it is a way of utterly denying and finally renouncing all ungodliness, and so a way of self-denial or self-renunciation.

Many natural men, under the means used with them and God’s strivings with them to bring them to forsake their sins, treat their sins as Pharaoh treated his pride and covetousness, which he gratified by keeping the children of Israel in bondage, when God strove with him to bring him to let the people go. When God’s hand pressed Pharaoh hard, and he was troubled with fears of God’s future wrath, he had some thoughts of letting the people go, and promised he would do it. But time after time he broke his promises when he saw there was a respite.
