When God filled Egypt with thunder and lightning, and the fire ran along the ground, then Pharaoh is brought to confess his sin with seeming humility, and to make a great resolution to let the people go. Exod 9:27, 28: “Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron. ‘This time I have sinned,’ he said. ‘The Lord is righteous, and I and my people are wicked. Pray to the Lord, for there has been enough of God’s thunder and hail. I will let you+ go; you+ do not need to stay any longer.’ ” So sinners are sometimes brought by thunders and lightnings, and great terrors of the law, to a seeming work of humbling, and to all appearance to part with their sins. But they are no more thoroughly brought to a disposition to let them go than Pharaoh was to let the people go. Pharaoh, in the struggle between his conscience and his lusts, was for contriving a way in which God might be served and he might also enjoy his lusts, which were gratified by the slavery of the people. Moses insisted that Israel’s God should be served and sacrificed to. Pharaoh was willing to consent to that, but would have it done without parting with the people. “Go, sacrifice to your+ God within this land,” he says (Exod 8:25). So many sinners are for contriving to serve God and enjoy their lusts too. Moses objected to complying with Pharaoh’s proposal, on the ground that serving God and yet staying in Egypt under their taskmasters did not agree together, and were inconsistent with each other. (There is no serving God and continuing as slaves to such enemies of God at the same time.) After this Pharaoh consented to let the people go, provided they would not go very far away. He was not willing to part with them finally, and so would have them within reach. So do many hypocrites with their sins. Afterward Pharaoh consented to let the men go, if they would leave the women and children (Exod 10:8, 9, 10). And then after that, when God’s hand was still harder on him, he consented that they should go, women and children as well as men, provided they would leave their cattle behind. But he was not willing to let them go with all they had (Exod 10:24). So it often is with sinners. They are willing to part with some of their sins, but not all. They are brought to part with the grosser acts of sin, but not to part with their lusts in lesser indulgences of them. Yet we must part with all our sins, little and great, and all that belongs to them, men, women, children and cattle. They must all be let go, with their young and their old, with their sons and their daughters, with their flocks and their herds; not a hoof must be left behind, as Moses told Pharaoh concerning the children of Israel. At last, when it came to the extreme, Pharaoh consented to let the people all go, with all they had. But he was not steadfastly of that mind. He soon repented, and pursued them again. And the reason was that those lusts of pride and covetousness that were gratified by Pharaoh’s dominion over the people, and the gains of their service, were never really mortified in him, but only forcibly restrained. And so, being guilty of backsliding after his seeming compliance with God’s commands, he was destroyed without remedy. In the same way there may be a forced parting with ways of disobedience to the commands of God that may seem to be universal, as far as appears, for a little while. But because it is mere force, without the mortification of the inward principle of sin, they will not persevere in it, but will return like the dog to its vomit, and so bring on themselves dreadful destruction without remedy. There were many false disciples in Christ’s time who followed him for a while. But none of them followed him to the end; some on one occasion and some on another went back and walked with him no more.90

From what has been said it is clear that Christian practice, or a holy life, is a great and distinguishing sign of true and saving grace. But I may go further and assert that it is the chief of all the signs of grace, both as an evidence of the sincerity of professing Christians to others and also to their own consciences.

But then it is necessary that this be taken rightly, and that it be well understood and observed in what sense and manner Christian practice is the greatest sign of grace. So, to set this matter in a clear light, I will try to prove particularly and distinctly that Christian practice is the principal sign by which Christians are to judge of the sincerity of godliness, both their own and others’. At the same time I will observe some things that need to be particularly noted for a right understanding of this matter.

(1.) I will consider Christian practice and a holy life as a manifestation and sign of the sincerity of a professing Christian to the eye of his neighbors and brothers.

And that this is the chief sign of grace in this respect is very evident from the word of God. Christ, who knew best how to give us rules for judging others, has repeated and pressed home that we should know them by their fruits. Matt 7:16: “By their fruit you+ will recognize them.” And then, after arguing the point and giving clear reasons in the following verses why men’s fruits must be the chief evidence of what sort they are, he closes by repeating the assertion in verse 20: “So then, by their fruit you+ will recognize them.” Again, ch. 12:33: “Make a tree good and its fruit will be good, or make a tree bad and its fruit will be bad.”—As much as to say: it is a very absurd thing for anyone to suppose that the tree is good and yet the fruit bad, that the tree is of one sort and the fruit of another; for the proper evidence of the nature of the tree is its fruit. Nothing else can be meant by the last clause of the verse, “for a tree is known by its fruit,” than that the tree is chiefly known by its fruit: that this is the main and most proper diagnostic by which one tree is distinguished from another. So Luke 6:44: “Each tree is known by its own fruit.” Christ nowhere says, “You+ will know the tree by its leaves or flowers,” or “You+ will know men by their talk,” or “You+ will know them by the good story they tell of their experiences,” or “You+ will know them by the manner and air of their speaking, and the emphasis and pathos of their expression,” or “by their speaking feelingly,” or “by their making a very great show by an abundance of talk,” or “by many tears and heartfelt expressions,” or “by the affections you+ feel in your+ hearts toward them.” He says, by their fruit you+ will recognize them; a tree is known by its fruit; each tree is known by its own fruit. And as this is the evidence Christ has directed us mainly to look at in others when we judge them, so it is the evidence Christ has mainly directed us to give to others, by which they may judge of us. Matt 5:16: “Let your+ light shine before men, that they may see your+ good works and glorify your+ Father in heaven.” Here Christ directs us to show our godliness to others. Godliness is, as it were, a light that shines in the soul. Christ directs that this light should not only shine within, but should shine out before men, so that they may see it. But in what way will this be? It is by our good works. Christ does not say, “that others, hearing your+ good words, your+ good story, or your+ moving expressions,” but “that they may see your+ good works and glorify your+ Father in heaven.” Doubtless when Christ gives us a rule for making our light shine, so that others may have evidence of it, his rule is the best there is. And the apostles mention Christian practice as the principal ground of their esteem of persons as true Christians. So the apostle Paul does in the 6th chapter of Hebrews. At the beginning of the chapter the apostle speaks there of those who have great common illuminations, who have been enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift, have shared in the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the coming age, and afterward fall away, and are like barren ground, whose curse is imminent; in the end it will be burned. And then he immediately adds in the 9th verse (expressing his charitable judgment of the Christian Hebrews, as having the saving grace that is better than all these common illuminations), “Even though we speak like this, beloved, we are convinced of better things in your+ case—things that accompany salvation.” And then in the next verse he tells them why he had such good thoughts of them. He does not say that it was because they had given him a good account of a work of God on their souls and talked very experientially. It was their work and labor of love: “For God is not unjust. He will not forget your+ work and labor of love that you+ have shown for His name as you+ have ministered to the saints and continue to do so.” And the same apostle speaks of faithfully serving God in practice as the proper proof to others of men’s loving Christ above all and preferring his honor to their private interest. Phil 2:21, 22: “For all the others look after their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you+ know the proof of him, that as a child with his father he has served with me to advance the gospel.” So the apostle John expresses the same thing as the ground of his good opinion of Gaius. 3 John 3, 4, 5, 6: “For I was overjoyed when the brothers came and testified of the truth that is in you.” But how did the brothers testify of the truth that was in Gaius? And how did the apostle judge of the truth that was in him? It was not because they testified that he had given them a good account of the steps of his experiences, and talked like one who felt what he said, and had the very language of a Christian. They testified that he walked in the truth, as it follows: “just as you continue to walk in the truth. I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth. Beloved, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you. They have testified to the church about your love.” In this way the apostle explains what the brothers had borne witness to when they came and testified of his walking in the truth. And in this same place the apostle seems to give it to Gaius as a rule for how he should judge others. In verse 10 he mentions one Diotrephes, who did not conduct himself well and led others away after him. Then in the 11th verse he directs Gaius to beware of such men and not to follow them, and gives him a rule by which he may know them, exactly agreeing with the rule Christ had given before, By their fruit you+ will recognize them. The apostle says, “Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God.” And I would further observe that the apostle James, expressly comparing the way of showing others our faith and Christianity by our practice or works with other ways of showing our faith without works, or not by works, plainly and abundantly prefers the former. Jas 2:18: “But someone will say, ‘You have faith and I have works.’ Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith by my works.” A manifestation of our faith without works, or in a way different from works, is a manifestation of it in words, by which a man professes faith. As the apostle says in v. 14: “What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith?”—So here are two ways of showing our neighbor what is in our hearts: one by what we say, and the other by what we do. But the apostle abundantly prefers the latter as the best evidence. Now certainly all the accounts we give of ourselves in words (our saying that we have faith and that we are converted, and telling the manner in which we came to have faith, and the steps by which it was worked, and the manifestations and experiences that accompanied it) are still only showing our faith by what we say. It is only showing our faith by our words, which the apostle speaks of as falling vastly short of showing it by what we do, and showing our faith by our works.

And as Scripture plainly teaches that practice is the best evidence of the sincerity of professing Christians, so reason teaches the same thing. Reason shows that men’s deeds are better and more faithful interpreters of their minds than their words. The common sense of all mankind, through all ages and nations, teaches them to judge men’s hearts chiefly by their practice in other matters: whether a man is a loyal subject, a true lover, a dutiful child or a faithful servant. If a man professes a great deal of love and friendship to another, reason teaches all men that such a profession is not so great an evidence of his being a real and hearty friend as his showing himself a friend in deeds: being faithful and constant to his friend in prosperity and adversity, ready to spend himself, and deny himself, and suffer in his personal interest, to do him a kindness. A wise man will trust such evidences of the sincerity of friendship further than a thousand earnest professions and solemn declarations and most affectionate expressions of friendship in words. And there is equal reason why practice should also be looked on as the best evidence of friendship toward Christ. Reason says the same as Christ said in John 14:21: “Whoever has My commandments and keeps them is the one who loves Me.” So if we see a man who in the course of his life seems to follow and imitate Christ, and greatly to exert and deny himself for the honor of Christ and to promote his kingdom and interest in the world, reason teaches that this is an evidence of love to Christ more to be depended on than if a man only says he has love to Christ and tells of the inward experiences he has had of love to him, what strong love he felt, and how his heart was drawn out in love at such and such a time, when perhaps little imitation of Christ appears in his behavior. He seems reluctant to do any great thing for him, or to put himself out of his way to promote his kingdom, but seems inclined to excuse himself whenever he is called to deny himself for Christ. So it is if a man, in declaring his experiences, tells how he found his heart weaned from the world and saw its vanity, so that it all looked like nothing to him at such and such times, and professes that he gives up all to God, and calls heaven and earth to witness it; but yet in his practice he is violent in pursuing the world, and what he gets he keeps tight hold of. He is exceedingly unwilling to part with much of it for charitable and pious uses; it comes from him almost like his heart’s blood. But there is another professing Christian who does not say a great deal, yet in his behavior appears ready at all times to forsake the world whenever it stands in the way of his duty, and is free to part with it at any time to promote religion and the good of his fellow creatures. Reason teaches that the latter gives by far the more credible manifestation of a heart weaned from the world. And if a man appears to walk humbly before God and men, and to be of a conduct that savors of a broken heart, appearing patient and resigned to God under affliction and meek in his behavior among men, this is a better evidence of humbling than if a person only tells how great a sense he had of his own unworthiness, how he was brought to lie in the dust, and was quite emptied of himself, and saw himself as nothing and as altogether filthy and abominable, etc., but yet acts as if he looked on himself as one of the first and best of saints, and by just right the head of all the Christians in the town, and is presumptuous, self-willed and impatient of the least contradiction or opposition. We may be sure in such a case that a man’s practice comes from a lower place in his heart than his profession. So (to mention no more instances) if a professing Christian shows in his behavior a pitying, tender spirit toward others in calamity, ready to bear their burdens with them, willing to spend his substance for them, and to suffer many inconveniences in his worldly interest to promote the good of others’ souls and bodies: is not this a more credible manifestation of a spirit of love to men than a man’s merely telling what love he felt for others at certain times, how he pitied their souls, how his soul was in labor for them, and how he felt a hearty love and pity for his enemies, when in his behavior he seems to be of a very selfish spirit, tight-fisted and stingy, all for himself and nothing for his neighbors, and perhaps envious and quarrelsome? Persons in a sudden surge of affection may think they have a willing heart for great things, to do much and to suffer much, and so may profess it very earnestly and confidently, when really their hearts are far from it. In this way many, in their surges of affection, have thought themselves willing to be damned eternally for the glory of God. Passing affections easily produce words, and words are cheap; and godliness is more easily feigned in words than in actions. Christian practice is a costly, laborious thing. The self-denial required of Christians, and the narrowness of the way that leads to life, do not consist in words but in practice. Hypocrites may much more easily be brought to talk like saints than to act like saints.

So it is plain that Christian practice is the best sign or manifestation of the true godliness of a professing Christian to the eye of his neighbors.

But then the following things should be well observed, so that this matter may be rightly understood.

[1.] First, it must be observed that when Scripture speaks of Christian practice as the best evidence to others of sincerity and truth of grace, a profession of Christianity is not excluded but presupposed. The rules mentioned were given to the followers of Christ to guide them in their thoughts of professing Christians, and of those who offered themselves as members of their society, so that they might judge by them of the truth of their claims and the sincerity of the profession they made. They were not given for the trial of heathens, or of those who made no claim to Christianity and with whom Christians had nothing to do. This is as plain as possible in the great rule Christ gives in the 7th chapter of Matthew, By their fruit you+ will recognize them. He gives a rule there for judging those who professed to be Christians, indeed who made a very high profession: false prophets, who come in sheep’s clothing, as in verse 15. So it is also with the words of the apostle James, ch. 2:18: “Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith by my works.” It is evident that both these sorts of persons, offering to give these different evidences of their faith, are persons who profess faith. This is implied in each of them offering to give evidences of the faith he professed. And it is evident from the preceding verses that the apostle is speaking of those who profess faith in Jesus Christ. So it is very plain that the apostle John, in the passages observed in his third epistle, is speaking of professing Christians. In these rules the Christian practice of those who profess is spoken of as the greatest and most distinguishing sign of their sincerity in their profession, much more of an evidence than their profession itself. Yet a profession of Christianity is plainly presupposed. It is not the main thing in the evidence, nor anything distinguishing in it; yet it is a thing required and necessary in it. In the same way, having an animal body is nothing that distinguishes a man from other creatures, and is not the main thing in the evidence of human nature; yet it is a thing required and necessary in the evidence. So if any man should say plainly that he was not a Christian, and did not believe that Jesus was the Son of God, or a person sent by God, these rules of Christ and his apostles do not at all oblige us to look on him as a sincere Christian, whatever his visible practice and virtues may be. And these rules have no place not only with respect to a man who explicitly denies Christianity and is a professed deist, Jew, heathen or open unbeliever, but also with respect to a man who merely refrains from making a profession of Christianity. For these rules were given us only for judging professing Christians. Fruits must be joined with open flowers; bells and pomegranates go together.

But here this question will naturally arise: when may a man be said to profess Christianity, or what profession may properly be called a profession of Christianity?

I answer in two things.

1st. For a man to be properly said to make a profession of Christianity, there must undoubtedly be a profession of all that is necessary to his being a Christian, or of as much as belongs to the essence of Christianity. Whatever is essential in Christianity itself, the profession of that is essential in the profession of Christianity. The profession must be of the thing professed. For a man to profess Christianity is for him to declare that he has it. And so, as much as belongs to a thing, so as to be necessary for its being truly called that thing, so much is essential to the declaration of that thing, for it to be truly called a declaration of that thing. If we take only a part of Christianity, and leave out a part that is essential to it, what we take is not Christianity, because something of its essence is missing. So if we profess only a part, and leave out a part that is essential, what we profess is not Christianity. So, to make a profession of Christianity, we must profess that we believe that Jesus is the Messiah, for this reason: such a belief is essential to Christianity. And so we must profess, either expressly or implicitly, that Jesus made satisfaction for our sins, and other essential doctrines of the gospel, because belief of these things is also essential to Christianity. But there are other things as essential to religion as an orthodox belief, and so it is just as necessary that we profess them if we are truly to be said to profess Christianity. So it is essential to Christianity that we repent of our sins; that we are convicted of our own sinfulness and have a sense that we have justly exposed ourselves to God’s wrath; that our hearts renounce all sin; that we embrace Christ with our whole hearts as our only Savior; that we love him above all and are willing for his sake to forsake all; and that we give ourselves up to be entirely and forever his, etc. Such things as these belong as much to the essence of Christianity as the belief of any of the doctrines of the gospel, and so the profession of them belongs as much to a Christian profession. Not that, to be professing Christians, it is necessary to make an explicit profession of every single thing that belongs to Christian grace or virtue. But certainly there must be a profession, either express or implicit, of what is of the essence of religion. And as to the things Christians should express in their profession, we ought to be guided by the precepts of God’s word, or by the Scripture examples of the public professions of religion God’s people have made from time to time. So they ought to profess their repentance of sin, as of old, when persons were admitted as professing believers, they came confessing their sins and showing that they were humbled for sin (Matt 3:6). And the baptism they were baptized with was called the baptism of repentance (Mark 1:4). And John, when he had baptized them, urged them to bring forth fruit in keeping with repentance (Matt 3:8), that is, agreeing with the repentance they had professed. He encouraged them that if they did so, they would escape the wrath to come and be gathered like wheat into God’s barn (Matt 3:7, 8, 9, 10, 12). So the apostle Peter says to the Jews in Acts 2:38, “Repent and be baptized,” which shows that repentance is a qualification that must be visible for baptism, and so ought to be publicly professed. So when the Jews who returned from captivity entered publicly into covenant, it was with confession, or a public profession of repentance of their sins (Neh 9:2). This profession of repentance should include or imply a profession of conviction that God would be just in our damnation: see Neh 9:33, together with verse 35, and the beginning of the next chapter. They should profess their faith in Jesus Christ: that they embrace Christ and rely on him as their Savior with their whole hearts, and that they joyfully welcome the gospel of Christ. So Philip, before baptizing the eunuch, required that he should profess that he believed with all his heart. And those who were received as visible Christians at the great outpouring of the Spirit that began on the day of Pentecost appeared gladly to receive the gospel. Acts 2:41: “Those who gladly received his message were baptized, and about three thousand were added to the believers that day.” They should profess that they rely only on Christ’s righteousness and strength, that they are devoted to him as their only Lord and Savior, and that they rejoice in him as their only righteousness and portion. It is foretold that all nations would be brought to make this profession publicly (Isa 45:22 to the end): “Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other. By Myself I have sworn; truth has gone out from My mouth, a word that will not be revoked: Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance. Surely they will say of Me, ‘In the Lord alone are righteousness and strength.’ All who rage against Him will come to Him and be put to shame. In the Lord all descendants of Israel will be justified and will exult.” They should profess to give themselves up entirely to Christ, and to God through him, as the children of Israel did when they publicly acknowledged their covenant with God. Deut 26:17: “Today you have proclaimed that the Lord is your God and that you will walk in His ways, keep His statutes and commandments and ordinances, and listen to His voice.” They ought to profess a willing heart to embrace religion with all its difficulties, and to walk in a way of obedience to God universally and perseveringly (Exod 19:8, and 24:3, 7; Deut 26:16, 17, 18; 2 Kgs 23:3; Neh 10:28, 29; Ps 119:57, 106). They ought to profess that all their hearts and souls are in these commitments to be the Lord’s and to serve him forever (2 Chr 15:12, 13, 14). God’s people’s swearing to God, and swearing by his name, or to his name, as it might be translated (which seems to signify their solemnly giving themselves up to him in covenant, and vowing to receive him as their God and to be entirely his, to obey and serve him), is spoken of as a duty to be performed by all God’s visible Israel (Deut 6:13, and 10:20; Ps 63:11; Isa 19:18; chapter 45:23, 24, compared with Romans 14:11 and Phil 2:10, 11; Isa 48:1, 2, and 65:15, 16; Jer 4:2, and 5:7, and 12:16; Hos 4:15, and 10:4). So, for persons to be entitled to full esteem and charity from their neighbors as sincere professing Christians, by the rules of Christ and his apostles mentioned before, there must be a visibly holy life, together with a profession either expressing or plainly implying such things as have now been mentioned. We are to know them by their fruits; that is, we are to know by their fruits whether they are what they profess to be. We are not to know by their fruits that they have something in them which they do not so much as claim to have.

And moreover,

2nd. The profession of these things that is properly called a Christian profession, and that must be joined with Christian practice for persons to be entitled to the benefit of those rules, must be made with understanding (as far as appears). That is, they must be persons who appear to have been instructed in the principles of religion far enough to be in an ordinary capacity to understand the proper meaning of what is expressed in their profession. For sounds signify or declare nothing any further than men understand the meaning of their own sounds.

But for persons to make a proper profession of Christianity, such as Scripture directs, and such as the followers of Christ should require before accepting those who profess with full charity as members of their society, it is not necessary that they give an account of the particular steps and method by which the Holy Spirit, perceptibly to them, worked and brought about those great essential things of Christianity in their hearts. There is no trace in Scripture of any such practice of the apostles, or of the first ministers and Christians, requiring any such account before they received and treated others as their Christian brothers in every respect, or of their first examining them about the particular method and order of their experiences. They required of them a profession of the things worked, but no account of the manner of working was required of them. Nor is there the least shadow in Scripture of any such custom in the church of God from Adam to the death of the apostle John.

I am far from saying that it is not required that persons give any sort of account of their experiences to their brothers. For persons to profess the things in which the essence of Christianity lies is the same thing as to profess that they experience those things. So it is when persons solemnly profess the following: that in a sense and full conviction of their own utter sinfulness, misery and helplessness, and totally undone state in themselves, and of their just desert of God’s utter rejection and eternal wrath without mercy, and of the utter insufficiency of their own righteousness, or of anything in them, to satisfy divine justice or recommend them to God’s favor, they depend only and entirely on the Lord Jesus Christ and his satisfaction and righteousness; that they believe the truth of the gospel of Christ with all their hearts; that in a full conviction and sense of his sufficiency and perfect excellence as a Savior, as set forth in the gospel, they cling to him with their whole souls and rest in him as the refuge and rest of their souls and the fountain of their comfort; that they repent of their sins, utterly renounce all sin, and give themselves up wholly to Christ, willingly submitting to him as their King; that they give him their hearts and their whole selves; that they are willing and resolved to have God for their whole and everlasting portion, and, depending on his promises of a future eternal enjoyment of him in heaven, to renounce all the enjoyments of this vain world, selling all for this great treasure and future inheritance, and to comply with every command of God, even the most difficult and self-denying, and to devote their whole lives to God’s service; and that, in forgiveness of those who have injured them and a general benevolence to mankind, their hearts are united to the people of Jesus Christ as their people, to cling to them and love them as their brothers, and to worship and serve God and follow Christ in union and fellowship with them, being willing and resolved to perform all the duties that belong to them as members of the same family of God and mystical body of Christ. I say, for persons solemnly to profess such things as these, as in the presence of God, is the same thing as to profess that they are conscious of, or experience, such things in their hearts.

Nor do I suppose that persons’ giving an account of their experience of particular exercises of grace, with the times and circumstances, gives others no help in forming a judgment of their state; or that persons may not properly be asked about these in some cases, especially cases of great importance, where all possible assurance about persons’ piety is especially to be desired and sought, as in the ordination or approval of a minister. It may help in forming a judgment in several respects; among others in this, that by it we may be better satisfied that the one who professes speaks honestly and with understanding in what he professes, and that he does not make the profession as a mere formality. For a profession of Christianity to be accepted to any purpose, there ought to be good reason, from the circumstances of the profession, to think that the one who professes does not make it out of mere customary compliance with a prescribed form, using words without any distinct meaning, or in a very loose and ambiguous way, as confessions of faith are often subscribed; but that he signifies with understanding and honesty what he is conscious of in his own heart. Otherwise his profession can be of no significance, and is no more to be regarded than the sound of lifeless things. But in fact (whatever help an account of particular exercises may give in judging this) it must be granted that the best evidence of it is that the one who professes has first been thoroughly instructed by his teachers, and gives good proof of his sufficient knowledge, together with a practice agreeing with his profession.

Nor do I deny that when a person who is asked about particular episodes, times and circumstances of his Christian experience seems, among other things, to be able to give a distinct account of the manner of his first conversion, in a way that has often been observed in true conversion, so that things seem perceptibly and distinctly to follow one another in the order of time according to the order of nature, this is an illustrating circumstance that, among other things, adds luster to the evidence he gives his brothers of the truth of his experiences.

But what I speak of as unscriptural is insisting on a particular account of the distinct method and steps in which the Spirit of God perceptibly proceeded in first bringing the soul into a state of salvation, as a thing required before receiving one who professes into full charity as a real Christian; or insisting on it so much that, for lack of such an account, other things in the evidence persons give their neighbors of their Christianity, things vastly more important and essential, are disregarded.

[2.] Secondly, to understand rightly how Christian practice is the greatest evidence others can have of the sincerity of a professing Christian, we need to bear in mind what was said before in showing what Christian practice is, and to consider how far this may be visible to others. That a professing Christian is merely what is commonly called an honest man and a moral man (that is, we have no particular transgression or iniquity to charge him with that might bring a blot on his character) is no great evidence of the sincerity of his profession. This is not letting his light shine before men. This is not that work and labor of love shown for Christ’s name which gave the apostle such persuasion of the sincerity of the professing Hebrews (Heb 6:9, 10). It may be that we see nothing in a man to show anything but that he may be a good man. Nothing may appear in his life and conduct that is inconsistent with his being godly, and yet there may not be any great positive evidence that he is so. But there may be great positive appearances of holiness in men’s visible behavior. Their life may appear to be a life of the service of God. They may appear to follow the example of Jesus Christ, and to come up in a great measure to the excellent rules in the 5th, 6th and 7th chapters of Matthew, and the 12th of Romans, and many other parts of the New Testament. There may be a great appearance of their being universal in their obedience to Christ’s commands and the rules of the gospel. They may appear to be universal in performing the duties of the first table, showing the fear and love of God; and also universal in fulfilling the rules of love to men, love to saints and love to enemies; rules of meekness and forgiveness; rules of mercy and charity, of looking not only to our own interests but also to the interests of others; rules of doing good to men’s souls and bodies, to particular persons and to the public; rules of temperance and mortification and of a humble conduct; rules of bridling the tongue, and of using it to glorify God and bless men, showing that the law of kindness is on their tongues. They may appear to walk as Christians in all places and at all seasons: in the house of God, in their families and among their neighbors, on Sabbath days and every day, in business and in company, toward friends and enemies, toward superiors, inferiors and equals. Persons in their visible walk may appear to be very earnestly engaged in the service of God and mankind, to labor and spend themselves much in this work of a Christian, and to be very constant and steadfast in it under all circumstances and temptations. There may be great evidences of a spirit willing to deny themselves and suffer for God and Christ, for the interest of religion and for the benefit of their brothers. There may be great appearances in a man’s walk of a disposition to forsake anything rather than forsake Christ, and to make everything give way to his honor. There may be great evidences in a man’s behavior that such religion as this is his element, and that he places the delight and happiness of his life in it. And his conduct may be such that he carries with him a sweet fragrance of Christian graces and heavenly dispositions wherever he goes. And when it is like this with those who profess Christianity, here is an evidence to others of their sincerity in their profession to which all other manifestations are not worthy to be compared.

There is doubtless a great variety in the degrees of evidence professing Christians give of their sincerity in their life and practice, just as there is a variety in the fairness and clearness of the accounts persons give of the manner and method of their experiences. But undoubtedly such a manifestation of a Christian spirit in practice as has been described is vastly beyond the fairest and brightest story of particular steps and episodes of experience that was ever told. And in general a manifestation of the sincerity of a Christian profession in practice is far better than an account of experiences.

But yet,

[3.] Thirdly, it must be noted, in agreement with what was observed earlier, that no outward manifestations and appearances whatever that are visible to the world are infallible evidences of grace. The manifestations that have been mentioned are the best mankind can have. They are such as oblige Christians to embrace wholeheartedly as saints those who profess, and to love them and rejoice in them as the children of God. They are enough to give them as great assurance concerning them as is ever needed to guide them in their conduct, or for any purpose that needs to be served in this world. But nothing that appears to them in their neighbor can be enough to produce absolute certainty about the state of his soul. For they do not see his heart; nor can they see all his outward behavior, for much of it is in secret and hidden from the eye of the world. And it is impossible to determine with certainty how far a man may go, from other principles, in many outward appearances and imitations of grace. Yet undoubtedly, if others could see as much of what belongs to men’s practice as their own consciences may see of it, it might be an infallible evidence of their state, as will appear from what follows.

Having considered Christian practice in this way as the best evidence of the sincerity of professing Christians to others, I now go on

(2.) to observe that Scripture also speaks of Christian practice as a distinguishing and sure evidence of grace to persons’ own consciences. This is very plain in 1 John 2:3: “By this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments.” And the testimony of our consciences concerning our good deeds is spoken of as something that may give us assurance of our own godliness. 1 John 3:18, 19: “Little children, let us love not in word and speech, but in action” (in the original it is ΕΡΓΩ, in work) “and truth. And by this we will know that we belong to the truth, and will assure our hearts in His presence.” And the apostle Paul in Hebrews 6 speaks of the work and labor of love of the Christian Hebrews both as what persuaded him that they had something above the highest common illuminations, and as the evidence that tended to give them the highest assurance of hope concerning themselves. V. 9, etc.: “Even though we speak like this, beloved, we are convinced of better things in your+ case—things that accompany salvation. For God is not unjust. He will not forget your+ work and labor of love that you+ have shown for His name as you+ have ministered to the saints and continue to do so. We want each of you+ to show this same diligence to the full assurance of hope to the very end.” So the apostle directs the Galatians to examine their behavior or practice, so that they might have rejoicing in themselves in their own happy state. Gal 6:4: “Each one should test his own work. Then he will have reason to rejoice in himself alone, and not in someone else.” And the psalmist says in Ps 119:6, “Then I would not be ashamed when I heed all Your commandments”; that is, then I will be bold, assured and steadfast in my hope. And so it is with our Savior’s words in Matt 7:19, 20: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. So then, by their fruit you+ will recognize them.” Though Christ gives this first as a rule by which we should judge others, yet in the words that follow next he plainly shows that he also intends it as a rule by which we should judge ourselves: “Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only he who does the will of My Father in heaven. Many will say to Me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord,’ etc.—Then I will tell them plainly, ‘I never knew you+; depart from Me, you+ workers of lawlessness!’ Therefore everyone who hears these words of Mine and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock.—But everyone who hears these words of Mine and does not act on them is like a foolish man who built his house on sand.” I will have occasion later to mention other texts that show the same thing.

But for greater clearness in this matter, I would first show how Christian practice, doing good works or keeping Christ’s commandments, is to be taken when Scripture represents it as a sure sign to our own consciences that we are real Christians. And secondly, I will prove that this is the chief of all the evidences men can have of their own sincere godliness.

[1.] First, I would show how Christian practice, or keeping Christ’s commandments, is to be taken when Scripture represents it as a sure evidence to our own consciences that we are sincere Christians.

And here I would observe that we cannot reasonably suppose that when Scripture speaks in this case of good works, good fruit and keeping Christ’s commandments, it has in view merely what is outward, the motion and action of the body, without including anything else, with no regard to any aim or intention of the agent, or to any act of his understanding or will. For consider men’s actions in that way, and they are no more good works or acts of obedience than the regular motions of a clock. Nor are they considered as the actions of the men, or as any human actions at all. The actions of the body, taken in that way, are neither acts of obedience nor of disobedience, any more than the motions of the body in a convulsion. But the obedience and fruit spoken of is the obedience and fruit of the man; and so not only the acts of the body, but the obedience of the soul, consisting in the acts and practice of the soul. Not that I suppose that when Scripture speaks in this case of gracious works and fruit and practice, these expressions include all inward piety and holiness of heart, both principle and exercise, both spirit and practice. For then, in giving these things as signs of a gracious principle in the heart, the same thing would be given as a sign of itself, and there would be no distinction between root and fruit. What is meant, and given as the sign of the holy principle and good state, is only the gracious exercise and holy act of the soul. Nor is every kind of inward exercise of grace meant, but the practical exercise: the exercise of the soul and exertion of inward holiness that there is in an act of obedience; or the exertion of the mind and act of grace that issues and ends in what are called the imperate acts of the will, the acts in which the soul directs and commands something to be done and brought about in practice.

Here, for a clearer understanding, I would observe that there are two kinds of exercises of grace. 1. There are what some call immanent acts: that is, exercises of grace that remain within the soul, that begin and end there, without any immediate relation to anything to be done outwardly or brought about in practice. Such are the exercises of grace the saints often have in contemplation, when the exercise in the heart does not proceed directly to, or end in, anything beyond the thoughts of the mind, however they may tend to practice more remotely (as all exercises of grace do). 2. There is another kind of acts of grace, which are more strictly called practical or effective exercises, because they immediately concern something to be done. They are the exertions of grace in the commanding acts of the will, directing the outward actions. So it is when a saint gives a cup of cold water to a disciple in and from the exercise of the grace of charity, or willingly endures persecution in the way of his duty immediately from the exercise of a supreme love to Christ. Here is the exertion of grace producing its effect in outward actions. These exercises of grace are practical and productive of good works, not only in the sense that they are of a productive nature (for so are all exercises of true grace), but they are the producing acts. This is properly the exercise of grace in the act of the will, and this is properly the practice of the soul. And the soul is the immediate actor of no other practice but this. The motions of the body follow from the laws of union between the soul and body, which God, and not the soul, has fixed and maintains. The act of the soul, and the exercise of grace that is exerted in the performance of a good work, is the good work itself, as far as the soul is concerned in it, or as far as it is the soul’s good work. The determinations of the will are indeed our very actions, as far as they are properly ours, as Dr. Doddridge observes.91 This practice of the soul includes the aim and intention of the soul, which is the agent. For not only would we not look on the motions of a statue doing justice or giving alms by clockwork as any acts of obedience to Christ in that statue; but no one would call the voluntary actions of a man that outwardly and materially agree with a command of Christ by the name of obedience to Christ, if he had never heard of Christ or any of his commands, or had no thought of his commands in what he did.—If the acts of obedience and good fruits spoken of are looked on not as mere motions of the body but as acts of the soul, then the whole exercise of the spirit of the mind in the action must be taken in, with the end it acts for and the regard the soul then has to God. Otherwise they are no acts of self-denial, or obedience to God, or service done to him, but something else. Many of the martyrs have experienced in a high degree such effective exercises of grace as I have now described. And all true saints live a life of such acts of grace as these, since they all live a life of gracious works, of which these working exertions of grace are the life and soul. And this is the obedience and fruit God mainly looks at, since he looks at the soul more than the body, as much as the soul is the superior part in the make of human nature. As God looks at the obedience and practice of the man, he looks at the practice of the soul; for the soul is the man in God’s sight: “The Lord does not see as man does. … the Lord sees the heart.”

And this is how obedience, good works and good fruit are to be taken when Scripture gives them as a sure evidence to our own consciences of a true principle of grace: as including the obedience and practice of the soul, which precedes and governs the actions of the body. When Scripture gives practice as the main evidence of our true Christianity to others, it means that part of our practice which is visible to them, our outward actions. But when practice is given as a sure evidence of our real Christianity to our own consciences, it means that part of our practice which is visible to our own consciences. This is not only the motion of our bodies, but the exertion and exercise of the soul that directs and commands that motion, which is more directly and immediately under the view of our own consciences than the act of the body. And that this is the meaning of Scripture is shown not only by the nature and reason of the thing; it is plain from Scripture itself. So it is evident that when Christ, at the conclusion of his Sermon on the Mount, speaks of doing or practicing these sayings of his as the grand sign that those who profess are true disciples (without it he likens them to a man who built his house on the sand, and with it to a man who built his house on a rock), he has in view not only the outward behavior but the inward exercise of the mind in that behavior. This is evident if we observe what those preceding sayings of his are that he refers to when he speaks of our doing or practicing them. We will find they are such as these: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” “Blessed are those who mourn,” “Blessed are the meek,” “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness,” “Blessed are the merciful,” “Blessed are the pure in heart,” “anyone who is angry with his brother without a cause,” etc., “anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her,” etc., “love your+ enemies,” “do not worry about your+ life,” and others of the same nature, which imply inward exercises. And when Christ says in John 14:21, “Whoever has My commandments and keeps them is the one who loves Me,” he evidently has special regard to the command repeated several times in the same discourse (which he calls, by way of eminence, his commandment), that they should love one another as he had loved them (see ch. 13:34, 35, and ch. 15:10, 12, 13, 14). But this command chiefly concerns an exercise of the mind or heart, though exerted in practice. So when the apostle John says in 1 John 2:3, “By this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments,” he plainly has chief regard to the same command, as appears from what follows, verses 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 2nd Epistle, verses 5, 6. And when we are told in Scripture that men will be judged at the last day according to their works, and that all will receive according to the things done in the body, it is not to be understood only of outward acts. For if it were, why is God so often spoken of as searching the hearts and testing the inmost minds, so that he may give to every one according to his works? As in Rev 2:23: “And all the churches will know that I am the One who searches minds and hearts, and I will repay each of you+ according to your+ works.” Jer 17:9, 10: “I, the Lord, search the heart; I examine the mind to reward a man according to his way, according to the fruit of his deeds.” But if by his way and the fruit of his deeds only the actions of his body are meant, what need is there of searching the heart and examining the mind in order to know them? Hezekiah in his sickness pleads his practice as an evidence of his title to God’s favor, including not only his outward actions but what was in his heart. Isa 38:3: “Please, O Lord, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion.”

Though in this great evidence of sincerity that Scripture gives us what is inward is of the greatest importance, yet what is outward is included and intended, as connected with the practical exertion of grace in the will directing and commanding the actions of the body. And by this every claim any man can make to evidences of godliness while he lives wickedly outwardly is effectually cut off. For the great evidence lies in the inward exercise and practice of the soul that consists in the act of the will commanding outward acts. But it is well known that these commanding acts of the will do not go one way and the actions of the bodily organs another. For the unalterable law of nature is that they are united, as long as soul and body are united, and the organs are not so destroyed as to be incapable of the motions the soul commands. So it would be ridiculous for a man to plead that the commanding act of his will was to go to public worship while his feet carry him to a tavern or a brothel; or that the commanding act of his will was to give a coin he had in his hand to a poor beggar while his hand at the same instant kept it back and held it tight.

[2.] Secondly, I go on to show that Christian practice, taken in the sense that has been explained, is the chief of all the evidences of a saving sincerity in religion to the consciences of those who profess it. It is much to be preferred to the method of the first convictions, enlightenings and comforts in conversion, or to any immanent manifestations or exercises of grace whatever that begin and end in contemplation.92 The evidence of this appears from the following arguments.

Argument I. Reason plainly shows that the things which put to the proof what men will actually hold to and prefer in their practice, when left to follow their own choice and inclinations, are the proper trial of what they really prefer in their hearts. Sincerity in religion, as has already been observed, consists in setting God highest in the heart, in choosing him before other things, in having a heart to sell all for Christ, etc.— But a man’s actions are the proper trial of what his heart prefers. For instance, when God and other things come to stand in competition, when God is, as it were, set before a man on one hand and his worldly interest or pleasure on the other (as often happens in the course of a man’s life), his behavior in such a case, in actually holding to the one and forsaking the other, is the proper trial of which he prefers. Sincerity consists in forsaking all for Christ in heart. But to forsake all for Christ in heart is the very same thing as to have a heart to forsake all for Christ. And certainly the proper trial of whether a man has a heart to forsake all for Christ is his being actually put to it: Christ and other things coming into competition, so that he must actually or practically hold to one and forsake the other. To forsake all for Christ in heart is the same thing as to have a heart to forsake all for Christ when called to it. But the highest proof to ourselves and others that we have a heart to forsake all for Christ when called to it is actually doing it when called to it, or as far as we are called to it. To follow Christ in heart is to have a heart to follow him. To deny ourselves in heart for Christ is the same thing as to have a heart to deny ourselves for him in fact. The main and most proper proof of a man’s having a heart to anything about which he is free to follow his own inclinations, and either to do it or not as he pleases, is his doing it. When a man is free to speak or keep silent, the most proper evidence of his having a heart to speak is his speaking. When a man is free to walk or sit still, the proper proof of his having a heart to walk is his walking. Godliness does not consist in a heart to intend to do the will of God, but in a heart to do it. The children of Israel in the wilderness had the former, as we read in Deut 5:27, 28, 29: “Go near and listen to all that the Lord our God says. Then you can tell us everything the Lord our God tells you; we will listen and obey.” “And the Lord heard the words you+ spoke to me, and He said to me, ‘I have heard the words that these people have spoken to you. They have done well in all that they have spoken. If only they had such a heart to fear Me and keep all My commandments always, so that it might be well with them and with their children forever.’ ” The people showed that they had a heart to intend to keep God’s commandments, and to be very eager in those intentions. But God shows that this was far from being the thing he desired, in which true godliness consists: a heart actually to keep them.

So it is exceedingly absurd, and even ridiculous, for anyone to claim that he has a good heart while he lives a wicked life, or does not bring forth the fruit of universal holiness in his practice. For it is proved in fact that such men do not love God above all. It is foolish to argue against plain fact and experience. Men who live in ways of sin, and yet flatter themselves that they will go to heaven, or expect to be received hereafter as holy persons without a holy life and practice, act as though they expected to make a fool of their judge. This is implied in what the apostle says (speaking of men’s doing good works and living a holy life, and so showing evidence of their title to everlasting life) in Gal 6:7: “Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return.” As much as to say: Do not deceive yourselves with an expectation of reaping life everlasting hereafter if you do not sow to the Spirit here. It is useless to think that God will be made a fool of by you, that he will be shamed and tricked with shadows instead of substance, and with empty claims instead of the good fruit he expects, when the contrary of what you claim appears plainly in your life before his face. The word mock is sometimes used in Scripture in this way. So Delilah says to Samson, “You have mocked me and lied to me!” (Judg 16:10, 13), that is, “You have tricked me, as though you would make a fool of me, as if I might easily be turned away with any empty pretense instead of the truth.” So it is said that when Lot told his sons-in-law that God would destroy that place, he seemed to his sons-in-law like one who was mocking (Gen 19:14), that is, he seemed like one who would make a game of them, as though they were such credulous fools as to pay attention to such bugbears. But the great judge, whose eyes are like a flame of fire, will not be mocked or tricked with any claims without a holy life. Men may have prophesied in his name, and worked miracles, and had faith so that they could move mountains, and cast out devils. However high their religious affections have been, however great the resemblances of grace they have had, and though their hiding place has been so dark and deep that no human skill or search could find them out, yet if they are workers or practicers of iniquity, they cannot hide their hypocrisy from their judge. Job 34:22: “There is no darkness or deep shadow where the workers of iniquity can hide.” Would a wise prince allow himself to be fooled and tricked by a subject who claimed that he was a loyal subject? Suppose he told his prince that he had an entire affection for him, that at such and such a time he had experience of it and felt his affections working strongly toward him, and came expecting to be accepted and rewarded by his prince as one of his best friends on that account, though he lived in rebellion against him, following some pretender to his crown and from time to time stirring up sedition against him. Or would a master allow himself to be shamed and duped by a servant who claimed great experiences of love and honor toward him in his heart, and a great sense of his worthiness and kindness to him, when at the same time he refused to obey him, and he could get no service done by him?

Argument II. As reason shows that the things that occur in the course of life which put to the proof whether men will prefer God to other things in practice are the proper trial of the uprightness and sincerity of their hearts, so Scripture represents the same things as the proper trial of the sincerity of those who profess. There we find such things called by that very name, trials or temptations (which, as I observed before, are words of the same meaning). The things that put to the proof whether men will prefer God to other things in practice are the difficulties of religion, the things that occur which make the practice of duty difficult and contrary to other principles besides the love of God. For in them God and other things are both set before men together for their actual and practical choice, and it comes to this: we cannot hold to both, but one or the other must be forsaken. And all through Scripture these things are called by the name of trials or proofs.93 And they are called by this name because by them those who profess are tried and proved, what sort they are, whether they are really what they profess and appear to be; and because in them the reality of a supreme love to God is brought to the test of experiment and fact. They are the proper proofs in which it is truly settled by experience whether or not men have a thorough disposition of heart to hold to God. Deut 8:2: “Remember that these forty years the Lord your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep His commandments.” Judg 2:21, 22: “I will no longer drive out before them any of the nations Joshua left when he died. In this way I will test whether Israel will keep the way of the Lord.” So also ch. 3:1, 4, and Exod 16:4. And when Scripture calls these difficulties of religion by the name of temptations or trials, it explains itself to mean by this the trial or experiment of their faith. Jas 1:2, 3: “Consider it pure joy, my brothers, when you+ encounter trials of many kinds, because you+ know that the testing of your+ faith develops perseverance.” 1 Pet 1:6, 7: “Though now for a little while you+ may have had to suffer grief in various trials so that the trial of your+ faith—more precious than gold,” etc. So the apostle Paul speaks of the costly duty of parting with our substance to the poor as the proof of the sincerity of the love of Christians (2 Cor 8:8). And the difficulties of religion are often represented in Scripture as the trial of those who profess, in the same way that the furnace is the proper trial of gold and silver. Ps 66:10, 11: “For You, O God, have tested us; You have refined us like silver. You led us into the net; You laid burdens on our backs.” Zech 13:9: “This third I will bring through the fire; I will refine them like silver and test them like gold.” What has the color and appearance of gold is put into the furnace to try whether it is what it seems to be, real gold or not. So the difficulties of religion are called trials because they try those who have the profession and appearance of saints, whether they are what they appear to be, real saints. If we put true gold into the furnace, we will find its great value and preciousness. So the truth and priceless value of the virtues of a true Christian appear when they are under these trials. 1 Pet 1:7: “so that the trial of your+ faith—more precious than gold, which perishes …—may result in praise, glory, and honor.” True and pure gold will come out of the furnace at full weight; so true saints, when tried, come forth as gold (Job 23:10). Christ distinguishes true grace from counterfeit by this, that it is gold refined by fire (Rev 3:17, 18). So it is evident that these things are called trials in Scripture chiefly because they try or prove the sincerity of those who profess. And from what has now been observed it is evident that they are the most proper trial or proof of their sincerity, since the very meaning of the word trial, as it is ordinarily used in Scripture, is the difficulty occurring in the way of a professing Christian’s duty, as the trial or experiment of his sincerity. If trial of sincerity is the proper name of these difficulties of religion, then doubtless these difficulties of religion are properly and eminently the trial of sincerity. For doubtless they are eminently what the Holy Spirit calls them; God gives things their names from what is eminently their nature. And if these things are the proper and eminent trial, proof or experiment of the sincerity of those who profess, then certainly the result of the trial or experiment (that is, persons’ behavior or practice under such trials) is the proper and eminent evidence of their sincerity. For they are called trials or proofs only with regard to the result, and because the effect is eminently the proof or evidence. And this is the most proper proof and evidence to the consciences of those who undergo these trials. For when God is said by these things to try men and prove them, to see what is in their hearts, and whether or not they will keep his commandments, we are not to understand that it is for his own information, or so that he may obtain evidence of their sincerity for himself (for he needs no trials for his information), but chiefly for their conviction, and to set evidence before their consciences.94 So when God is said to prove Israel by the difficulties they met with in the wilderness, and by the difficulties they met with from their enemies in Canaan, to know what was in their hearts, whether or not they would keep his commandments, it must be understood that it was to show them to themselves, so that they might know what was in their own hearts. So when God tempted or tried Abraham with the difficult command to offer up his son, it was not for God’s own assurance, whether or not Abraham feared God, but for Abraham’s own greater assurance and comfort, and the clearer manifestation of the favor of God to him. When Abraham had proved faithful under this trial, God says to him, “Now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your only son from Me.” This plainly implies that in this practical exercise of Abraham’s grace under this trial there was a clearer evidence of the truth of his grace than there ever was before, and the greatest evidence to Abraham’s conscience. For God himself gives it to Abraham as such, for his comfort and rejoicing, and speaks of it to him as what might be the greatest evidence to his conscience of his being upright in the sight of his judge. This proves what I say, that holy practice under trials is the highest evidence of the sincerity of those who profess to their own consciences. And we find that Christ again and again took the same method to convict the consciences of those who claimed friendship with him, and to show them what they were. This was the method he took with the rich young man (Matt 19:16, etc.). He seemed to show great respect to Christ. He came kneeling to him, and called him good Teacher, and made a great profession of obedience to the commandments. But Christ tried him by telling him to go and sell all that he had and give to the poor, and come, take up his cross and follow him, telling him that then he would have treasure in heaven. So he tried another we read of in Matthew 8:20. He made a great profession of respect to Christ. “Lord,” he says, “I will follow You wherever You go.” Christ immediately puts his friendship to the proof by telling him that foxes had dens and the birds of the air had nests, but the Son of Man had no place to lay his head. And in this way Christ still usually tries professed disciples in general in his providence. So it is with the seed sown in every kind of ground, stony ground, thorny ground and good ground. Though in all of them it looks alike when it first springs up, yet it is tried, and the difference is made to appear, by the burning heat of the sun.

Since, then, these are the things God uses to try us, it is undoubtedly the surest way for us to pass a right judgment on ourselves to try ourselves by the same things. These trials of his are not for his information but for ours, so we ought to take our information from them. The surest way to know our gold is to look at it and examine it in God’s furnace, where he tries it for this very end, that we may see what it is. If we want to know whether or not a building stands strong, we must look at it when the wind blows. If we want to know whether what has the form of wheat has the real substance of wheat, or is only chaff, we must watch it when it is winnowed. If we want to know whether a staff is strong, or a rotten, broken reed, we must watch it when it is leaned on and weight is put on it. If we want to weigh ourselves justly, we must weigh ourselves in God’s scales, the ones he uses to weigh us.95 These trials in the course of our practice are, as it were, the balances in which our hearts are weighed; or in which Christ and the world, or Christ and his rivals, are weighed as to the esteem and regard they have in our hearts, or are put into opposite scales, so that there is opportunity to see which outweighs the other. When a man is brought to the parting of paths, one of which leads to Christ and the other to the objects of his lusts, to see which way he will go; or is brought and, as it were, set between Christ and the world, Christ on the right hand and the world on the left, so that if he goes to one he must leave the other, to see which his heart inclines to most, or which outweighs the other in his heart: this is just the same thing as laying Christ and the world in two opposite scales. And his going to the one and leaving the other is just the same thing as the sinking of one scale and the rising of the other. So a man’s practice under the trials of God’s providence is as much the proper experiment and evidence of the superior inclination of his heart as the motion of the balance, with different weights in opposite scales, is the proper experiment of the superior weight.

Argument III. Another argument that holy practice, in the sense explained, is the highest kind of evidence of the truth of grace to the consciences of Christians is this: in the language of Scripture, grace is said to be made perfect, or to be finished, in practice. So the apostle James says in Jas 2:22: “You see that his faith was working with his works, and his faith was perfected by his works,” or finished (as the word in the original properly means). So the love of God is said to be made perfect, or finished, in keeping his commandments. 1 John 2:4, 5: “If anyone says, ‘I know Him,’ but does not keep His commandments, he is a liar, and the truth is not in him. But if anyone keeps His word, the love of God has been truly perfected in him.” The commandment of Christ the apostle especially has in view when he speaks here of our keeping his commandments is (as I observed before) that great commandment of his which concerns deeds of love to our brothers, as appears from the following verses. Again, the love of God is said to be perfected in the same sense in ch. 4:12: “If we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us.” Here doubtless the apostle still has in view loving one another in the way he had explained in the preceding chapter, where he speaks of loving one another as a sign of the love of God, verses 17, 18: “If anyone with earthly possessions … withholds his compassion from him,” etc., “how can the love of God abide in him? Little children, let us love not in word and speech, but in action” (or in work) “and truth.” By loving in work in this way, the apostle says, the love of God is perfected in us. Grace is said to be perfected or finished in holy practice because in it grace is brought to its proper effect, and to the exercise that is the end of the principle. In it the tendency and design of grace is reached, and its working completed and crowned. So the tree is made perfect in the fruit. It is not perfected in the seed’s being planted in the ground. It is not perfected in the seed’s first stirring of life and in its putting out root and shoot. Nor is it perfected when it comes up out of the ground, nor in bringing forth leaves, nor yet in putting forth blossoms. But when it has brought forth good ripe fruit, then it is perfected. In this it reaches its end; the design of the tree is finished; all that belongs to the tree is completed and brought to its proper effect in the fruit. So it is with grace in its practical exercises. Grace is said to be made perfect or finished in its work or fruit in the same way as is said of sin. Jas 1:15: “Then after lust has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is finished, gives birth to death.” Here are three steps. First, sin in its principle or habit, in the being of lust in the heart. Next, here is its conceiving, consisting in its immanent exercises in the mind. And lastly, here is the fruit that was conceived actually brought forth, in the wicked work and practice. And this the apostle calls the finishing or perfecting of sin, for the word in the original is the same as is translated perfected in the places mentioned before.

Now certainly, if this is so, if grace is made perfect in its fruit in this way, if these practical exercises of grace are the exercises in which grace is brought to its proper effect and end, the exercises in which whatever belongs to its design, tendency and working is completed and crowned, then these exercises must be the highest evidences of grace, above all other exercises. Certainly the proper nature and tendency of every principle must appear best and most fully in its most perfect exercises, or in the exercises in which its nature is most completely exerted, and its tendency most fully answered and crowned in its proper effect and end. If we want to see the proper nature of anything whatever, and to see it fully distinguished from other things, let us look at it in its finishing. The apostle James says, faith was perfected by works, and brings this in as an argument to prove that works are the chief evidence of faith, by which the sincerity of those who profess faith is justified (Jas 2). And the apostle John, after telling us again and again that love was made perfect in keeping Christ’s commandments, observes in 1 John 4:18 “that perfect love drives out fear,” meaning (at least in part) love made perfect in this sense. This agrees with what he had said in the preceding chapter, that by loving in deed, or work, we know that we belong to the truth, and will assure our hearts (vv. 18, 19).

Argument IV. Another thing that makes it evident that holy practice is the principal evidence we ought to use in judging the sincerity both of ourselves and of others is that Scripture insists on this evidence above all others. A common acquaintance with Scripture, together with a little attention and observation, will be enough to show anyone that throughout Scripture, from the beginning of Genesis to the end of Revelation, this is insisted on as a mark of true piety ten times more than anything else. And in the New Testament, where Christ and his apostles expressly and with declared purpose lay down signs of true godliness, this is insisted on almost entirely. It may be observed that Christ and his apostles not only often say things in their discourses on the great doctrines of religion that show what the nature of true godliness must be, or from which its nature and signs may be inferred by sound reasoning, and often mention in passing many things that belong to godliness. They also often, on set purpose, give signs and marks for the trial of those who profess, urging them to try themselves by the signs they give, and introducing what they say with expressions like these: By this you+ will know that you+ know God; by this the children of God and the children of the devil are made plain; he who has this builds on a good foundation; he who does not have it builds on the sand; by this we will assure our hearts; he is the man who loves Christ, etc. But I can find no place where either Christ or his apostles give signs of godliness in this way (and the places are many) in which Christian practice is not almost the only thing insisted on. It is true that in many of these places love to the brothers is spoken of as a sign of godliness; and (as I have observed before) there is no one virtuous affection or disposition so often expressly spoken of as a sign of true grace as our having love for one another. But then the Scriptures explain themselves to mean chiefly this love as exercised and expressed in practice, or in deeds of love. So the apostle John (who above all others insists on love to the brothers as a sign of godliness) most expressly explains himself in 1 John 3:14: “We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love our brothers. The one who does not love remains in death.—If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him? Little children, let us love not in word and speech, but in action” (that is, in deeds of love) “and truth. And by this we will know that we belong to the truth, and will assure our hearts in His presence.” So when Scripture insists so much on our loving one another as a great sign of godliness, we are not to understand by it the immanent workings of affection that men feel toward one another so much as the soul’s practicing all the duties of the second table of the law, all of which, the New Testament tells us again and again, a true love for one another includes (Rom 13:8, and 10; Gal 5:14; Matt 22:39, 40). So in reality there is no place in the New Testament where the declared design is to give signs of godliness in which holy practice and keeping Christ’s commandments is not the mark chosen out of all others to be insisted on. This is an invincible argument that it is the chief of all the evidences of godliness, unless we suppose that when Christ and his apostles deliberately set about this business of giving signs by which professing Christians in all ages might determine their state, they did not know how to choose signs as well as we could have chosen them for them. But if we make the word of Christ our rule, then undoubtedly the marks Christ and his apostles chiefly laid down and gave us, so that we might try ourselves by them, are the same marks we ought especially to receive and chiefly to use in trying ourselves.96 And surely the things Christ and his apostles chiefly insisted on in the rules they gave, ministers ought chiefly to insist on in the rules they give. To insist much on things Scripture insists little on, and to insist very little on things Scripture insists much on, is a dangerous thing. For it is going out of God’s way, and judging ourselves and guiding others in an unscriptural manner. God knew which way of leading and guiding souls was safest and best for them. He insisted so much on some things because he knew they needed to be insisted on; and, as a wise God, he left other things more alone because he knew it was not best for us to lay so much of the weight of the trial there. As the Sabbath was made for man, so the Scriptures were made for man, and infinite wisdom has fitted them for our use and benefit. So we should make them our guide in all things, in our thoughts of religion and of ourselves. And for us to make great what Scripture makes little, and little what Scripture makes great, tends to give us a distorted idea of religion, and (at least indirectly and gradually) to lead us wholly away from the right rule and from a right opinion of ourselves, and to establish delusion and hypocrisy.
