Argument V. Christian practice is plainly spoken of in the word of God as the main evidence of the truth of grace, not only to others but to men’s own consciences. Not only is it spoken of and insisted on more than other signs, but in many places where it is spoken of it is represented as the chief of all evidences. This is plain from the manner of expression again and again. Suppose God were now to speak from heaven to settle our doubts about the signs of godliness, and were to give some particular sign by which all might know whether or not they were sincerely godly, with such emphatic expressions as these about the man who has such a quality or mark: That is the man who is a true saint; that is the very man; by this you+ may know; this is the thing by which it is made plain who are saints and who are sinners; such men as these are saints indeed. Should we not look on it as beyond doubt that this was given as a special and eminently distinguishing mark of true godliness? But this is the very case with the sign of grace I am speaking of. God has spoken in his word again and again in this very way about Christian practice. So in John 14: “Whoever has My commandments and keeps them is the one who loves Me.” Christ gives this to the disciples in this place not so much to guide them in judging others as to apply to themselves for their own comfort after his departure, as appears from every word of the context. And by the way I would observe that it is not only the emphasis with which Christ speaks that is remarkable, but also his insisting on and repeating the matter so much, as he does in the context. V. 15: “If you+ love Me, you+ will keep My commandments.” Verse 23: “If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word.” And v. 24: “Whoever does not love Me does not keep My words.” And over and over in the next chapter. V. 2: “He cuts off every branch in Me that bears no fruit, and every branch that does bear fruit, He prunes.” Verse 8: “This is to My Father’s glory, that you+ bear much fruit, proving yourselves+ to be My disciples.” Verse 14: “You+ are My friends if you+ do what I command you+.” We have this mark laid down with the same emphasis again in John 8:31: “If you+ continue in My word, you+ are truly My disciples.” And again in 1 John 2:3: “Hereby we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments.” And v. 5: “If anyone keeps His word, the love of God has been truly perfected in him. By this we know that we are in Him.” And ch. 3:18, 19: “Let us love … in action and truth. And by this we will know that we belong to the truth.” What is translated hereby would have been a little more emphatic if it had been rendered more literally from the original, by this we know—. And how evidently holy practice is spoken of as the grand mark of distinction between the children of God and the children of the devil in v. 10 of the same chapter! “By this the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil.” He is speaking of a holy and a wicked practice, as may be seen in all the context, as in v. 3: “Everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as Christ is pure.” Verses 6, 7, 8, 9, 10: “No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning. No one who continues to sin has seen Him or known Him. Little children, let no one deceive you+: The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Christ is righteous. The one who practices sin is of the devil.—Anyone born of God refuses to practice sin.—Anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God.” So we have the same emphasis in 2 John 6: “And this is love, that we walk according to His commandments.” That is (as we must understand it), this is the proper evidence of love. So 1 John 5:3: “For this is the love of God, that we keep His commandments.” So the apostle James, speaking of the proper evidences of true and pure religion, says in Jas 1:27: “Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.” We have similar emphatic expressions used about the same thing in the Old Testament. Job 28:28: “And He said to man, ‘Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.’ ” Jer 22:15, 16: “Did not your father have food and drink? He administered justice and righteousness.—He took up the cause of the poor and needy. … Is this not what it means to know Me?” declares the Lord. Ps 34:11, etc.: “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you+ the fear of the Lord.—Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from deceitful speech. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.” Ps 15 at the beginning: “O Lord, who may abide in Your tent? Who may dwell on Your holy mountain? He who walks with integrity,” etc. Ps 24:3, 4: “Who may ascend the hill of the Lord? Who may stand in His holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart,” etc. Ps 119:1: “Blessed are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the Law of the Lord.” Verse 6: “Then I would not be ashamed when I heed all Your commandments.” Prov 8:13: “To fear the Lord is to hate evil.”

So Scripture never uses such emphatic expressions about any other signs of hypocrisy and unsoundness of heart as it does about an unholy practice. So Gal 6:7: “Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return.” 1 Cor 6:9, 10: “Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters,” etc., “will inherit the kingdom of God.” Eph 5:5, 6: “For of this you+ can be sure: No immoral or impure person,” etc., “has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no one deceive you+ with empty words.” 1 John 3:7, 8: “Little children, let no one deceive you+: The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Christ is righteous. The one who practices sin is of the devil.” Chapter 2:4: “If anyone says, ‘I know Him,’ but does not keep His commandments, he is a liar, and the truth is not in him.” And ch. 1:6: “If we say we have fellowship with Him yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.” Jas 1:26: “If anyone considers himself religious and yet does not bridle his tongue, he deceives his heart and his religion is worthless.” Chapter 3:14, 15: “But if you+ harbor bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your+ hearts, do not boast in it or deny the truth. Such wisdom does not come from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic.” Ps 125:5:

“Those who turn to crooked ways the Lord will banish with the evildoers.” Isa 35:8: “And there will be a highway called the Way of Holiness. The unclean will not travel it.” Rev 21:27: “But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who practices an abomination or a lie.” And in many places: “Depart from Me; I do not know you+, you+ who work iniquity.”

Argument VI. Another thing that makes it evident that holy practice is the chief of all the signs of the sincerity of those who profess, not only to the world but to their own consciences, is that this is the grand evidence that will be used hereafter before the judgment seat of God. His judgment will be governed by it, and the state of every professing Christian will be determined by it beyond change. In the future judgment there will be an open trial of those who profess, and evidences will be used in the judgment. For God’s future judging of men, for their eternal reward or punishment, will not be his trying and finding out the state of men’s hearts and passing judgment on it in his own mind. It will be a declarative judgment, and its end will not be God’s forming a judgment within himself, but the manifestation of his judgment, and of its righteousness, to men’s own consciences and to the world. That is why the day of judgment is called the day “when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed” (Rom 2:5). And the end of God’s future trial and judgment of men, as to the part each one in particular is to have in the judgment, will be especially the clear manifestation to his conscience of God’s righteous judgment concerning him, as is plain from Matthew 18:31 to the end; chapter 20:8–15; chapter 22:11, 12, 13; chapter 25:19–30, and verse 35 to the end; Luke 19:15–23. And so, though God needs no means of making the truth evident to himself, yet evidences will be used in his future judging of men. And doubtless the evidences used in their trial will be those best fitted to serve the ends of the judgment, namely, the manifestation of the righteous judgment of God not only to the world but to men’s own consciences. But the Scriptures abundantly teach us that the grand evidences the judge will use in the trial for these ends, by which the judgment of everyone will be governed and the irreversible sentence passed, will be men’s works or practice here in this world. Rev 20:12: “And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne. And there were open books.—And the dead were judged according to their deeds, as recorded in the books.” So verse 13: “The sea gave up its dead, and Death and Hades gave up their dead, and each one was judged according to his deeds.” 2 Cor 5:10: “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad.” So men’s practice is the only evidence by which Christ represents the future judgment as governed in the most detailed description of the day of judgment we have in the holy Bible, at the end of Matt 25. See also Rom 2:6–13; Jer 17:10; Job 34:11; Prov 24:12; Jer 32:19; Rev 22:12; Matt 16:27; Rev 2:23; Ezek 33:20; 1 Pet 1:17. At the day of judgment the judge will not (for the conviction of men’s own consciences, and to show them to the world) set about examining men as to the method of their experiences, or set every man to tell his story of the manner of his conversion. Rather, his works will be brought out as evidences of what he is, of what he has done in darkness and in light. Eccl 12:14: “For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil.” In the trial those who profess will undergo in the future judgment, God will use the same evidences to show them to themselves and to the world as he uses to show them in the temptations or trials of his providence here, namely, their practice in cases where Christ and other things come into actual and immediate competition. At the day of judgment, to show his righteous judgment, God will weigh those who profess in a balance that is visible. And the balance will be the same one he weighs men in now, which has already been described.

From this we may undoubtedly infer that men’s works (taken in the sense explained) are the highest evidences by which they ought to try themselves. Certainly what our supreme judge will chiefly use to judge us by when we come to stand before him, we should chiefly use to judge ourselves by.97 If it had not been revealed in what manner, and by what evidence, the judge would proceed with us hereafter, how natural it would be for someone to say: “Oh, that I knew what token God will chiefly look for and insist on in the last and decisive judgment, which he expects all who would then be accepted by him to be able to produce, and by which sentence will be passed; so that I might know what token or evidence especially to look at and seek now, as I would be sure not to fail then.” And since God has so plainly and abundantly revealed what this token or evidence is, surely if we act wisely we will regard it as of the greatest importance.

Now from all that has been said I think it is abundantly clear that Christian practice is the most proper evidence of the gracious sincerity of those who profess, to themselves and to others, and the chief of all the marks of grace: the sign of signs and evidence of evidences, the thing that seals and crowns all other signs.—I would rather have the testimony of my conscience that I have on my side such a saying of my supreme judge as John 14:21, “Whoever has My commandments and keeps them is the one who loves Me,” than the judgment and fullest approval of all the wise, sound and experienced divines who have lived in the last thousand years, after the most exact and critical examination of my experiences as to the manner of my conversion. Not that there are no other good evidences of a state of grace but this. There may be other exercises of grace besides these exercises that produce action, which the saints may have in contemplation, that may be very satisfying to them. But still this is the chief and most proper evidence. There may be several good evidences that a tree is a fig tree, but the highest and most proper evidence of it is that it actually bears figs. It is possible that a man may have a good assurance of a state of grace at his first conversion, before he has had opportunity to gain assurance by this great evidence I am speaking of.—Suppose a man hears that a great treasure is offered him in a distant place, on condition that he prizes it so much as to be willing to leave what he possesses at home and make a journey for it, over the rocks and mountains in the way, to the place where it is. It is possible that the man may be well assured, as soon as the offer is made him, that he values the treasure to the degree spoken of. He may feel within him, beyond all doubt, a willingness to go for the treasure. But still this does not prevent his actually going for it from being the highest and most proper evidence of his being willing, not only to others but to himself. But then, as an evidence to himself, his outward actions and the motions of his body on his journey are not considered alone, apart from the action of his mind, and an inward consciousness of what moves him and of the end he goes for. Otherwise his bodily motion is no evidence to him of his prizing the treasure. It is in this way that Christian practice is the most proper evidence of a saving value set on the pearl of great price and the treasure hidden in the field.

Christian practice is the sign of signs in this sense: that it is the great evidence that confirms and crowns all other signs of godliness. There is no grace of the Spirit of God of whose truth Christian practice is not the most proper evidence. As it is with the members of our bodies and all our tools, the proper proof of their soundness and goodness is in their use, so it is with our graces. They are given to be used in practice, as much as our hands and feet, or the tools we work with, or the weapons we fight with; and the proper trial and proof of them is in their exercise in practice. Most of the things we use are serviceable to us, and so have their serviceableness proved, under some pressure, straining, shaking or collision. So it is with a bow, a sword, an axe, a saw, a cord, a chain, a staff, a foot, a tooth, etc. And those that are so weak as not to bear the strain or pressure we need to put them to are good for nothing. So it is with all the virtues of the mind. Their proper trial and proof is in their being exercised under the temptations and trials God brings us under in the course of his providence, and in their being put to such service as strains hard on the principles of nature.

Practice is the proper proof of the true and saving knowledge of God, as appears from the apostle’s words already mentioned: “By this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments.” It is useless for us to profess to know God if by our works we deny him (Titus 1:16). And if we know God, but do not glorify him as God, our knowledge will only condemn us and not save us (Rom 1:21). The great mark of the knowledge that saves and makes happy is that it is practical. John 13:17: “If you+ know these things, you+ will be happy if you+ do them.” Job 28:28: “To turn away from evil is understanding.”

Holy practice is the proper evidence of repentance. When the Jews professed repentance, when they came confessing their sins to John, who preached the baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, he directed them to the right way of getting and showing proper evidences of the truth of their repentance when he said to them, “Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance” (Matt 3:8). This agreed with the practice of the apostle Paul; see Acts 26:20. Pardon and mercy are again and again promised to the one who has this evidence of true repentance, that he forsakes his sin (Prov 28:13, and Isa 55:7, and many other places).

Holy practice is the proper evidence of a saving faith. It is evident that the apostle James speaks of works as what eminently justifies faith, or (which is the same thing) justifies those who profess faith, and vindicates and shows the sincerity of their profession, not only to the world but to their own consciences. This is evident from the instance he gives of Abraham (Jas 2:21–24).—And in verses 20 and 26 he speaks of the practical and working nature of faith as its very life and soul, in the same way that the active nature and substance in the body of a man is its life and soul. And if so, doubtless practice is the proper evidence of the life and soul of true faith, by which it is distinguished from a dead faith. For doubtless practice is the most proper evidence of a practical nature, and working the most proper evidence of a working nature.

Practice is the best evidence of a saving belief of the truth. It is spoken of as the proper evidence of the truth’s being in a professing Christian that he walks in the truth. 3 John 3: “For I was overjoyed when the brothers came and testified of the truth that is in you, just as you continue to walk in the truth.”

Practice is the most proper evidence of a true coming to Christ, and accepting him and embracing him. A true and saving coming to Christ is (as Christ often teaches) a coming in such a way as to forsake all for him. And as was observed before, to forsake all for Christ in heart is the same thing as to have a heart actually to forsake all. But the proper evidence of having a heart actually to forsake all is actually to forsake all, as far as we are called to it. If a prince seeks the hand of a woman in a far country, asking her to forsake her own people and her father’s house and come to him to be his bride, the proper evidence that her heart complies with the king’s suit is her actually forsaking her own people and her father’s house and coming to him. By this her compliance with the king’s suit is made perfect, in the same sense in which the apostle James says faith was perfected by works.98 Christ promises us eternal life on condition of our coming to him. But it is such a coming as he directed the young man to, who came to ask what he must do to obtain eternal life. Christ told him to go and sell all that he had, and come to him and follow him. If he had consented in his heart to the proposal (and so had come to Christ in his heart), the proper evidence of it would have been his doing it; and in that his coming to Christ would have been made perfect. When Christ called Levi the tax collector, as he sat at the tax booth in the midst of his worldly gains, Levi’s embrace, in his heart, of this invitation of his Savior to come to him was shown and made perfect by his actually getting up, leaving all and following him (Luke 5:27, 28). Christ and other things are set before us together, for us practically to hold to one and forsake the other. In such a case a practical holding to Christ is a practical acceptance of Christ, as much as a beggar’s reaching out his hand and taking a gift that is offered is his practical acceptance of the gift. Indeed, the act of the soul that is in holding to Christ in practice is itself the most perfect coming of the soul to Christ.

Practice is the most proper evidence of trusting in Christ for salvation. The proper meaning of the word trust, in its more ordinary use, both in common speech and in the holy Scriptures, is the emboldening and encouraging of a person’s mind to run some risk in practice, or in something he does, on the credit of another’s sufficiency and faithfulness. And so the proper evidence of his trusting is the risk he runs in what he does. A man is not properly said to run any risk in dependence on anything if he does nothing on that dependence, or if his practice is no different from what it would be if he had no dependence. For a man to run a risk in dependence on another is for him to do something from that dependence by which he seems to expose himself, and which he would not do if it were not for that dependence. And so it is in complying with the difficulties and seeming dangers of Christian practice, in dependence on Christ’s sufficiency and faithfulness to bestow eternal life, that persons are said to venture themselves on Christ and trust in him for happiness and life. They depend on such promises as Matt 10:39: “Whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.” And so they part with all, and venture their all, in dependence on Christ’s sufficiency and truth. And this is the Scripture idea of trusting in Christ in the exercise of a saving faith in him. In this way Abraham, the father of believers, trusted in Christ, and by faith forsook his own country, relying on the covenant of grace God established with him (Heb 11:8, 9). In this way also Moses, by faith, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing to suffer oppression with the people of God rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin (Heb 11:24, etc.). So by faith others exposed themselves to be stoned and sawed in two, or put to death by the sword; they endured the trial of cruel mocking and flogging, chains and imprisonment, and went around in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, mistreated. And in this sense the apostle Paul by faith trusted in Christ and committed himself to him, venturing himself and his whole interest in dependence on the ability and faithfulness of his Redeemer, under great persecutions and in suffering the loss of all things. 2 Tim 1:12: “For this reason, even though I suffer as I do, I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day.”

Suppose a man had word brought to him from the king of a distant land that he intended to make him his heir. If on receiving the news he immediately leaves his native land and friends and all he has in the world to go to that country, in dependence on what he hears, then he may be said to venture himself, and all he has in the world, on it. But if he only sits still and hopes for the promised benefit, inwardly pleasing himself with the thought of it, he cannot properly be said to venture himself on it. He runs no risk in the case. He does nothing different from what he would do if he had received no such news, nothing by which he would be exposed to any suffering in case it all failed. So he who, on the credit of what he hears of a future world, and in dependence on the report of the gospel concerning life and immortality, forsakes all, or at least does so as far as there is occasion, making everything give way entirely to his eternal interest: he, and he only, may properly be said to venture himself on the report of the gospel. And this is the proper evidence of a true trust in Christ for salvation.

Practice is the proper evidence of a gracious love, both to God and to men. The texts that plainly teach this have been mentioned so often already that there is no need to repeat them.

Practice is the proper evidence of humility. The expression and manifestation of humility of heart that God speaks of as its great expression, the one he insists on, is the one we should look on as its proper expression and manifestation. But this is walking humbly. Mic 6:8: “He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the Lord require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?”

This is also the proper evidence of the true fear of God. Prov 8:13.

“To fear the Lord is to hate evil.” Ps 34:11, etc.: “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you+ the fear of the Lord.—Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from deceitful speech. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.” Prov 3:7: “Fear the Lord and turn away from evil.” Prov 16:6: “By the fear of the Lord one turns aside from evil.” Job 1:8: “Have you considered My servant Job?—a man who is blameless and upright, who fears God and shuns evil.” Chapter 2:3: “Have you considered My servant Job?—a man who is blameless and upright, who fears God and shuns evil. He still retains his integrity, even though you incited Me against him.” Ps 36:1: “An oracle is in my heart regarding the transgression of the wicked man: There is no fear of God before his eyes.”

So practice, in repaying according to the benefits received, is the proper evidence of true thankfulness. Ps 116:12: “How can I repay the Lord for all His goodness to me?” 2 Chr 32:25: “But … Hezekiah did not repay the favor shown to him.” In the 50th Psalm, paying our vows to God and ordering our way rightly seem to be spoken of as the proper expression and evidence of true thankfulness. Verse 14: “Sacrifice a thank offering to God, and fulfill your vows to the Most High.” Verse 23: “He who sacrifices a thank offering honors Me, and to him who rights his way, I will show the salvation of God.”

So the proper evidence of gracious desires and longings, and what distinguishes them from those that are false and empty, is that they are not idle wishes and would-be wishes, like Balaam’s, but are effectual in practice, stirring persons up to seek earnestly and thoroughly the things they long for. Ps 27:4: “One thing I have desired of the Lord that will I seek.” Ps 63:1, 2: “O God, You are my God. Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You. My body yearns for You in a dry and weary land without water, to see Your power and Your glory.” Verse 8: “My soul follows hard after You.” Song 1:4: “Draw me after you—let us run!”

Practice is the proper evidence of a gracious hope. 1 John 3:3: “Everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as Christ is pure.” Patient continuance in doing good, through the difficulties and trials of the Christian course, is often mentioned as the proper expression and fruit of a Christian hope. 1 Thess 1:3: “Continually recalling … your+ work of faith, your+ labor of love, and your+ patience of hope.” 1 Pet 1:13, 14: “Therefore prepare your+ minds for action. Be sober-minded. Set your+ hope fully on the grace to be given you+ at the revelation of Jesus Christ. As obedient children,” etc. Ps 119:166: “I hope for Your salvation, O Lord, and I carry out Your commandments.” Ps 78:7: “that they should set their hope in God, not forgetting His works, but keeping His commandments.”

A cheerful practice of our duty and doing of the will of God is the proper evidence of a truly holy joy. Isa 64:5: “You welcome those who gladly do right.” Ps 119:111, 112: “Your testimonies are my heritage forever, for they are the joy of my heart. I have inclined my heart to perform Your statutes, even to the very end.” Verse 14: “I rejoice in the way of Your testimonies as much as in all riches.” 1 Cor 13:6: “Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth.” 2 Cor 8:2: “Their abundant joy … overflowed into rich generosity.”

Practice is also the proper evidence of Christian fortitude. The trial of a good soldier is not in his chimney corner but on the field of battle (1 Cor 9:25, 26; 2 Tim 2:3, 4, 5).

And as the fruit of holy practice is the chief evidence of the truth of grace, so the degree to which experiences influence a person’s practice is the surest evidence of the degree of what is spiritual and divine in his experiences. Whatever claims persons may make to great manifestations, great love and joys, they are to be regarded no further than they influence their practice. Allowances must indeed be made for the natural disposition. But that does not prevent the degree of grace from being justly measured by the degree of the effect in practice. For the effect of grace is as great, and the change as remarkable, in a person of a very bad natural disposition as in another. Although a person of such a disposition will not behave as well as another with the same degree of grace, the difference from what he was before conversion may be as great, because a person of a good natural disposition did not behave so badly before conversion.

So I have tried to set out the evidence that Christian practice is the chief of all the signs of saving grace. And before I conclude this discourse, I would say something briefly in answer to two objections that some may possibly make against what has been said on this head.

Objection 1. Some may be ready to say that this seems contrary to the opinion so widely received among good people, that those who profess should judge their state chiefly by their inward experience, and that spiritual experiences are the main evidences of true grace.

I answer: it is doubtless a true opinion, and justly much received among good people, that those who profess should chiefly judge their state by their experience. But it is a great mistake to think that what has been said is at all contrary to that opinion. That the chief sign of grace to the consciences of Christians is Christian practice, in the sense explained, and according to what has been shown to be the true idea of Christian practice, is not at all inconsistent with Christian experience being the chief evidence of grace. Christian or holy practice is spiritual practice. And that is not the motion of a body that does not know how, or when, or why it moves. Spiritual practice in man is the practice of a spirit and body jointly, or the practice of a spirit animating, commanding and moving a body to which it is united, and over which the Creator has given it power. And so the main thing in this holy practice is the holy acts of the mind, directing and governing the motions of the body. And the motions of the body are to be looked on as belonging to Christian practice only secondarily, and as they depend on and follow from the acts of the soul. The exercises of grace that Christians find, or are conscious of, within themselves are what they experience within themselves, and so Christian experience lies in this. And this Christian experience consists as much in the working exercises of grace in the will that are immediately concerned in managing the behavior of the body as in other exercises. These inward exercises are no less a part of Christian experience because outward behavior is immediately connected with them. A strong act of love to God is no less a part of spiritual experience because it is the act that immediately produces and brings about some self-denying and costly outward action that is much to the honor and glory of God.

To speak of Christian experience and practice as if they were two things properly and entirely distinct is to make a distinction without consideration or reason. It is true that not all Christian experience is properly called practice; but all Christian practice is properly experience. And the distinction made between them is not only an unreasonable but an unscriptural distinction. Holy practice is one kind or part of Christian experience, and both reason and Scripture represent it as its chief, most important and most distinguishing part. So it is represented in Jeremiah 22:15, 16: “Did not your father have food and drink? He administered justice and righteousness.—He took up the cause of the poor and needy. … Is this not what it means to know Me?” declares the Lord. Our inward acquaintance with God surely belongs under the head of experiential religion; but God represents this as consisting chiefly in the experience there is in holy practice. So the exercises of the graces of the love of God and the fear of God are a part of experiential religion; but Scripture represents these as consisting chiefly in practice, in the texts mentioned before. 1 John 5:3: “This is the love of God, that we keep His commandments.” 2 John 6: “This is love, that we walk according to His commandments.” Ps 34:11, etc.: “Come, children, … I will teach you+ the fear of the Lord.—Turn away from evil and do good.” Such experiences as these were what Hezekiah chiefly took comfort in on his sickbed, when he said, “Please, O Lord, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion.” And such experiences as these are what the psalmist chiefly insists on in the 119th Psalm and elsewhere. Such experiences as these are what the apostle Paul mainly insists on when he speaks of his experiences in his epistles. So Rom 1:9: “God, whom I serve with my spirit in preaching the gospel of His Son, is my witness.”—2 Cor 1:12: “And this is our boast: Our conscience testifies that we have conducted ourselves in the world … in the grace of God.” Chapter 4:13: “And in keeping with what is written: ‘I believed, therefore I have spoken,’ we who have the same spirit of faith also believe and therefore speak.” Chapter 5:7: “For we walk by faith, not by sight.” Verse 14: “For Christ’s love compels us.” Chapter 6:4–7: “As servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: in great endurance; in troubles, hardships, and calamities;—in labor, sleepless nights, and hunger; in purity, knowledge, patience, and kindness; in the Holy Spirit and in sincere love;—in the power of God.” Gal 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. The life I live in the body, I live by faith in the Son of God.” Phil 3:7, 8: “But whatever was gain to me I count as loss for the sake of Christ. More than that, I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. … I consider them rubbish, that I may gain Christ.” Col 1:29: “To this end I also labor, striving with all His energy working powerfully within me.” 1 Thess 2:2: “In the face of strong opposition, we were bold in our God to speak to you+ the gospel of God.” Verses 8, 9, 10: “We cared so deeply that we were delighted to share with you+ not only the gospel of God, but our own lives as well. That is how beloved you+ have become to us. Surely you+ recall, brothers, our labor and toil. We worked night and day.—You+ are witnesses, and so is God, of how holy, righteous, and blameless our conduct was among you+.” And it was such experiences as these that this blessed apostle chiefly comforted himself in considering when he was going to martyrdom (2 Tim 4:6, 7): “For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.”

And not only does the most important and distinguishing part of Christian experience lie in spiritual practice; but such is the nature of the sort of exercises of grace in which spiritual practice consists that nothing is so properly called by the name of experiential religion. For the experience that is in those exercises of grace that are sound, and prove effectual, at the very point of trial, where God tests which we will actually hold to, whether Christ or our lusts, is, as has already been shown, the proper experiment of the truth and power of our godliness. In it its victorious power and efficacy, in producing its proper effect and reaching its end, is found by experience. This is properly Christian experience, in which the saints have opportunity to see by actual experience and trial whether or not they have a heart to do the will of God and to forsake other things for Christ. As the philosophy that brings opinions and ideas to the test of fact is called experimental science, so the religion that brings religious affections and intentions to the same test is properly called experimental religion.

There is a sort of outward religious practice in which there is no inward experience; God takes no account of it, but counts it good for nothing. And there is what is called experience that is without practice, neither accompanied nor followed by Christian behavior; and this is worse than nothing. Many persons seem to have very wrong ideas of Christian experience and of spiritual light and manifestations. Whenever a person finds within him a heart to treat God as God at the time he is put to the trial, and finds his disposition effectual in the experiment, that is the most proper and most distinguishing experience. And to have at such a time the sense of divine things, the grasp of the truth, importance and excellence of the things of religion, which then sways and prevails and governs his heart and hands: this is the most excellent spiritual light, and these are the most distinguishing manifestations. Religion consists much in holy affection; but the exercises of affection that most distinguish true religion are these practical exercises. Friendship between earthly friends consists much in affection; yet the strong exercises of affection that actually carry them through fire and water for each other are the highest evidences of true friendship.

There is nothing in what has been said contrary to what some sound divines assert when they say that there are no sure evidences of grace but the acts of grace. For that does not prevent these working, productive acts, the exercises of grace that are effectual in practice, from being the highest evidences, above all other kinds of acts of grace. Nor does it prevent the evidence from being heightened still further when there are many of these acts and exercises following one another in a course, under various trials of every kind, as one act confirms another. A man may have good evidence of his neighbor’s presence by seeing him once; but by seeing him day after day, and conversing with him regularly in various circumstances, the evidence is established. When the disciples first saw Christ after his resurrection, they had good evidence that he was alive. But by conversing with him for forty days, and by his showing himself alive to them with many convincing proofs, they had still higher evidence.99

The witness or seal of the Spirit that we read of doubtless consists in the effect of the Spirit of God in the heart, in the implanting and exercises of grace there, and so it consists in experience. And it is also beyond doubt that this seal of the Spirit is the highest kind of evidence of their adoption that the saints ever obtain. But in these exercises of grace in practice that have been spoken of, God gives witness and sets his seal in the most conspicuous, eminent and evident way. The experience of the Christian church has abundantly found it to be true in fact that Christ commonly gives his saints by his Spirit the greatest and most joyful evidences of their sonship in those effectual exercises of grace under trials that have been spoken of. This is plain in the full assurance and unspeakable joys of many of the martyrs. It agrees with 1 Pet 4:14: “If you+ are insulted for the name of Christ, you+ are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you+.” And with Romans 5:2, 3: “We rejoice in the hope of the glory of God. Not only that, but we also rejoice in our sufferings.” And it agrees with what the apostle Paul often declares of what he experienced in his trials. And when the apostle Peter in my text speaks of the joy unspeakable and full of glory that the Christians he wrote to experienced, he has in view what they found under persecution, as appears from the context. Christ’s manifesting himself in this way as the friend and Savior of his saints, who hold to him under trials, seems to have been represented of old by his coming and manifesting himself to Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the furnace. And when the apostle speaks of the witness of the Spirit in Romans 8:15, 16, 17, he has more immediately in view what the Christians experienced in their exercises of love to God in suffering persecution, as is plain from the context. In the preceding verses he is encouraging the Christian Romans under their sufferings, telling them that though their bodies are dead because of sin, yet they will be raised to life again. But it is especially plain from the verse immediately following, v. 18: “I consider that our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us.” So the apostle evidently has their persecutions in view in all he says to the end of the chapter. So when the apostle speaks of the earnest of the Spirit that God had given him, in 2 Corinthians 5:5, the context plainly shows that he has in view what was given him in his great trials and sufferings. And in the promise of the white stone and the new name to the one who overcomes (Rev 2:17), it is evident that Christ has special regard to a benefit Christians would obtain by overcoming in the trial they had in that day of persecution. This appears from v. 13, and many other passages in this epistle to the seven churches of Asia.

Objection 2. Some may also be ready to object against what has been said of Christian practice being the chief evidence of the truth of grace that this is a legalistic doctrine: that making practice a thing of such great importance in religion magnifies works, and tends to lead men to make too much of their own doings, lessening the glory of free grace, and does not seem to agree well with the great gospel doctrine of justification by faith alone.

But this objection is altogether without reason. In what way is it inconsistent with the freeness of God’s grace that holy practice should be a sign of God’s grace? It is our works being the price of God’s favor, and not their being the sign of it, that is inconsistent with the freeness of that favor. Surely the beggar’s looking on the money in his hands as a sign of the kindness of the one who gave it to him is in no respect inconsistent with the freeness of that kindness. It is his having money in his hand as the price of a benefit that is inconsistent with the free kindness of the giver. The idea of the freeness of the grace of God to sinners, as it is revealed and taught in the gospel, is not that no holy and lovely qualities or actions in us will be a fruit, and so a sign, of that grace. It is that it is not the worthiness or loveliness of any quality or action of ours that recommends us to that grace; that kindness is shown to the unworthy and unlovely; that there is great excellence in the benefit bestowed, and no excellence in the one who receives it as the price of it; that goodness goes forth and flows out from the fullness of God’s nature, the fullness of the fountain of good, without any loveliness in the object to draw it. And this is the idea of justification without works (as this doctrine is taught in Scripture): that it is not the worthiness or loveliness of our works, or of anything in us, that is in any way accepted by God as a balance for the guilt of sin, or as a recommendation of sinners to his acceptance as heirs of life. So we are justified only by the righteousness of Christ, and not by our own righteousness. And when works are set against faith in this matter, and it is said that we are justified by faith and not by works, what is meant is that it is not the worthiness or loveliness of our works, or of anything in us, that recommends us to a share in Christ and his benefits, but that we have this share only by faith, by our souls’ receiving Christ, or clinging to him and embracing him. But that the worthiness or loveliness of nothing in us recommends us to a share in Christ and brings us into it is no argument that nothing in us is a sign of a share in Christ.

If the doctrines of free grace and justification by faith alone are inconsistent with the importance of holy practice as a sign of grace, then they are equally inconsistent with the importance of anything whatever in us as a sign of grace: any holiness, or any grace in us, or any of our experiences or religion. For it is as contrary to the doctrines of free grace and justification by faith alone that any of these should be the righteousness we are justified by as that holy practice should be. It is with holy works as it is with holy qualities. It is as inconsistent with the freeness of gospel grace that a title to salvation should be given to men for the loveliness of any of their holy qualities as that it should be given for the holiness of their works. It is inconsistent with the gospel doctrine of free grace that a share in Christ and his benefits should be given for the loveliness of a man’s true holiness: for the loveliness of his renewed, sanctified, heavenly heart, his love to God and likeness to God, or his experience of joy in the Holy Spirit, self-emptiness, a spirit that exalts Christ above all and gives all glory to him, and a heart devoted to him. I say, it is inconsistent with the gospel doctrine of free grace that a title to Christ’s benefits should be given out of regard to the loveliness of any of these, or that any of these should be our righteousness in the matter of justification. And yet this does not lessen the importance of these things as evidences of a share in Christ. It is just the same with holy actions and works. To make light of works because we are not justified by works is in effect the same thing as to make light of all religion, all grace and holiness, indeed true evangelical holiness, and all gracious experience. For all of it is included when Scripture says we are not justified by works. For by works in this case is meant all our own righteousness, religion or holiness, and everything that is in us: all the good we do and all the good we are conscious of; all outward acts, and all inward acts and exercises of grace; all experiences; all the holy and heavenly things in which the life and power and very essence of religion consist; all the great things Christ and his apostles mainly insisted on in their preaching, and tried to promote as of the greatest consequence in the hearts and lives of men; all good dispositions, exercises and qualities of every kind whatever; and even faith itself, considered as a part of our holiness. For we are justified by none of these things; and if we were, we would in a Scripture sense be justified by works. And so if it is not legalistic, and contrary to the gospel doctrine of justification without works, to insist on any of these as of great importance as evidences of a share in Christ, then neither is it legalistic to insist on the importance of holy practice. It would be legalistic to suppose that holy practice justifies by bringing us to a title to Christ’s benefits as the price of it, or as recommending us to it by its preciousness or excellence. But it is not legalistic to suppose that holy practice justifies the sincerity of a believer, as its proper evidence. The apostle James did not think it legalistic to say in this sense that Abraham our father was justified by works. The Spirit who inspired the Scripture did not think the great importance and absolute necessity of holy practice in this respect to be inconsistent with the freeness of grace, for it commonly teaches them both together. So in Revelation 21:6, 7 God says, “To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life,” and then adds in the very next words, “The one who overcomes will inherit all things,” as though behaving well in the Christian race and warfare were the condition of the promise. So in the next chapter, in the 14th and 15th verses, Christ says, “Blessed are those who do His commandments, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates,” and then declares in the 15th verse how those of a wicked practice will be shut out. And yet in the next two verses he gives out with very great solemnity an invitation to all to come and take of the water of life freely: “I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star. The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’ Let the one who hears say, ‘Come!’ And let the one who is thirsty come, and the one who desires the water of life drink freely.” So ch. 3:20, 21: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me.” But then it is added in the next words, “To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to sit with Me on My throne.” And in the great invitation of Christ at the end of Matt 11, “Come to Me, all you+ who are weary and burdened, and I will give you+ rest,” Christ adds in the next words, “Take My yoke upon you+ and learn from Me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you+ will find rest for your+ souls. For My yoke is easy and My burden is light,” as though taking up the burden of Christ’s service and imitating his example were necessary for obtaining the promised rest. So in the great invitation to sinners to accept free grace in Isa 55: “Come, all you+ who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you+ without money, come, buy, and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost!” Even there, in the continuation of the same invitation, the sinner’s forsaking his wicked practice is spoken of as necessary for obtaining mercy. Verse 7: “Let the wicked man forsake his own way and the unrighteous man his own thoughts; let him return to the Lord, that He may have compassion, and to our God, for He will freely pardon.” So the riches of divine grace in the justification of sinners are set forth together with the necessity of holy practice in Isa 1:15, etc.: “Wash and cleanse yourselves+. Remove your+ evil deeds from My sight. Stop doing evil! Learn to do right; seek justice and correct the oppressor. Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow.” “Come now, let us reason together,” says the Lord. “Though your+ sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow; though they are as red as crimson, they will become like wool.” And in the most solemn invitation of wisdom in Prov 9, after it is described what great provision is made, and how all things were ready, the house built, the animals slaughtered, the wine mixed and the table set, and the messengers sent out to invite the guests, we then have the free invitation, vv. 4, 5, 6: “ ‘Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!’ she says to him who lacks judgment” (that is, who has no righteousness). “ ‘Come, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed.’ ” But then in the next breath it follows, “ ‘Leave your+ folly behind, and you+ will live; walk in the way of understanding,’ ” as though forsaking sin and going in the way of holiness were necessary for life. So the freeness of grace and the necessity of holy practice, which Scripture joins together in this way again and again, are not inconsistent with one another. Nor does it at all lessen the honor and importance of faith that the exercises and effects of faith in practice should be counted its chief signs, any more than it lessens the importance of life that action and motion are counted its chief signs.

So in what has been said of the importance of holy practice as the main sign of sincerity there is nothing legalistic; nothing that takes away from the freedom and sovereignty of gospel grace; nothing in the least clashing with the gospel doctrine of justification by faith alone, without the works of the law; nothing in the least tending to lessen the glory of the Mediator and our dependence on his righteousness; nothing infringing on the special prerogatives of faith in the matter of our salvation; nothing in any way detracting from the glory of God and his mercy, or exalting man, or lessening his dependence and obligation. So if any are against such an importance of holy practice as has been spoken of, it can only be from a senseless aversion to the letters and sound of the word works. For there is no reason in the world that can be given for it which may not be given with equal force for having an aversion to the words holiness, godliness, grace, religion, experience, and even faith itself. For to make a righteousness of any of these is as legalistic, and as inconsistent with the way of the new covenant, as to make a righteousness of holy practice.100

It is greatly to the hurt of religion for persons to make light of, and insist little on, the things Scripture insists on most as of the most importance in the evidence of our share in Christ (supposing that to lay weight on these things is legalistic, an old-covenant way); and so to neglect the exercises and effectual workings of grace in practice, and to insist almost wholly on manifestations, and on the method and manner of the immanent exercises of conscience and grace in contemplation, depending on an ability to make fine distinctions in these matters, and on a skill in discerning them accurately, from philosophy or experience. It is useless to look for any better or further signs than the ones the Scriptures have most expressly mentioned and most often insisted on as signs of godliness. Those who claim a greater accuracy in giving signs, or claim by their extraordinary experience or insight into the nature of things to give more distinguishing marks, which will search out and expose the hypocrite more thoroughly, are only subtle in darkening their own minds and the minds of others. Their refinements and fine discernings are in God’s sight only refined foolishness and shrewd delusion. The words of Agur apply here, Prov 30:5, 6: “Every word of God is flawless; He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him. Do not add to His words, lest He rebuke you and prove you a liar.” Our wisdom and discernment concerning the hearts of men is not much to be trusted. We can see only a little way into the nature of the soul and the depths of man’s heart. The ways in which persons’ affections may be moved without any supernatural influence are so many; the natural springs of the affections are so various and so secret; so many things often have a joint influence on the affections (the imagination, and that in innumerable and unsearchable ways; natural disposition; education; the common influences of the Spirit of God; a surprising coming together of moving circumstances; an extraordinary coincidence of things in the course of men’s thoughts; together with the subtle management of invisible malicious spirits) that no philosophy or experience will ever be enough to guide us safely through this labyrinth and maze unless we closely follow the thread God has given us in his word. God knows his own reasons why he insists on some things, and plainly sets them out as the things we should try ourselves by, rather than others. Perhaps it is because he knows that these things are accompanied by less perplexity, and that we are less liable to be deceived by them than by others. He knows our nature best. He knows the nature and manner of his own workings, and he knows best the way of our safety. He knows what allowances to make for different states of his church, and different dispositions of particular persons, and varieties in the manner of his own workings; how far nature may resemble grace, and how far nature may be mixed with grace; what affections may arise from imagination, and how far imagination may be mixed with spiritual illumination. And so it is our wisdom not to take his work out of his hands, but to follow him, and to lay the weight of our judgment of ourselves where he has directed us. If we do otherwise, no wonder if we are bewildered, confounded and fatally deluded. But if we had got into the way of looking chiefly at the things Christ and his apostles and prophets chiefly insisted on, and so, in judging ourselves and others, chiefly regarding the practical exercises and effects of grace, while not neglecting other things, it would have many happy consequences. It would above all things tend to the conviction of deluded hypocrites, and to prevent the delusion of those whose hearts were never brought to a thorough compliance with the strait and narrow way that leads to life. It would tend to deliver us from innumerable perplexities arising from the various inconsistent schemes there are about methods and steps of experience. It would greatly tend to keep professing Christians from neglecting strictness of life, and to promote their commitment and earnestness in their Christian walk. It would become the custom for men to show their Christianity more by a lovely, distinctive behavior than by an abundant and excessive declaring of their experiences. We would get into the way of appearing lively in religion more by being lively in the service of God and of our generation than by the liveliness and forwardness of our tongues, and by making a business of proclaiming on the housetops with our mouths the holy and eminent acts and exercises of our own hearts. Christians who are close friends would talk together of their experiences and comforts in a way that better becomes Christian humility and modesty, and more to each other’s profit, their tongues not running ahead of their hands and feet but rather going behind them, after the prudent example of the blessed apostle (2 Cor 12:6). Many occasions of spiritual pride would be cut off, and so a great door shut against the devil. A great many of the main stumbling blocks against experiential and powerful religion would be removed. And religion would be declared and shown in such a way that, instead of hardening onlookers and greatly promoting unbelief and atheism, it would above all things tend to convince men that there is a reality in religion, and greatly awaken them and win them, by convincing their consciences of the importance and excellence of religion. So the light of those who profess would so shine before men that others, seeing their good works, would glorify their Father in heaven.

80. He who claims to be godly and turns aside to crooked ways is a hypocrite. For those who are really godly live in a way of obedience. Ps 119:1, 2, 3: “Blessed are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the Law of the Lord. … They do no iniquity.” Luke 1:6: “Both of them were righteous in the sight of God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and decrees of the Lord.” But those who live in ways of sin are deceivers, for all such will be rejected in the day of judgment. Matt 7:23: “Depart from Me, you+ workers of lawlessness!” We have the same in Luke 13:27. If men live in a way of disobedience, they do not love God, for love will make men keep God’s commandments. 1 John 5:3: “This is the love of God, that we keep His commandments. And His commandments are not burdensome.” If men live in a way of disobedience, they do not have a spirit of faith, for faith sanctifies men. Acts 26:18: “sanctified by faith in Me.” If men live in a way of disobedience, they are not Christ’s sheep, for his sheep hear his voice (John 10:27). Men who live in a way of disobedience are not born of God. 1 John 3:9: “Anyone born of God refuses to practice sin.” Men who live in a way of disobedience are the slaves of sin. John 8:34: “Everyone who sins is a slave to sin.”—A course of outward sin is an evidence of hypocrisy, whether it is a sin of omission or of commission. If men live in the neglect of known duties, or in the practice of known evils, that will be their condemnation, whatever the sin may be: profaneness, impurity, lying or injustice.—If men allow themselves in malice, envy, lustful thoughts or profane thoughts, that will condemn them, even though those corruptions do not break out in any scandalous way. These thoughts are an evidence of a rotten heart. Titus 3:3: “At one time we too were foolish, disobedient, misled, and enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures—living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another.” If a man allows himself in malice and envy, even though he thinks he does not, he is a hypocrite. Though his conscience disapproves of it, yet if his heart allows it, he is no saint.—Some make claims to godliness by which they deceive not only others but also (which is a great deal worse) themselves. But this will condemn them: that they live in a course of sin, and so must go with ungodly men. Ps 125:5: “Those who turn to crooked ways the Lord will banish with the evildoers.” If there is a great change in a man’s conduct, and he is reformed in several particular things, yet if there is one evil way, the man is an ungodly man. Where there is piety there is universal obedience. A man may have great weaknesses and yet be a godly man. So it was with Lot, David and Peter. But if he lives in a way of sin, he does not merely make his godliness doubtful; it is full evidence against him. Men who are godly have respect to all God’s commandments (Ps 119:6). There are a great many commands, and if there is one of them that a man has no respect for, he will be put to shame another day. If a man lives in one evil way, he is not subject to God’s authority, but lives in rebellion. That will take away all his pleas and cut off all his claims at once, and he will be condemned in the day of judgment.—One way of sin is objection enough against the man’s salvation, even though the sin he lives in is only small. Such persons will not be guilty of perjury, stealing, drunkenness or fornication. They look on these as heinous things, and they are afraid of them. But they do not much care if they take a little unfair advantage in a bargain, if they praise too highly a thing they are about to sell, if they break a promise, if they spend the Sabbath unprofitably, if they neglect secret prayer, if they talk rudely and insult others. They think these are only small things. If they can keep clear of great transgression, they hope that God will not insist on small things. But in fact all the commands of God are established by divine authority. A small shot may kill a man as well as a cannonball. A small leak may sink a ship. If a man lives in small sins, that shows he has no love to God, no sincere care to please and honor God. Little sins are of a damning nature as well as great ones. If they do not deserve as much punishment as greater ones, yet they do deserve damnation. There is a contempt of God in all sins. Matt 5:19: “Whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do likewise will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.” Prov 19:16: “He who keeps a commandment preserves his soul, but he who despises his ways will die.” If a man says, “This is a great command,” and so lays weight on it, and “That is a little commandment,” and so does not regard it but will allow himself to break it, he is in a perishing condition. Stoddard’s way to know sincerity and hypocrisy.

81. Deut 5:29. Deut 32:18, 19, 20. 1 Chr 28:9. Ps 78:7, 8, 10, 11, 35, 36, 37, 41, 42, 56, etc. Ps 106:3, 12, 13, 14, 15. Ps 125:4, 5. Prov 26:11. Isa 64:5. Jer 17:13. Ezek 3:20. And 18. 24. 82. Gen 22:1. Exod 15:25. Chap. 16. 4. Deut 8:2, 15, 16. Chap. 13. 3: Judges 2. 22. Chap. 3. 1, 4. Job 23:10. Ps 66:10, 11. Ezek 3:20. Dan 12:10. Zech 13:9. Matt 8:19, 20. Chap. 18. 21, 22. Luke 1:35. 1 Cor 11:19. 2 Cor 8:8. Jas 1:12. 1 Pet 4:12. 1 John 2:19. Heb 11:17. Rev 3:10.

83. One way of sin is objection enough against men’s salvation, even though their temptations are great. Some persons delight in iniquity; they take pleasure in rudeness and in intemperate practices. But there are others who do not delight in sin. When they can conveniently avoid it, they do not choose it; unless they are under some great necessity, they will not do it. They are afraid to sin; they think it is dangerous, and take some care to avoid it. But at times they force themselves to sin. They are brought into difficulties and cannot see how to avoid it well; it seems a dangerous thing not to do it. If Naaman does not bow down in the house of Rimmon, the king will be in a rage with him and take away his office, perhaps take away his life; and so he complies (2 Kgs 5:18).—So Jeroboam forced himself to set up the calves at Dan and Bethel. He thought that if the people went up to Jerusalem to worship, they would return to Rehoboam and kill him, so he must think of some way to deliver himself in this strait (1 Kgs 12:27, 28).—He was driven by what seemed necessity to take this wicked course. So the stony-ground hearers were willing to keep the profession of the true religion, but the case was such that they thought they could not well do it. Matt 13:21: “When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away.”—So Achan and Gehazi had unusual opportunities to get an estate. If they lived twenty years they were not likely to have such an advantage again; so they force themselves to stretch a point and break the law of God. They lay a necessity on estate and liberty and life, but not on obedience. If a man is willing to serve God in ordinary cases, but excuses himself when there are great difficulties, he is not godly. It is a small matter to serve God when men have no temptation. But Lot was holy in Sodom, and Noah was righteous in the old world. Temptations try men, but they do not force men to sin; and grace will establish the heart in a day of temptation. Those who endure temptation are blessed (Jas 1:12), but those who fall away in a day of temptation are cursed. Stoddard’s way to know sincerity and hypocrisy.

84. From this we learn what verdict to pass and give concerning those men who decay and fall away from the Lord. They never had oil in the vessel; they never had a dram of grace in their heart. So 1 John 2:19: “For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us.” It seems they were men so eminent and excellent that there were no brands or marks on them to warn the churches that they were marked out for apostasy; they were found to be unsound only by their apostasy. And this was argument enough. Shepard’s parable, Part I. P. 226.

85. When a man’s rising is the cause of his fall, or seals him up in his fall, or at least is the cause of it through his corruption. For example, there was a time when a man lived a loose, careless, carnal life. By the ministry of some word, or the reading of some book, or speaking with some friend, he comes to be convicted of his misery and woeful condition, and sees no good or grace in himself; he has been deceived up to this time. At last he comes to get some light, some taste, some sorrows, some heart to use the means, some comfort and mercy and hope of life. And when it is like this with him, now he falls; he grows full and falls, and this rising is the cause of his fall. His light is darkness and death to him, and grows into a form of knowledge. His rising makes him fall into formality, and then into profaneness. So his tasting satisfies him; his sorrows empty his heart of sorrow for sin; his sorrows for his falls harden his heart in his falls; and all the means of recovering him harden him.—It is as it is in diseases: if the medicine and the food turn to poison, then there is no hope of recovery; the man is sick to death now. The saint’s little measure makes him forget what is behind. Shepard’s parable, Part I. P. 226.
