87. To profess to know much is easy; but to bring your+ affections into subjection, to wrestle with lusts, to cross your+ wills and yourselves+ on every occasion, this is hard. The Lord looks for us to be serviceable to him in our lives and useful to men. What is within, the Lord and our brothers are never the better for; but the outward obedience flowing from it glorifies God and does good to men. The Lord will have this done. What else is the end of our planting and watering, but that the trees may be filled with sap? And what is the end of that sap, but that the trees may bring forth fruit? What does the farmer care for leaves and barren trees? Dr. Preston of the Church’s carriage.

88. What is the end of every grace, but to soften the heart and make it pliable to some command or other? Look how many commandments there are: so many graces there are in virtue and efficacy, although not so many separate names are given them. The end of every such grace is to make us obedient. So the end of temperance is chastity, to bow the heart to these commands: “Be sober-minded,” etc., “not in sexual immorality and debauchery,” etc. When the Lord commands us not to be angry with our brother, the end of meekness, and the reason the Lord infuses it, is to keep us from thoughtless, rash anger. So with faith: its end is to take Jesus Christ, to make us obedient to the command of the gospel, which commands us to believe in him. So all graces join together only to frame and fashion the soul to obedience. Then as much obedience as there is in your+ lives, so much grace is there in your+ hearts, and no more. Therefore ask your+ hearts how subject you+ are to the Lord in your+ lives. It was the counsel Francis Spira gave to those around him. “Learn from me, all of you+,” he said, “to take heed of separating faith and obedience. I taught justification by faith, but neglected obedience; and that is why this has come upon me.” I have known some godly men whose comfort on their deathbeds came not from the inward acts of their minds, which, considered by themselves, might be open to misunderstanding, but from the course of obedience in their lives that issued from them. Let Christians see to it in all their conduct, in every relation they stand in, as scholars, tradesmen, husbands, wives; let them see to this, that when they come to die, they have been subject in all things. This will give comfort. Dr. Preston’s Church’s carriage.

89. There is no unregenerate man, however far he goes and however much he does, who does not live in some one sin or other, secret or open, little or great. Judas went far, but he was covetous. Herod went far, but he loved his Herodias. Every dog has his kennel, every pig has his swill, and every wicked man his lust. Shepard’s sincere convert, 1st edition, p. 96. There is not one unsound heart in the world but, as they say of witches that they have some familiar spirit that sucks them, so they have some lust that is beloved by them; there is some beloved one to whom they have given a promise never to forsake it. Shepard’s parable, Part I. P. 15. There is no man married to the law whose fig leaves do not cover some nakedness. All his duties always brood some lust. There is some one sin or other the man lives in, which either the Lord shows him and he will not part with, as with the young man, or else is so spiritual that he cannot see it all his lifetime. Read through the strictest of them all, and see this (Matt 23): “whitewashed tombs.” Paul, who was blameless, yet (Eph 2:3; Titus 3:3) was “enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures.” And the reason is that the law is not the ministry of the Spirit (2 Cor 3:8, 9), which breaks a man off from every sin. There is no law that can give life (Gal 3:21). And this is why many men make strong resolutions and break them all again. This is why men sin and sorrow, and pray again, and then go on with more ease in their sin. Examine yourself: is there any living lust alongside your righteousness? Then it is certain that it is righteousness you are married to, and you were never yet matched to Christ. Shepard’s parable, Part I. P. 19, 20. There is no hypocrite, though he takes up with Christ and for a time grows in knowledge of and communion with Christ, who does not have at that time hidden lusts and thorns that overgrow his growth and choke everything at last; and in the end he seeks to make a league between Christ and his lusts, and to reconcile them together. Shepard’s parable, Part I. P. 109. —Their faith is found in such a person as was never yet thoroughly torn away from sin. And here is the great wound of the most cunning hypocrites living.——Let a man be cast down as low as hell with sorrow, and lie under chains, quaking in dread of terror to come. Let a man then be raised up to heaven in joy, so that he is not able to live. Let a man reform and shine like an angel on earth. Yet if he is not torn away from lust, so that either you+ never saw it, or, if you+ did, you+ have not followed the Lord to remove it, but are proud, surly, worldly and sluggish still, false in your+ dealings, cunning in your+ trading, devils in your+ families, images in your+ churches, then you+ are objects of pity now, and will be objects of terror at the great day. For where sin remains in power, it will bring faith, and Christ, and joy into bondage and service to itself. Shepard’s parable Part I. P. 125. It seems to me that it is with the best hypocrites as it is with various old merchants. They prize and desire the gain of trade, but to take the trouble to prepare the ship, to put themselves to the hazards and dangers of the ship, to go and fetch the treasure they prize, this they will never do. So many prize and earnestly desire the treasures of heaven. But to take the trouble of a voyage to heaven to fetch this treasure, to pass through the valley of Baca, through tears, temptations, the powers of darkness, the breaches, opposition and contradictions of a sinful, unbelieving heart, through good report and evil report, to pass from one depth and wave to another: in this the best hypocrite fails, and so loses all at last. And I take this to be one of the great differences between the strong desires and esteem of hypocrites and of saints.—It is as it is with men who have two trades or two shops: one is as much as they can ever follow or tend, so at last they are forced to give up one, and they must neglect one. So it is here.—The spirit of sloth and slumber that the Lord always leaves the best hypocrite to so mightily oppresses all their senses that they cannot use all means effectually to accomplish their ends. And so a man desires the end but does not have it (Prov 13:4). Shepard’s parable, Part I. P. 150, 151. Read through all of Scripture: constantly there were never any hypocrites who did not have this brand (Matt 7:23), “you+ workers of iniquity.” Shepard’s parable, Part I. P. 195. A carnal man may hit upon some good duty God commands, and refrain from some sin God forbids; but to go all the way through, he cannot. To take up reproach and disgrace, to lose his good name, to forsake his friends, to lose honor and riches and pleasures: this he will not do until he is humbled. Dr. Preston, on Paul’s conversion. So it is with men, because they lack humbling. That is why their profession and they do not continue together, but part from each other willingly. They will do some things, but not all things; and they will give up some things, but not all things. And that is why our Savior says in Luke 14, “Whoever will not forsake all for My sake is not worthy of Me.” He is not worth saving who does not prize me above all things whatever. And a man will not prize Christ, or forsake all things for Christ, until he is humbled. Ibid.

90. The counterfeit and common grace of foolish virgins, after some time of glorious profession, will certainly go out and be quite spent. It is consumed in the using and shining and burning.—Men who have been most zealous decay: their gifts decay, their life decays.——It is so after some time of profession; for at first it grows rather than decays and withers, but afterward they have had enough of it, and it withers and dies.—The Spirit of God comes on many hypocrites in an abundant and plentiful measure of awakening grace. It comes on them as it did on Balaam, and as it is with overflowing waters, which spread far, and grow very deep, and fill many empty places.—Though it does come on them so, yet it never rests within so as to dwell there, to take up an eternal mansion for himself.—That is why it decays little by little until at last it is quite gone, like ponds filled with rainwater that comes upon them, not spring water that rises up within them: it dries up little by little until it is quite dry. Shepard’s parable, Part II. P. 58, 59. Some men may lay hold of Christ neither out of fear of misery nor only to preserve some sin. Rather, God lets in the light and heat of the blessed beams of the glorious gospel of the Son of God, showing that there is mercy, rich, free and sweet, for damned, great, vile sinners. “Good Lord,” says the soul, “what a sweet ministry, word, God and gospel this is!” And there it rests. This was the frame of the stony ground, which heard the word and received it with joy, and for a time believed. And this is the case of thousands who are much moved by the promise and mercy of Christ, and hang on free grace for a time. But like sweet smells in a room they do not last long; or like flowers they grow old and withered, and then fall. In time of temptation, lust and the world and sloth are sweeter than Christ and all his gospel. Shepard’s parable, Part II. P. 168. There was never any carnal heart in whose soil some root of bitterness did not grow up at last. Shepard’s parable, Part I. P. 195. We will see it in experience: take the best professing Christians living; though they may come to the Lord, as they and others judged, and follow the Lord, yet in time they will depart.—The Spirit was never given effectually to draw them, nor yet to keep them. Shepard’s parable, Part I. P. 205.

91. Scripture doctrine of salvation. Sermon 1. P. 11.

92. Look at John, Christ’s beloved disciple and bosom companion. He had received the anointing to know him who is true, and he knew that he knew him (1 John 2:3). But how did he know that? He might be deceived (for it is strange to see what a melancholy imagination will do, and its effects; as honest men are reputed to have weak brains, and never to have seen the depths of the secrets of God). What is his final proof? Because we keep his commandments. Shepard’s Par. Part I. P. 131. A man may know his present union with the Lord Jesus by a work. 1 John 2:4: “If anyone says, ‘I know Him,’ but does not keep His commandments, he is a liar.”—Yes, that is true negatively; but may a man, ought a man, to see or know his union positively by this? Answer: verse 5. Many said they did know and love the Lord, but “if anyone keeps His word”—Oh, they are sweet! It is heaven to cling to him in every command; it is death to depart from any command. “By this we know that we are in Him.” If it were possible to ask the angels how they know they are not devils, they would answer, “The Lord’s will is ours.” Shepard’s Par. Part I. P. 134. If the question is, whom does the Lord Jesus love, you need not go to heaven for the answer; the word is near you: those who love Christ. Who are those? Those who keep his commandments. Shepard’s Par. Part I. P. 138. Will you have Christ sit in heaven, and not look for him to subdue your lusts by the work of his grace, and so rule your hearts? Then you despise his kingdom. Do you seek pardon in the blood of Christ, and never look for the virtue and end of that blood, to wash you and make you without spot, etc.? Then you despise his priesthood and blood. Do you look for Christ to do work for you, while you do not do Christ’s work and bring forth fruit to him? Then you despise his honor (John 15:8). If I were to point out a hypocrite, or a false heart, this is what I would say: it is he who will set up Christ but loathe his work. Shepard’s parable Part I. P. 140.

93. 2 Cor 8:2. Heb 11:36. 1 Pet 1:7. Chapter 4:12. Gen 22:1. Deut 8:2, 16. Chapter 13:3. Exod 15:25. And 16. 4. Judg 2:22. Chapter 3:1, 4. Ps 66:10, 11. Dan 12:10. Rev 3:10. Job 23:10. Zech 13:9. Jas 1:12. Rev 2:10. Luke 8:13. Acts 20:19. Jas 1:2, 3. 1 Pet 1:6.

94. I am persuaded, as Calvin is, that all the various trials of men are meant to show them to themselves, and to the world, that they are only counterfeits, and to make saints better known to themselves.—Rom 5:4: Tribulation works trial, and trial hope. Prov 17:3. If you want to know whether it will hold its weight, the trial will tell you. Shepard’s parable Part I. P. 191.

95. Dr. Sibbs, in his bruised reed, says: When Christ’s will comes into competition with any worldly loss or gain, if the heart will stoop to Christ then, in that particular case, it is a true sign. For the truest trial of the power of grace is in such particular cases as touch us most nearly, for there our corruption gathers the greatest strength. When Christ came home to the young man in the gospel, he lost a disciple in him. Mr. Flavel speaks of a holy practice under trials as the greatest evidence of grace. “No man,” he says, “can say what he is, whether his graces are true or false, until they are tried and examined by the things that are to them as fire is to gold.” Touchstone of sincerity, ch. 4. Sect. 1. Again, speaking of great difficulties and sufferings in the way of duty, in which a person must actually part either with what is dearest to him of a worldly nature or with his duty, he says: That such sufferings as these will show the falseness and rottenness of men’s hearts cannot be doubted, if you+ consider that this is the fire God designed for this very use and purpose, to separate the gold from the dross. So you+ will find it in 1 Pet 4:12: “Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial that has come upon you+ to try you+”; that is, the very design and aim of providence in permitting and ordering these sufferings is to try you+. On this account you+ find the hour of persecution (in a fitting sense) called the hour of temptation or testing (Rev 3:10). For then those who profess are sifted to the very bran, searched to their very deepest principles. This is the day burning like a furnace, when every evildoer will be stubble (Mal 4:1). For in that day the ruling interest must appear and be shown; it can be hidden no longer. “No servant can serve two masters,” says Christ (Luke 16:13). A man may serve many masters if they all command the same thing, or things subordinate to each other; but he cannot serve two masters if their commands clash and conflict with each other. And such are the commands of Christ and of the flesh in an hour of suffering:—so the two interests come into full opposition. And now only have patience and wait a little, and you+ will discern which is ruling. A dog follows two men while they both walk the same way, and you+ do not know which of the two is his master. Only wait a little, until their paths part, and then you+ will quickly see who is his master. So it is in this case. Ibid ch. 8. Sect. 3. And in another chapter he says: Great numbers of persons are deceived and destroyed by trusting to grace that seems real but is untried. This was the miserable condition of the Laodicean professing Christians: they counted themselves rich, but were really poor. All that glitters is not gold. Their gold (as they counted it) was never tried in the fire. If a man’s whole estate lay in some precious stone, suppose a rich diamond, how concerned he is to have it thoroughly tried, to see whether it will bear a sharp blow with the hammer, or fly to pieces like a Bristol diamond! Ibid ch. 10. Sect. 3. Again in the same place: The promises of salvation are made over to tried grace, and only to such grace as will endure the trial. The Lord will try you+. God has his trying times, and they were never sent except to show who were dross and who were gold. And the main end of all God’s trials is to show this truth that I am now pressing on you+. Some have a thorough work, and then the trial shows the truth, as in Abraham (Heb 11:17). Some have a superficial work, and they fall in the trial, as in Saul; and it shows that it was only a shallow work. For this is the question God puts: is it thorough or not? “Ay,” says the carnal heart; “yes,” says a gracious heart. That is why it is strange to see what men will do when a trial comes. Shepard’s Par. Part I. P. 219. There is an hour of temptation that tries men, which will show what men really are. Shepard’s parable Part II. P. 60.

96. It is a sure rule (says Dr. Preston) that what the Scriptures spend many words on, we should spend many thoughts on; and what the Holy Spirit urges most, we should prize most. Churches carriage.

97. What God makes the rule of his own judgment, by which he judges every man, is a sure rule for every man to judge himself by. What we will be judged by at the last day is a sure rule to apply to ourselves now. Now he judges us by our obedience and works: he “will repay each one according to his deeds.” Dr. Preston’s churches carriage.

98. Our real taking of Christ appears in our actions and works. Isa 1:19: “If you+ consent and obey, you+ will eat the best of the land.” That is, if you+ will consent to take Jehovah for your+ Lord and King. If you+ give consent: there is the first thing. But that is not enough: but if you+ also obey. The truth of the consent that stands in the inward act of the mind will be seen in your+ obedience, in the acts of your+ lives. If you+ consent and obey, you+ will eat the best of the land; that is, you+ will take of all he has that is fitting for you+. For then you+ are married to him in truth, and have a share in all his goods. Dr. Preston Church’s carriage.

99. The more these visible exercises of grace are renewed, the more certain you+ will be. The more often these actings are renewed, the more lasting and confirmed your+ assurance will be. A man who has been sure of such visible exercises of grace may soon afterward be in doubt whether he was not mistaken. But when such actings are renewed again and again, he grows more settled and established about his good state. If a man sees a thing once, that makes him sure. But if afterward he fears he was deceived, when he comes to see it again he is surer that he was not mistaken. If a man reads certain passages in a book, he is sure it is so. Some months later some people may argue him down, saying he was mistaken, so that he questions it himself; but when he looks and reads it again, he is abundantly confirmed. The more men’s grace is multiplied, the more their peace is multiplied. 2 Pet 1:2: “Grace and peace be multiplied to you+ through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.” Stoddard’s way to know sincerity and hypocrisy.

100. You say you know Christ, and the love and goodwill of Christ toward you, and that he is the propitiation for your sins. How do you know this? “If anyone says, ‘I know Him,’ but does not keep His commandments, he is a liar” (1 John 2:4). True, some might reply, he who does not keep the commands of Christ has in this a sure evidence that he does not know him and is not united to him; but is it any evidence that we do know him, and that we are united to him, if we do keep his commandments? Yes indeed, says the apostle: “By this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments.” And again, v. 5: “By this we know that we are in Him.” What can be plainer? What vanity it is to say that this is running on a covenant of works!—O beloved, it is a sad thing to hear such questions, and such cold answers too: that sanctification possibly may be an evidence. May be? Is it not certain? Surely to deny it is as bad as to affirm that God’s own promises of favor are not sure evidences of it, and so that they are lies and untruths.—Our Savior, who was no legalistic preacher, pronounces, and so gives evidence of, blessedness by eight or nine promises expressly made to such persons as had inherent graces (Matt 5:3, 4, etc.). Shepard’s sound believer. P. 221, 222, 223.
